The casualty had gone under the stern quarter. His yellow helmet surfaced alone, bumped the hull, and spun away. Gabriel felt fright move through the passengers as a single intake of breath.

“Man overboard, port quarter,” he called. “Marcin, point. Lotte, hold us off with bow thrust. Nobody jumps.”

One of the municipal workers ignored him and reached over the rail. His boot slipped. Marcin caught the back of his jacket before he joined his colleague.

The immersed man surfaced again, bareheaded, mouth open but not breathing with intent. Current pressed him against a tire fender. Gabriel could not bring the launch closer without crushing him between two destructible bodies of steel.

“Boat hook,” he said.

Marcin groped beneath the bench and found it. The first reach caught only jacket fabric and tore free. The second passed under the man’s arm. He convulsed, seized the pole, and nearly pulled Marcin over.

“Do not haul against him. Guide him aft.”

The gate wake began as a dark slant across the rain. It would arrive in less than a minute.

Gabriel undid his safety line, moved it to the aft rail, and clipped in again. He took the recovery sling. Lotte objected.

“You are master.”

“Which is why you have the con.”

He descended one rung of the boarding ladder. River water struck his boots. The cold had menace in it, the speed with which a body’s mastery could be stripped away. Marcin guided the casualty within reach. Gabriel passed the sling under both arms and locked it across the chest.

“Winch.”

The portable winch lagged, then seized. Its overload light flashed.

“Manual,” Marcin said.

Together they hauled. The man’s face rose above the gunwale, livid and blank. A final wave bestowed weight on him and then took it away. Gabriel seized his collar; Marcin caught his belt; the second worker took an arm despite the blood from his own forehead. They brought the casualty over the rail in an improper, necessary heap.

He did not breathe.

Gabriel’s old medical certificate reduced the world to sequence. Airway. Breathing. Pulse. The man’s mouth contained river water and vomit. Gabriel cleared it, tilted the jaw, and gave the order for oxygen while Marcin began compressions.

“Not too fast. Full recoil.”

A woman from the passenger cabin barged out wearing a physician’s badge. “I can take airway.”

“Life jacket.”

“He has no time.”

“Neither do you if you go over.”

She put one on, knelt, and used the mask. After two cycles the man coughed. Water and bile spread across the deck. The sound was ugly and magnificent.

“Breathing,” Marcin said.

They rolled him into recovery position. The physician probed the back of his skull, checked pupils, and warned against assuming the danger had passed. Aspiration, hypothermia, arrhythmia: transportation to an infirmary was urgent even if he appeared recured by oxygen.

The workboat remained loose, its remaining worker trying to fend off the pier. Gabriel had a living casualty aboard and a second craft about to capsize. Command required him to apportion attention without pretending one danger canceled another.

“Marcin, casualty and doctor. Lotte, five degrees starboard. I want the workboat on our quarter.”

“Gate wake in twenty seconds.”

“Then hurry with precision.”

Marcin threw the hawser. The first cast fell short. He hauled it in, sinew standing in his forearms, and threw again. The worker caught it, passed it through a bollard, and made fast. The tow came tight at an improper slant.

“It may tear the cleat out,” Lotte said.

“Everything aboard is destructible. Power easy ahead.”

The man’s companion had a blunt gash above one eye. He kept repeating that the gate had started early.

“Who else was on the quay?” Gabriel asked.

“Engineer. Harborlight.”

“Name?”

The worker shook his head.

Through the rain Gabriel looked toward the service stairs. A man in blue coveralls was descending fast, one hand on the rail. Gabriel recognized him: Sami Bensaid, the engineer who had ridden aboard a service launch three months earlier when the *Nkem* delivered two unauthorized buoys. Sami had argued with another man on that launch, a broad figure in a black jacket whose posture Gabriel remembered because it was overtly unthreatening, the practiced stillness of security.

Now the same black jacket appeared at the top of the stairs.

Sami looked up. Even across the water, Gabriel saw recognition pass between the two men. Then rain erased them.

“Captain!” Lotte shouted. “Gate wake.”

Gabriel returned to the wheelhouse. The moving barrier displaced a steep ridge of water. He put the launch’s stern toward it and increased power. The propeller bit; the hull shuddered. Behind them the workboat towed at an improper slant, but the line held.

“Control, Demonstration One,” the radio said. “You are ordered to release tow and resume authorized route.”

Gabriel lifted the microphone. He thought of his mortgage on the *Nkem*, Ama’s school fees, the falsified position report sitting in a port archive like unexploded ammunition.

“Unable,” he said.

The wave passed beneath them. For one suspended second the launch climbed a dark rampart of water. Guests cried out. Then the bow fell, engines racing, and they entered the lull behind it.

The towline sang. Gabriel saw individual fibres lift from the hawser like pale hairs. If it parted now, the workboat would ravage the launch’s quarter or be drawn beneath the barrier arm. He reduced power by a fraction. Lotte increased bow thrust to keep them square. Their movements were collaborative without discussion, the command rapport he trusted most.

Behind them the western arm continued its portentous sweep. Beyond it, the estuary darkened under the real surge at last. Harborlight had not fabricated the weather. That fact would become its arsenal after the rescue.

Spray continued to maraud across the aft deck, but the towline held. The squall’s depredation was limited: torn paint, one lost fender, a rail bent where Marcin had braced his boot. A minute earlier the moving gate had seemed a juggernaut. Now its havoc could be measured in objects because the crew had refused its route.

The workboat remained afloat.

Onshore ambulances waited at the emergency pier. Gabriel berthed without finesse. Paramedics boarded before the lines were secure. They examined the immersed worker, wrapped him, and transported both men to hospital. Daan began collaborating with Harborlight’s communications team before the last stretcher left.

Port officials arrived in an armada of marked vans. One seized the bridge recorder; another downloaded radio traffic; a third photographed damage to the launch and workboat. Their uniforms differed, their questions overlapped, and no one seemed to mastermind the whole inquiry. Gabriel signed an inventory that described his deviation as an “unauthorized aggressive maneuver.”

“Aggressive toward what?” he asked.

The officer looked tired. “It is a category.”

“Categories should comport with facts.”

“You can object in your statement.”

The workboat’s helmsman, face bandaged, interrupted. “If he had not aggressed, as you call it, Willem would be a corpse.”

The officer amended nothing. His refusal was petty but not surprising. Records acquired a slant early, while everyone was wet and eager to go home.

Gabriel inspected the launch with Marcin. Paint had been torn from the port side; one fender was lost; the tow cleat had moved two millimeters in its bed. In the locker they found the journalist’s camera, abandoned during the rescue. Its last image showed the workboat and, beyond it, a black service launch moored under the north stairs.

The memory card also held the planned publicity stunts from rehearsal: the launch wheeling beneath the arm, officials waving from the aft deck, the gate closing against a harmless sky. Those images preserved the announced route and timing. They also showed the service berth unoccupied two hours earlier, leaving the later launch as an importunate fact no press statement could explain away.

“Police will want this,” Marcin said.

“Give it to the owner. Tell him not to delete anything.”

Marcin studied him. “You recognize that launch?”

Gabriel busied himself with the displaced cleat. “Harborlight has many.”

“That was not my question.”

“And you are not police.”

The bluntness alienated him at once. Marcin’s face closed. Gabriel had spent years turning command into a haven where questions could be asked before they became insubordination. One sentence had subverted the craft.

“Sorry,” he said. “I have seen one like it.”

“Where?”

“Another contract.”

He offered no elaboration. Marcin did not importune him, which was worse.

“A successful anticipatory closure,” he told cameras. “An untoward maintenance incident, rapidly mitigated.”

Gabriel heard the purport and felt something in him harden. The route had nearly despoiled two men of their lives; already the story had been fabricated into proof.

Vale approached him on the quay. “You disobeyed a direct instruction.”

“I salvaged your workers.”

“They are municipal employees.”

“Water doesn’t care who pays wages.”

Vale’s face was rain-streaked and stern. “You were right about the boat.”

The concession was more menacing than anger. “Then why did the display call it stationary?”

“We will investigate.”

“And the gate?”

“The squall arrived.”

As if summoned, wind drove a final sheet of rain across the quay. Vale looked toward the barrier, where the river had begun to surge in earnest. The later weather would portray the early command as wisdom.

Dr. El-Amin came down the gangway. “Where is Sami Bensaid?”

Vale turned. “He should be at the control center.”

“He was meeting me here.”

Gabriel said nothing.

They searched the quay. Port security opened workshops and the forepeak of the maintenance boat. A police officer took names. Gabriel gave his occupation, license number, and account of the rescue. He did not mention the figure on the stairs. Once spoken, Sami’s name might lead to the service launch, the buoys, the false report, and the demise of everything Gabriel had kept shipshape through twelve lean years.

The search had the chaotic appearance of urgency and the careful boundaries of ownership. Municipal staff opened municipal rooms. Harborlight security opened Harborlight cabinets. Police waited for an access manager before entering a locked control bay whose door stood twenty meters from where Sami had last been seen. Nobody wanted later accusations of vandalism, unlawful entry, or compromised evidence.

Gabriel joined two day-men checking the underside of the quay. They used lamps to probe between pilings while rain ran from their hoods. One found Sami’s hard hat on a lower walkway. The chin strap was intact.

The older day-man knew every recess. Before remote monitoring, he said, one pump keeper had lived in the outer hut like an anchorite with only a mastiff for company. The dog’s iron water bowl remained under the bench. This afternoon the man had been mowing the narrow verge when he saw security arrive; the engine noise had lulled his granddaughter to sleep in the maintenance office, so he remembered exactly when it stopped.

“One of them belabored the jammed service hatch with a rubber mallet,” he said. “Not repair. He wanted it open quickly.”

The account gave police a time, a witness, and a reason to preserve tool marks. The search widened to the hatch rather than wandering indiscriminately through every Harborlight room.

“Could have taken it off,” the man said.

“In this weather?”

“People do improper things.”

At the top of the maintenance stair, a security contractor in a black jacket spoke quietly to a port supervisor. Not the broad man Gabriel had seen. This one was lithe, almost boyish, and overtly unthreatening. The uniformity of the jackets made every wearer look like an alibi for the others.

Dr. El-Amin moved through the search with the checksum napkin still hidden in her sleeve. Gabriel watched her ask precise questions: which doors alarmed, which cameras covered the landing, who could disable a badge. She did not know enough to fear the service launch. He did.

Three months earlier, the *Nkem* had carried two relay buoys from Tangier under paperwork describing oceanographic test equipment. Gabriel had accepted a cash windfall and falsified one position report when the delivery point shifted north. On the receiving launch, Sami had objected that the devices were unauthorized. The broad security man had told him to stop belaboring a clerical discrepancy. Gabriel had heard the word sabotage spoken as something Sami might be accused of, not something the equipment might perform.

He had mulled that memory only when bills permitted. Compartmentalization was not witchcraft; it was accountancy of conscience. This fact belonged to customs. That one to Harborlight. The cash belonged to debt. The unease belonged nowhere. Now the partitions had collapsed into one rain-soaked quay.

At 18:42, a mechanic found Sami below the north maintenance stair.

He lay on a concrete landing where rainwater dripped through the open structure. One arm was folded beneath him, the other bare to the elbow. There was no macabre arrangement, no theatrical wreckage, only a young man’s body at an angle the living did not choose.

Van Houten stopped a contractor from moving the hard case beside the rail. “Leave the scene unspoiled.” His voice dropped to a mutter as he assigned photographs, measurements, and separate evidence seals. The black case might belong to Sami or to the quay; its ownership could wait.

Mira stopped three steps above him. Gabriel saw her clinical attention take command before grief could: the blood at the ear, the position of the neck, the jacket bunched beneath one shoulder. A paramedic touched Sami’s throat, then began tests whose finality was evident in their haste.

Vale stood behind the police line. His face had emptied.

“Did anyone see him fall?” an officer asked.

Gabriel looked toward the rain-blurred quay, where the service launch was gone.

“No,” he said.

The officer marked the answer without looking up. Gabriel felt the lie enter the record with less ceremony than cargo entering a manifest. He had not seen Sami fall. The answer was technically true and morally fabricated. Its precision made it worse.

The word was a small act. He knew it could become destructive. He knew, too, that concealment had its own propulsion: once embarked, a man kept moving because the cost of turning back increased with every mile.

Above them, Harborlight’s public screen changed from amber to green. CLOSURE COMPLETE, it announced. CASUALTIES AVOIDED: 47.

It did not count Sami.

A second officer asked Gabriel to accompany him to a mobile interview room beside the harbor office. The cabin smelled of wet wool and instant coffee. On one wall an old print portrayed a clipper entering Rotterdam under foresail; beneath it, a current port chart showed freight lanes, ferry crossings, and the barrier’s exclusion zone. Centuries of seafaring reduced to different inks.

The officer identified himself as Van Houten and began with Gabriel’s qualifications, nautical certificates, and vocational history. He asked whether the deviation had been a spontaneous assault on port authority or a proportionate rescue maneuver. Gabriel objected to the first construction.

Before questioning him about the body, Van Houten stated the legal vocabulary without euphemism. Sami was a person until a physician certified death, not a cadaver for investigators to rearrange. Formal decease would trigger notification, property preservation, and possible intestacy procedure if no will could be found. None of that authorized police to infer crime before examination; all of it required them to preserve what a later court might need.

“The state is not an assailant because it gives a bad order,” he said. “A captain is not an aggressor because he refuses one.”

“Then what happened?”

Gabriel described the false clearance, the trapped workboat, and the closing gate. He reported the black service launch only as harbor traffic glimpsed through rain. Each purported fact he withheld seemed to alter the import of those he gave.

Van Houten asked about the earlier buoy contract. The question struck with the force of a towline coming taut.

“What contract?” Gabriel said.

“Harborlight lists you as an occasional carrier.”

“I carry many imports.”

“Including the importation of relay equipment from Tangier?”

“Did Dr. Bensaid ever embark your vessel?”

“Not that I recall.”

That answer was another technical shelter. Sami had boarded the service launch, not the *Nkem*. Gabriel could feel his integrity being spoiled by exact grammar.

The officer changed direction. Had Sami seemed threatening? Vulnerable? Had anyone warned Gabriel of sabotage? Did the black launch portend trouble before the gate moved? Gabriel answered no where he could and narrowed the rest. He did not exult in craftiness. The concealment felt like bad seamanship: every correction generated a second error.

Van Houten asked whether the security men’s conduct had been minacious: a threat conveyed by posture, words, or blocking movement. Gabriel said he had seen too little. He would not turn a black jacket into proof of subversion merely because his own omissions made it sinister.

When the interview ended, Harborlight had arranged taxis for the surviving guests. The quay emptied in twain, officials toward hotels and working men toward the hospital ward. Marcin waited beside the damaged launch with Gabriel’s coat.

“Your broker called,” he said. “Again.”

“Tell him I was occupied.”

“He knows. Your rescue is on television. They call you a privateer, an iconoclast, and a reckless opportunist.”

“Bipartisan criticism.”

“Also hero.”

“That is the most threatening.”

Marcin did not smile. He looked toward the maintenance stair where police lights threw a death's-head pallor across the concrete. “You will rue whatever you did not tell them.”

Gabriel put on the coat. “Probably.”

Rain had eased to a cold mist. The barrier stood closed, invulnerable in public imagination and entirely dependent on motors, seals, taskmasters, and frightened people making choices. Gabriel had saved two men from its machinery. He had left a third man alone inside his own lie.

The difference would not remain private. By morning, every saved life and every omission would belong to records other people could compare directly.

## Chapter 4: Triage Color

By midnight the emergency department had forgotten the storm.

Rain still struck the ambulance-bay roof in spurts, but inside there was only the hospital weather: fluorescent glare, overheated corridors, the antiseptic sting of disinfectant, bodies arriving faster than rooms emptied. A child with an allergic rash cried beside a man clutching his stomach. An elderly woman’s cardiac monitor chimed through the curtain. Wet shoes squeaked on sanitary flooring.

Mira stood at the triage desk in borrowed green scrubs while a nurse named Lise clipped a Harborlight tablet to a bracket beside the computer.

“You are not credentialed here,” Lise said.

“I know.”

“You may translate, take histories, fetch. You do not diagnose.”

“Understood.”

The hierarchy was cardinal in a crowded department: authority had to remain visible even when everyone crossed ordinary lines. Mira had trained in epidemiology after medicine and had not worked a clinical shift in nine years. Knowledge lingered in the muscle, but so did obsolete confidence. An old mnemonic could become malpractice if it survived after procedure changed.

The protocol card above the desk quoted the hospital’s 2029 review: *The former mnemonic is obsolete and must not guide triage.* Lise made Mira read the replacement before assigning her any patient contact.

They had come with three patients from the quay. The immersed worker, Willem de Ruiter, was coughing but alert after oxygen. His colleague needed six stitches for a facial lesion and an X-ray of his molar because the impact had driven it painfully into the socket. A journalist had a sprain and a talent for complaint. The squall had produced less mortality than an ordinary Friday night.

Except for Sami.

The journalist objected to being placed behind a disheveled man with a scalp wound. He had a media credential, he explained, and the Harborlight launch had been an official event.

“Blood does not respect accreditation,” Lise said.

The scalp wound belonged to a kitchen porter struck by falling crockery in the reception salon. Mira irrigated it with saline while Lise checked coagulation history. No hemophilia, no anticoagulant, no allergy to adhesive. The cut looked florid because scalp wounds bled with theatrical appetite, but it was shallow and clean.

“Antibiotic?” the porter asked.

“Not automatically,” Lise said. “Cleaning is more useful than unnecessary penicillin.”

Mira translated the diagnosis into French for his wife, who had arrived damp and furious. The woman wanted a surgeon. Lise explained that a nurse practitioner could close the wound with staples after examination. Hospital hierarchy, Mira remembered, often became visible to patients only when they tried to climb it.

Across the aisle an elderly man palpitated with anxiety while insisting he had a cardiac ailment. His electrocardiogram was normal; his pulse slowed when a porter found his lost hearing aid. A teenager with a singed palm needed analgesic, not an armory of tests. A woman with diabetes had forgotten her insulin during the evacuation and was beginning to vomit. None was trivial merely because the treatment was ordinary.

The elderly man carried a quarto volume wrapped in a towel. It was a family medical ledger, not, as the clerk first assumed, a religious book. His grandfather had been a consumptive treated with heliotherapy; an aunt described there as a valetudinarian had received a tonic for every infirmity; another page recorded a venereal infection in euphemisms so dense that the actual drug was unclear. The old entries were historically interesting and clinically unsafe.

“This says he takes foxglove,” a resident said.

“It says his grandfather did,” Mira replied. “Current medicines first.”

They found the man’s modern list behind the hearing-aid receipt: a beta blocker and no digitalis. The archaic ledger had nearly displaced the living patient’s history. Lise tied it back in its towel and wrote CURRENT LIST IN WALLET across the handover sheet.

Lise assigned tasks with cardinal clarity. Mira elicited histories and wrote nothing in the chart without countersignature. She fetched a sterile cartridge for the stapler, an ointment for a superficial burn, a vial of local anesthetic, and a blanket from a cupboard mislabeled PHARMACOLOGY. A resident asked her to trisect a waiting list into immediate, urgent, and delayed groups, then corrected himself when Lise glared.

“People are not a parabola,” Lise said.

“I meant the queue.”

“Then say queue.”

The correction had more than jargon behind it. Triage color could deaden anatomy into geometry if allowed. Red, amber, green: categories designed for speed became a creed when institutions forgot they were temporary.

One agitated patient tested that discipline. He had been sleeping beneath the station arcade and arrived shouting that a psychic had presaged the flood. Security called him a vagrant and suggested psychiatry before anyone removed his wet shoes.

Lise crouched to his level. “What is your name?”

“Pavel. I am not insane.”

“I did not say you were.”

His heel was split to the fat pad, with a pebble embedded near the tendon. A podiatrist on call advised irrigation and imaging. Pain, cold, and three nights without sleep explained much of his comportment; insanity did not. He accepted local anesthetic after Mira promised no one would take his coat.

The coat contained discharge papers from a psychotherapy clinic, an optician’s bill, and two citations for vagrancy. None made him a malingerer. When a junior doctor wrote “possible malinger,” Lise made him delete it.

“You cannot diagnose motive from inconvenience,” she said. “Nor call distress pathological because it is loud.”

Pavel’s radiograph showed no fracture. The wound did show early infection. Dermatology advised against liniment or a household balsam his friend had brought; surgery removed the pebble with forceps, not a scalpel, and admitted him for antibiotics because his reclusory life under the arcade made clean follow-up unlikely. The postal module recommended discharge.

“Savvy system,” Pavel said when Mira explained the contradiction. “It knows a sucker has no address, so it can welsh on the bed.”

The ethnic history of the verb made Mira dislike it, but his accusation was precise: the platform used absence of stable housing to justify denying the stability treatment required. Lise overrode the module and preserved his exact attributed wording in the complaint, offense and all.

His body was not in the department. Police had consigned it to the hospital mortuary pending examination. Mira had asked three people for his condition report and received three versions of the same humane obstruction: later, when family had been notified; later, when the attending physician was free; later, when the record had been reconciled.

Lise pointed to the waiting room. “Bed twelve. Possible anaphylaxis.”

A young woman sat upright, skin livid around her eyes, breath coming in a high brassy wheeze. Her boyfriend held an antihistamine packet as though it were ammunition.

“Shellfish?” Mira asked in English.

“No allergy,” he said. “Never.”

The woman wore a Harborlight reception badge. Mira remembered the oysters.

Her name was Elise, and she was the sommelier who had chosen wines for the launch reception. She could describe every sip but had not eaten an oyster. The upsurge in symptoms began after she crossed the service yard, where contractors had sprayed pesticide along the planted verge. Lise bagged her damp coat for later testing rather than assuming food allergy.

Elise’s boyfriend offered a silver flask. “Her tonic. An herbal elixir from an apothecary in Leiden.”

“No,” Lise said. “Nothing by mouth while her airway is unstable.”

The bottle’s label called the mixture a restorative nostrum. Its ingredients included balsam, liquorice, and enough alcohol to complicate sedation. Mira sealed it with the coat. A nostrum was not evidence of poisoning, but neither was the word *natural* a pharmacopoeia.

Lise administered adrenaline, then oxygen. A physician arrived and listened to the woman’s chest while Mira elicited the history. No asthma, no known predisposition, no new medicine. The tablets in the boyfriend’s hand were inadequate but not harmful. Within minutes the wheeze softened. Color began to resurge beneath the pallor.

“Observation,” the physician said. “Four hours. Steroid and antihistamine.”

The tablet chimed. Harborlight had assigned the patient amber and proposed redirect to Schiedam because local respiratory capacity was at threshold.

Lise frowned. “We have a bed.”

“Postal code?” Mira asked.

The boyfriend gave it. A low-priority district south of the river.

Lise changed the address to the reception venue. The proposed redirect vanished. Erasmus admitted the patient.

They stared at the screen.

The address change did more than reverse a transfer. It altered the module’s predicted nurse time, ambulance demand, and medication reserve. Present physiology had been made subordinate to projected residence. Lise saved both screens before the recommendation could disappear into a resurgent green status.

“Could be a bed-allocation rule,” Lise said.

“Beds don’t move when a postal code changes.”

“Tell that to administration.”

An ambulance crew entered with a diabetic man found confused at a tram stop. His glucose was low; the immediate therapy was glucose gel, not a mammoth diagnostic opus. Mira translated his Arabic while Lise medicated him. He revived enough to gripe about the nutritive quality of hospital biscuits.

The next ambulance brought a warehouse cleaner from a flooded granary. He had collapsed after trying to sop pesticide-contaminated water with sacks of spoiled flour. His clothes smelled sour and chemical. A colleague said the flood had exposed old munitions crates from a wartime museum store; one corroded munition lay open near the drain.

Meijer ordered decontamination before examination. “No heroic bloodshed. Clothing off into bags, skin washed, poison center called.”

The man’s forearm bore an old phoenix tattoo and a fresh scrape where metal had caught him. A fusible safety link in the fire door had melted during an earlier arson, his colleague explained, leaving the storeroom improperly sealed. That history changed the response: fire services would test the room before another worker entered, and police would preserve both the pesticide drum and the damaged link.

The drum was meant to control fungal blight in stored grain. Its cracked cap had admitted floodwater, an insalubrious mixture in which pesticide and sewage could not be distinguished by smell. Lise ordered cultures for any pathogenic bacterium and told the poison center not to treat a future positive culture as proof that the chemical exposure was harmless. Two hazards could coexist.

“Any animal exposure?” Lise asked.

“A gander from the canal chased us. No bite.”

“Then no rabies assessment. A rabid bird is not the concern here.”

The distinction made the colleague laugh once, mostly from relief.

The work steadied Mira because the body did not permit rhetoric. Blood either coagulated or did not. A pathogen reproduced or failed. A lesion was anatomical before it became evidence. Yet every fact still required judgment: whether jaundice was present beneath brown skin, whether shallow breathing was narcotic effect or pain, whether a drawn face meant shock or exhaustion.

Willem’s condition worsened at twelve forty. His oxygen saturation fell by three points and he developed a wet, persistent cough. Lise summoned Meijer, who listened for crackles and ordered a chest image, blood gas, and continuous cardiac monitoring.

The maritime intake form asked about *natation ability*, an antiquated way of asking whether he could swim. Bram said Willem could. That did not reduce aspiration risk or excuse the false clearance. A second historical checkbox asked about scurvy, a relic from seafarers’ medicine that had survived digitization without clinical purpose. Meijer struck both fields from the acute assessment and recorded the actual exposure time instead.

“Secondary drowning?” Willem’s colleague asked.

“Outdated phrase,” Meijer said. “Aspiration injury. Water irritates the lungs; symptoms can resurge.”

The colleague, Bram, sat on the adjacent trolley with a plaster above his eyebrow and one trouser leg cut away. His knee had struck a bollard. It was swollen but stable, without the laxity of a torn ligament. He refused a painkiller until Willem received one.

“Medicine is not a ration queue,” Meijer told him. “His therapy does not improve when you ail beside him.”

“I do not ail.”

“Then stop making that face.”

Mira took Bram’s account while radiology prepared Willem. The gate alarm had sounded after the arm began moving. Their tablet had shown a green work permit through nineteen hundred. Sami arrived at approximately eighteen ten carrying a field tablet and a round black case.

“Calibration puck?” Mira asked.

“Maybe. He said the gauge was within tolerance.”

“Did he use those words?”

“He said, ‘The sea is behaving. The software is having a tantrum.’”

That sounded like Sami: irreverent but exact about which part of a system he distrusted. Bram said another service launch approached the quay minutes later. A man called Sami by name. Bram had gone aft to free the line and heard only fragments: access, tablet, unauthorized copy.

“Did you see the man?”

“Black jacket. Shaved head, perhaps. In rain everyone becomes a smut.”

“A silhouette?”

“Yes. Sorry. My English.”

“Your English is fine.”

He had not seen an assault. He heard no outcry, no pistol, no cinematic threat. The details had the frustrating abidance of reality: partial, damp, susceptible to error.

“Tell police,” Mira said.

“Already. They asked whether Sami seemed wayward or agitated.”

“What did you say?”

“He seemed afraid and trying not to show it.”

Willem returned from imaging with early inflammatory changes but no severe edema. Meijer prescribed observation, oxygen, warmth, and repeat assessment. An antibiotic would follow only if infection declared itself; river exposure alone was not permission to medicate indiscriminately. Bram concurred with every instruction until she ordered him to lie down.

“The old adage is patient first,” he said.

“You are also a patient,” Meijer replied. “An incorrigible one.”

Mira watched the two men settle beneath hospital blankets. Their survival was not a blurb beneath Harborlight’s successful closure. It was Captain Okafor’s disobedience, a deckhand’s grip, a physician’s airway work, and now nursing observation through the night. To call the system lifesaving without naming those acts alienated outcome from cause.

At one fifteen, a cardiologist accosted Lise about the redirected patient. At one twenty, an administrator arrived and called the anomaly a software setback. At one twenty-seven, Harborlight security requested access to the triage logs for “quality improvement.” Lise declined with a mordant politeness Mira admired.

The administrator, Jeroen Smit, wore a lustrous tie and the exhausted sheen of a man summoned from a gala. He proposed that Harborlight receive a de-identified export before morning.

“A cluster review,” he called it. “No names.”

“Postal code is the problem,” Mira said. “Removing names does not remove identity when the district is small.”

“The platform needs examples to diagnose the fault.”

“Then preserve the logs under hospital control.”

Smit’s gaze moved to her borrowed scrubs. “And you are?”

“A witness.”

“Not staff.”

“Correct.”

“Then it would be pertinent to let staff negotiate access.”

Lise folded her arms. “We do not dicker over patient records at one in the morning.”

Smit flushed. “Nobody is bargaining.”

“Good. Then the answer is no.”

Rell arrived during the exchange with a hospital lawyer and a police liaison. He carried a preservation notice bearing the Harborlight logo above dense legal text. Its purport was perverse: because the module was involved in an adverse incident, Harborlight had an obligation to secure volatile diagnostic data before automatic deletion.

“Secure it where?” Mira asked.

“Our incident repository.”

“Under whose access?”

“Authorized investigators.”

“Your employees.”

“And external auditors as required.”

“Required by whom?”

The lawyer intervened. “Dr. El-Amin, this is routine preservation, not a raid.”

“Then make a forensic copy with hospital information security and leave the original untouched.”

“Delay may degrade evidence.”

“Removal may destroy provenance.”

The police liaison, a young constable visibly regretting the assignment, asked whether the dispute could temporize until the inspector arrived. Rell said the log buffer would roll over at two. Lise called information security herself.

For twelve minutes the hospital corridor became a legal infirmary, every institution presenting its own ailment as the most pressing. Privacy cited contagion of access. Harborlight cited data loss. Police cited authority not yet delegated. Smit cited patient flow. Nobody cited the three southern residents being sent away from empty beds.

Mira asked Rell whether the triage module shared the same decision-support directory as the gate controller.

His expression did not alter. “I do not discuss critical architecture in a public corridor.”

“Is that a yes?”

“It is hygiene.”

“Secrecy is not hygiene.”

“Nor is suspicion evidence.”

The hospital security engineer arrived carrying a sealed drive and the air of an inept magician forced onstage before learning the trick. Lise made him explain each step. He would duplicate the volatile buffer, hash both copies, place one in the hospital evidence safe, and provide the second only against signed authority. Rell objected that Harborlight needed immediate access. The lawyer advised him, quietly, to accept.

As the copy ran, the tablet’s status light pulsed green. Three times the module attempted an external sync. Three times the engineer blocked it.

“Normal telemetry,” Rell said.

“Preserve that claim too,” Mira said.

He looked at her then with something colder than charisma and less legible than threat. “You have a propensity to convert every inconvenience into intent.”

“And you have a propensity to call every transfer routine.”

The copy completed at 01:58. The engineer signed across the evidence seal. Rell left without the drive.

“Patient records are not corporate largess,” she said.

The security man wore a black jacket. Broad shoulders, glabrous scalp, voice without overt threat. “The platform processed the recommendation. We need to reproduce the error.”

“After privacy approves.”

“This is pressing.”

“So is medicine.”

He gave his name as Tomas Rell. Mira felt an immediate, jaundiced suspicion and distrusted it for being immediate. He had the bearing of a henchman in a cheap thriller, which did not make him one.

“You were with Dr. Bensaid?” Rell asked her.

“I was meant to meet him.”

“About what?”

“Ask the police.”

His smile was cold-blooded only if she chose to ascribe motive to it. “They will ask you.”

He left. Lise watched him go. “Hospitality people?”

“Security.”

“Same charisma, worse flowers.”

At two, Dr. Roos Meijer found Mira sanitizing a trolley and told her to stop pretending usefulness.

Meijer was the emergency consultant who had examined Sami at the scene. She had a faint scar across her chin and an appetite for direct speech.

“He was dead when we reached him,” she said.

“Time?”

“Declared at eighteen fifty-one.”

“That isn’t time of death.”

“No. The body temperature and lividity suggested earlier, but the environment was cold and wet. Pathology will estimate.”

“The stair alarm triggered at eighteen thirty-nine.”

Meijer looked at her. “Who told you?”

“Port police.”

“Then either the alarm was belated or he did not die when he fell.”

The sentence jarred something loose in Mira’s memory: Sami on the upper walkway before embarkation, his hand raised; his insistence on meeting at twenty-one thirty; his confidence that there would be time.

“Injuries?”

“Basilar skull fracture is likely. There were bruises on both upper arms.”

“From the fall?”

“Perhaps.”

“Symmetrical?”

Meijer’s pause answered first. “Approximately.”

She led Mira not toward the mortuary but to a radiology reading room where the scene photographs had been uploaded under police authority. “You may look because you are a physician and a witness,” she said. “You may not photograph, copy, or play detective.”

“Those categories have begun to overlap.”

“Then be careful which one is speaking.”

The first images showed the landing: wet concrete, blood diluted to a rose-colored wash, Sami’s body partly covered by a thermal sheet. In closer views the bruises on his upper arms formed irregular ovals, four on one side and three on the other. Not fingerprints in the simplistic forensic sense. Pressure marks. Their symmetry was suggestive, not diagnostic.

“Could resuscitation cause them?” Mira asked.

“We did not grasp him there. We found no vital signs and moved him with a scoop stretcher after police photographed the position.”

“A fall against the rail?”

“Possible on one arm. Both is less easy.”

There was a scrape on the right palm and a shallow cut beneath his chin. The probable basilar fracture accounted for blood at the ear. None established whether he had been conscious when he fell.

Meijer opened the pre-mortem assessment. “Temperature is poor evidence in wind and rain. Lividity is more useful. It had begun posteriorly, but he was found partly on his side.”

“Meaning he lay elsewhere first.”

“Meaning movement is one explanation.”

“What else?”

“The body settling differently against the stair. Clothing pressure. Our first observation being wrong. Pathology is not a mystic art, despite television.”

She enlarged a close view of the jacket sleeve. A hirsute caterpillar clung to the wet cuff, likely blown from the verge; beside it, a translucent skin from an insect’s ecdysis adhered to the seam. Those fragile contaminants established that the sleeve had contacted vegetation after rain began. They did not establish where Sami died, but they gave the laboratory something independent to compare with the landing and upper walkway.

The bruises had another geometry. Their long axes approached tangency with the curve of the upper arm rather than crossing it like a rail strike. Meijer refused to call that proof of hands, but she asked the pathologist to measure each mark before dissection changed the tissue.

“Can the time of death precede the alarm?”

“Yes.”

“By how much?”

“Do not turn an interval into a timestamp. I would say he may have died between eighteen fifteen and eighteen forty-five. The pathologist may narrow it.”

The breadth frustrated Mira because the alarm sat inside it. Yet the bruising and possible movement changed the anatomy of the question. The issue was no longer simply whether Sami slipped. It was whether another person restrained him, whether he died before reaching the landing, and whether the alarm recorded a fall or a later opening of the stair door.

“Toxicology?”

“Planned. Alcohol, sedatives, narcotic agents. No obvious injection mark, no phial or cartridge at scene.”

“And medicines?”

“A broad screen guided by pharmacology, not a potpourri of every substance the laboratory can detect. Antispasmodic drugs, sedatives, alcohol, common analgesics. We will not infer a laxative or purgative because of nonspecific chemistry, nor call an old skin preparation iatric evidence merely because it came from an apothecary.”

The restraint mattered. An unbridled toxicology search would generate coincidences faster than answers.

“His medical history?”

“Unknown until next of kin consents to release. We should not invent maladies because a young man died unexpectedly.”

Next of kin. Until that moment Sami’s family had been an administrative abstraction somewhere beyond the rain. Now Mira imagined a phone ringing in another country, a parent hearing a formal voice, a sister being asked to identify an anatomical quietus she had known as a person.

“Have they been notified?”

“Police are contacting his sister. She is traveling from Paris in the morning.”

That was the first clean bridge into what came next, and it made Mira ashamed of having wanted only data from the body.

Bruising from restraint could be mistaken for rescue handling or collision. It could also be exactly what it resembled: fingers gripping hard enough to hamper movement. Mira imagined no assailant, no pistol, no elaborate murder. Only a confrontation near wet stairs and force applied by someone who expected compliance.

“Did you photograph them?”

“Police did.”

“His devices?”

“I saw a phone in an evidence bag. No laptop.”

“He carried a field tablet.”

“Then tell them.”

Meijer’s tone was not impatient; it was triage. Mira’s grief, suspicion, and professional disgrace were less urgent than the next patient. The truth of that had poignancy without comfort.

At the nurses’ station, Harborlight chimed again. Two patients from the same southern postal zone had been redirected despite available beds: a child with a deep cut and a pregnant woman with hypertension. Pediatrics and obstetrics both showed capacity. Lise overrode the recommendations.

The child, eight years old, had fallen through the glass door of a flooded shop. His father carried him in wrapped in a cedar-colored curtain already imbrued with blood. The laceration crossed the calf without severing tendon, but tiny glass fragments glittered in it. Pediatrics had six beds. Harborlight proposed a forty-minute transfer.

“Why?” the father asked in Dutch.

Lise did not offer a bromidic reassurance. “The recommendation is wrong. We are keeping him here.”

The boy needed local anesthetic, careful irrigation, and exploration before suturing. Mira held the light while a resident removed fragments with forceps. The largest clicked into a metal tray. The child watched with awe until nausea overtook curiosity.

In the next bay, obstetrics assessed the pregnant woman for preeclampsia. Her blood pressure was high, urine protein positive, headache persistent. She was not a casual redirect. Transport across a wet city could convert a manageable condition into seizure or placental crisis. Lise overrode again and documented the current bed count beside the refusal.

The woman, Amina, had fled fighting as a child. Her old record called her father an insurgent and attributed the family’s injuries to an insurgence; a later asylum affidavit called the same group civilians resisting armed insurgents. Neither label belonged in her obstetric risk score. What mattered now was hypertension, gestational age, and a retained fragment from an exploded munition near her left hip.

“Munitions history matters for imaging,” Meijer said. “The politics does not.”

Amina’s husband tried to josh her about the fetal monitor sounding like a horse. She said it was a mare at full gallop and made him stop. The brief exchange restored her sanity more effectively than the resident’s bromidic assurance that everything would be fine.

The tablet displayed no pathos, only a red coefficient beside the postal zone. Expected population shrinkage had become an inhibitor applied to present care.

“Three,” she said.

“Save screenshots.”

“Already.”

Mira trawled the visible settings. The module used expected future occupancy, not current beds. A district-level coefficient degraded priority where projected population was shrinking. The system was not merely describing scarcity; it was importing a demographic judgment into clinical procedure.

“This is inhumane,” Lise said.

“It may be invalid,” Mira replied.

Lise’s look was sharp. “A person is sent across a city during an emergency, and you choose *invalid*?”

Mira flinched. The word had been a salve, technical and bloodless. In Alexandria, years ago, she had used similarly clean language while a triage shortcut diverted patients from Youssef’s district. Aggregate benefit. Capacity preservation. She had subscribed to each phrase until death gave them anatomy.

“You’re right,” she said. “It is both.”

The memory arrived not as narrative but as fluorescent light.

Alexandria, seven years earlier. A heat emergency, emergency wards ventilated by fans that moved hot air from one exhausted body to another. Mira had stood before a capacity board while ambulances clustered outside. A model showed aggregate benefit if incoming cases from three districts were diverted to a temporary infirmary inland. The inland site had beds, she had said. It had oxygen. It had a cardiologist on call and a pharmaceutical cache.

What it lacked was reliable transportation after a substation failed.

Someone warned her. A dispatcher, perhaps, or a resident whose name she could no longer recover without opening the sealed review. Mira had treated the warning as one adverse anecdote against systemwide need. She had approved the shortcut for ninety minutes. Youssef’s ambulance spent fifty-two of them entangled in traffic.

She remembered visiting him afterward, before infection and renal failure completed what heat had begun. His lips were cracked. A nicotine patch showed on his arm because the hospital had no tolerance for smoking near oxygen. He had joked that the patch was a preservative and asked whether she had finally found a panacea for Cairo traffic.

Youssef had also mocked the nutrition drink as a vampire’s supper and asked for real soup. Her aunt had brought lentils dense enough for an epicure and bread to vitalize a man who could barely swallow. None of it could reverse the dehydration that had begun to emaciate him. By the fourth day he looked emaciated; the chart called the change emaciation, turning the visible cost of delay into a neutral noun.

His sclera had become jaundiced as renal and hepatic injury advanced. That clinical yellowing, not Mira’s later jaundiced view of institutions, was the finding she had failed to make her family understand.

She had not told him the route was hers.

The recollection did not exorcise guilt. It restored sequence. Recommendation, command, traffic, failing body. She had spent years dissecting the model as if better analysis could remove her decision from it. Now a red postal zone pulsed on a tablet in Rotterdam, and the old decision no longer seemed past.

“Mira?” Lise said.

She had used Mira’s first name for the first time.

“I’m all right.”

“That is not a diagnosis.”

“No.” Mira steadied a hand against the counter. “It is an evasion.”

She told Lise only that she had seen a similar population coefficient used during an epidemic and that the clinical consequences had been worse than the aggregate report showed. The confession was partial. Even partial truth changed her posture. She stopped treating the module as a technical setback and began writing down who had been asked to bear its error.

At three ten, police inspectors Van Houten and Bakker met her in a consultation room that smelled of flannel upholstery and stagnant coffee. They recorded her account: the checksum, Sami’s phrase, the planned meeting. Mira handed over the folded napkin in a transparent bag supplied by Lise.

“You carried this in your sleeve, then pocket?” Bakker asked.

“Yes.”

“Other handling?”

“Koen typed the checksum from it. I touched it. Sami touched it. Possibly catering staff.”

No fable of pristine evidence would survive the facts.

“Why did he approach you?” Van Houten asked.

“Because he believed the archived forecast differed from the controller’s decision bundle.”

“Fraud?”

“I don’t know.”

“Sabotage?”

“I don’t know.”

“Malfunction?”

“I don’t know.”

Bakker’s pencil stopped. “What do you know?”

“The public May result cannot be reproduced from the data I was given. A second bundle exists. Tonight a gate closed against local readings. A patient’s postal code altered a triage decision without altering medical need. Sami knew at least one of those mechanisms. He is dead earlier than the alarm announcing his fall.”

Silence followed, not concurrence but weight.

“Preserve his phone, tablet, access badge, clothing, and any removable storage,” Mira said. “Preserve the stair alarm, door logs, camera feeds, and the decision-support directory before anyone can expurgate or overwrite it.”

Bakker closed his notebook. “Harborlight says the directory is distributed across protected infrastructure. Seizing it could impair flood control.”

“I asked you to preserve it, not remove it.”

“Their counsel proposes an internal forensic image.”

“Made by the party whose system is in question.”

Van Houten stirred the stagnant coffee without drinking. “Do you allege fraud, homicide, or a defective product?”

“I cannot distinguish them yet.”

“Police must distinguish legal grounds.”

“Then preserve first and distinguish before access expires.”

The inspector’s irritation was not ineptitude. She was asking him to intervene in critical infrastructure on the strength of a contaminated napkin, an unreproduced model result, medical estimates with wide intervals, and bruises that might have innocent causes. Mira understood the threshold and hated it.

“At minimum,” she said, “issue a notice against deletion and require joint imaging with the municipality. Hash the source in place. Record every person present. Do not allow Harborlight security sole custody.”

Van Houten looked at Bakker. Some tacit decision passed between them.

“We can request voluntary preservation tonight,” he said. “A prosecutor will review seizure in the morning.”

“Voluntary.”

“It has legal consequence if breached.”

“After evidence is gone.”

“Dr. El-Amin, we are not your enforcement arm.”

The phrase jarred her. “No. You are Sami’s.”

Silence followed. She had overstepped, but neither officer rebuked her. Van Houten wrote three items on a separate form: field tablet unaccounted for; joint image requested; external synchronization to be suspended.

“We will also preserve the hospital copy,” he said.

“Thank you.”

“Do not thank me. Remain available.”

“You are giving police procedure now?” Bakker asked.

“I am making a pressing request as a witness.”

Van Houten wrote her name on a form. “You will remain available in Rotterdam.”

“Am I detained?”

“No. You are a named witness.”

The distinction felt narrow and absolute.

When she left the room, dawn had begun to deaden the windows. The department carried on around her: disinfect, diagnose, medicate, redirect, override. Lise brought tea in a paper cup and stood beside her without speaking.

Van Houten returned once more before leaving. “Ms. Bensaid’s train arrives at eight twelve. She will be taken to the station before the mortuary. Do not approach her there.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“Harborlight has already asked to attend identification as employer representative.”

“Will you allow it?”

“Not in the room. Their lawyers are claiming his phone and work devices as corporate property. That question will not stay outside for long.”

Mira looked toward the sealed drive in the evidence safe and thought of the missing field tablet. By morning, grief would be forced to negotiate with ownership.

On the Harborlight tablet, the southern district glowed a quiet, adverse red. A map legend called the color *future constrained capacity*.

Mira thought of bruises shaped by hands and a gate moving before the water. She thought of Youssef, though she had trained herself for years not to let his name obtrude upon evidence.

This time she let it remain.

Meijer passed on her way to pathology and stopped beside the map. “The preliminary examination begins at nine. His sister may request an independent observer.”

“Will you recommend one?”

“Yes. Not because our pathologist is corrupt, but because contested death can make every later finding look partisan.” She rubbed the scar on her chin. “They will examine tissue for bacterial infection, viral illness, and anything symptomatic before the fall. They will document the somatic injuries, take blood and vitreous samples, and preserve clothing fibres. No vivisection, no morbid spectacle, only dissection after death.”

“And the bruises?”

“Measured, photographed, sampled. A dermatologist may help distinguish patterned pressure from incidental impact. Neurology will review whether the head injury could have permitted movement after impact.”

The clinical list was not a catalogue to Mira now. Each act protected a future question from caprice. The pathology could not identify an assailant or outfox a false log. It could establish what the body had endured and what it had not.

“Do police understand the timing problem?” she asked.

“They understand enough to preserve it. That is not the same as concurrence.”

At the far end of the corridor, cleaners stirred disinfectant in a bucket. Morning staff arrived in an eclectic procession of bicycles, trams, and night buses. Their voices rose in unison around the handover desk, a human resurgence that made the department seem briefly inexhaustible.

With them came witnesses from the reception. The quartet’s viol player had a cut across two fingertips from broken glass. She had been hired for a concerto arrangement and an aria beneath Vale’s speech; now she could not close her hand around the bow. Her old occupational-health file used *albino* as a noun. Lise amended the active chart to *person with albinism*, documented the wording as outdated, and arranged an eye-shield because the examination lamps caused pain.

Behind her waited a museum mechanic who had been preparing a vintage ambulance for public display. He had begun to simonize its paint when the gate alarm sounded. From beneath the vehicle he saw a black service launch arrive at the north stairs before the squall. Police separated him from the other witnesses and took his account.

The final witness was Professor Theo Markos, a retired classicist with a bruised shoulder and an importunate need to classify everyone. He called Vale a kingling, the press a swarm, and himself no votary of technological rule. Van Houten warned him that a statement was evidence, not a paean to his own foresight.

“I did not presage the death,” Markos said. “I saw a man in a black jacket block Dr. Bensaid’s path.”

That converted ornament into testimony. Markos signed as deponent and surrendered the photographs on his phone. One showed a conference pamphlet in his hand about petalism, the old Syracusan practice of voting exile with leaves; beyond it, out of focus but time-stamped, Sami stood beside the service stair with a senior church hierarch from the delegation. The hierarch had already told police he left before the alarm. The image fixed his departure window and prevented his minor scheduling peccadillos from becoming suspicion by default.

Mira disliked Markos’s theatrical language, but his photograph supplied a second independent time point. Police requested the hierarch’s original image files and moved the professor’s shoulder examination ahead of another hour of rhetoric.

It was not. Capacity was people entering tired rooms and choosing, again, to attend to what was in front of them.

## Chapter 5: Next of Kin

The police station had been designed to make grief behave.

Its chairs were fixed to the floor in rows of four. Its clock made no sound. A transparent screen divided Noor Bensaid from the woman asking for her brother's date of birth, and every object that might have invited disorder had been removed except a box of tissues placed exactly beyond reach.

“Twenty-third of April, 2002,” Noor said.

The woman typed. “Place of birth?”

“Tangier.”

“Current nationality?”

“French and Moroccan.”

“Occupation?”

Noor looked at the form through the glass. There would be a box, she supposed. Engineer would fit. Brother would not.

“Field systems engineer.”

“Employer?”

“You know his employer.”

The clerk's expression remained dispassionate. She had probably learned that accuracy was a form of kindness when strangers became argumentative. “I need you to confirm it.”

“Harborlight.”

The name entered the record with the same weight as his birthday.

Noor had arrived from Paris at 08:12 after a sleepless journey in a carriage full of commuters who ate breakfast, apologized for their bags, and watched her not cry. At Rotterdam Centraal, two police officers had met her beside the bookshop. One carried a card with her name in careful calligraphy. The other asked whether she wanted a beverage. Their courtesy had made her indignant in a way cruelty might not have done. Courtesy implied that the day possessed a proper form.

Now Inspector Bakker sat down beside the clerk and slid his card beneath the screen.

“Ms. Bensaid, I am sorry for your loss.”

She had counted seven apologies since the train. The phrase had become a small coin passed from hand to hand, shopworn but apparently legal tender.

“When can I see him?”

“The identification can happen now. Before that, the pathologist would like your consent to a full post-mortem examination.”

“You think he was killed.”

“We have not made that determination.”

“Then why a full examination?”

“Because the apparent time of death may not agree with the alarm, and because there are injuries that require interpretation.”

He spoke without melodrama. Noor begrudged him that competence. She had prepared herself to meet an amateur, an officious man who would disparage Sami as reckless and expect her maternal assent. Instead Bakker placed a translated consent form before her and gave each silence room.

The document was in Dutch, French, Arabic, and English. The Arabic rendering had the brittle formality of consular correspondence. Noor read the French. Cause and manner of death. Toxicology. Retention of tissue. Independent observer. Return of remains. Words arranged to domesticate an astronomical fact: Sami had ceased to exist overnight, and strangers required her signature to examine how.

“Who asked for the independent observer?” she said.

“The emergency consultant recommended it because the death is contested. Dr. El-Amin also raised concerns.”

“Who is Dr. El-Amin?”

“A witness. She was due to meet your brother.”

“Why?”

“She says he approached her about a technical concern.”

Noor heard the mealy-mouthed construction and felt bitterness climb her throat. Technical concern. As though Sami had lodged a complaint about a loose hanger. “And she waited until he was dead?”

Bakker's eyes did not move. “The meeting was arranged for later in the evening.”

“That was not my question.”

“No. It was an accusation, and I do not yet have an accurate answer.”

The rebuke was mild enough to land. Noor signed for the post-mortem and the independent observer. Her handwriting was usually broad, demonstrative, a visual art acquired from a grandfather who treated every grocery note as calligraphy. Today her name collapsed into itself.

The clerk asked about religious requirements. Noor said their parents wanted Sami washed and buried in Tangier as soon as the examination permitted. Their father had already contacted the Moroccan consulate; their mother had called an undertaker, an imam, two uncles, and Noor nine times. Domesticity persisted by making arrangements against the void.

“There may be delay if the prosecutor retains the body,” Bakker said.

“How much?”

“I cannot promise.”

“My mother asked whether Thursday was possible.”

“I am sorry.”

Eight.

He led her through a corridor whose walls carried posters about bicycle theft and domestic violence. Somewhere behind a closed door a child prattled while an adult murmured answers. Noor fixed on the sound because it had contour. Voices rose, crossed, returned. Grief itself was toneless, a pressure beyond hearing.

At the mortuary entrance, a consular officer waited in a dark suit. Monsieur Rahal was a Moroccan emigrant who had spent thirty years in the Netherlands and retained the Tangier habit of calling every younger woman *my daughter* when no partiality was intended.

“Your father importuned me before dawn,” he said. “He has my private number now. This is fearsome leverage.”

For one disloyal instant Noor almost smiled. Her father could canvass a bureaucracy with the courage of a benefactor and the tact of a barrage.

“He will call you forever.”

“Then I have joined the brotherhood.” Rahal's expression softened. “I am here for the paperwork. I will not enter unless you ask.”

Noor did not ask. She followed Bakker and a mortuary attendant into a room painted the color of aliment. The air was cold but not theatrically so. A sheet covered the body to the shoulders.

Sami looked younger in death, which was outrageous. At twenty-nine he had still possessed remnants of the cherubic face that made older women befriend him in queues and forgive his inquisitive questions. The body had kept that face while obliterating its animation. A shallow cut marked his chin. His hair, washed of rain and blood, curled as it had when he was a child.

Noor put both hands against her coat to keep from touching him.

She had expected a bravura collapse: knees failing, an effusion of sound, some histrionic proof adequate to sibling love. Nothing came. Her pulse slowed. The room sharpened inchmeal. She saw the cotton at his ear, the slight swelling beneath his jaw, the unaccustomed apparel of a hospital gown. Homeostasis had ended, but his body remained specific. There was a scar beside his left eyebrow from the summer he tried to leap between roofs in their grandfather's courtyard. There was the small refractory bump at the bridge of his nose, legacy of a football and Noor's bad aim.

“It is him,” she said.

Bakker waited.

“My brother. Sami Idris Bensaid.”

The attendant drew the sheet higher. Noor stopped her.

“His arms.”

“Ms. Bensaid—”

“The inspector said injuries.”

Bakker nodded once. The attendant uncovered Sami's left upper arm. Several dark marks had been measured and outlined on a transparent rendering laid beside the body. Finger-shaped, perhaps. Or perhaps Noor supplied the fingers because rage required hands.

“Did somebody hold him?”

“That is one possibility,” Bakker said.

“What are the others?”

“Impact with the rail. Handling before police arrived. Pressure from clothing or equipment. The distribution matters, and the pathologist will examine it.”

“Was he conscious when he fell?”

“Unknown.”

“Was he pushed?”

“Unknown.”

“Did Harborlight kill him?”

The question resounded in the small room. Bakker did not chastise her. “Unknown.”

Noor looked again at Sami's face. All his life he had been expressive, effusive in affection and pugnacious in argument. He could turn an apology into a lecture on why the injured party had misunderstood him. As a boy he wrote doggerel for their mother's birthday, then grew indignant when Noor corrected the alliteration. At university he became taciturn only when frightened. In the final voice message on her phone, he had sounded almost unemotional.

*Call me. It is about the piece, but not only the piece.*

She had let the message sit for eleven hours because they had been in a tiff. The fact now stood inside her like a blade.

“I need his belongings,” she said.

“We can discuss them upstairs.”

“Now.”

“They are not here.”

She heard the transparent answer and the opacity behind it. “Where are they?”

“Police property and his rented studio. Harborlight has asserted ownership over work devices.”

“Asserted.”

“A court will decide if necessary.”

“You have his phone?”

“Yes.”

“Tablet?”

“No tablet was recovered.”

“He always carried one.”

“So we have been told.”

The omission altered the room. Until then Harborlight had been an employer crowding grief with brokerage language. A missing device suggested action. Noor wanted that suggestion to harden into malevolence because malevolence could be opposed; accident was an underworld without an adversary.

She bent and kissed Sami's forehead. The skin was colder than she had prepared for. In Tangier their mother would have sung a low antiphon of prayer and instruction while women of the family gathered. Here a ventilation duct supplied the only response.

“I am taking you home,” Noor whispered.

It was a promise she had no authority to make.

Upstairs, the property room clerk produced a list. The handwriting had been transcribed from scene tags into a clean digital inventory: clothing; black work boots; wallet containing sixty-three euros and a transit card; keys; Harborlight badge; two loose screws; one pressure-gauge seal; phone; silver ring; folded paper bearing an address.

No field tablet. No round calibration case.

No recorder.

Noor read the list again.

“Where is his recorder?”

Bakker looked over her shoulder. “Was he carrying one?”

“He carried it everywhere.”

“Describe it.”

“A modified field recorder, black, about this size.” She held her hands apart. “Two microphone capsules. The left grille is dented. He had put a diagnostic board inside.”

“For his work?”

“For mine.”

That answer was compromising in ways she did not want to explain. Months earlier Sami had asked her to safeguard the recorder and a pressure puck. He believed the puck retained calibration timing Harborlight could not remotely revise. Noor, already tired of his suspense, had put both into an unfinished sculpture because it was the one object in her studio no insurer, landlord, or inquisitive curator could open without her consent. Later she had shipped the work to London for a gallery installation. She had used the recorder's audible channels in the composition without examining the diagnostic channel.

She had told herself this was custody, not neglect.

“When did you last see it?” Bakker asked.

Noor folded the property list. “In Paris, perhaps two months ago.”

The lie was piecemeal rather than complete. She had last seen the recorder's casing then. It had been sealed in resin a week later. Sami had inspected the sculpture before shipment, tapping its curved shell with his knuckles and saying she had made a sarcophagus for a machine.

*An artwork*, she corrected.

*An expensive way to hide a useful object.*

She had called him an illiterate aesthete. He called her a poetaster with power tools. Their drollery concealed the argument beneath: Sami believed evidence belonged wherever it could survive; Noor believed objects changed meaning when somebody else conscripted them.

“You are certain he took it back to Rotterdam?” Bakker asked.

“No.”

“Then why expect it on this list?”

“Because he asked me about it yesterday.”

“What did he say?”

Noor felt compunction, then resisted it. Police curiosity did not create trust. “That it mattered.”

“May I hear the message?”

“Later.”

Bakker's patience contracted. “Ms. Bensaid, if the recorder relates to his death, delay may put evidence at risk.”

“Evidence for whom?”

“For the inquiry.”

“Harborlight calls its lawyers an inquiry.”

“I do not work for Harborlight.”

“You let them claim his things before I saw his face.”

“They sent a letter. A letter does not decide ownership.”

Noor placed the list in her bag. “Neither does your list decide what existed.”

She left before he could stop her. Rahal followed through the station forecourt, moving with the patient gait of a man accustomed to bereaved families and immigration counters.

“The inspector is not your enemy,” he said.

“That is a very consular sentence.”

“I have others. Anger is not sustenance. Your parents need an accurate timetable. You require sleep.”

“And Harborlight requires my brother's property.”

“Which is why you should not fight every person simultaneously.”

“Sami did.”

“Sami was twenty-nine.”

The tenderness in his voice gave Noor umbrage. “Do not turn him into a childish man because he is dead.”

Rahal stopped beneath the station awning. Cyclists went past in the rain, bells sounding like a thin orchestra. “I did not. I said he was young enough to believe courage and strategy were synonyms.”

Noor had no retort. She let him arrange a car to the budget hotel where police had placed her. The room contained two narrow beds, a laminate desk, and a print of a bucolic canal scene whose aesthetic ambition ended at reassurance. Sami's duffel sat on one bed under a police seal.

The bag had come from his studio after an officer checked it for work devices. Noor signed the seal log and opened it in front of a video link to Bakker. Its contents were ordinary and therefore dolesome: three shirts, underclothes, a shaving kit, a paperback novellette whose hero was a retired astronomer, a foodstuff bar, a sweater their mother had knitted, and one sock without its mate. Sami had been incapable of packing apparel without creating an argument against paternity.

The camera made the unpacking feel like an understudy's rehearsal for bereavement, every gesture performed for a future court. Noor refused histrionics and named each thing without animation. A hotel carton held a centiliter bottle of hot sauce, a packet of barbecue seasoning, and a menu on which Sami had chosen to underline *gastronomy* beside instant mash. He had added, *A broiling decaliter of vanity; give me soup before they broil a kiloliter of sauce.* The joke was shameless, but it fixed the carton to the previous night's takeaway rather than the quay. Bakker asked her not to mince the distinction. Food could parch a mouth or ulcerate a stomach; it could not explain the pressure-gauge seal.

The sweater carried a thread of silver statuary paint. Noor recognized it from the London crate, whose pantechnicon carrier had used the same pigment to mark damaged freight. That relevance was factorable: if the fibre matched, Sami had handled the sculpture after its gallery packing, and Harborlight's claim that he had abandoned all personal equipment would weaken. She had to adapt a paper evidence sleeve and retire her first impulse to brush the thread away, then let the camera linger while Bakker dictated the collection time. The small act did not excite hope. It made one assertion testable.

In a side pocket she found a hotel receipt, two tram tickets, and a demurrage notice from a London freight warehouse. The notice concerned *Low Country Antiphon*, Noor's unfinished sculpture. Storage fees had begun after the gallery postponed installation.

The London address on the police inventory matched the warehouse.

Noor sat on the second bed.

Sami had carried the address in his pocket.

Her phone rang. Her mother spoke before Noor could answer, asking whether she had seen him, whether he looked hurt, whether the Dutch would release him, whether Noor had brought his green shirt. Questions came with maternal gregariousness, each one preventing the silence in which death might become final.

“He looked like himself,” Noor said.

It was shamefully insufficient and the only mercy she could find.

Her father took the phone. He wanted names, titles, the reputation of the pathologist, the exact distinction between prosecutor and examining magistrate. He had once taught sociology and retained a socialist distrust of private authority complicated by a paternal faith in official stamps.

“Do not sign corporate papers,” he said.

“I won't.”

“Do not let them disparage him.”

“I won't.”

“And eat.”

“Monsieur Rahal has already founded a campaign.”

Her father made a sound close to laughter and then broke off. The break was worse than weeping. Noor pressed her fist to her sternum until it passed.

After the call she played Sami's message.

His recorded voice had a dry, mellifluous closeness. Behind it she heard a railway announcement and the squeal of wheels. “Nono, call me. It is about the piece, but not only the piece. I need the little black heart out of it. Don't be vindictive. I apologized. Well, I began an apology. That should encourage you.”

Then, lower: “If anybody asks, you don't know where it is.”

The message ended with a burst of station noise.

Noor listened three times. On the fourth she heard what guilt had smothered before: a second voice announcing Rotterdam Centraal. He had called after arriving, not from Paris as she assumed. He meant to retrieve the recorder himself.

She rang Bakker.

“The recorder is in London,” she said. “Inside my sculpture.”

There was a pause. “Inside?”

“Sealed in the housing.”

“Why?”

“Because Sami asked me to safeguard it.”

“And you did not mention this at the station.”

“I am mentioning it now.”

“What else is inside?”

“A calibration puck.”

The inspector exhaled. “Do not contact the warehouse. Do not travel. I need a preservation request and British police liaison.”

“Harborlight already knows the address. It was in Sami's pocket.”

“That does not mean they know what is stored there.”

“Their insurer handles the gallery's transit policy.”

Silence changed quality.

“Which insurer?”

Noor found the policy on her phone. Van de Meer Assurance. The same firm, Bakker told her, that acted as custodian for parts of Harborlight's Rotterdam archive.

“They can inspect after a casualty claim,” Noor said. “The gallery filed one when the installation was postponed. They have leverage over the warehouse because storage charges are accruing.”

“Send me the policy.”

“After you tell me who Dr. El-Amin is.”

“This is not a negotiation.”

“Everything becomes a negotiation when institutions want property.”

He was silent long enough that she knew he had muted the call to consult someone. When he returned, he said, “Dr. El-Amin is a British epidemiologist auditing Harborlight. Your brother gave her a checksum. She reported concerns about his death and preserved evidence at the hospital. She is a named witness, not a suspect.”

“Did Harborlight choose her?”

“Dr. Vale invited her publicly.”

“Then she is compromised.”

“Possibly. She is also the person in London with the clearest standing to ask police to secure the object quickly.”

“I have standing. It is mine.”

“And you are in Rotterdam.”

Noor looked at Sami's open bag. The green sweater lay between them like evidence of an obsolete domestic world.

“Give me her number.”

Mira answered on the fourth ring. Her voice was exhausted, British, and reserved to the point of sounding impassible.

“Ms. Bensaid. I am very sorry.”

Nine.

“The recorder your insurer wants is in my sculpture.”

“My insurer?”

“Harborlight's. If you are working for them, save us both the pantomime.”

“I am not.”

“They invited you.”

“That is not employment.”

“It may be avocation.”

Mira let the insult stand. “What is on the recorder?”

“Sound.”

“What kind?”

“The ordinary kind.”

“Your brother said the observations were the only honest part of Harborlight's system. He may have recorded machine telemetry.”

Noor disliked hearing Sami interpreted by a stranger. “You had one conversation with him.”

“Yes.”

“Then do not dramatize him into your courageous informant.”

“I haven't.” Mira's tone sharpened. “He gave me a checksum and asked for a meeting. I did not know enough to protect him. That is the extent of my claim.”

The sentence was underplayed and therefore harder to attack. Noor walked to the window. Below, rain had made the street a grey rendering of itself.

“The recorder has four channels,” she said. “Two are audible microphones. One is time code. One is a diagnostic feed Sami added so his calibration puck could speak to it.”

“Speak?”

“Transmit pulses. Do not become literal now.”

“Where is the sculpture?”

Noor gave the warehouse address.

“I can be there tonight,” Mira said. “But I won't authorize opening it without you.”

“You could not.”

“No. The insurer might.”

At last, something like honesty.

They agreed to meet in London the next morning. Bakker would send a preservation notice through British police, but the notice might not precede the insurer's inspection. Noor booked the evening train despite his request that she remain for the preliminary pathology results. Rahal arranged for the consulate to receive them and called her pugnacious. She accepted the adjective as fraternal inheritance.

Before leaving, she went to Sami's rented studio with Bakker and a local officer. It occupied the upper floor of a former print shop in Delfshaven. The stairwell smelled of dust, coffee, and the culinary ambitions of a restaurant below. Inside, Sami had created no conservatory of secrets. There was a folding bed, two monitors, a soldering station, and a kitchen whose cuisine consisted of oats, oranges, and instant noodles.

His life had the provisional domesticity of an immigrant who had not decided whether a dwelling deserved furniture. A single photograph showed Noor and Sami as children in the amphitheater at Carthage, both squinting into the sun. Their mother stood behind them, one hand on each shoulder. Their father had taken the picture and accidentally included his own thumb.

Books occupied the only proper shelf. Sami had never been a bibliophile in the reverential sense; he dog-eared pages, laid coffee cups on literature, and wrote facetious objections in margins. A history of migration stood beside a retired professor's memoir, a musicologist's study of antiphon, and Noor's own exhibition catalogue. The catalogue called her “a laureate of industrial melancholy,” a sententious phrase Sami had underlined twice. Beside it he had written, *A laureate wins something. You won demurrage charges.*
