The catalogue had become an argument between siblings. A cineaste had called the installation an extravaganza; Sami wrote that one slow motor did not make an extravaganza. A versemonger praised its “plaintive eclogue in steel,” and Sami scanned the sentence as faulty pentameter. An emeritus dramatist compared Noor to a thespian who would not emote, while a comedienne admired her unimpassioned refusal to woo an audience. Sami's verdict ran beneath both: *Every critic wants the artist as understudy to the critic.* The mordant notes mattered because they changed beside the technical pages. There he stopped teasing and drew speaker positions.

One review described the work's esthetic lineage as preliterate ritual. Noor had taken umbrage at the lazy primitivism; Sami, more meddlesome and more exact, wrote, *She is literate. So is the calligrapher whose notation you cropped.* Across a photograph he marked the umbrageous rear of the resin housing and a supernumerary reed omitted from the gallery plan. A retired acoustics devotee had noticed that extra reed in person and likened its response to a cathedral antiphon. The review called him an archbishop of resonance. Sami crossed out the jingoism of the title but preserved the man's measured frequency.

Noor photographed the spread. These were not the frolicsome quarrels of a fretter correcting art prose for sport. The measured note corresponded to the hidden spacer. Even Sami's puerility had boundaries; when evidence appeared, the acrobat landed. She told Bakker the annotation might show how to open the work without turning conservation into an extravaganza of cutting tools.

Noor felt a twinge of fondness so violent it almost nauseated her. She put the book down.

The downstairs restaurant owner came up when the officers knocked. Mrs. Van Dijk was a retiring woman with flour on one sleeve and the querulous vigilance of a landlord who had spent years mediating between tenants and drains. Sami, she said, was quiet except when friends visited. He paid promptly, carried groceries for her uxorious husband, and once rehabilitated the restaurant freezer after a technician declared it dead.

“Any visitors yesterday?” Bakker asked.

“A woman from his company, perhaps. Very neat. She waited in the vicinity for twenty minutes but did not enter. Later, two men.”

“Could you describe them?”

“One tall, one broad. Dark apparel. They had no tools.”

Noor showed her a photograph of Harborlight staff from the demonstration. Mrs. Van Dijk refused the invitation to become certain. “Maybe this one. Maybe not. A face seen from my kitchen is not a passport.”

That restraint gave her more credibility than bravura recognition would have done. She recalled that the broad man had been snappish when Sami came downstairs. Sami said something in French. The men did not understand, but Mrs. Van Dijk had studied it at school.

“What did he say?” Noor asked.

“Something about a hanger-on. Then, *You cannot make me ashamed of being accurate.*”

Noor translated for Bakker. The first phrase was mordacious but ordinary Sami; the second was not. Shame had always been the weapon that found him. As children, Noor could make him apologize by calling him brattish, even when she was the malefactor. Their father's disappointment could embitter him for days. Harborlight might have discovered the same leverage without understanding its parentage.

Mrs. Van Dijk produced a parcel from behind the stairs. It had arrived for Sami that morning from an antiquarian emporium in Dublin. The label rendered Ireland as Hibernia, an affectation that would have delighted him. Inside was a small volume of Hibernian verse, purchased not for patriotism or philology but for one handwritten page: a radio engineer's notes on how low frequencies traveled through resin and stone. The engineer had alliterated his tests into a rough decasyllable, perhaps to remember them. Sami had marked one line in an online auction image before ordering the book.

“This is why he asked about the sculpture,” Noor said.

The page described sympathetic release: a hidden pin could be induced to move when a housing's resonant frequency was excited. No code, no confession. Merely a practical forefather of the method Sami had adapted.

Bakker photographed the page. “Would a stranger recognize its relevance?”

“A conservator might. A dilettante would call it poetic. Sami would call that disparagement of both engineering and poesy.”

“And you?”

“I would call it incomplete.”

Noor examined the room again, no longer for an object but for a sequence. Sami had received the warehouse's demurrage warning. He ordered the book after seeing its page online. He carried the London address to the demonstration and called Noor from Rotterdam. The facts did not reveal why he went to the quay instead of the station, but they made his intended journey apparent.

On a peg near the door hung a visitor badge from a philharmonic concert Noor had taken him to in Paris. He had disliked the conductor's effusive rendition and spent the interval befriending an elderly cellist who knew more about vibration in old wood. Later he confessed a predilection for musicians because they argued from what they could hear. Noor accused him of turning every avocation into engineering. He accused the artistic literati of pretending engineering was not artistry whenever an invoice arrived.

The badge brought back the supper after that concert, when their parents' friends had filled a cramped chateau restaurant in the environs of Paris. The extroverted host, a self-declared philogynist, praised every woman present until his gallantry became its own vanity; his introverted wife replied that affection required listening, not applause. A quidnunc at the next table reported their exchange as conjugal warfare. Sami, then a sloven in a borrowed jacket, called matrimony a connubial committee and misogamy its permanent opposition. Their mother rebuked his puerility. Their father, a devotee of socialism rather than matriarchy or patriarchy, said domestic power was not improved by slogans.

Noor had defended Sami with an older sister's reflex to mollycoddle him, then attacked him herself. She accused him of confusing amatory display with amorous feeling and of treating every marriage as a specimen. He answered that a family could be loving without making a cult of kinship, and that xenophilia was no cure for contempt at home. The argument sounded shameless now, but its extent clarified the final message: Sami distrusted institutions that advertised devotion while withholding care. Harborlight's memorial language would have enraged him precisely because he was not unsociable. He wanted fellowship without ownership.

Another memory attached itself, less flattering. At a cousin's wedding, an acrobat and a frolicsome children's troupe had delayed the meal; a hungry Sami threatened to shoplift pastries from the caterer. Noor called him a meddlesome whelp, and he replied lugubriously that the family treated every appetite as moral failure. A visiting comedienne made the quarrel into a joke, the bride laughed, and Noor's rage dissolved. No such comic release existed now. The recollection did not absolve her for ignoring his call, but it stopped guilt from rewriting him as either saint or malefactor.

The memory was endearing and unbearable. Noor sat on the folding bed. Grief did not remain sorrowful; it changed register without warning, now lachrymose, now dry, now almost comic. Sami had mocked the idea that siblings possessed a mystical fraternity. Brotherhood and sisterhood, he said, were words institutions used when they wanted devotion without wages. Yet he called her whenever his courage failed.

And she had not answered.

“Did your brother have enemies?” Bakker asked.

“He had arguments.”

“Serious ones?”

“All his arguments were serious while they occurred.”

She told him about Sami's Harborlight supervisor, about colleagues he admired, about his invidious habit of correcting a person's premises before acknowledging their emotion. She did not dramatize ordinary office resentment into conspiracy. Nor did she absolve herself. She played the final message into the evidence recorder and stated when she had received it, when she heard it, and why she had delayed.

“We had quarreled,” she said.

“About the device?”

“About his belief that asking forgiveness in advance was an apology.”

“Was he contrite?”

“Sami could perform contrition. Feeling it took longer.”

The inspector did not offer comfort. Noor was grateful. Comfort would have been a palinode, an invitation to retract the guilt before its facts were known.

The police searched without artistry. They photographed cables, canvassed neighbors, bagged a broken access card, and checked the waste. Noor moved among the remains of her brother's thought: a pressure diagram askew on the wall, a half-written letter of apology to a colleague, a limerick about a pompous manager. No manifesto. No confession. No grand plot adequate to his death.

On the desk lay a postcard of Noor's sculpture. Sami had written on the back: *The pulse is beneath the chorus. Nono knows the seam.*

She pocketed nothing. Bakker photographed it and gave her a copy.

“What seam?” he asked.

“There isn't one.”

The sculpture's housing was a continuous resin shell around a steel armature. She had designed it to frustrate the eye's penchant for joints. To reach the recorder with a saw would shear the shell, possibly damaging both device and calibration puck.

“Then how do you open it?”

Noor looked at the postcard. She remembered Sami tapping the curved housing, each knock returning at a different pitch. She remembered their final tiff: his insistence that the work was not a tomb, her refusal to let engineering reduce sculpture to container. Beneath the resentment, another memory surfaced. Sami had asked her to preserve a sequence of tones from the installation, not because he admired the melody but because the resin had been cast around temporary spacers that could be released by vibration.

He had built a way back in.

“Not with a blade,” she said. “With sound.”

Bakker stared at her.

“Do not look so anxious, Inspector. It is not magic.”

“That was not my concern.”

“What was?”

“That Harborlight's insurer has already scheduled a structural inspection at nine tomorrow.”

The fact entered the studio like another person.

Noor closed Sami's duffel and lifted it from the bed. Grief had not made her courageous or contrite. It had made direction possible. London lay between the insurer and the object Sami had entrusted to her, then tried to reclaim.

For the first time since the mortuary, she knew what the next hour required.

## Chapter 6: Privileged

At nine in the morning, Harborlight's headquarters applauded a death.

Not the death itself. The distinction was tangible and, to Elena Varga, insufficient. Employees had assembled beneath the atrium's gleaming flood map while Adrian Vale praised the Rotterdam team for an audacious response to the squall. On the screen behind him, green districts radiated from the closed barrier. A caption reported forty-seven casualties avoided. Sami Bensaid's name appeared only in a black band at the bottom: FIELD ENGINEER, COLLEAGUE, FRIEND.

Vale asked for silence. The silence lasted twelve seconds. Then somebody near the rear began to clap, perhaps for the rescue, perhaps because grief in an office required a cue. Applause spread along the marble axis until even those who looked ashen had joined it.

The cellist lowered her bow, but a piccolo continued above a recorded cello from the memorial film. On screen, Harborlight crews crossed a palmy airfield while storm cloud began to scud above a relief hangar. A condor wheeled over another project's mountain dam; children on bleachers waved paper flags; Vale carried a coughing whelp from a flooded kennel. The montage was harrowing by design and voluptuous in execution, imbued with a grief meant to stun dissent. It turned dearth, moldy grain, and a refugee clinic's mash into a panegyric for intervention. Elena could not decide which was worse: the coronation music or the caption promising that useful work made a colleague immortal.

Sami appeared for three seconds, explaining a pressure seal to a local mechanic. He did not smile. Communications had placed a digital shroud over the frame and reduced his words to music. The treatment would have dumbfound him, Elena thought. It also deprived police of his voice and his kinsfolk of his unedited image while seeming to devote the whole film to him. Its pervading sorrow left no room for the fact that he had challenged his employer.

Elena did not.

She stood beside Tomas Rell beneath a potted tree whose leaves had collected office dust. Rell's black jacket was gone, replaced by a settled grey suit. Without the uniform he looked less like security and more like a prosperous bureau chief, affable until a datum resisted him.

“This is inimical to an inquiry,” Elena said.

“It is a staff briefing.”

“It is a verdict with catering.”

On trestle tables, coffee stood beside pastries and little glass vessels of vanilla yogurt. Employees had been told to gather before commencing work. A cellist from the company quintet played something placid near the lifts until the applause submerged her.

Rell said, “Public confidence is a resource.”

“So is silence before facts.”

“Silence creates a void. Others fill it.”

“That is not a legal principle.”

“No. It is modernity.”

He turned away as Vale descended from the low platform. Staff formed an entourage around the founder: engineers wanting instruction, managers offering concern, communications people carrying tablets like votive objects. Vale accepted condolences without either ecstasy or false modesty. His discipline was almost sacerdotal. He could preside over institutional emotion while appearing immune to its appetite.

Elena had come from the Compact's EU liaison office with one concrete goal: contain Harborlight's liability without obstructing the police investigation. The formulation had seemed pragmatic at dawn. Here, beneath the applause, *contain* revealed its obverse. A container did not merely prevent spill. It kept pressure from being seen.

Vale reached them. “Elena. Thank you.”

“For attending your fete?”

“For coming before Brussels sends a cavalcade.”

“Brussels has already sent me.”

“Not officially.”

That was true. Officially she was deputy counsel to the Compact secretariat, a liaison without investigative authority. Unofficially her supervisor had blurted at six forty that she should stop the Dutch pilot from becoming a referendum on ratification.

“What do police have?” Vale asked.

Rell answered. “Phone, badge, clothing. They issued preservation requests to the municipality, hospital, and us. They want a joint image of the decision-support directory.”

“Give it to them.”

“The directory is live critical infrastructure.”

“Then give them a mirror.”

Elena watched the exchange. Vale's willingness was genuine as far as it went. The mirror would be selected by Harborlight, delimited by privilege, and certified under an emergency regime Harborlight had helped design.

“Police also want Sami's work devices,” she said.

Rell's expression remained placid. “Corporate devices. We are obligated to secure them.”

“One is missing.”

“The field tablet.”

“And a recorder.”

“Art equipment, according to his sister.”

He knew about Noor's call to police less than an hour after it happened. Elena felt the familiar refraction of authority around him: every lawful outlet supplied a different sliver, and Rell stood where they converged.

“How did you learn that?” she asked.

“Our insurer received notice of a stored sculpture.”

“Did you ask the insurer to inspect it?”

“The inspection was already scheduled.”

“Did you accelerate it?”

“No.”

The denial was timely, narrow, and probably veracious. Elena had spent twenty years among people who believed a flawless sentence could redeem a pernicious act.

Vale looked toward the screen, where floodwater animation crossed Rotterdam and flattened into green. “What is on the recorder?”

“Unknown,” Rell said. “Possibly proprietary telemetry.”

“Then police must preserve it.”

“Police have no jurisdiction in London. The insurer does.”

Elena said, “Insurance rights do not obviate evidential duty.”

“They facilitate it. Chain of custody begins with recovery.”

“By an interested party.”

“By a regulated custodian.”

The sophism was adept: convert conflict into qualification, then qualification into confidence. Elena had drafted enough codicils to recognize the morphology of an excuse.

“No insurer opens that sculpture without the owner's consent or British authority,” she said.

Rell's eyes shifted to her. “Under which prohibition?”

“Conversion, interference with goods, privacy, potentially obstruction.”

“The policy authorizes inspection after a casualty claim.”

“Structural inspection. Not disinterment of a recorder.”

“Machines are not buried.”

“Then stop using the word recovery.”

Vale raised one hand. “Enough. Tomas, instruct the insurer to await police liaison.”

Rell gave a slight obeisance that managed to tarnish obedience. “And if evidence disappears while jurisdictions confer?”

“Then we will endure the criticism.”

“Criticism is not the only risk.”

“I know.” Vale's baritone dropped. “Do it.”

Rell walked away. Elena watched him summon an aide before he reached the lifts.

“He believes delay is danger,” Vale said.

“Do you?”

“I have seen delay incinerate settlements.”

The allusion to his humanitarian past was not allegory. Elena had read the reports: cyclone warnings inhibited by election concerns, roads clogged, a hospital transfer ending in death. Vale's wound had become paradigm, then policy.

“Urgency does not validate every shortcut,” she said.

“No. But procedure can become an apathetic way to allocate harm.”

“You invoke procedure when it protects you.”

“As do governments.”

He led her upstairs through an access gate that recognized his face. The executive floor had none of the atrium's corporate jocularity. Doors shut without sound. A palette of pale timber and granite conveyed affluence without the vulgarity of display. Through broad windows the river lay liquid and dark beneath scudding cloud.

Vale's office contained no triumphal photographs. One wall held a relief map of the Mediterranean, another a child's drawing of a sphericity-defying earth. On a shelf stood an extant fragment of fired brick from a clinic he had helped rebuild. Elena had seen the same fragment in profiles. It functioned as emblem, relic, and argument.

The brick's display card said workers had found it after galvanism from a faulty generator stunned a mason and scorched the clinic wall. An earlier card, still visible beneath the replacement, used the vocative *O brave hands* and called the rebuilding a new cosmogony. Vale had crossed out that fustian himself. Yet he kept the relic lit as though every visitor belonged to its audience. Even restraint could become pageantry when curated long enough.

“Coffee?” he asked.

“No.”

“You look exhausted.”

“That is not remedied by your coffee.”

He gulped his own and sat. “Tell me the Compact's exposure.”

Elena opened her bureau file. “The demonstration operated under a municipal pilot agreement. Harborlight has ordinary contractual liability unless the emergency-immunity provision applies. The municipality will invoke it for the gate closure. You may invoke it for integrated recommendations made in good faith during an imminent hazard.”

“May?”

“A death on a maintenance stair is not an integrated recommendation.”

“Nobody says it is.”

“Rell wants the clause used to interdict police access to devices and systems.”

Vale's face tightened. “On what basis?”

“Operational continuity.”

“That is not what it says.”

“It says protected functions shall not be impaired by seizure, injunction, or disclosure while emergency status persists.”

“And there is a reporting obligation.”

“After stabilization.”

“The system is stable.”

“Your security director says the next forty-eight hours remain a continuation event.”

Vale stood and went to the window. Below, barges moved along the river with menial steadiness. “The weather network shows another front.”

“A front is not a magic word.”

“Nor is privilege.”

Elena almost laughed. “You have discovered restraint at an opportune hour.”

“I asked for immunity to prevent a prosecutor from shutting down rescue coordination because one supplier breached a by-law.”

“You asked for broad operational continuity. I supplied the legal code.”

“And you regret it.”

“I am concerned by its use.”

“That is lawyer for regret.”

She did not repudiate the word because it would invite him to console her. The clause had been her audacious contribution to the treaty architecture. Governments were loath to share ambulances and hospital beds if every cross-border error exposed them to ruinous litigation. Elena had argued that good-faith emergency allocation required a protected sphere. Legislators added little. Vale encouraged more. She had adjusted the language until ministries signed.

Now Rell had found the underlying power in her text: immunity from interruption could become immunity from observation.

Vale touched the brick fragment on his shelf. “In Mozambique, an inquiry seized the dispatch server after a fuel contractor was accused of poaching public stock. It took four days to restore mobility. People died because evidence had prestige and operations looked menial.”

“That does not make every seizure pernicious.”

“No. It means preservation must not arouse a second emergency.”

“You are arguing with a position I did not take.”

“I am telling you why public confidence matters. A warning system depends on response. If every alert arrives captioned by suspicion, people delay.”

“Confidence obtained by repressing a death inquiry is not confidence.”

“We are not repressing it.”

“Then direct Rell not to invoke my clause.”

Vale looked at her. The refusal formed before speech.

“I will direct him to cooperate within it.”

“That is not the same.”

“It is the responsible course.”

The difference between them was not honesty. Vale did not lie to her. He ranked harms, chose one, and treated the remainder as a regrettable substance to be contained.

Her phone signaled a message from her liaison office. Rell had filed an emergency continuity notice with Elena's supervisor at 07:14, before the staff memorial. The notice asserted privilege over “all integrated field artifacts,” including the missing tablet, recorder, calibration devices, and derivative data.

“He already invoked it,” she said.

Vale read the notice. Surprise showed as a scintilla, then vanished. “Without consulting me.”

“He did not need you. The delegated security principal may act during imminence.”

“Who drafted that?”

“I did.”

The answer mortified her because his question had been sincere.

Vale called Rell. “Suspend external enforcement of the continuity notice until counsel reviews it.”

Rell's voice came through the console. “Police have requested direct access to the live network. Suspension would be irresponsible.”

“Nobody is giving direct access.”

“Then the notice changes nothing.”

“It changes posture.”

“Our posture should deter compromise.”

“Suspend it.”

There was a fractional hiatus. “Aye.”

The line ended.

Elena closed her file. “He will comply with the letter.”

“You say that as though compliance were disobedience.”

“Under a broad clause, it can be.”

Vale's secretary entered to announce a delegation from the Dutch ministry. The officials waited in a conference room named after a delta. Elena gathered her papers.

“I need access to Sami's protected-disclosure record,” she said.

“Ask compliance.”

“They say security restricted it.”

“Then ask Tomas.”

“I am asking you.”

Vale held her gaze. “Access it.”

The authorization was oral. Elena asked him to put it in writing.

“You think I will renege?”

“I think networks remember differently from people.”

He signed a one-line instruction on her tablet. She watched the cryptographic seal appear beneath his name.

Compliance occupied a lower floor without windows. Its manager, Marit Vos, was a gangly woman whose office was crowded with sprigs of rosemary in laboratory beakers. She greeted Elena with a sullen exhaustion that suggested a night spent answering questions from every rank above her.

“We have no extant complaint from Bensaid,” Marit said.

“He told Dr. El-Amin he filed one.”

“People confuse drafts with submissions.”

“Search receipts.”

Marit opened the protected channel. Its interface was deliberately simple: a whistleblower could submit without naming a supervisor, receive a ciphered receipt, and petition for status through an external portal. The design had won an ethics award. A little bronze bust of the award stood beside Marit's monitor.

They searched Sami's employee key. Nothing.

“Anonymous channels do not index by employee,” Marit said.

“Then search device, network origin, and time.”

“That will catch scads of records.”

“Do it.”

The query returned forty-three submissions in six months. Most concerned procurement, rank discrimination, or data handling. One complained that a manager had gormandized at a company retreat and charged the feast to field safety. Another alleged cronyism in a promotion panel. Elena read none beyond what was needed to delimit the search.

She did read the safety abstracts because their device fields could identify Sami's terminal. One described a technician ordered to disrobe after nonradioactive tracing powder entered his sleeve; another recorded an inflamed extensor tendon and a bruised bronchus after a security drill became excessive. A warehouse complaint said a supervisor let chemical rinse macerate sacks of seed until moldy runoff crept beneath a partition. The complainant had written, “We sow food, not obedience.” Security marked the sentence depraved and its author a ruffian. Elena preserved the terms because the abusive characterization, not the spill, had triggered restricted handling.

A fourth record concerned a staff forum that collapsed into what its chair called an orgy of accusation. An employee had called a manager a troll; the manager answered *freak* and *whelp*. Compliance removed the insults but retained the threat to disinter private medical files. That distinction mattered. A protected channel existed to separate actionable conduct from noise, not to punish vulgarity or let a loud label pervade the record.

Sami's likely complaint originated from a service terminal in the Rotterdam control complex three weeks earlier. The record contained no text. Status: RESOLVED. Resolution authority: E. VARGA. Closure basis: DUPLICATIVE / NON-ACTIONABLE.

Elena stared at her name.

“You resolved it?” Marit asked.

“No.”

The word fell inert between them.

Marit checked the audit facet. “Your credential signed at 22:16 Central European Time.”

“I was in Zagreb.”

“Remote access is permitted.”

“I was at my mother's apartment. The network failed during a landslide. I had no access for two days.”

Marit looked bemused rather than alarmed. Institutional betrayal first appeared as a technical puzzle because terror was not yet useful.

“Could you have pre-authorized closure?”

“Never. Open the underlying submission.”

The system displayed a privilege interdict. Because the complaint concerned critical infrastructure and had been adjudged duplicative, its text had moved to a restricted crypt. Access required the original adjudicator or a security principal.

“It thinks you are the adjudicator,” Marit said.

Elena supplied her passkey. Rejected.

“Your current credential differs from the signing credential.”

“Show the certificate.”

The certificate bore her name, title, and an obsolete middle initial used in an early Compact drafting account. Its root chain led not to the secretariat but to Harborlight's liaison environment.

Marit opened the retired authority's test manifest. Its multilingual module used a jay call to test audio compression, a diphthong and a vocative to test name parsing, and a seven-sided heptagon whose diagonal formed a measured hypotenuse to test image scaling. The absurd variety had a purpose: expose corruption across media before credentials went live. Beside those fixtures sat a neural classifier tagged SURREALISM because its output once turned a face into disjointed planes. None should have had adjudicative power. The manifest's very oddity made the active certificate harder to dismiss as an ordinary service copy.

“A test root should not creep into production,” Elena said.

“Nor should a painted heptagon resolve a whistleblower complaint,” Marit replied.

“A service copy,” Elena said.

Marit shook her head. “Service copies cannot resolve concerns.”

“Apparently this one could.”

She felt nausea, cold and precise. Somebody had not merely forged her name. They had used privity between the Compact and Harborlight to embody her authority inside Harborlight's network. The fraud depended on bureaucratic intimacy: test credentials left alive, a trusted root, privileges adjusted inchmeal until a copy could act.

“Who issued the certificate?”

Marit opened the chain. The issuing service had been retired eighteen months ago. Its administrator field was void. Migration logs showed a network maintenance task authorized by security.

“Rell?” Elena asked.

“Security is a role, not a person.”

“Every role ends in a person.”

“Usually several.”

Marit looked frightened now. She tried to print the audit page. The printer remained somnolent. She exported instead, but the file flattened into a summary without the certificate chain.

“Normal control,” she said. “Restricted metadata cannot leave the network.”

“Then photograph the screen.”

“Personal devices are banned.”

“Use the incident camera.”

Marit hesitated. “That could be misconduct.”

“So could falsely resolving a protected concern.”

“Not by me.”

“No. Which is why we preserve it before somebody claims it was.”

The appeal was unfair but effective. Marit fetched an aseptic-looking evidence camera from a wall cabinet. Elena made her capture the full screen, the certificate detail, the time source, and the active user list. They hashed the images and lodged one copy in compliance's internal evidence store.

The active user list changed while they watched. A remote security session appeared, touched the complaint index, and vanished.

“They know,” Marit said.

Elena's pulse began to quaver. “Disconnect this terminal from remote administration.”

“I cannot obstruct security.”

“You can contain an incident.”

Marit pulled the network cable. The screen went dark, then resumed on battery with a red signal warning. It was a menial act, almost droll in a building devoted to networks: truth preserved by unplugging a cord.

Someone knocked. Rell stood outside the glass door.

He did not enter. “Elena. The Dutch delegation is asking for you.”

“I am occupied.”

“With privileged records.”

“Authorized by Vale.”

“Authorization does not abrogate handling controls.”

“Neither does handling control validate forged credentials.”

Marit's face went blank. Elena had spoken too early, but the words could not be recalled.

Rell opened the door. “What forged credentials?”

“Mine.”

He looked at the disconnected cable, then the evidence camera. “Reconnect the terminal.”

“No.”

“You are inhibiting a protected system.”

“I am preserving a compromised one.”

“On whose authority?”

Elena displayed Vale's signed instruction. Rell read it without touching the tablet.

“That authorizes access, not seizure.”

“Nothing has been seized.”

“A camera removed data from the system.”

“Into its own evidence store.”

“Which security administers.” His mouth almost smiled. “Reconnect it, and we can investigate.”

There was the trap made visible. Rell did not need to threaten, wheedle, or swear. The network itself was his holster.

Elena said, “Compliance will retain the terminal offline pending an external forensic examiner.”

“The continuity notice forbids impairment.”

“Vale suspended enforcement.”

“External enforcement. Internal continuity remains.”

Exact compliance, as predicted.

Rell's phone vibrated. He read, then looked at Elena with a new and unreadable keenness. “British police have placed a temporary hold on the London sculpture. Your concern is obviated.”

“Which concern?”

“That we would interfere.”

“This concern has your network address.”

“It has a role label. Do not distort technical architecture into accusation.”

“And do not simplify authority into code when a person benefits.”

Vale appeared behind him with two ministry officials. For a moment the narrow compliance corridor held every stratum of the institution: founder, security director, treaty counsel, compliance manager, and two bewildered diplomats whose badges gave them access to none of the substance.

Elena told Vale what they had found.

He examined the certificate chain on the offline screen. “Could Sami have created it?”

The question stunned her more than denial would have.

“Why would he forge my credential to squash his own concern?”

“To demonstrate the channel was unsafe. To implicate the Compact. I am not saying he did. I am asking.”

Rell said, “An internal red-team exercise is also possible.”

“Without compliance knowledge?” Marit asked.

“Tests are not useful if everyone knows.”

Vale looked at him. “Was there a test?”

“Not one I authorized.”

Again, a narrow and possibly veracious answer.

Elena copied the complaint's audit reference by hand onto her legal pad. Not its text, which remained sealed. Not the certificate images, which stayed in compliance custody. Only the immutable reference, timestamp, and root fingerprint. Three strings that would allow an independent system to summon the same record if it still existed.

Rell noticed. “That metadata is privileged.”

“Privilege belongs to the whistleblower, not the institution accused by him.”

“The complaint's substance is unknown.”

“Its disappearance is not.”

Vale ordered Marit to keep the terminal offline and requested an external examiner by noon. It was the right decision. Elena saw the cost it gave him: Rell's sullen withdrawal, the ministry officials' alarm, the certainty that rumor would pervade headquarters before lunch.

“We contain this until authentication,” Vale told her.

“We preserve it.”

“Both.”

They parted without concurrence.

At the EU liaison office, Elena sat in a borrowed room overlooking a dank courtyard. Her supervisor called from Brussels and chastised her for disabling a Harborlight terminal. She explained that she had disabled nothing. The distinction sounded feckless even to her.

Before answering his next accusation, she summoned Pieter De Smet from cyber liaison and Ana Kovač from treaty translation. Pieter arrived carrying a floppy canvas tool case whose childish appearance concealed an array of forensic keys. Ana brought the Compact in four languages, each version furred with paper flags.

“I need two things delineated,” Elena told them after ending the call. “How my obsolete certificate acquired power, and whether the continuity clause reaches the protected channel.”

Pieter was a brawny man with the cautious hands of a watchmaker. He did not touch Elena's written reference. He asked her to read the root fingerprint aloud, then decoded its segments against the liaison registry. The first radix identified a Harborlight test authority. The second pointed to a certificate batch issued during treaty-system migration. The final digits should have been random; instead they reproduced the date Elena had first logged into Harborlight's drafting environment.

The batch had been called CORONATION in the migration notes, a name Pieter found embarrassing rather than sinister. Its privilege map resembled a heptagon with Elena's old account at one point and security at another. A line between them supplied the missing hypotenuse: a temporary bridge authorized for one demonstration and never removed. Whoever used it did not need to be a cyber ruffian. They needed only to know that a palmy test environment had survived inside the live one.

“That does not happen by chance,” he said.

“Could Sami have built it?”

“If he had your original token, administrative access to a retired root, and an appetite for a cryptogram whose only triumph was closing his own report.” Pieter shrugged. “Technically possible. Humanly strange.”

“Rell proposed a red-team exercise.”

“Then there should be a manifesto of scope, even if sealed: authority, target, duration, restoration. Otherwise it is not a test. It is a bandit with stationery.”

Ana gave him a look.

“A legal metaphor,” he said.

“A fallacy wearing a holster,” Elena replied. “But useful.”

They projected the clause on a square of white wall. In English, protected functions could not be impaired while emergency status persisted. The French emphasized obstruction; the Croatian implied operational stagnation; the Dutch used a verb that could mean hinder or inhibit. None expressly placed whistleblower records inside protected operations.

“The reporting channel is oversight,” Ana said. “It exists because operations may be wrong.”

“Security will say oversight is a facet of operational integrity.”

“Then security may ensorcell anything with the word integrity.”

Ana's dry dictum made Pieter laugh. She had begun her career translating ordination records and brought to technical prose a keen distrust of abstract nouns. “A protected channel cannot be immune from inquiry into its own compromise. That would make the remedy insensible.”

Elena traced the proviso beneath the immunity grant. Every protected emergency act incurred a duty to retain contemporaneous assumptions and report material system hazards to the designated public authority.

“Hazard,” she said.

“A forged adjudicator qualifies,” Pieter said.

“If it can alter access, yes. But the report itself is sealed. We cannot infer substance from its disappearance.”

“We can infer that your credential acted.”

“And that Sami's concern was repressed.”

Ana tapped the word *hazard*. “The reporting duty is unceasing while immunity applies. It is not postponed until the platform feels placid.”

That reading startled Elena. She had treated the duty as an after-action safeguard because the Compact's procedures prescribed periodic reporting. But the substantive obligation contained no delay. If an imminent systems hazard could be shown, immunity itself generated present disclosure.

“Do not become ecstatic,” Pieter said. “A certificate anomaly is not yet danger to the public.”

“No. But it gives us a lawful tract to examine.”

They worked for an hour. Pieter explained that a certificate could be enciphered yet still malevolent in use; Ana separated privilege from secrecy; Elena tested each construction against the treaty's purpose. The exercise did not exonerate Harborlight or convict it. It prevented legal language from becoming fustian.

A ministry aide entered with a sopping coat and reported that reporters had gathered in the forecourt. One claimed Harborlight's founder had buried a firebrand engineer's complaint. Another called Sami a quisling who had tried to depopulate Rotterdam by sabotaging its barrier. The polar stories required no evidence because each enthralled an existing audience.

“Issue no comment,” Elena said.

“That lets the stories stagnate.”

“A false rebuttal makes them indelible.”

“What may I say?”

Elena dictated: a protected record was under independent review; no conclusion had been reached about its author, substance, or closure; evidence preservation was commencing under Dutch and Compact procedures. Ana removed *independent* because no examiner had yet been appointed. Pieter removed *evidence* because the status of the record had not been adjudicated. What remained was thin but true.

She sent the final language to police liaison, the municipal authority, and Harborlight at the same minute. The simultaneous service mattered. No recipient could later claim that another had enjoyed a privileged interval in which to alter the record. She requested acknowledgment by named officers rather than generic mailboxes, ordered the liaison copy retained under a new hash, and wrote the time by hand in her file. These were small protections, precarious beside a live network, but law often began as a refusal to let sequence become folklore. When all three receipts arrived, she printed them and sealed them with the audit reference.

The Harborlight receipt came from Rell himself. It acknowledged preservation but reserved every claim of privilege and operational necessity. Elena read the sentence twice. He had not resisted the order; he had built a future argument around obedience. She added his message to the sealed packet, noting that the reservation arrived after Vale's suspension instruction and before any examiner was named. If the record changed, sequence would matter. If it did not, the precautions would look excessive. She had learned to prefer the embarrassment of visible caution to the prestige of being quietly right too late.

“This is why people think lawyers addle language,” the aide said.

“We are removing claims,” Elena replied. “Not meaning.”

When he left, Pieter packed his keys. “If security used the certificate once, assume it can again. Change your current credential.”

“That will not revoke the service copy.”

“No. But it will signal any attempted use. A trip wire.”

“Can you install it lawfully?”

“I can petition. Lawful things take longer.”

“Today they must be tenacious.”

He saluted with two fingers and went to file the request.

Ana remained. “You wrote this clause.”

It was not a question.

“Yes.”

“Did you imagine this episode?”

“I imagined a prosecutor seizing a dispatch network because of bribery, leaving ambulances without routes. I imagined a government using litigation to renege on aid. I did not imagine a private security office invoking rescue against inspection of itself.”

“That is not lack of imagination,” Ana said. “It is confidence in the groom because you feared the unruly horse.”

The folk image would have seemed droll from anyone else. From Ana it carried no jocularity. Elena had disciplined state power and left its private delegate holding the reins.

“The flaw may be irremediable,” she said.

“No. The clause contains its own reporting duty.” Ana gathered the language versions. “You gave yourself a way back, whether you recognized it or not.”

Elena looked again at *hazard*. A route was not a victory. It might narrow to nothing under adjudication. But it was more concrete than regret.

“Your mandate is ratification readiness,” he said. “Not a private criminal inquiry.”

“My credential closed a protected report.”

“Then adjust the credential.”

“It was forged.”

“Allegedly. Do not let one cryptic log eclipse the Compact.”

There it was again: aggregate benefit deployed against a concrete contradiction. Elena looked down at the audit reference. She had believed good procedure could domesticate bad power. Now her procedure had been made to speak in her absence.

She opened an encrypted message service outside both institutional networks. Mira El-Amin's witness contact appeared in the police liaison packet. Elena typed, deleted, and began again.

*Dr. El-Amin. Sami filed a protected concern. The system marks it resolved by my credential, but I did not receive or resolve it. I have an audit reference, not the complaint. Harborlight security knows it has been found. This communication is off record until we establish lawful disclosure.*

She attached nothing. She copied the reference into a ciphered note and sealed the original pad in her office safe.

Before sending, she considered the obligation she owed her office, the treaty, Vale, police, and the dead man whose substance she had never read. Privilege had once seemed a clean shelter where candid advice could occur. Now it resembled the atrium applause: a collective act whose author could not be located afterward.

Elena pressed send.

Across the courtyard, rain began to stipple the paving stones. The message showed delivered, then read.

For the first time that morning, an action taken under her name was hers.

## Chapter 7: The Ordinary House

Mira's mother had changed the locks and forgotten to tell her.

At half past seven on Day Five, Mira stood on the narrow step of the Walthamstow terrace with her overnight bag sopping against one leg and tried three keys in a door that rejected them all. Behind the frosted glass, a familiar shape waddled into view.

“Who is it?” her mother called.

“A burglar with keys.”

“Mira?”

Bolts moved. The door opened on Samira El-Amin in a peach dressing gown, her grey hair askew and her expression already peevish.

“You did not say you were coming.”

“I sent two messages.”

“Messages are not saying. They are homework for the recipient.”

The distinction was maternal and unanswerable. Mira stepped inside.

The ordinary house had survived her absences by becoming more itself. Shoes accumulated beneath the radiator. A canvas shopping trolley leaned beside an umbrella stand. The hallway smelled of coffee, furniture polish, and cumin from last night's cooking. On the wall, family photographs had multiplied around the cheap gilt mirror until kinship crowded out reflection.

Samira touched Mira's wet sleeve. “You have no proper coat.”

“I own several.”

“Then why do you arrive dressed as a forager?”

“I did not forage the rain.”

“Take it off. You will chafe.”

Mira surrendered the coat and shoes. In the kitchen, a pan of oatmeal thickened on the hob beside a skillet of tomatoes and eggs. Her mother believed breakfast should furnish a person against catastrophe. A morsel was never enough; appetite implied need, and need was answered by grub.

“Sit,” Samira said.

“I have to meet someone at a warehouse.”

“At nine.”

“How do you know?”

“Your message.”

Mira sat.

On the radio, an announcer discussed the Rotterdam death with the false animation of morning broadcast. Harborlight, she said, faced questions about an engineer's fatal fall and a disputed gate closure. A panel would follow. The word panel made inquiry sound like auditorium entertainment.

Samira turned it off. “Was he your friend?”

“No.”

“You say that quickly.”

“I met him once.”

“And now his sister is coming here.”

“To the warehouse.”

“London is here when you are in Rotterdam.”

Mira ate. The oatmeal had cinnamon and too much honey. Her mother's culinary method had always been to cosset a basic ingredient until it confessed sweetness.

“You look hungry,” Samira said.

“I am eating.”

“That is observable. Hunger is different.”

The phrase had Layla's cadence, though Samira would have denied borrowing anything from her older sister. Layla collected arguments; Samira collected people who needed feeding. Between them, Mira had learned that affection could be both analysis and assault.

“I slept on the train,” Mira said.

“You leaned against a window with your mouth open. That is not sleep. I saw a photograph.”

Mira stopped. “What photograph?”

Her mother showed her a news site. The image captured Mira arriving at St Pancras, head tilted, eyes shut, the collar of her coat muffle-high around her face. The caption called her “the disgraced model critic at the center of the Harborlight tragedy.”

“Libel,” Samira said.

“Only if false and damaging.”

“Disgraced is both.”

“It is opinion.”

“A canard can be opinion.”

“Where did you learn *canard*?”

“Your aunt.”

“Of course.”

Samira replenished Mira's coffee. “The article says patients were sent away by district.”

“Three attempted diversions. Staff overrode them.”

“Like Alexandria.”

The spoon struck Mira's cup. A tiny phonic accident, metal against ceramic, but it seemed to resound through the kitchen.

“Not the same,” she said.

“No two tragedies are the same. That is why people can repeat them and say they have learned.”

“I have to go.”

“You have ten minutes.”

Mira's irritation dilated into anger because her mother had earned the right to ask. “What do you want me to say?”

“Something literal.”

“The Rotterdam module used projected population to deprioritize current care. In Alexandria, the model used available beds and travel times.”

“And the travel time was inaccurate.”

“Yes.”

“For Youssef's quarter.”

“Yes.”

“You never say his name unless somebody else says it first.”

The house seemed to lean around them, every familiar object becoming audience. A psalm embroidered by Mira's grandmother hung above the sink. Youssef's photograph stood on the dresser in the adjoining room, much-loved enough to be dusted daily.

“I am saying it now,” Mira said. “Youssef.”

“That is not an answer.”

“There is no answer you will like.”

“Do not be arrogant. I am not grading you.”

Mira felt bile rise. Fatigue made every correction feel like a grudge preserved for its own sake. “You think I don't grieve him because I don't perform it correctly.”

“I think you turn grief into a site you can leave.”

The sentence landed with the clean force of a dart.

Mira stood and took her cup to the sink. “Noor's brother is dead. There is evidence in a sculpture that Harborlight's insurer may seize. This morning is not about Youssef.”

“That is what I said. London is here when Rotterdam needs you. Alexandria is elsewhere when London needs you. You are always useful at a distance.”

Mira turned. Her mother did not look wrathful. She looked fretful and old, one hand palsied slightly around the edge of the table. Mira had noticed the tremor at Christmas and accepted Samira's explanation that it came from coffee. Now the cup before her was untouched.

“How long?” Mira asked.

Samira drew her hand into her sleeve. “How long what?”

“The tremor.”

“Do not diagnose me to dodge the conversation.”

“I am asking.”

“And I am going to the clinic next week.”

“Which clinic?”

“My clinic.”

“Who is taking you?”

“I can jog there.”

“You do not jog.”

“Then I will walk with uncommon poise.”

The jocose answer failed to hide fear. Mira wrote the appointment time in her phone and told her mother she would come. Samira scoffed.

“You will be in The Hague or the Antarctic.”

“I will come.”

“Do not adore promises. Keep them.”

At the door, Samira handed her a carton of food. “For the dead man's sister.”

“Her name is Noor.”

“Then for Noor.”

Inside were spinach pastries, dates, two apples, and a jar of coffee Mira's mother considered drinkable. The offering was not reconciliation. It was viand, which in Samira's moral order came first.

“Change the lock back,” Mira said.

“Learn to knock.”

They kissed without resolving the feud.

Mira paused in the front room to retrieve a charger she kept in the desk. The furnishings had altered by accretion rather than design. Her father's reading chair remained beside the greenhouse window though he had been dead twelve years; a new duplex socket climbed the skirting; crocheted covers protected the arms from visitors who no longer came. On the mantel, a plaster cast of Youssef's hand stood beside a cheap figurine of a ballerina. He had made the cast at seventeen in a school art room and given it to Samira as a comic tribute to “the family surgeon.” He became an architect instead.

The desk drawer held the neighborhood association archive because Samira had become its unwilling custodian. Mira found a sopped programme from the first street festival, when newly arrived immigrants and older emigrants from half a dozen countries had argued over whether homesick songs belonged before or after the raffle. Her father, a jazz buff with no musical authority, chose to adlib an epic welcome. Aunt Layla supplied a sonnet; Youssef turned its final stanza into an epigram about rain. Samira, then peachy with wrath, told them that needy families required dry coats, not poetics. She also refused the donor table's attempt to divide the street into castes of giver and recipient.

An older school atlas lay beneath it. One caption used the dated plural “eskimos.” Samira had struck it through years ago and written *Inuit where Inuit is meant; ask people their own name.* Mira remembered the argument that followed when a teacher called the correction meddlesome. Her mother did not emote in public, but injustice could enrage her more reliably than insult. She treated bad language as tinder because it taught a child which people could be made scenery.

Family photographs complicated the archive's tidy chronology. In one, her father wore the garment of a fop and attempted to woo Samira beside an idyllic painted fountain. In another, Youssef played mime behind a cousin flirting with a park ranger. A school pageant cast him as a patriot with a cardboard crown; another programme called him the mentor of younger astronomers. He had mocked the peerage implied by the title and treasured it anyway. Mira felt the old jealousy of how easily he gathered affection, followed by hatred of herself for converting love into rivalry.

Samira saw the papers in her hands. “Your dear cousin abhors a solemn photograph,” she said.

“He did.”

“And your father immigrated with one suit, then dressed as though a novel prince had lost his utopia.”

Mira touched the photograph rather than fondle the memory into innocence. Her parents' marital life had contained amour and fatigue, quarrels about money, long intervals of bliss, and no blissful immunity from regret. That was dearer and less consoling than the family epic she carried abroad.

Mira had always detested the hand. Not the object, she told herself, but its sentimentality. In truth its open palm seemed to ask for an account.

Beside it lay a gallery card for Noor's London show. Samira had circled the date.

“You were going?” Mira asked.

Her mother came to the doorway. “Aunt Layla sent it. She says the sculptor is an emigrant from Tangier and the piece concerns water.”

“Noor was born there. She lives in Paris.”

“That is what emigrant means from one vantage. Immigrant from another.”

“Layla has been teaching you philology.”

“Your aunt likes people to know she is a philologist. I humor her.”

The card showed *Low Country Antiphon* installed in a white gallery: grey housing, black reeds, an audience blurred into casts of motion. The critic called the work an elegy for places made unsafe by abstraction. Another praised its “soulful industrial prosody,” the sort of phrase Mira would normally loathe.

“It was postponed,” she said.

“Why?”

“Freight damage.”

“And her brother put something inside it?”

Mira stared. “How do you know?”

“The morning news. You should listen before you erupt at it.”

Samira lifted the card. “When you were little, you hid my gold bracelet inside the upright piano.”

“I was six.”

“You said music would guard it.”

“I was an idiot.”

“You were jealous because I wore it to your cousin's nuptial party and would not let you play with it. Your cousin said you had the choler of a small king.”

“Which cousin?”

“Youssef.”

The name returned without warning, not accusation now but domestic fact. Mira remembered the party: women adjusting wigs in the hall mirror, men arguing over jazz versus an old wedding hymn, children stealing sugared almonds. Youssef had found her beneath the piano, guilty and queasy, and helped Rake the bracelet out with a wire coat hanger. He kept her secret until adulthood, when he retold it whenever she became too confident in her immunity to irrational acts.

“He was fond of you,” Samira said.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Mira closed the desk drawer harder than necessary. “Must every memory be cross-examination?”

“No. Some are curative.”

“That is not how memory works.”

“It is how houses work. They keep the version you left behind.”

Mira looked around the homely room. She had treated it as a mirage of continuity, a place where her mother and dead cousin waited unchanged while she pursued each urgent quest. But Samira's hand had begun to tremble. Youssef's plaster cast had acquired a chip at the wrist. Even the photograph glass was fading to a sultry yellow.

“I will come to the clinic,” she said.

“We shall see.”

The answer discouraged hope without refusing it. Samira touched Mira's cheek, a doting gesture she underplayed by immediately straightening her collar.

“Go. Do not make the other sister wait.”

On the Underground, Mira read about Noor's work. She did not do this to become an art fancier. She needed to understand what might be destroyed. Noor had trained in musicology before sculpture, studied the timbre of industrial spaces, and rejected the renown attached to art-world novelty. In one interview she railed against curators who treated every immigrant artist as a ventriloquist for homeland grief. In another she described her brother as a “much-loved goof with a phobia of untested assumptions.”

The sentence saddened Mira because it returned Sami's voice more accurately than the eulogistic captions.

The catalogue showed earlier works: a canvas pierced by radio wire; an ode transmitted through a lift shaft identified in the quoted 1962 survey as “derelict,” meaning abandoned; a five-part canto built from harbor sirens; a sculpted carton that slowly swelled with humidity until printed promises became illegible. The pieces did not enchant machines into speech. They used ordinary materials to expose what rooms, institutions, and listeners suppressed.

One work adapted an epode, the answering movement of an ancient choral form, to the butt of a demolished stair. A critic called the juxtaposition mere virtu; Noor replied that virtu without structural knowledge would bring the ceiling down. Another accused her of trying to flirt with engineering while scorning engineers. Her answer was material rather than rhetorical: load readings printed beside every crack. Mira understood why Sami had trusted her with a diagnostic instrument. Noor made claims that objects could resist.

One review accused Noor of arrogance, another of being too literal, a third of harboring malice toward the gallery class. She answered none. Her silence had been interpreted as uptight, playful, soulful, wroth, blissful, and shy according to the critic's prepossession. Mira recognized the violence of that projection. An undemonstrative woman became whatever feeling an audience required.

At King's Cross, a school troupe performed beneath the departure board. One child in a paper crown missed his cue; another adlibbed until the chorus found him. Their teacher, acting as composer, designer, and harried stagehand, restored order with a glance. The performance made Mira think of Noor's hidden diagnostic track. A public melody could contain a second system of signals audible only to those who knew the cast.

Her phone vibrated with a message from Noor: *Warehouse says insurer brought cutting tools.*

Mira began to run.

The freight warehouse stood in a converted tram depot near Tottenham Hale, its brick flank crossed by old girders and new security cameras. A tractor unit idled beside the loading bay. Pallets of gallery equipment occupied the forecourt beneath plastic sheeting, while shoppers waded through puddles toward a retail park beyond.

Noor waited at the gate with Inspector Bakker on video and a British constable in person. She wore black raiment that had been slept in and held herself with the vocal stillness of someone containing rage. Beside her stood a conservator named Judith Reeve, small, nimble, and wrapped in a shaggy coat.

“Dr. El-Amin,” Noor said.

“Mira.”

“I know.”

Mira offered the food carton. Noor looked at it as though it might be a lure.

“My mother sent breakfast.”

“Does she feed evidence?”

“Only people.”

Noor accepted it. “Thank her.”

The warehouse manager, Colin Pash, emerged with two insurer representatives and a docket. He was jaunty in the manner of a man who believed jocularity could smother conflict.

“Quite the troupe,” he said. “Police, scientist, artist, conservation. We only need a bard.”

Noor did not smile. “Open the bay.”

Pash's expression soured. “There is a procedure. Van de Meer filed the original inspection request, so their assessor observes.”

The assessor, a designer-suited woman named Helen Saye, said the insurer did not claim ownership. It sought only to verify whether damage during transit had rendered the sculpture unsafe.

“Unsafe for whom?” Noor asked.

“Handlers and audience. The work weighs eight hundred kilos and is leaning five degrees outside its declared tolerance.”

“It was designed with that crest.”

“The packing specification says two degrees.”

“The packing specification is wrong.”

Saye glanced at her tablet. “Submitted by the sculptor.”

“Submitted by a gallery intern who copied an early cartoon.”

The dispute had the shape of farce but material consequence. If the housing leaned because its steel axle had shifted, moving it could rupture the resin. If the declared tolerance was simply inaccurate, the insurer's inspection became a pretext with legal force.

Judith asked to see the crate before anyone opened it. Pash led them into a bay smelling of damp timber, diesel, and dregs of machine oil. Noor's sculpture occupied a shipping frame beneath opaque membrane wrap. A mother-of-pearl sheen showed where the plastic touched resin.

Mira had seen photographs: a crescent housing suspended above a field of thin metal reeds. In person it was neither crescent nor instrument. Its mass lured the eye toward the floor while the reeds suggested upward motion. The work seemed caught between swell and collapse.

Noor walked around it without touching. Her attention moved by sound even in silence: footfall on concrete, forklift throb beyond the wall, rain pop against roof lights. She tapped the shipping frame. The answering note was dull.

“The armature moved,” Saye said.

“The crate absorbed humidity,” Noor replied.

“You cannot infer that by tapping.”

“You cannot infer movement from a photograph.”

Their enmity was professional, not personal, which made it more exact.

Judith cut the outer wrap with shears. The resin housing emerged, smoke-grey and mottled, its surface holding scraps of musical notation, tide maps, and calligrapher's strokes beneath translucent layers. A rail of narrow reeds curved beneath it like a frozen chorus.

A loose fold of wrap caught Noor's sleeve. She did not fret over the snag; she cut the plastic away from her garment and asked Judith to retain it for the insurer. Pash made a joke about artists' wrath. Noor told him to freeze traffic at the adjoining bay before a forklift vibration crossed the floor. The appointment of a safety boundary altered the process at once: engines stopped, doors shut, and the sculpture's faint responses emerged from the auditorium-sized depot.

At the rear, a shallow impact scar had obliterated part of the finish.

Noor's face changed.

“That was not there.”

Pash consulted the intake photographs. “It was.”

“The photograph shows a reflection.”

Saye enlarged it. The mark existed on arrival, though less pronounced. Transit vibration had widened it.

“We need to inspect the internal girder,” she said.

“No cutting,” Noor replied.

“Ultrasound first.” Judith opened her case. “Then borescope through an existing aperture if necessary.”

“There is no aperture.”

“Every hollow casting has one.”

“This is not hollow.”

Mira heard the dodge. “The recorder occupies a cavity.”

Noor looked at her with ire. “A cavity is not an opening.”

“How do we reach it?”

“We release the temporary spacers.”

“With sound.”

Saye gave a faint sneer. “The policy excludes experimental extraction.”

Noor rounded on her. “Conservation is not an insurer's synonym for timidity.”

Judith intervened. “Nobody performs anything until I map the internal stress. If the shell is unsound, resonant vibration may extend the fracture.”

For two hours, action slowed into measurement. Judith moved an ultrasonic probe across the housing while Mira logged coordinates. Noor corrected the early design cartoon against the as-built form. Pash kept warehouse traffic clear, grumbling whenever a forklift route was ousted. Saye photographed each step for subrogation, the insurer's right to pursue whichever carrier had caused damage.

The probe revealed a steel armature, four resin spacers, the recorder, and a puck-shaped object nested near the lower axle. The impact scar did not reach them. It did, however, make the original release frequency unsafe.

“Then we cut,” Saye said.

“No,” Noor said.

Saye invoked the insurer's right of subrogation against the carrier: after paying a loss, Van de Meer could assume Noor's claim. Noor replied that subrogation might transfer a remedy; it did not transfer authorship or permit destructive handling. She was the designer and composer of the work, and Judith, not an insurer's cartoon of the internal frame, would govern conservation.

“Your brother's device may concern a criminal inquiry.”

“Do not use him to debase the work.”

“I am trying to expose the evidence.”

“You are trying to expose your company to the least liability.”

Mira watched them seethe across the resin shell. Noor's custody had become indistinguishable from control; Saye's concern for evidence from concern for contract. Mira recognized the pattern because she had practiced it with data. Preserve the object, preserve the model, preserve the possibility of being right, while time accumulated around living need.

“What did Sami design?” she asked.

Noor turned on her. “I designed it.”

“The release.”

Silence.

“He suggested four temporary spacers,” Noor said. “They hold the inner cradle while the shell cures. Each has a spring tongue. At the correct frequency, the tongues retract in sequence and the cradle slides to the maintenance quarter.”

“Like tumblers.”

“Not locks. Harmonic thresholds.”

“And the composition contains the sequence?”

Noor looked toward the reeds. “Perhaps.”

“You told Bakker you knew the seam.”

“There is no seam.”

“Sami's postcard says otherwise.”

Grief moved across Noor's face like weather. “Sami used *seam* for any place an object admitted it was made. He abhorred perfect surfaces.”

“Where does this one admit it?”

Noor struck the first reed with her fingertip. A low note sounded, reedy at its edge. She struck the next. Its pitch was higher by nearly an octave. The reeds formed no piano scale but a spatial melody heard by walking around the work. In gallery installation, microphones caught each visitor's movement and returned delayed tones from another quarter, making audience and object appear to answer one another.

“The piece is called *Low Country Antiphon*,” Mira said.

“Yes.”

“Call and response.”

“Do not become poetic.”

“I am being literal.”

Noor's mouth twitched despite herself. “That is worse.”

They found the composition files on a storage drive in the crate. Noor opened a session labeled FINAL, then another labeled FINAL-2, then one called NO REALLY FINAL. Sami had added a hidden track beneath the public mix. Its waveform looked almost flat.

“Diagnostic pulse,” Mira said.

“Maybe.”

Noor routed it through a portable speaker. Nothing audible emerged. Judith's vibration meter registered a pattern below ordinary hearing, four pulses separated by irregular pauses.

“Those pauses are the spacer positions,” Noor said.

“Can you transpose the sequence away from the damaged frequency?” Judith asked.

Noor frowned. “The tongues respond to pitch, not melody. Change the pitch and they stay fettered.”

“Could we damp the fracture locally?”

They built a temporary brace around the scar using foam, canvas straps, and a curved plate from the shipping frame. Judith calculated tolerances. Noor adjusted speaker placement by ear. Mira watched expertise cross boundaries no model would have assigned: the conservator understood stress, the artist understood resonance, the epidemiologist understood neither enough to lead.

Her urge was to seize the process because evidence might vanish. Instead she asked, “What do you need?”

Noor looked surprised. “Silence.”

Mira sent everyone unnecessary out of the bay. Pash mutinied briefly over warehouse operations until the constable gave him a thirty-minute safety closure. Saye remained as observer but surrendered her phone to prevent its alerts from entering the sound field.

Noor placed four contact speakers against the housing. She did not perform like a composer at a concert. She crouched on the concrete in a dusty coat, checking cables, adjusting a brace, asking Judith for readings. Her artistry resided in attention rather than pageant.

Pash peered through the office glass like a magpie denied a bright object. Saye's face had become a specter of professional calm. Neither could cavort through the bay or turn the extraction into spectacle; the court hold required them to observe. Mira felt no bliss in excluding them, only relief that Noor's expertise had displaced their arrogance.

“Ready,” Judith said.

Noor played the first pulse.

It entered the sculpture below hearing, visible only as a tremor in a cup of coffee somebody had abandoned on the floor. The resin throbbed. A faint click came from within.

“One,” Noor said.

The second pulse produced no response.

She stopped, changed the angle of one speaker by a finger's width, and tried again. The click came sharper.

“Two.”

At the third, the damaged shell gave a tiny groan. Judith raised her hand. Noor cut the signal.

The fracture had extended less than a millimeter. They added a second brace. Time moved. At 12:17 Bakker warned that Harborlight counsel was seeking a court order to freeze Sami's property. At 12:24 Saye received a message and refused to disclose it. At 12:31 the constable said their voluntary hold might be superseded within the hour.

“Then hurry,” Mira said.

Noor's head snapped around. “This is why I did not trust you.”

“Because time exists?”

“Because when you are frightened, everything else becomes dregs.”

The charge was just enough to hurt. Mira saw her mother at the kitchen table, hiding the tremor in her sleeve. She saw Youssef's ambulance as a point moving through a model while a dispatcher warned that the road was blocked.

“You are right,” she said.

Noor seemed almost disappointed by the absence of feud.

“Tell us when it is safe,” Mira said.

They reinforced the shell and resumed. The third tongue released. The fourth required a harmonic Noor had buried beneath a fragment of ragtime, a playful revolt against the work's otherwise austere score. Sami had complained that it made the sculpture sound like a haunted musicale. Noor kept it from spite.

Now the pulse beneath that jocular refrain opened the last spacer.

The inner cradle lurched six centimeters. Everyone froze.

No fracture spread. Judith inserted wedges and drew the cradle out inchmeal. A black recorder appeared first, dented grille packed with resin dust. Behind it lay a calibration puck in an antistatic sleeve.

Noor touched neither.

The constable photographed the position. Judith lifted each object with nitrile gloves and placed it on clean foil. Saye recorded serial numbers. Noor signed as owner and transferring custodian; the constable signed for temporary police custody; Judith signed for extraction; Mira signed only as witness.

Custody became a chorus of names rather than one person's possession.

While the constable called Bakker to confirm seal numbers, Noor kept vigil beside the foil. She looked frigid despite the warm bay, arms locked across her chest, gaze fixed on the dented recorder.

“You can sit,” Mira said.

“I am not tired.”

“That is likely untrue.”

“You diagnose people whenever silence becomes uncomfortable?”

“Only when they sway.”

Noor sat on the edge of a pallet. The anger had gone out of her posture, leaving something nearer guilt but not available for inspection.

“Sami thought objects were lovable because they failed honestly,” she said. “A machine clicked, overheated, lost time. People called that character. When people failed, he wanted a technical cause.”

“Did he?”

“It was easier than remorse.”

Mira felt a twinge of recognition. “Models are good at making sequence visible. They are poor at deciding what sequence means.”

“And yet you let them.”

“Sometimes.”

The answer drew no outrage. Noor rubbed resin dust from one thumb. “He would have enjoyed this. Police around a sculpture, an insurer sulking, you trying not to become the grouch in charge.”

“I was not aware I had succeeded.”

“You have not.”

For an instant the exchange approached humor. Neither woman trusted it enough to laugh.

The constable returned with confirmation that the seals would travel under escort to a secure evidence room. Noor demanded the route, names, and access conditions. Mira expected the questions to sound possessive. Instead they sounded precise. Noor was not relinquishing concern with the object; she was learning what shared custody required.

When she signed the final receipt, her hand shook once. She covered it by closing the pen.

The recorder's battery was dead. Its removable card contained the audible composition and no secret message. Noor's disappointment showed as a blush of anger.

“He said the pulse was beneath the chorus,” she said.

“The diagnostic channel,” Mira replied.

Judith connected the recorder through an isolated reader. A second storage partition appeared, encrypted but intact. Its metadata showed brief captures from pressure pucks, controller handshakes, and machine time codes. No exposition, no confession, no voice naming a perpetrator. Telemetry.

Noor listened to the raw channel through headphones. Mira heard only what escaped the ear cups: faint pops, a hiss, an irregular octave of machine sound.

“There,” Noor said.

“What?”

She replayed a segment. “A diagnostic pulse beneath the composition. It is not part of my score.”

On screen, the pulse preceded a recorded controller event by eleven minutes, but the time bases were unauthenticated. It might prove everything or nothing. The puck could be inaccurate. The firmware could have drifted. Extraction could have altered neither file nor time, but they needed somebody independent to establish that.

Mira felt the old hunger for a clean result and refused it.

“We need a metrology lab,” she said.

Noor removed the headphones. “We need one that will let me remain present.”

“Police custody will impose conditions.”

“Then police can explain them to me, not through you.”

The rancor had not vanished. It had become workable.

Outside, a court courier arrived with Harborlight's freeze application. The constable accepted service but noted that the devices were already in police custody under the voluntary preservation agreement. Saye's phone began to ring in the property tray. Nobody answered it.

Noor closed the sculpture's cradle. The scar remained visible beneath its brace, a wound conservation could stabilize but not pretend away.

“Sami hated flawless surfaces,” she said.

Mira thought of the zero residuals in Harborlight's Rotterdam graph. “So do I.”

Noor gave her a guarded look. It was not liking, much less affection. It was recognition of a shared phobia: an object that concealed how it had been made.

Mira's phone showed three missed calls from her mother and one encrypted message from Elena Varga. Noor saw the name.

“The lawyer?”

“Compact counsel. She says Sami's protected complaint was closed using her credentials without her knowledge.”

“Do you believe her?”

“I believe the claim can be tested.”

Noor almost sneered, then did not. “That is the closest you come to trust?”

“At present.”

They carried the sealed devices toward the loading-bay office while rain drummed a new refrain on the roof. The recorder had survived resin, freight, grief, and three competing claims of ownership. It had not delivered Sami back to them or explained his death. It had given them machine telemetry whose meaning depended on lawful access and patient measurement.

For evidence, Mira thought, that was not a failure. It was simply the next obligation.

Before leaving, she requested a duplicate seal log for Elena and the Dutch investigators, ensuring that the legal argument in The Hague would begin from the same witnessed transfer rather than competing institutional accounts.

## Chapter 8: Narrow Construction

The chambers occupied a house too narrow for its own staircase.

Elena climbed sideways beneath a skein of electrical cable while rainwater from her sopping coat marked each tread. Through a window on the landing she could see the Peace Palace beyond bare aspen trees, its tower radiant in a brief interval of sun. The proximity was a professional vanity. No international court had summoned them. They were four lawyers, two investigators, an artist, and a model auditor attempting to decide whether listening to a dead man's recorder would itself be unlawful.

An apologetic tinker had braced the banister that morning but left the garish carpet exposed, piebald with plaster and damp. A leak began to gush through the ceiling rose whenever wind drove rain beneath the tiles. The cable hung like a pallium over the landing, ceremonial in shape and dangerous in fact. Elena had no spunk to spare for the torturous ascent. The building's defects were within any tenant's ken; nobody could call them extraterrestrial merely because repair crossed a lease boundary.

At the top, a bailiff in shirtsleeves took phones into numbered pouches. He was not a court officer but the chambers' intern, elevated for the morning because every solicitor present distrusted every device.

“No frisk?” Noor asked.

The intern faintly blushed. “Please do not joke.”

“I was not.”

Mira touched Noor's elbow before the exchange could growl into dispute. The gesture was brief and apparently effective. Elena noticed because she had expected alliance to be slower.

The conference room had a floral carpet, a mottled ceiling, and a table built for six. Ten people compressed around it. Advocate Saskia Holt, an adept Dutch barrister with an English mother, chaired from beneath a bookcase teeming with treaty commentaries. Beside her sat Yusuf Rahman, British evidence counsel; Inspector Bakker; a Dutch prosecutor named De Wilde; and Ana Kovač from treaty translation. Elena took the chair nearest the door.

Holt opened without courtesy. “We have three polar questions. May police access the recorder? May experts decrypt and interpret its telemetry? May any result cross from criminal inquiry into Compact reporting or civil litigation? A yes to one does not answer the others.”

De Wilde added a fourth question: whether any interference with the reporting channel had been premeditated. A premeditated closure could support obstruction; an unpremeditated credential error might be negligent yet still peccable under systems law. They could not premeditate a suspect into existence merely because the result looked designed. Intent required evidence of planning, not a reprise of public anger in legal vocabulary.

Noor said, “It is my recorder.”

“Possibly.”

“I bought it.”

“Your brother modified it. Harborlight alleges the diagnostic board and telemetry are corporate property.”

“They allege the weather is corporate property when it passes through their sensor.”

Holt did not retort. “Ownership is not dispositive. The device may contain personal communications, trade secrets, critical-infrastructure data, and evidence of a felony or misdemeanor. Each legal stratum imposes a different obligation.”

“Sami is dead,” Noor said. “His privacy cannot be a bait to keep his killers safe.”

“We do not know that he was killed,” Bakker replied.

Noor's jaw set.
