Elena watched the room divide before argument had properly begun. Police feared prejudgment. Noor feared confiscation. Mira feared corrupted data. Harborlight's absent counsel, embodied by three threatening letters on the table, feared disclosure. Elena feared her own hand in the statute none of them yet understood.

Holt turned to Rahman. “English custody?”

“The Metropolitan Police hold the recorder and puck under a voluntary preservation agreement pending Dutch mutual assistance. They have not searched the encrypted partition. Van de Meer Assurance sought an emergency injunction in Chancery last night, claiming spoliation risk and contractual inspection rights. The judge preserved the objects but declined to adjudicate access without the Dutch prosecutor.”

“Harborlight?”

“Filed this morning to join as an interested party. They seek a ban on examination outside an accredited critical-systems lab under nondisclosure.”

“Reasonable on its face,” Holt said.

“And ruinous in effect,” Mira replied. “Their accredited labs use Harborlight firmware and network validation. Connecting the recorder could trigger synchronization.”

“Can you evidence that?”

“The hospital triage module attempted three external synchronizations while its log was copied. That system is not this recorder, but it demonstrates the hazard.”

“Inference, not evidence.”

“Yes.”

Holt seemed to admire the concession. “What examination do you propose?”

Mira described a write-blocked image, hash verification, firmware isolation, environmental control, and separate authentication of the puck's clock. Technical language remained actionable because every term changed who could touch what. She did not boast that the method was flawless. No method was.

Noor added conditions: she would retain visual custody, the sculpture extraction log would accompany the devices, and no audible channel would be published without her consent.

“Visual custody is not a juridical category,” De Wilde said.

“Then legalize your vocabulary,” Noor replied.

“We cannot legislate at this table.”

“You legislate ownership every time you say my presence is trivial.”

Elena intervened. “Shared observation can be written as a handling proviso. It need not grant Ms. Bensaid control over forensic decisions.”

Noor looked at her. “You are the Compact lawyer.”

“Yes.”

“Did you close Sami's complaint?”

The question came without premeditation, or appeared to. Mira had probably told her about the credential.

“No.”

“Your name did.”

“A certificate bearing my name did.”

“That is legal waffle.”

“It is technical precision.”

“Those are not opposites.”

Elena accepted the blow. “I did not receive, read, adjudicate, or resolve his concern. I found the closure record and preserved its audit reference. My office is investigating the credential.”

“Your office,” Noor said.

“Among others.”

Holt tapped the table. “The credential issue may establish a systems hazard, but it also creates Ms. Varga's conflict. Elena, do you represent the Compact, the secretariat, or yourself?”

“The secretariat.”

“Then your personal evidential position is adverse to your client. You may be a witness to misuse of its authority.”

“The authority was mine.”

“Derived from office.”

“Misused in Harborlight's environment.”

“That is a debate for another panel. For this one, disclose your role and do not advise on your own liability.”

Noor asked whether that liability could disbar Elena.

“Only professional misconduct proved through the proper process,” Holt said. “Not an unpopular interpretation, and not the fact that an opponent calls counsel a shyster. That word is a pejorative, not a finding.”

Elena felt the rebuke on both sides. Harborlight could not make her a scofflaw by announcement; she could not make its lawyers corrupt by motive alone.

Elena felt the familiar impulse to narrow conflict until it vanished. She could say she had no knowledge of the forgery, no privity with its perpetrator, no tortious act, no criminal intent. All true. None addressed her authorship of the clause Rell now invoked.

“There is a further conflict,” she said.

The room stilled.

“I was principal drafter of the Compact's emergency-immunity provision.”

Noor gave one short, arrant laugh. “Of course.”

“Harborlight did not draft it,” Elena said.

“Did they ask for it?” Holt asked.

“Vale advocated continuity protection. Governments requested liability limits. I wrote the provision and reporting duty.”

“And Rell invokes it against examination.”

“Yes.”

Mira's expression did not change, but Elena saw judgment withheld rather than absent.

Holt said, “You should have disclosed that at the outset.”

“Yes.”

“Why didn't you?”

“Because I believed authorship improved my interpretation.”

“It improves historical evidence. It may distort advice.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?” Noor asked. “Or do lawyers absolve themselves by naming the flaw after it is found?”

The words were actionable in another setting. Here they were grief, and Elena would not hide behind defamation doctrine.

“No,” she said. “Disclosure does not exonerate me.”

Holt ordered a ten-minute recess while she considered whether Elena could remain. They moved into the forecourt, where rain had stopped and traffic hissed on wet stone. The Peace Palace tower appeared close enough to confer authority by shadow.

Mira stood beside Elena beneath the awning. “Why did you write it?”

“To keep governments from abandoning cross-border rescues over liability.”

“That is the public reason.”

“It is also mine.”

“No pressure from Vale?”

“Pressure, yes. Extortion, no. He described cases where seizure and litigation interrupted aid. The cases were bona fide.”

“And you inferred a broad immunity was necessary.”

“I concluded it.”

“Those are not the same.”

Elena looked at her. “You enjoy that sentence.”

“I have needed it.”

Noor remained by the door speaking to Bakker. Her anger had the restless sway of a person forced to wait while professionals converted danger into jurisdiction.

“If Holt excludes me,” Elena said, “Ana has the audit reference.”

“And the exception?”

“There may be one.”

“May?”

“The clause imposes a reporting duty for material system hazards. It does not define when inspection is permitted to establish one.”

“Narrow construction.”

“Exactly.”

Mira studied the palace tower. “A narrow route can still go somewhere.”

“Or terminate.”

“Then we find out.”

The absence of entreaty steadied Elena. Mira did not ask her to make law merciful. She asked her to test the route.

Back inside, Holt allowed Elena to remain as a factual resource, not counsel. Her interpretation would be treated as a submission against interest and checked against all authentic treaty texts. It was professionally humiliating and procedurally correct.

Rahman placed Harborlight's application on screen. The company argued that telemetry was a trade secret; unauthorized decryption could be tortious, potentially criminal under systems-interference legislation, and irremediable once disclosed. It proposed an internal examiner under judicial supervision.

De Wilde objected that a suspected perpetrator could not choose the forensic lab.

“Harborlight is not a defendant,” Rahman said.

“Not yet.”

“Nor may we forejudge it into one.”

Holt turned to Elena. “What protection does the immunity clause actually provide?”

Elena opened the treaty text. “Good-faith acts or omissions undertaken through a designated emergency function are immune from interim restraint and damages while provisional status persists, provided the operator retains contemporaneous assumptions, reports material hazards, and permits review required by implementing authority.”

“Does decrypting telemetry restrain an emergency function?”

“Not physically. Harborlight argues it deters candid internal communication and risks disclosure of live architecture.”

“Can a recorder be a function?”

“No. But data upon it may be integral to one.”

Noor muttered, “A courtier's answer.”

Elena continued. “The immunity grant should be construed narrowly because it derogates ordinary remedies. It protects operation, not every artifact connected to operation. The onus is on Harborlight to show concrete impairment.”

“And the reporting duty?”

“Broad enough to prevent concealment, narrow enough not to outlaw confidentiality. A material systems hazard must be reported contemporaneously.”

“To whom?”

“The designated public authority. For the Rotterdam pilot, the municipal controller, Compact liaison, and Dutch emergency ministry.”

Holt looked over her glasses. “You are Compact liaison.”

“Yes.”

“Could you demand the telemetry?”

“Not merely because I hanker after it. The duty is triggered by a hazard, not suspicion.”

Mira slid forward the hospital preservation record, gate timeline, and credential reference. “We have a premature gate closure against local readings, a false clearance of an occupied workboat, a triage module whose recommendation changed with postal code, repeated synchronization attempts during preservation, and a protected concern closed by a credential its owner denies using.”

Holt said, “A skein of anomalies.”

“A pattern,” Mira replied.

“Patterns can be distorted by selection.”

“Then inspect the source that may connect or separate them.”

The argument gathered mettle. De Wilde wanted a criminal warrant, but Dutch law required a specified offense and locus. Rahman warned that a broad search could violate British privacy law and render results inadmissible. Holt proposed imaging without interpretation. Mira objected that a bitwise copy alone could not establish imminent danger. Noor demanded that no one banish the audible composition from consideration merely because lawyers preferred machine data.

Ana translated key provisions into French for the prosecutor and back into English for Rahman. Every translation risked contraction or expansion. *Material hazard* became *danger substantiel*, which carried a different shade; *review* became a term closer to control. Ana refused fluent equivalence where jurisprudence differed.

“The English rider cannot govern alone,” she said. “All treaty texts are authentic.”

“Then we have four laws,” Noor said.

“One obligation seen through four legal fabrics.”

“That sounds worse.”

“It is more honest.”

Holt divided the whiteboard into three columns: WARRANT, CONSENT, DUTY. “We will test each route as if the others fail. Courts dislike remedies built from a fog of alternatives.”

Under warrant, De Wilde identified possible offenses: unlawful systems interference, obstruction of an inquiry, and computer misuse through Elena's credential. Each required a factual nexus to the recorder. The credential anomaly might justify seizure of Harborlight logs, but it did not prove that Sami's device contained evidence of the same perpetrator.

He drew the distinction as a branching line rather than let rhetoric rally the branches into one offense. The recorder might show a command, the complaint might show concealment, and the credential might show access. Chaff from one source could not fill a gap in another. Even a simian resemblance between two digital handshakes, he said, would be analogy until an examiner established a shared mechanism. Noor disliked the adjective; De Wilde withdrew it and said superficial resemblance. The retraction improved the record rather than disguising the correction.

“He filed the complaint from a field terminal,” Bakker said.

“And the recorder contains field telemetry,” De Wilde replied. “Connection is plausible. A magistrate may still call it inference stacked on inference.”

“What would obviate that?”

“The complaint text, which we cannot access because the disputed closure marked it resolved.”

The circularity was almost flawless. A possibly unlawful act had removed the fact needed to investigate it.

Rahman proposed a narrower warrant limited to metadata: creation dates, device identifiers, and communication endpoints. Mira objected that timing metadata could not be authenticated without examining the puck. Noor objected that the audible composition would become legally invisible merely because it did not resemble what a prosecutor expected evidence to be.

“A warrant is not a primer on the investigator's imagination,” Holt said. “It must specify what may be searched and why.”

Noor leaned forward. “Then specify that machine pulses may be embedded in an audio work. I can identify which are mine.”

“Would you swear to that?” De Wilde asked.

“Orally, in writing, before a tribunal, upside down if the court prefers spectacle.”

“The first two will suffice.”

Holt wrote her role beneath the warrant column: SOURCE-SEPARATION WITNESS. The designation was clumsy but actionable. Noor copied it into her notebook with a faint, moody satisfaction.

Consent appeared simpler. Noor consented as purchaser and owner of the audible recordings. Police held the device. Sami had modified it and might possess rights in the diagnostic board. His estate had not yet been constituted; Moroccan succession law, French nationality, Dutch death jurisdiction, and British location made the chain tortuous.

Rahal joined by secure video from Rotterdam to speak for consular practice, not the estate. His image occupied a small square on the screen, tie askew after a morning with Noor's parents.

He clarified that he was attending as a consular officer, not pretending that the title consul made him physician, executor, or judge. Noor's mother had asked whether grief could cause her hands to tan at the knuckles; a clinician had arranged an examination rather than let diplomatic courtesy become diagnosis. A scene photograph also showed Sami's broken sandal beside the stair, but Rahal refused to treat footwear as proof of a struggle before pathology assessed the body. The family obligation delayed his call but strengthened his point: capacity decisions belonged to qualified people, and consent required advice the family could understand.

“The family does not oppose examination,” he said. “They oppose Harborlight's appropriation. They will sign a limited consent if advised independently.”

“Who can advise today?” Holt asked.

“A French attorney has been retained. Moroccan counsel is reviewing burial and succession. Neither will adjudge title before tomorrow.”

“Then consent is supportive, not sufficient,” Holt said.

Harborlight's claim rested on contract. Employee agreements assigned inventions made within work duties and confidential information acquired through employment. Elena read Sami's contract for the first time. It defined invention broadly enough to include firmware, calibration routines, test data, and derivative improvements, but reserved an employee's preexisting artistic collaboration and personal equipment.

“When was the diagnostic board built?” Rahman asked.

“Before Sami joined Harborlight,” Noor said. “He made it for my first installation in Lyon.”

“Can you prove that?”

“Invoices, photographs, a gallery catalogue, and a room full of people who complained that its signal made the lights flicker.”

“That supports ownership of the board. Not telemetry captured later.”

“A notebook belongs to its owner even when an employer dislikes what is written in it.”

“Unless the writing is a trade secret.”

Noor's cup struck the table. “You keep making ownership a hall of mirrors. When Harborlight wants the device, it is corporate equipment. When we want to inspect it, it is private data. When police want it, it is immune infrastructure. Does the object have any nature beyond what deters the next person?”

Nobody answered quickly. Elena thought of the word *privileged*, elastic enough to denote confidential advice, social vantage, and exemption from ordinary consequence.

Holt said, “Its legal character is plural. That is frustrating, not necessarily corrupt.”

“Plural for whom? My brother cannot litigate.”

“No. Which is why we are here.”

Rahal asked for a recess to call the family. Twenty minutes later he returned with their instruction: they consented to non-destructive examination for the sole purpose of determining risk to life or integrity of the death inquiry. They did not waive any claim against Harborlight, police, insurer, gallery, or carrier.

“Your father added the carrier?” Rahman asked Noor.

“My father believes no document is complete until it anticipates a quarrel with freight.”

Even Holt smiled.

The consent strengthened equity but did not defeat Harborlight's statutory immunity. DUTY remained.

Before turning to it, Holt called Harborlight counsel and offered a voluntary stipulation. The company could nominate an independent lab from a panel, receive notice of every test, preserve trade-secret objections, and attend through a technical observer. In exchange, it would waive emergency restraint of the first forensic image.

Counsel asked for thirty minutes. During the wait, an associate brought case law from the judiciary database. One decision concerned a hospital ventilator seized after a fatal malfunction; another, a satellite operator ordered to disclose orbital telemetry; a third, a litigious manufacturer who invoked emergency law to block inspection of a cracked reservoir gate. None matched. Law developed through analogies that became less terrestrial with every difficult fact.

A fourth case concerned a ceramic cooperative whose insurer refused to inspect a kiln after heat cracked its crown. The court allowed a limited shutdown because molten glaze could plague the adjoining workshop. A fifth followed a political rally at which a temporary platform failed; organizers could not cavort behind emergency immunity while injured workers waited for the bolts to be examined. Neither case solved theirs, but both treated separable evidence as evidence rather than sacred machinery.

Elena read the reservoir judgment. The court held that immunity protected continued gate operation but not evidence physically separable from it. The operator had been required to provide a replica sensor for testing. Here the recorder was separable, but its data might expose the live architecture Harborlight claimed to protect.

“This helps,” she said.

Holt shook her head. “It helps both sides. Harborlight will emphasize architecture; we emphasize separability.”

“The reporting proviso was not in that statute.”

“Then stop hankering after precedent and read your own text.”

The rebuke was deserved. Elena returned to the authentic versions.

Harborlight counsel called back at the thirty-minute mark. The company would stipulate only if its own security team created the first image, retained encryption keys, and could redact any material it adjudged unrelated.

“That is not independent examination,” Holt said.

“It is standard handling for protected architecture.”

“Your client is implicated in a false credential closure.”

“Allegedly. Ms. Varga's service account may have been compromised through her office.”

Elena felt the accusation as a crimp in breath. It was plausible. The Compact could be the intrusion locus. Her certainty that Harborlight's environment was responsible rested on certificate chain, not proof of who controlled it.

Holt said, “Would your client permit an independent image if the keys remain sealed with the court?”

“No.”

“Then no stipulation.”

“We will seek costs against every litigant and officer involved.”

“There is no plaintiff yet.”

“There will be.”

The call ended.

Holt drew a line through CONSENT as a complete basis and placed a question mark beneath WARRANT. “Duty is not our preferred embellishment. It is what remains.”

Elena looked around the crowded room. Institutions liked to enshrine narrow construction as judicial modesty. Today modesty required them to use the smallest lawful instrument that could still reach the danger. Anything narrower would be no remedy at all.

At noon, the chambers' clerk brought sandwiches and scalding coffee. Nobody ate except Bakker, who consumed half a cheese sandwich while reading a draft warrant. Noor drank from a paper cup and winced at the liquor-like strength.

Holt asked the question they had circled for three hours. “What imminent act will occur if we do nothing?”

Mira answered carefully. “We do not know.”

“Then imminence fails.”

“The recorder may contain a timing relationship between Harborlight's decision bundle and physical measurements. If the same architecture remains live, another premature command is possible.”

“Possible is not imminent.”

“The Rotterdam pilot continues. Rell's continuity notice defines the next forty-eight hours as one emergency event.”

Elena looked up.

Rell had used imminence to invoke immunity. The position could not be reversed without consequence. If an emergency persisted, the reporting duty persisted. If no emergency existed, the immunity claim protecting the devices weakened.

“They have pleaded themselves into the exception,” she said.

Holt's eyes narrowed. “Explain.”

“Harborlight cannot simultaneously claim continuing imminence to deter examination and deny that anomalies in the same live architecture are reportable hazards. The grant and duty share a temporal trigger.”

Rahman opened the continuity notice. “They may say the hazard is weather, not their system.”

“The clause does not say *weather hazard*. It says material hazard arising in, affecting, or disclosed by a protected function.”

Outside, Elena could observe a compact nebula of rain crossing the palace tower while the barometer in Holt's window rose. Weather was present and measurable; that did not prove Harborlight's command architecture was sound.

Ana checked the other texts. “The French supports that. Croatian too. Dutch is broader.”

“Does the duty authorize inspection?” Holt asked.

“Not generally. But it requires the operator to permit review necessary to determine the nature and extent of a reported hazard.”

“No hazard has been reported.”

Elena touched the audit reference. “Sami reported one. Harborlight's system marked it resolved by a credential that did not belong to the actor. The content is sealed, but the closure anomaly itself is now a reported systems hazard. I report it in my official capacity.”

The sentence entered the room without drama. It changed everything.

Holt leaned back. “You are both reporting authority and implicated credential holder.”

“Which is why the review must be independent and its scope fixed by this panel.”

“Your office may repeal the report.”

“It may attempt to. The treaty does not permit retraction of a contemporaneous hazard notice, only adjudication.”

De Wilde said, “A magistracy could supervise.”

Rahman was already reading the implementing statute. “The British court can recognize the Compact duty as a statutory public-interest basis for limited processing. Privacy rights remain, but they are balanced against the specified hazard.”

Ana traced the provision's legislative history. One lawmaker had proposed a broad immunity; another demanded the reporting proviso. The final legislation was a contraction of the grant and an expansion of review, not permission to contort every protected object into an untouchable function. Elena's reading was therefore narrow construction, not legislative invention.

“Trade secret?”

“Protective order. Named experts, sealed results, no publication beyond hazard findings.”

Noor said, “And me.”

“You are not an expert.”

“I am the only person here who can distinguish my composition from Sami's diagnostic pulse.”

Holt nodded. “She is a necessary factual observer.”

It was the first legal sentence all morning that recognized Noor's expertise without transforming her into owner or obstacle. Mira glanced toward her. Noor's face remained guarded, but her shoulders lowered.

The terms assembled quickly once the basis existed. An independent metrology laboratory outside Delft would authenticate the recorder and puck under Dutch supervision. A British forensic officer would create the image and transfer a sealed copy. Noor would attend, with no unilateral handling right. Mira could observe model and timing interpretation but not operate original evidence. Harborlight could send one technical representative subject to exclusion if the lab found network risk. All findings would remain sealed except a yes-or-no hazard report and supporting measurements necessary to act.

Noor asked that Judith, her former conservation tutor, review photographs if the recorder emitted a mechanical whimper or the resin dust shifted during unpacking. Holt allowed remote consultation but no second extraction. They would not reprise the warehouse procedure or let observers cavort around the bench.

“How long?” Bakker asked.

Holt checked the injunction timetable. Harborlight's full hearing was scheduled in fifty-one hours. Travel and transfer consumed three.

“Forty-eight hours,” she said. “After that, the court may freeze interpretation pending adjudication.”

“Can you summon the lab?” Noor asked.

“We can request.”

Mira had already found one. The Netherlands Metrology Annex outside Delft maintained isolated electronics benches and could take them at eight the next morning if the order arrived by four.

Holt drafted the determination as a memorandum for parallel submission in London and The Hague. She refused expansive rhetoric. The court need not declare Harborlight corrupt, Sami a whistleblower in substance, or the telemetry public. It need only adjudge that a documented closure anomaly in a protected reporting channel, coupled with live emergency status and related operational anomalies, justified narrowly tailored inspection.

“No finding of criminality,” she dictated.

“No finding of ownership beyond temporary custody.”

“No waiver of privilege except as necessary to report imminent system hazard.”

“No publication of personal or proprietary content unrelated to that hazard.”

The limitations did not dilute the remedy. They made it harder to overturn.

At three forty, the London judge endorsed the agreed protocol on an interim basis. At three fifty-two, the Dutch prosecutor issued the transfer authority. At three fifty-eight, the lab confirmed its bench.

Then Harborlight's attorney called.

The voice came through Holt's speaker, smooth with professional restraint. He called the protocol brazen, the hazard report self-interested, and Elena's interpretation a contortion of legislation she had no power to amend. He threatened civil liability, professional discipline, and an emergency appeal.

Holt let him finish. “Which relief do you seek before five?”

“A stay.”

“On what new evidence?”

“The recorder contains critical architecture.”

“That supports controlled examination.”

“It could expose untold vulnerabilities.”

“Then they may be hazards.”

“You are torturing the clause.”

“No. We are applying its proviso.”

He shifted to Elena. “Ms. Varga, your conduct is irresponsible. You may be liable for every loss caused by disclosure.”

Elena felt the threat enter old professional seams. Disbarment, damages, loss of office: not torture, but the ordinary instruments by which a career taught obedience.

“The protocol prohibits disclosure,” she said. “Do you contest the credential anomaly?”

“We contest your characterization.”

“Do you deny that my credential marked the report resolved?”

“We have not authenticated your claim.”

“Then attend the review.”

He asked whether this was her final position.

Elena looked at the table: Noor's hands around a cold cup, Mira's annotated timeline, Bakker's warrant, Ana's four treaty texts. The institution had not acted by itself. People had forced its conflicting duties into the same room and refused to let immunity erase obligation.

“It is the reporting authority's position,” she said.

“You presume to speak for the Compact.”

“On this notice, I am designated to do so.”

“We will appeal.”

“That is your lawful right.”

The call ended without verdict or triumph.

They left after dark. Wind wafted rain from the trees, and the palace forecourt shone beneath streetlights. A courier carried the sealed protocol toward the prosecutor's office. Bakker went to arrange evidence transport. Noor and Mira stood beneath the awning discussing who would travel with the recorder.

Elena remained on the top step. She had used the clause against Harborlight's preferred outcome, but the act did not absolve her authorship or make the provision benevolent. It proved only that law was not a fiat spoken once by a lawgiver. Its meaning depended on who could enter the room, what facts survived, and whether a duty was allowed to have mettle when power preferred a technicality.

Her phone, returned from its pouch, showed a message from Vale.

*You have made the inquiry possible. You may also have made the platform impossible to operate. I hope your judgment is sound.*

Elena read it twice. He did not rant, extort, or threaten. He placed the onus of every future harm in her hands with the courtesy of a colleague.

She wrote back: *Then the review should establish which danger is real.*

At 06:30 the recorder would leave London under seal. At 08:00 the lab outside Delft would receive it. Forty-eight hours after that, Harborlight's injunction could close around them.

Bakker circulated the transfer sheet before anyone left. The recorder and puck would travel in separate shock cases, each with temperature and humidity indicators, escorted by a British forensic officer to the Dutch border handoff at Schiphol. Noor's extraction video would remain sealed on a third drive so that damage to one item could not contaminate the history of another. The laboratory was instructed to photograph resin dust before cleaning, preserve every connector state, and begin with passive clock measurement rather than power. Mira added that no Harborlight time server should enter the room, even through an automatic instrument update. Noor required a window into the bench area and the right to challenge any handling step on the record. Holt accepted both conditions, then made the challenge right nonbinding: objection would pause work long enough for the supervising prosecutor to decide, not give any observer a veto.

The protocol was slower than trust and more useful. By the time the last person signed, the laboratory appointment had become not a destination but a chain of acts whose failures could be named.

Narrow construction had opened a narrow door.

They would have to carry the evidence through before it shut.

By dawn, every objection would travel with it, preserved beside the machines it sought to restrain.

## Chapter 9: Baseline

The laboratory had windows for people who did not trust walls.

At eight minutes past eight on Day Seven, Noor stood behind laminated glass and watched a technician photograph dust. The recorder lay in a stainless-steel tray under a white light, its dented grille still maculate with grey resin. In the adjacent tray the calibration puck looked trifling, a black capsule no wider than her palm. Each object had arrived in a separate shock case. Each case had its own seal, temperature strip, humidity card, and custody sheet. The unabridged extraction video waited on a third drive inside a fourth container. Nobody had yet joined the histories merely because the objects had once occupied the same sculpture.

The fastidiousness ought to have reassured her. Instead it aggravated the feeling that Sami was being translated into facilities.

What she felt in its place was the incipience of another fight, colder than grief: who would get to say first what these objects meant, and how much the first naming could undo every careful qualification that followed.

Beyond the bench, Dr. Marijke Vos wore a bald cap of close-cropped silver hair, denim trousers under her lab coat, and an expression that discouraged blather. She photographed the corrugated impression left by packing foam, then changed gloves before lifting a single resin splinter with ceramic tweezers. Her assistant, Pieter Lang, transcribed the seal numbers aloud. A British forensic officer checked them against the transfer sheet. Inspector Bakker watched the check. Mira watched the instruments. Noor watched everybody.

“Object one, recorder,” Pieter said. “No power applied. No connector engaged.”

“You have called it object one three times,” Noor said through the intercom. “Its designation on the order is recorder R-Bensaid-one.”

Marijke looked up. “Correct the oral record, Pieter.”

He did, without defensive commentary.

At the far end of the observation room, Harborlight’s representative gave a small, exasperated croak. Dirk van Hove had introduced himself as a principal integrity engineer and then spent twelve minutes badgering Bakker about the absence of a network link. His company had demanded the right to observe; now he objected to every precaution that made observation cumbersome.

“The serial alone divulges architecture,” he said. “Your panoramic photographs are excessive.”

“The serial is already on the insurer’s extraction record,” Bakker replied. The company had been trying since dawn to knit confidentiality and custody into one indivisible right.

“That record is proscribed from disclosure.”

“Nothing here is being disclosed.”

“Six outsiders are looking at it.”

Noor glanced at him. “Your definition of outside appears dependent on who owns the door.”

Van Hove pretended not to hear. He had a florid face, glamorous spectacles with turquoise arms, and the cautious coiffure of a man who believed expensive disorder counted as ease. He placed one hand on the glass whenever Marijke approached the recorder, as if appeal to the barrier might stop her.

He also had the corporate habit of making a sentence longer when it had begun to fail. In a municipal chamber, the polish might have bought him time. Here it only made Marijke look more dangerous: she listened until the objection ran out of mechanism, then returned to the object in the tray. Noor, who had spent too many years watching patrons confuse volume with authority, felt the room choose its own standard. Proof was not persuaded. It was handled, measured, repeated.

The laboratory occupied a former materials annex at the edge of Delft, between an aquifer monitoring station and a yard where railway components rusted behind bunting left from some municipal anniversary. Across the service road, the quondam ceramics works had become offices, its deposed kiln stack cut down to a stump. A foxhole of a guard booth crouched by the gate. Near the loading apron, a maintenance van idled with a loose muffler while orange-brown slag devoured the bases of two retired signal posts. When the wind shifted off the drainage canal, it carried a marshy miasma with it. A locomotive moved beyond the perimeter at intervals, slow enough that its vibration emerged as a trend on the bench seismometer. The building had linoleum corridors, sealed doors, and a machine shop whose muffled lathe supplied a faint orthogonal rhythm beneath the ventilation. Noor apprehended each sound before she learned its source. The room was not silent. It was coherent.

At 08:17 Marijke began the contamination map. She used raking light to distinguish resin transferred during extraction from older material embedded around the recorder grille. One patch coruscated; another remained matte. She assayed loose debris with infrared spectroscopy and found two related but nonidentical polymers.

“Outer fracture resin and cradle adhesive,” Judith Reeve said by secure video from London. The conservator’s image had been admitted only for source identification. “The adhesive was applied during fabrication. It should contain a blue pigment.”

Pieter enhanced the spectrum. A small peak emerged.

“Cobalt aluminate,” he said.

“Not radioactive, not volatile, not relevant to timekeeping,” Marijke said. “Record and retain.”

Van Hove pressed the intercom. “The cobalt may affect magnetic components.”

“At this fractional concentration?” Mira asked.

“You cannot conclude immateriality before modeling it.”

“I can conclude the burden is yours if you want delay.”

He launched into a disclaimer about unknown interactions between pigments, adhesives, and legacy storage media. The possibility was not bogus. It was simply unbounded, a stratagem by which any examination could be postponed until every molecule had been given counsel.

His objections followed a sclerotic corporate logic: if a fact could be called architecture, it could be withheld; if a question touched the withheld thing, the question itself became suspect. He was not inventing risks so much as refusing to rank them. Each protest only sharpened Marijke’s patience into something more dangerous than anger.

Marijke cut him off. “Submit an apposite mechanism in writing. We are not arbitrating every vision of calamity.”

Noor liked her then, which made her suspicious of liking her.

The puck came first because it could be measured without waking it. Its quartz oscillator still produced a weak periodic field through the casing. Marijke placed it inside a shielded enclosure beside a cesium-referenced counter. The counter’s authority ran back through a cesium isotope chain Noor did not pretend to master. The puck itself, Pieter said when she asked, was a descendant of a cheaper industrial sensor family Sami had once derided for promising ruggedness and delivering only sufficiency. A camera showed the setup from above; another showed her hands. Pieter entered room temperature, pressure, and humidity, then read them back.

Noor asked why pressure mattered if the counter measured frequency.

"Because the puck contains a pressure transducer," Marijke said. "We need to know whether its casing is intact before we compare the stored baseline. In materials work, impermeability is a claim, not a blessing."

“And if it leaked?”

“Then the oscillator may still be sound while the pressure readings are corrupt. We would sunder those conclusions.”

The answer was neither comforting nor evasive. Noor wrote it down.

For twenty minutes the counter accumulated cycles. A green trace crept across the screen, nearly parallel to the reference. Mira stood immovable, squinting at values as if concentration could quench drift. Van Hove paced. Bakker took a call in the corridor concerning the injunction appeal. Noor listened to the air handler and remembered Sami at twelve, tapping a cane against their parents’ cellar wall because he believed a cavity lay behind it. There had been no treasure, only a disused inlet and a damp smell. He had called the discovery a bounty anyway.

She had spent the previous six days refusing every narrative that made him a saint. Now memory kept trying to make him a boy.

At 08:52 Marijke displayed the first conclusion. The puck ran slow by 0.81 seconds per day at laboratory temperature. The uncertainty interval was narrow enough to exclude a drift of more than four seconds across the period since its last certified calibration.

“That does not authenticate its stored time,” Van Hove said rapidly.

“No,” Marijke replied.

“It does not establish where it was.”

“No.”

“It does not establish which controller it heard.”

“No.”

His triumph faltered under the litany of agreement.

“It establishes only present oscillator behavior,” she continued, “which is preparatory to reading its internal count. Your refusal to distinguish conclusions is becoming a hindrance.”

The next step required power, but not firmware boot. Marijke connected a passive inductive probe to read the puck’s maintenance register. Van Hove objected that the probe’s field might overwrite volatile memory. Pieter produced the manufacturer’s assay and demonstrated the field strength on a blank device. Mira asked for one additional control: place the blank beside the operating probe for the full planned interval, then compare its checksum.

“That adds forty minutes,” Bakker said.

“It removes an appeal ground,” Elena said from the observation table.

She had arrived without ceremony and taken the chair nearest the door, still constrained by the chambers’ ruling to factual participation. Her briefcase remained closed. She looked as if she had not slept, but her writing was exact.

Van Hove appraised her with open hostility. “You have no authority to enhance this protocol.”

“The supervising prosecutor does. I am noting that your company alluded to inductive corruption in its appeal filed at 07:43. A control answers your own point.”

“You have seen the appeal?”

“I am a named respondent.”

The blank puck spent forty minutes under the probe. Its checksum did not change. The actual puck then yielded a maintenance register with three fields: oscillator count, pressure samples, and device temperature. No location. No command text. No culprit obligingly embossed in the metal.

Before accepting the register, Marijke assessed the casing itself. A digital microscope revealed a jagged line beside the charging coil. Van Hove called it a fracture; Judith, looking through the remote feed, said it was the impression of a serrate clamp jaw used during fabrication. Marijke refused both conclusions until Pieter made a silicone cast and compared its scale with the manufacturer’s tooling marks. The line conformed to the clamp, but a shallow dimple at its end did not. They placed the puck in a small pressure vessel, raised the load by fractions, and watched for seepage with a helium assay.

“If it is impermeable, why test it?” Noor asked.

“Because saying *impermeable* does not make a surface so,” Marijke said. “And because a leak can render the stored pressure narrative false while leaving the clock coherent.”

No helium emerged. The puck had not been breached. Pieter paused to jot the result, then photographed the satiny convex seam from four angles. Van Hove objected that the test pressure exceeded field conditions. Marijke showed that it remained below the certified limit and invited him to divulge any apposite contrary specification. He had none.

The inspection also exposed a second problem. A camera above the observation room was not part of the laboratory system. Its indicator glinted once, then went dark. Bakker found that it belonged to the building’s general security network, a system the protocol had not proscribed because nobody had recollected that the observation room, unlike the bench, remained under ordinary surveillance. The feed showed faces and screens but not legible values. Even so, he ordered it disconnected, preserved its preceding hour, and notified the prosecutor.

“A precaution, or evidence that someone intervenes?” Noor asked.

“A precaution,” Bakker said. “No one absconded with data merely because a camera existed.”

Van Hove called the response farce. Elena answered that custody abounds in dull risks and that protocol apprehends them one by one; dullness did not make them immaterial. The camera’s network log was sealed apart from the device evidence; no one would graft suspicion onto it before the access record was read.

Noor watched an officer caulk the cable port with a tamper seal. The act was almost comically physical, a bright strip across a hole, but it clarified the room. Surveillance had been possible. Now its limit had been named, recorded, and made visual.

The glass did not exactly immure them, Noor thought. It ranked them. Inside the bench room Marijke and Pieter could alter the objects by named, documented acts. Outside, everyone else could only object, interpret, or wait.

Noor felt both relief and refusal. “That is all?”

“That is what a baseline device should contain,” Mira said.

“Sami hid a clock.”

“He preserved a comparison.”

“Do not make poverty sound merited.”

Mira accepted the rebuke. “No. It is incomplete.”

The word restored the object’s integrity. Incomplete did not mean failed. It meant no one was entitled to pretend it contained more.

Marijke exported the register twice through separate readers, hashed both images, and found them identical. She did not yet interpret the pressure samples. First she had to establish the recorder’s relation to the same interval.

At 10:21 the recorder moved beneath a microscope. Its casing bore a dent near the grille, resin in two screw wells, and a narrow rupture in the rear laminate. Pieter found lint caught beneath one edge and reached for forceps.

“Stop,” Noor said.

Every hand in the lab stopped.

The lint was red.

“It may be from the sculpture’s internal padding,” Noor said. “The cradle was lined with red felt before I replaced it.”

Judith checked the fabrication photographs. The early lining was visible, but later images showed black foam. The red fiber might date the recorder’s insertion or might be debris introduced during years of studio work.

Marijke photographed and packed it. “No conclusion.”

Van Hove sighed theatrically.

Noor turned on him. “Would you prefer they invent one?”

“I would prefer we reach material questions before the court proscribes the work.”

“You have spent two hours manufacturing delay.”

“Precaution becomes harassment only when you dislike the source.”

The charge struck close enough to disconcert her. She had objected to a corrected designation, a probe, a fiber, the position of a camera. Some objections mattered. Others gave her the sensation of guarding Sami when all she guarded was sequence.

Marijke was waiting. “Do you maintain an objection to removing the fiber?”

The protocol let Noor challenge a step; Bakker would decide whether the objection paused it. She could force the decision and keep her hands metaphorically on the recorder. Or she could acknowledge that the documented removal caused no loss she could name.

“No,” she said. “Retain it separately.”

“Agreed.”

The word hurt less than she expected.

They cleaned only enough resin to expose the service contacts. The fracture had not reached the memory package. Two hairline fractures in the solder mask stopped short of the bond pads, which was better news than Noor had allowed herself to expect. Power rails tested open, so direct current could not be applied without repair. Van Hove proposed a Harborlight adapter whose optimization routine, he said, could reconstruct the damaged board.

Mira laughed once, without humor. “A machine that edits the evidence in order to read it.”

“It creates a verisimilar virtual state.”

“We require the actual state.”

“Then you may require the impossible.”

Marijke chose chip-off imaging instead. Under magnification, Pieter would desolder the storage package, clean its contacts, and place it in an isolated reader. It was destructive to the recorder’s present configuration, though restorative repair might later be possible. The order permitted it only if no less invasive method sufficed.

Noor stared at the black package on screen. A faint plaque of cooked flux ringed one solder pad, amber under magnification. The package itself sat grafted to the board by tiny solder joints with the dumb finality of an implant. Cutting the sculpture had felt like violence because the work’s form would be changed. Here a technician would apply heat to something Sami had altered with his own hands.

“Can the board be imaged by micro-CT?” she asked.

“We can map it,” Marijke said. “We cannot retrieve the data.”

“Could you bridge the rupture?”

“Possibly, but energizing an uncharacterized repair risks erasure. Removing the package is the moderate course.”

“Moderate,” Noor repeated.

“Not harmless.”

That was what persuaded her. Harm named was easier to share than safety advertised.

Bakker recorded the decision. Noor signed acknowledgment as owner-observer, not consent to a transfer of title. The prosecutor authorized the step. Pieter wheeled the recorder through an air lock into the electronics room, where a flexible extractor arm waited above the bench, its nozzle angled toward the solder station.

The work took ninety minutes.

Noor went outside because the solder station’s fume extractor produced a whiff that transported her to Sami’s student room in Lyon: scorched flux, old ale, and the saliferous air of a window he never closed. He used to file solder tips flat, which was wrong, and wipe them on his jeans, which was worse. Once, after working through most of a night on a diagnostic board, he had lifted the iron too quickly and let it sear his own thumb. Their mother had called it the price of showing off. Noor had called it proof that confidence and competence were not the same trade. When she bought him a brass cleaner he called it bourgeois propaganda. Then he used it until it fell apart.

The laboratory yard sloped toward a drainage canal. Gulls stood on the bank. Across the road, an old ceramics factory had become offices, its brick facade retained while everything behind it was modernized. A pallet leaned against the fence, splintered by weather, and fresh splinters shone pale near Noor’s shoe. Somewhere beyond the gate a bicycle bell tinkled. High above, airplanes moved west in a slow file. Noor sat on a concrete ramp and watched a skiff pass between reeds, its little outboard leaving water spurting white behind it.

Mira came out carrying two paper cups.

“Tea,” she said.

“It smells like a wet splint.”

“The coffee was worse.”

Noor took it. “Did they send you to moderate me?”

“Marijke sent everyone out while they remove the chip.”

“Even Harborlight?”

“Especially Harborlight.”

They drank in the weak sun. A gust set the abandoned bunting singing against its cable, a thin metallic refrain.

The damp air began to frizz the loose hairs at Mira’s temples. She looked exhausted, but there was something resolute in the angle of her mouth, as if fatigue had burned away every gesture that was not essential.

“If the eleven minutes disappear,” Noor said, “what then?”

“Then we stop saying eleven minutes.”

“And Sami?”

Mira looked at the canal rather than at her. “Remains dead under suspicious circumstances. The hospital diversions remain real. The complaint closure remains false or misused. One failure of one hypothesis does not immunize the rest.”

“You sound as if you have rehearsed that.”

“I have needed it before.”

Noor heard the ellipsis but did not pursue it. Mira’s reserve was not a locked cellar Noor was entitled to maul open. Still, the woman’s hands had tightened around the cup.

“Your mother called twice,” Noor said.

Mira checked her phone and swore under her breath. “The clinic appointment.”

“Today?”

“Tomorrow afternoon.”

“During the injunction.”

“Yes.”

“Will you go?”

“I said I would.”

It was not an answer, and both knew it. Noor considered pressing, then recollected her own unanswered call from Sami. Advice from that foothold would be iniquity dressed as concern.

She said only, “Promises materialize in calendars.”

Mira gave her a perturbed look. “That sounds like something my mother would say.”

“I have met her food.”

Noor remembered Mira’s mother at a kitchen counter in Schiedam, using the flat of a cleaver to tenderize squid while lecturing everyone within reach. She had once heard Sami defend some late-night beer experiment, only for the older woman to say that swine at a trough made the same grateful noise and expected the same applause. The memory nearly lifted into laughter, but lassitude pressed it back down.

Noor also remembered a hospital briefing Mira had shown her weeks earlier, a jejune capacity handout that reduced whole wards to colored cells. Mira had said the clinician who wrote it preferred a sledgehammer to a conversation, as if enough force could cure uncertainty. Remembering that now, Noor surmised the clinic appointment was not a social courtesy her mother had invented out of piety.

The recorder image was ready at 12:46. Pieter had removed the package without visible substrate damage. The first read failed; the second produced a stable image. The two subsequent reads matched its hash. Marijke sealed the physical chip separately, sealed the recorder board, and created two forensic copies. One remained with Dutch police. One entered the court depository. Analysis would proceed on a third working copy derived in view of all parties.

By then the room had gone back to the grindstone of exact repetition. Whatever smoldered between the observers had to wait while hashes, timestamps, and witness initials were checked again.

Noor watched the multiplication with unease. Custody no longer meant a single thing in a single box. It meant originals, images, hashes, permissions, and people able to testify how one became another. Shared custody was not dilution. It was a chain whose strength depended on admitting every joint. For Noor, coherence came less from trust than from making every irreversible step visible.

The encrypted partition did not yield to Harborlight keys because none were used. Sami’s diagnostic board had an older key pair from Noor’s Lyon installation. She supplied the public half from her archived project files; the private half remained in the recorder’s secure element, which Pieter imaged separately. The cryptograms opened into packet captures and audio-linked time codes, just as the warehouse preview had suggested.

No confession emerged.

There were pressure packets from three field pucks, controller acknowledgments, battery states, and incomplete firmware labels. Several captures ended abruptly. One was garbled by a voltage collapse where the recorder had lost power. Another contained a checksum but no payload. The apparent event at 18:28:14 recorder time was a controller receipt whose command body had been stripped.

“Stripped by whom?” Bakker asked.

“By the recording filter, perhaps,” Mira said. “It may have stored headers by design.”

Van Hove seized the uncertainty. “Then your narrative is gone. A receipt does not identify a command.”

“It identifies a sender, destination class, bundle hash, and time,” Mira replied.

“According to an unauthenticated clock.”

“For another few minutes.”

Marijke aligned the recorder’s free-running oscillator against the laboratory reference. It had drifted fast by 2.4 seconds per day. The machine’s internal temperature history allowed her to model the drift across four days, but she refused to rely on that drift equation alone. She looked for an external event captured by both devices.

The puck had recorded a sharp pressure notch when its case was closed. The recorder’s microphone had captured the same closure as a tactile knock transmitted through the sculpture cradle. Noor identified the act in her studio log: at 14:12 on Day Two, Sami had packed the devices while they argued by video about the eccentric spacer release he still insisted would save two grams and three headaches. Her call metadata fixed the minute but not the second.

They needed greater fineness.

Pieter found a second paired event. At Rotterdam, a calibration transmitter had emitted a standard three-pulse handshake. The puck recorded its pressure side effect through a tiny diaphragm movement; the recorder logged the acoustic pulse and packet receipt. The intervals between pulses were distinctive: two seconds, then seven, then two. Both devices held them.

Noor heard the pattern through headphones. It was faint, almost a whisper under electrical sputtering. To her ear it was no homonym of Sami’s four-step diagnostic signature; it merely rhymed with it enough to tempt a careless listener. “That is not my score.”

“Can you say more?” Marijke asked.

“Only that. Sami’s diagnostic pulse used four intervals. This is three.”

Her expertise remained source separation, not authorship of the machine event. She did not pretend otherwise.

Marijke calculated offsets independently by three methods. Pieter repeated them without seeing her result. Mira wrote her own script on an isolated laptop and disclosed every assumption before running it. The offsets agreed within 0.37 seconds.

The recorder receipt was fixed at 18:28:11 local time, plus or minus 0.62 seconds.

The puck’s measured surge began at 18:39:06, plus or minus 0.41 seconds.

Ten minutes, fifty-five seconds.

Nobody spoke.

Outside the glass, the locomotive passed again. Its low vibration traversed the floor and appeared on the seismometer, an honest disturbance arriving after its sound.

Van Hove broke the silence. “A controller receipt is not a gate-close command.”

Mira enlarged the packet header. “Destination class barrier actuation. Bundle hash matches the checksum Sami gave me and the readiness acknowledgment Koen saw on Day Three.”

“It may be preparatory.”

“Then Harborlight can produce the bundle under seal.”

“Trade secret.”

Elena opened her briefcase for the first time. “The hazard exception now applies to the identified bundle. A command sent before measured surge is material to the live pilot. Refusal will be entered.”

“You are drawing a conclusion from coincidence.”

“No,” Marijke said. “I am not drawing your operational conclusion at all. My conclusion is metrological: the recorder received a packet in the barrier-actuation class ten minutes and fifty-five seconds before the puck measured the local pressure rise later cited in Harborlight’s incident account. Both times are traceable to independent standards within the stated uncertainty.”

It was less than Noor wanted and more than Van Hove could erase.

Mira’s face had gone still. “The published incident account says Harborlight issued closure after detecting the surge at 18:39.”

“Then the account and the authenticated sequence are incompatible,” Bakker said.

“Unless the command was based on a forecast,” Van Hove replied. “Which is what anticipatory systems do. They precede observations. You are treating efficacy as guilt.”

The argument had force. Noor hated it for having force.

The later squall had arrived. The gate closure might have averted harm at another berth. A forecast was supposed to act before measurement. Eleven minutes alone did not reveal intent, corruption, or Vale. Any inference beyond authenticated sequence remained refragable. It established only that Harborlight had inverted the public narrative: the physical surge had not triggered the command it was later used to justify, and that a true forecast elsewhere could not assoil a false chronology here.

Elena, hearing the same tension in the room, said quietly, “No one gets to blaspheme physics by calling this prophecy after the fact. And no one gets to cry larceny of trade secret to avoid the chronology.” Bakker added that the timing table did not identify who used the packet to perpetrate the closure logic or the later public account. It merely stripped away one convenient story. Uncertainty had not been eradicated. It had been narrowed.

Sami’s phrase returned to Noor not as prophecy but as technical prose. The forecast was downstream of the decision.

At 14:10 Harborlight filed an emergency request to halt interpretation. At 14:18 the supervising judge declined an immediate stay but ordered the lab to issue only the narrow hazard finding before the municipal hearing next morning. At 14:25 Rotterdam’s controller requested the finding. The pilot remained live.

Marijke dictated it without ornament. She described devices, seals, methods, uncertainty, paired events, and the incompatible chronology. She did not say deliberate. She did not say fraud. She did not say murder. Every word denied the prosecution and the defense a pretence of certainty they had not earned.

When the report was ready, Bakker asked Noor to sign the observation record and approve transfer of the derived timing table to the municipal controller.

“Approve?” she asked.

“Acknowledge. The prosecutor authorizes transfer. Your signature confirms the table derives from the observed examination and contains no audible composition.”

The distinction mattered. It was no adieu to scrutiny. It also deprived her of a veto she had half believed she retained.

She read every line. The table contained no music, no private speech, no images of the sculpture. It contained four time values and uncertainty bands. Sami’s work had become a sparse set of relations able to leave the room without his sister. She had feared the chain would treat him unjustly, or reduce him to a problem other people could solve on paper. Instead it forced everyone into the same narrow honesty.

“Who receives it?”

“Municipal controller, Dutch prosecutor, London court under seal, Compact reporting authority, Harborlight counsel.”

“Press?”

“No.”

“Vale?”

“Through counsel.”

Noor signed.

Her hand did not shake. That almost troubled her more.

Pieter sealed the original recorder components and puck for return to police storage. The working image remained on an encrypted laboratory server pending court order. Noor received no copy. She received the signed observation record and custody receipts. Ownership had not restored possession; grief had not conferred expertise; vigilance had not required command.

In the corridor, Van Hove overtook them.

“You believe you unveiled a conspiracy,” he said.

“No,” Mira replied. “We established sequence.”

“The distinction will vanish in tomorrow’s propaganda.”

“Then help keep it factual. Produce the bundle.”

He looked genuinely tired. “You think one person pulled one lever. The system allocates across gates, hospitals, roads, weather, crews, patients. Local measurements arrive late. If every municipality withdraws when one result looks suspicious, precaution becomes paralysis.”

He said it with less heat than before, though nothing in Elena’s face suggested she was dissuaded. Van Hove had not moved toward concession so much as toward exhaustion.

“And if no municipality can withdraw,” Elena said, “precaution becomes command without consent.”

Van Hove’s mouth tightened. “Florid nonsense.”

“An accurate legal outlook.”

He left through the security door, where a man in a dark parka waited beyond the fence. The man was thick-necked and watchful. He did not approach. He lifted a phone, apparently photographed the group, and walked toward a black car. Bakker, jaw tight, worked a peppermint against one cheek.

Bakker sent an officer to the gate. By the time she arrived, the car had pulled away. Its plate belonged to a rental agency; the booking name was not immediately available. As it turned through the junction, Noor caught the blue flare of the dashboard and the speedometer needle lifting.

“Rell?” Noor asked.

“You did not see Rell,” Bakker said.

“I asked a question.”

“And I am preventing it from hardening into recollection.”

The correction was scathing and sound. Noor wrote: *Unknown man. Dark parka. Photograph. Black rental. No identification.*

At the car park, Mira’s phone filled with municipal messages. The hearing had been moved to 09:00. Harborlight would argue that forecast lead time explained the discrepancy. Vale would appear in person, which meant the company wanted its best public orator on display. Protesters were already gathering outside city hall, some demanding shutdown, others carrying signs that said DON’T BLIND THE GATES. Reporters were already cramming the steps, and the finding had plainly ignited a fight none of them could still keep inside procedural walls.

“They are both right about the danger,” Mira said.

“That is an asinine campaign slogan,” Noor replied.

“It is not a slogan.”

Elena studied the report. “The finding can support a moratorium on the specific decision bundle. It cannot support a ban on Harborlight.”

“Will the municipality distinguish them?” Noor asked.

“Only if somebody gives them a decision they can lawfully make.”

Mira looked back at the laboratory windows. Through the glass, Marijke and Pieter were clearing the bench, each item moving into its proper container. The work had produced no panoramic revelation, only a baseline and a contradiction.

That contradiction would not pound by itself on the hearing-room door; they would have to carry it there and keep it exact.

Noor understood then why Sami had hidden the puck rather than a manifesto. He had not asked it to speak. He had asked it to stay still while another system moved around it.

She had spent days believing custody meant preventing other hands from altering what remained of him. In the laboratory, custody had required the opposite: permitting named hands to separate, heat, image, interpret, and transfer, while every irreversible act became visible enough to contest.

She folded the receipt into her notebook. The hearing now beckoned with the force of bad weather.

“Tomorrow,” Mira said, “we ask them to stop the pilot.”

“No,” Noor replied. “You ask. I listen for what they omit.”

It was not refusal. It was an allocation of work.

At 16:03 the municipal controller received the authenticated table. At 16:07 Harborlight acknowledged receipt. At 16:11 a new operational notice appeared on the public portal: pump priorities in the southern districts would be recalculated overnight because of forecast rainfall.

Mira read it twice.

“Is that normal?” Noor asked.

“It can be.”

“And is it?”

Mira showed her the affected map. The same postal zone whose patients had been diverted at the hospital sat along the lowest-ranked edge.

“I don’t know yet,” she said.

The honest answer did not avert danger. It gave danger a shape they could test.

They left Delft in the gloaming with the report sealed between them and the original evidence behind glass. The eleven minutes were no longer a rumor carried by a grieving sister or a suspicious auditor. They were measured time.

What that time meant would be fought over in public.

## Chapter 10: Self-Fulfilling

By nine in the morning the word *eleven* had acquired factions.

Outside Rotterdam city hall, one crowd chanted it as an accusation. Eleven minutes stolen. Eleven minutes falsified. Eleven minutes in which Sami Bensaid had still been alive or already dead, depending on which rumor had reached which phone. Across the tram tracks, Harborlight supporters held blue placards showing the barrier above a single sentence: FORECASTS MUST PRECEDE FLOODS. Police had opened a bar of wet pavement between them, and a hercules of a bailiff kept shifting the metal barriers whenever the crowd leaned too hard.

A woman near the front kept the accusation from collapsing into noise by giving each count a hard second beat. Beside her, a pensioner held up a damp cardboard drawing of Vale painting blue arrows over brown blocks labeled with insurance rates. Across from them, Harborlight volunteers lifted tablets that looped the same brochure animation: gates rising on cue, streets dry, a city saved before it knew to be afraid. The rain made the screens blur and brightened the verdigris on the tram shelter rail. A child in an oversized slicker watched the police line without blinking while his mother kept one hand on his hood.

Mira entered through a side door because the municipal commission had classified her as an expert witness and the protesters had classified her six other ways. Auditor. Traitor. Celebrity. Saboteur. One sign called her a coward for wanting the pilot stopped; another called her a shill for refusing to say Harborlight had murdered Sami. The antagonism was almost cheerful until somebody recognized her.

“Dr. El-Amin!”

Questions came like thrown gravel. Was the gate command bogus? Had Vale falsified the forecast? Would she swear Harborlight caused the death? A reporter asked whether the eleven-minute discrepancy vindicated her Westminster testimony. The premise was alluring: a clean line from suspicion to proof, herself at its meritorious end.

“The laboratory authenticated a sequence,” she said. “It did not identify who authorized the command or why.”

“Then why demand suspension?”

“Because the public incident account says the measured surge triggered the closure. It did not.”

“Is Vale lying?”

“That is a conclusion for evidence, not a chant.”

The restraint sounded halfhearted even to her. She crossed the foyer while the questions continued behind police glass.

The hearing room had once been a council chamber and still displayed an imperial tapestry whose ships sailed toward terrain rendered as a green frond. Temporary screens obscured half the wall. The chamber was lofty and faintly sweltering despite the rain outside, with verdigris along the bronze radiator grilles, scorching air around one old valve, and a chipped enamel number above the interpreter booth. The tapestry seemed to lace its ships past barren islands and improbable palms, so that the room's current technic of screens, witness microphones, and translation loops looked temporarily camped inside somebody else's empire. Commissioners sat in a shallow triad beneath the municipal seal. Chair Annika Smit, an orthopedic surgeon before politics, retained a surgeon's trimness and a clinician's eclecticism; she palpated each procedural dispute as if seeking the exact site of pain, and Mira suspected she had little patience for the municipal pantheism by which Harborlight's public advocates spoke as though residents, rain, and code belonged to one indivisible body. To her right sat infrastructure alderman Joost Vermeer; to her left, water commissioner Asha van Dijk.

Harborlight occupied one table. Vale sat at its center in a dark suit, no tie, with van Hove and two counsel beside him. Rell was absent. His absence seemed calculated without proving calculation.

At the opposing table, no unified party existed. The prosecutor had submitted the metrology finding but took no position on suspension. Elena attended for the Compact reporting authority under her restricted role. Mira had been retained by the municipality for this hearing only. Noor sat behind counsel as owner-observer to the evidence process. Gabriel waited near the rear in his best jacket, summoned because the command sequence included the harbor closure he had disobeyed.

Four people at three tables, not yet a team.

Smit opened with the restriction nobody wanted. “This is not an inquest into Mr. Bensaid’s death. It is not a criminal trial, a referendum on the Littoral Compact, or an appraisal of anticipatory government in general. Our mandate is whether the Rotterdam pilot presents a current operational hazard requiring modification, moratorium, or termination.”

Outside, the chant rose through the glazing: “Eleven. Eleven. Eleven.”

Smit waited for it to recede. “The public may prefer a broader mandate. We have the one law gives us.”

The first presentation belonged to Marijke Vos by video. She described traceable clocks, paired events, uncertainty bands, and the barrier-actuation packet received ten minutes fifty-five seconds before local pressure rise. Harborlight counsel attempted to dislodge the result by asking about resin, temperature, inductive fields, and the camera found in the observation room. Marijke answered with punctilious brevity.

“Did your laboratory conclude that the packet ordered gate closure?” counsel asked.

“No. We concluded its destination class was barrier actuation.”

“Did you conclude it was sent by Dr. Vale?”

“No.”

“Did you conclude it caused Mr. Bensaid’s fatal injury?”

“No.”

“Did you conclude it was abnormal for a forecast system to act before a measured surge?”

“That question exceeds metrology.”

The answers gave Harborlight what it needed without weakening the measurement. Vale’s counsel sat down with the radiance of a man who thought he could trounce an accusation nobody in the room had made. A young aide behind him allowed himself a petulant simper until one glance was enough to reprove him.

Mira was called next.

She explained the public account. Harborlight’s incident summary showed measured surge, confidence threshold breach, gate recommendation, controller acceptance, and actuation in that order. The authenticated packet preceded the first event. In ordinary speech, the summary said the water caused the decision. The devices showed the decision existed before that water.

“Could a probabilistic forecast properly precede local measurement?” Smit asked.

“Yes.”

Several protesters hissed. Smit threatened to clear the gallery.

“Could a system issue a preparatory actuation packet without actually moving the gate?”

“Yes.”

“Could the later surge vindicate the earlier forecast?”

“Yes.”

Vale watched her with neither gratitude nor surprise.

Smit leaned forward. “Then state the hazard.”

“The hazard is not precedence alone. It is that one decision bundle appears to feed physical commands and the archived forecast used to judge those commands. If the same bundle shapes action and later representation, the system can make its decision look externally validated even when the observation did not initiate it.”

“Can,” van Hove interjected.

“Yes,” Mira said. “Can. The architecture permits it. The incident account presents it as what happened. Harborlight has not produced the bundle to show otherwise.”

Vale’s lead counsel, Margot Rees, rose. “Dr. El-Amin, your phrasing externalizes uncertainty. You say the platform *appears* to do something, then invite the commission to impose a forcible restriction unless we disprove your scenario.”

“Your client controls the missing record.”

“Because it contains protected architecture.”

“Then disclose it under seal.”

“The court has not mandated that.”

“This commission can make continued operation conformable to disclosure.”

Rees smiled faintly. “You have become adroit at legal suggestions for an epidemiologist.”

“I am suggesting an audit condition.”

“You are demanding our blueprint.”

“For the command that closed a public gate.”

“A gate which closed before a real squall and may have saved lives.”

The sentence landed. The later squall was not apocrypha. Video showed vessels recalled, workers sheltered, loose equipment secured. Harborlight had issued warnings earlier than the ordinary service. At two berths, those warnings had plainly reduced danger.

Rees displayed the weather reconstruction. A pressure trough approached from the west. Radar returns intensified. Offshore gauges showed a variant surge. A model did not need to wait for Rotterdam water to arrive at Rotterdam instruments.

“You call this self-fulfilling,” Rees said. “But preparation changes outcomes. If a warning prompts protection, the absence of injury does not falsify the warning. That would be illogical.”

“I have not called the weather self-fulfilling.”

“Your public filing uses the phrase.”

“For validation, not weather.”

“A distinction without impact. You deprecate the system because its decisions alter the world against which efficacy is measured.”

“I object because the alteration is omitted.”

“Every intervention alters outcomes. Vaccination changes disease incidence. Triage changes waiting time. A drawbridge warning changes traffic. Must each model pretend it is insentient?”

Mira felt the old breach open under the analogy. In Alexandria, her triage shortcut had altered travel patterns and then measured the resulting queues as if they were demand. She had told herself the model adapted. She had not asked quickly enough which district had been made to wait.

“No,” she said. “It must record its own intervention as a cause.”

“Harborlight does.”

“Then produce the record.”

Rees returned to her table.

Vale asked to address the commission directly. Smit permitted ten minutes.

He did not grandstand. That was part of his power. He stood with one hand resting on the table and spoke in fluent, concrete terms about gates, pump stations, hospital beds, and the cost of waiting until hazard became obvious. He acknowledged that the incident account had condensed the sequence.

“Condensed?” Vermeer asked.

“For public comprehension. The technical log distinguishes forecast trigger from observed confirmation.”

“Why not say that?”

“We should have. The summary was facile. I will not defend it.”

The concession disarmed half the room.

Vale continued. “But a misleading summary does not make a correct warning factitious. Rotterdam was struck by a squall. The barrier sector became hazardous. Harborlight integrated offshore pressure, radar, shipping position, and pump capacity. It acted eleven minutes before one local puck registered surge. That is not scandal. It is the function the municipality commissioned.”

He offered a technical explanation for the shared bundle. Harborlight created a scenario object containing forecast state, proposed actions, and anticipated effects. When a controller accepted a recommendation, the scenario object became the active operational record. The archive later compared predicted conditions with observed outcomes. A single hash across those stages preserved integrity; it did not falsify chronology.

“Why did the public export place observation first?” Mira asked.

“Because the export is organized by event relevance, not database insertion time.”

“Why did it report the local gauge as trigger?”

“It reported it as confirmation.”

“The field says trigger.”

“A translation error in the dashboard layer.”

“And the occupied workboat that became cleared?” Gabriel called from the rear.

Smit struck her microphone. “Captain Okafor, you will be heard when called.”

Vale looked toward him. “That classification was wrong. Your refusal to follow it saved two men. Harborlight’s review has said so.”

Gabriel sat back, antagonized by praise he could not gainsay.

Vale’s explanation was plausible. Worse, parts were probably true. Scenario objects were common. Forecasts needed lead time. Dashboards did contain bad labels. Mira could imagine an engineering organization in which no conspirator sat in a tenebrous room falsifying values, only teams hardening a system whose outputs nobody saw whole.

Smit asked what remedy he proposed.

“Correct the dashboard. Add an external observer to incident review. Preserve the pilot while the criminal inquiry proceeds. Suspension would deprive the city of protection during forecast rainfall tonight.”

“Will you produce the scenario bundle?”

“Under a restriction preventing competitors from reconstructing our model.”

“To this commission?”

“To an agreed independent assessor.”

Mira knew the technique: make access contingent on a future negotiation, then invoke operational urgency against delay. Yet rejecting it made her look like a naysayer to any protection short of shutdown.

The hearing adjourned for thirty minutes.

Chairs scraped, doors swung, and the room’s stored heat escaped into the corridor. An attendant opened a window despite the rain. The astringent smell of wet stone displaced coffee and overheated cable. A black flex from the witness monitor snaked through the doorway where a cleaner had taped it flat with yellow strips. Argument had left Mira's body as if she had been gripping a rail, though she had done nothing more valorous than remain seated and answer.

In the corridor, Noor stood beside a vending machine and listened to the protest through the walls. The chant had become call and antistrophe: “Whose water?” “Our water.” It was euphonious enough to survive repetition and empty enough to admit sundry meanings.

“He has them,” Noor said.

“He has an explanation,” Mira replied.

“That is what I said.”

Gabriel joined them carrying coffee in paper cups. His jacket fit too tightly across the shoulders, and the knot of his tie had migrated. “An explanation that calls the workboat a mistake and the closure a success. Convenient.”

“Both can be true,” Mira said.

“You are a comfort.”

“Would you prefer dishonesty?”

“On a day like this? A little.”

Beside the vending machine, a security clerk had laid out paper bowls of canteen salmagundi, limp rolls, and condiment sachets with the municipal crest. There was plenty of food and no delectation in it, and Mira felt the futility of appetite returning before clarity did. The corridor carried the pervasion of onion, wet wool, and malodorous coffee from a silver urn; Gabriel took a stubborn swig anyway.
