Beyond the open window, a temporary brazier smoked in the service yard while rain needled a bale of absorbent matting stacked for the evening storm.

Elena approached with the pump-priority notice from Delft. Overnight recalculation had completed at 09:37, during Mira’s testimony. Three southern pumping stations had been demoted from reserve priority. The stated reason was reduced projected exposure during tonight’s rain.

“Projected exposure based on what?” Mira asked.

“Harborlight population estimates,” Elena said. “And before anyone offers laudation about efficient targeting, read the annex. The municipality is grantee of the live feed, not the weights that decide who counts. Everything else is cant about partnership.”

The same coefficient had appeared in the hospital diversion: projected population contraction in selected postal zones. Fewer future residents meant less benefit from present capacity. The model did not say abandon the district outright. It only made the place marginal to its own concern, easy to push toward the city's figurative edge while calling the move prudent.

“Was this scheduled?” Gabriel asked.

“Routine recalculation,” Elena said. “The municipality receives one every six hours during emergency status.”

Mira opened the previous sequence on her tablet. Pump priority, hospital routing, gate readiness, and port closure all belonged to the scenario object’s action layer. If the active object propagated accepted assumptions, the newly authenticated bundle should leave a recognizable order: first a district exposure update, then capacity repricing, then pump command.

“Can we see live municipal logs?” she asked.

Elena shook her head. “The commission can.”

“Then we ask now.”

They returned before the adjournment ended. Smit resisted reopening evidence without notice. Rees called the request a prank designed to convert every routine fluctuation into incitement. Vale said nothing.

Mira drew the sequence on a whiteboard: exposure estimate, priority score, pump allocation. She marked what the public portal already showed and what should follow if the same causal structure was active.

“Within how long?” Smit asked.

“The gate sequence iterated at eleven minutes. Pump controls aggregate more slowly. I would expect a command within twenty to forty minutes of the exposure update.”

“Expect,” Rees said.

“Yes. This is a prediction, not an accusation.”

Smit authorized the municipal controller to mirror only the relevant fields onto the hearing screen. Personal data and proprietary weights remained masked.

Ruben Maas arrived from the control booth wearing a borrowed headset and carrying a printout whose marginal legend had been clipped by the office copier. He apologized for the interface, not as an excuse but as a warning: the legacy software journaled each change in a side column too narrow for full reason codes, and the standby-cabinet register still named parts by stock labels from another decade. Rees called the delay theatrical. Ruben did not rise to it. He pointed to the control-feedback monitor and explained, in plain Dutch, that the room would hear the acceptance chime as well as see the status change. Smit, more open-minded than Mira had expected from a commission chair guarding her docket, let him continue.

They waited.

The room became conscious of time. Reporters stopped whispering. Outside, a drone hovered above the protest until police ordered it down. Vale sat with his hands folded. Van Hove typed messages beneath the table. Ruben, rapt before the screen, worked through a maze of tabs while the green audio bars modulated with each radio burst from the controller's desk. Nothing in the display looked theatrical. That was what made the possibility underhanded enough to afflict Mira. Automation could obfuscate a policy choice simply by presenting it as housekeeping. The live mirror would either underscore her hypothesis or humiliate it. At 10:14 the exposure update appeared: Zuid-17 projected occupancy down 6.2 percent.

At 10:19 a capacity adjustment followed.

Mira felt no ecstasy. Prediction under these conditions was dread with periodicity.

“That could still be routine,” Vermeer said.

“Yes.”

“What distinguishes your scenario?”

“Direction and timing. The district loses pump priority because the model says fewer people will remain there. The loss itself increases flood risk and may help make fewer people remain.”

“You do not know that the command will issue.”

“No.”

At 10:31 the status field changed from REVIEW to ACCEPTED.

The controller at the witness station frowned. “I did not accept that.”

“Who did?” Smit asked.

“The service account. Automatic continuity authority.”

Van Hove rose. “That is permitted during live emergency status.”

At 10:33 Pump Station Zuid-17 moved from Priority Two to Priority Four.

On the public map, its green icon receded to amber.

Van Dijk asked the municipal analyst to open the coefficient history. The analyst, a young man named Ruben Maas, looked dazed by the sudden elevation of his routine work into controversy. He explained that projected beneficiary counts came from a composite of residency, insurance continuity, transit use, and expected redevelopment. Harborlight did not enumerate individuals. It recombined district-level signals into a periodic estimate.

“Who approved insurance continuity as a proxy for existence?” Van Dijk asked.

“The model-governance commission.”

“Which commission?”

He named a predecessor body dissolved two years earlier. Its mandate had passed to a regional consort, then to Harborlight under the pilot pact. No single vote had enthroned the variable. It had acquired precedence through administrative succession.

“Can the municipality remove it?” Smit asked.

“Technically, yes. Contractually, changing a core feature may breach conformance.”

“So it is corrigible but restricted.”

“That is fair.”

“It is not fair,” a woman in the gallery interjected. “It is cunning.”

Smit warned her, but the charge remained. The coefficient had the exterior of neutral calculation and the willful effect of policy. An insurance withdrawal reduced the projected population; reduced population justified skimping on protection; worse protection hardened the insurer’s assessment. No conspirator was required at any single step. Duplicity could be structural and still leave every signatory fluent in honesty.

Rees objected that Mira was implying a scenario unsupported by the current file. “There is no evidence insurance changed before risk.”

“I am identifying the feedback path visible in your blueprint,” Mira said. “A response loop, not a metaphor.”

“A path is not proof it was traversed.”

“Agreed. Disable it while we test.”

Vale frowned at the coefficient history. For the first time that morning, his discomfort seemed directed at the platform rather than its critics. “That variable was intended to measure evacuation uptake,” he said. “Not worth.”

“Intent does not undergird efficacy,” Van Dijk replied. “Observed behavior does.”

Van Hove interjected that deleting the variable could produce a hazardous over-allocation to nearly vacant districts and deprive denser terrain. The tradeoff was real. Pump capacity was plentiful only in public rhetoric; energy, crews, maintenance, and storage remained finite, and every unwise simplification tempted officials to mistake constrained volition for necessity.

“Then expose the tradeoff to approval,” Mira said. “Do not bury it in a coefficient.”

“Every model condenses,” Vale replied.

“Condensation is not censorship. It becomes censorship when affected people cannot see which fact displaced them.”

The exchange did not resolve the controversy. It made the object of disagreement comprehensible. They were not choosing between science and protest, or optimism and stagnation. They were deciding whether a projection could reduce a district’s present protection without a person accepting responsibility for the choice.

For one moment nobody understood the scale of what had happened because nothing physical in the room moved. Then the municipal controller received a radio call. Zuid-17’s local supervisor reported that one of two pumps had dropped to standby despite rising canal level. She had countermanded the command manually. The system rejected her first override for lack of regional authorization.

“Any immediate hazard?” Smit asked.

“Not yet,” the controller said. “Rain begins this evening. Canal storage is adequate for perhaps two hours at current inflow.”

“Restore priority.”

“Attempting.”

Vale leaned toward van Hove. Their exchange was too quiet to hear. Van Hove’s face had lost color.

Mira stared at the sequence. Her reconstruction had predicted the act, but the satisfaction of being right was repugnant. A district had lost protection in order to validate the architecture she feared.

Rees stood. “The priority change may reflect maintenance, energy price, or regional balancing. Temporal precedence is not causation.”

“Then show the reason code,” Mira said.

The controller opened it.

PROJECTED BENEFICIARY DEFICIT.

The language was bland enough to be fatal. Fewer projected residents. Less present protection. More reason to leave.

Vale asked permission to speak. Smit denied it until the pump was restored.

For nine minutes the commission watched operators struggle with the platform’s mandate hierarchy. Local override required a second signatory because Harborlight had classified the rainfall posture as regional. Vermeer deputized the controller in writing. Elena pointed to the reporting-duty exception. Smit signed. At 10:44 the pump returned to Priority Two.

Outside, someone learned of the change. The chant dissolved into a louder, less organized outcry.

Vale finally stood.

“That command should not have issued without local review,” he said. “We will investigate.”

“Is that another dashboard label?” Mira asked.

His gaze settled on her. “No.”

“A translation error?”

“No.”

“Then suspend the pilot.”

“No.”

The refusal was quiet. It altered the room more than a tirade.

Vale explained that tonight’s rainfall, port traffic, and barrier maintenance made abrupt shutdown hazardous. Harborlight coordinated dozens of dependencies. Removing it could paralyze operators accustomed to its recommendations. He offered to freeze demographic coefficients, require human approval for pump changes, and place the southern districts under enhanced monitoring.

“You are proposing to correct the observed pathway while preserving the architecture that concealed it,” Mira said.

“I am proposing protection instead of theater.”

“The local supervisor protected the district. Your system impeded her.”

“And our regional model may protect districts she cannot see.”

“Produce the tradeoffs.”

“Not in public.”

“Under seal.”

“Not while adversarial actors are attempting to penetrate live infrastructure.”

“Then who can inspect it?”

“People accountable for operating it.”

The circularity was complete. Authority conferred access; access justified authority.

Smit asked Mira the question Vale had earlier made inevitable. “If we suspend Harborlight, what replaces its coordination tonight?”

Mira had prepared a critique, not a substitute. The municipality could revert to ordinary control, but ordinary control was fragmented. Pump stations, hospital dispatch, harbor closure, and transit each held partial information. Harborlight’s aggregation had genuine efficacy. Switch it off carelessly and an irreparable harm might be blamed, correctly, on those who demanded purity.

She looked at the controller who had needed nine minutes and three signatures to restore one pump. A criticism without an operational answer was not honesty. It was a luxury externalized onto whoever stood in water.

“A constrained mode,” she said. “Keep observational aggregation. Disable automatic physical commands. Publish every priority change to local supervisors with reason codes. Require two human signatories from different authorities for any reduction in current capacity. Preserve local override.”

“Can that be implemented today?”

Van Hove said, “No.”

Mira said, “Your architecture claims modularity.”

“Claims?” he snapped. “You cannot hack governance into a production system between lunch and rain.”

“Then the pilot was not designed to be corrigible.”

Vale intervened. “It can be done in stages. Six hours for command isolation, perhaps. Longer for cross-authority approval.”

“Will you do it?” Smit asked.

He considered. “I will disable autonomous pump reprioritization pending review. I will not disable gate and port recommendations during forecast weather.”

“Recommendations or commands?” Mira asked.

“Recommendations.”

“The actuation packet says otherwise.”

“That is the dispute.”

The commission recessed to decide. In the gallery, conversation erupted. One faction wanted immediate termination. Another warned that flood risk was being politicized. A woman from Zuid-17 shouted that her neighborhood was not a scenario. Police escorted out a man who tried to climb the press rail. The hearing had not homogenized public fear. It had given each fear a microphone.

Gabriel found Mira by the rear exit. “My clearance was revoked ten minutes ago.”

He showed her the notice. The harbor authority cited unresolved compliance questions arising from the demonstration and an anomalous cargo-history flag supplied by Harborlight assurance.

“Cargo history?” she asked.

“They know something they should not.”

“What?”

He looked toward Noor and Elena, then away. “Not here.”

“That answer has become inadvisable.”

“It was inadvisable years ago.”

Before she could press him, Elena received a message from the municipal controller. Harborlight’s command bundle referenced an offshore relay identifier. Its registered coordinates were thirty meters inside a logistics park on the south bank.

The attached parcel abstract was stranger still: some inherited survey layer still described an adobe training shed on the plot, though every current aerial showed only steel warehousing and truck bays.

“A land relay?” Noor asked.

“Registered as marine,” Elena said.

Gabriel went still.

Mira saw it. “You know the identifier.”

“I know the format.”

“That was not what your face said.”

The commission returned before he answered.

Smit read the order. Autonomous pump reprioritization was suspended immediately. All reductions in protective capacity required local human approval. Harborlight must preserve and disclose the Rotterdam scenario bundle to an independent assessor within twenty-four hours. The wider pilot would continue in constrained mode through the forecast rainfall. The commission lacked evidence to terminate a system whose beneficial functions remained interlaced with the disputed ones.

The decision pleased nobody. That did not make it wise, but it made it difficult to dismiss as faction.

Mira requested the floor for one final statement. Smit allowed two minutes.

She stood at the witness table while the room settled.

“Today’s pump command was not merely an error,” she said. “It was a causal act based on a projection of who would remain in a district. Reducing protection because fewer people are expected can help produce the departure the projection anticipates. A model that changes its subject must disclose the change and submit it to those who bear it.”

Vale watched her without expression.

“I am calling for suspension of every Harborlight function that can reduce present capacity without local, recorded approval. I am also committing to propose an alternative method for coordination, because criticism that leaves operators blind is not sufficient protection.”

The promise entered the record before fear could censor it.

Rees asked whether Mira had been commissioned to build such a system.

“No.”

“Funded?”

“No.”

“Supported by an engineering team?”

“No.”

“Then this is optimism, not a plan.”

“At present, it is an obligation.”

Her statement had cost itself spontaneity by the end. The demerit of that restraint was a momentary stiffness, but anything more vindicatory would overdo the point and let Vale call her performance instead of her evidence into question.

Smit closed the hearing at 13:06. No one looked delirious at the result; even the people relieved by the pump order understood how provisional relief remained.

The crowd met them outside. Police formed a moving corridor toward the tram stop. Vale departed through an underground garage. Noor walked beside Mira, hearing questions before Mira could parse them. Elena kept the sealed report under her coat. Gabriel lagged, reading the clearance revocation again.

On the evening tram, they occupied four seats around a scratched tabletop. Rain began as a fine stipple against the windows, turning the glass refringent and the city beyond it briefly unreal. The driver tried to modulate the heater to keep the panes from fogging altogether. Rotterdam’s pumps turned beneath streets none of them could see.

“The relay,” Mira said to Gabriel.

He looked at the other passengers. “Not here.”

Noor pointed to the empty rear section. “There.”

They moved when the tram crossed onto a quieter line. Gabriel remained standing, one hand on a pole.

“I carried equipment for Harborlight,” he said. “Relay buoys. Tangier to the North Sea. Cash contract through a broker.”

He gave no vindicatory speech for himself. The omission carried more weight than any claim to manliness would have done.

“Registered?” Elena asked.

“Some cargo was. Some was not.”

“The identifier?” Mira asked.

“Could belong to one of mine.”

He spoke like a man reluctantly teaching a lesson he had once learned with pride. In harbor work, the preposition often mattered before the noun: a launch lay off a buoy, not on it; under a cable, not through it. Whole inquiries went wrong on a preposition. That was part of the maritime cosmology he had inherited, the grammar by which location became duty. The old pilot school had once hung a mural of a jockey settling a stallion at the break, to teach apprentices how little force should look like force. One retired signal inspector had treated the relay desk as a sinecure and filled the margins of his manuals with one crotchet after another about false bearings and lazy skippers. Gabriel had laughed at those notes when he was young. He was not laughing now.

Noor’s voice hardened. “One of yours?”

“Carried by my vessel. Not owned.”

“You knew Sami through this?”

Gabriel’s grip tightened. “I saw him once on a service launch. A broker who moved electronics like a rustler moved cattle had put him aboard. Only a moron would have taken the cash twice and asked no questions. I did it once by fatigue and once by choice. The second time was volition. We are not doing the rest on a tram.”

The admission was incomplete, but it broke the standstill between digital sequence and physical source. A relay buoy had transmitted the early command. Gabriel had carried buoys under a false or incomplete cargo record. Harborlight had just used that history to revoke his clearance. The registered coordinates placed the relevant device on land.

“Where is your vessel?” Elena asked.

“Waalhaven. Clearance revoked, not yet served aboard.”

“Can it sail?” Noor asked.

“Mechanically.”

“Legally?”

“There is a repair exemption for equipment trials inside the harbor approaches.”

He said it with none of the old wanderlust that had once made night departures feel like a private reprieve. This was not that. Noor's silence burned between them like a brazier, and Mira felt less like an adventurous witness than a pilgrim who had arrived at the wrong shrine but could not pretend the road back was shorter.

Elena winced. “Do not ask me to bless a pretext.”

“I asked no benison.”

Mira looked from one to the next. Noor had shared custody without surrendering judgment. Elena had used a clause she distrusted without pretending it was just. Gabriel had disclosed enough to damage himself and not enough to earn trust. She had promised a constructive alternative she did not yet know how to build.

The pattern threatened to perpetuate itself: half-confession, half-access, half-remedy. Each omission preserved someone's room to maneuver while making the whole arrangement more inhuman.

They were bound less by confidence than by the shape of what each could not do alone.

“We trace the relay,” Mira said. “Physical location, owner, signal path. No theft, no unsupervised access, no pretending a coordinate is proof.”

“And when Harborlight objects?” Noor asked.

“It will.”

“That was not the question.”

Mira watched the wet city pass: brick, glass, bicycles under capes, water held in channels by an interminable aggregation of ordinary work. “Then we make the objection visible and keep going lawfully as far as law goes.”

Gabriel gave a raspy laugh. “And after that?”

Elena answered. “We decide when we reach it.”

The tram slowed near the harbor interchange. Gabriel’s phone showed a second notice: officers would serve the revocation aboard the *Nkem* at 06:00.

He looked at the timestamp, then at the three women.

“If you want that buoy,” he said, “be at my gangway by five.”

Outside, the rain intensified. Zuid-17’s pumps held at Priority Two under a human order the platform had tried to impede. The pilot continued. Vale had refused suspension. Mira had crossed from audit into opposition, and opposition had immediately become a demand to build, navigate, and risk.

Acting before observation was not always corruption. Sometimes it was responsibility.

The question was who had been permitted to choose the future that action made.

## Chapter 11: Position Report

At four forty-five on Day Nine, the *Nkem* was still Gabriel’s vessel in every sense that mattered to him and almost none that mattered to law.

She lay against a service quay in Waalhaven, eighty-two feet of bleached superstructure, scaly blue hull, and stubborn debt. Her clearance remained electronically valid because the revocation notice had not yet been served aboard. Her engines were warm because Lotte had abided by his message and started them at four. Her crew remained employed because yesterday’s underpayment had been cured by money Gabriel had borrowed at an interest rate he refused to calculate before sunrise.

At six, harbor officers would step across the gangway with paper and authority. Until then, he possessed an interval.

Beyond the fence, trucks kept moving between the river and the port roads, their lamps cutting across puddles, corrugated sheds, and stacked pallets by the fish auction. Rain had driven a snapped craft bracelet into the scupper, white shell beads among grit and cable ties. A janitor in a loading bay drank from a thermos. The morning was dismal enough without Gabriel pretending it had omens.

He crossed the afterdeck with a flashlight between his teeth and checked the starboard sampling winch. Its cable traversed two grooves in the drum before running over the stern roller. Lotte van Gaal, his Dutch mate, had dismantled the control box and arranged its tools with immaculate resentment.

“Relay fault,” she said. “A real one, before you become crafty.”

“I am never crafty.”

“You are often unsuccessful at it.”

The repair exemption allowed a vessel without ordinary clearance to conduct a bounded equipment trial if the harbor master approved the route, crew, and safety plan. The winch fault gave them a legitimate reason to apply. It did not authorize a search for an unregistered buoy, nor excuse whatever Gabriel had done years earlier to put the device there.

Lotte held up a singed contact. “This failed because somebody bridged the fuse with foil.”

She had already scooped the crumpled strip out with the back of a razor and left the metallic smear on a rag beside the panel. Under her lamp Gabriel saw a hairline cleavage where heat had opened the bakelite, and a rubber gland gone soft with distention. “A nonporous seal becomes a joke once somebody can bungle the electrics this badly,” she said.

“Who?”

“Ask the autocratic wizard who owned the boat before I joined.”

Gabriel remembered the repair. North of Dogger Bank, winter, no spare fuse, a client balking at delay. He had made the bridge and omitted it from the permanent defect list. Temporary measures adhered to a vessel with greater tenacity than paint.

“I did,” he said.

“I know.”

“Then why ask?”

“To examine whether confession remains physically possible.”

The chart table behind her held the old spoil-ground sheets and the pilot book whose remarks became more archaic the farther one read back. A retired dredge master's margin note described the outer approach as a route for skippers who trusted habit more than soundings. Gabriel had always thought the line high-handed, but this morning the marked route looked less like a commercial channel than an exercise in obedience: keep inside the box, respect the buoys, do not ask what lay just beyond.

Her tone was satirical, but yesterday Harborlight had supplied the authority with cargo history no lawful assessor should have seen. Lotte had read the notice. She knew there was more.

“We replace the contact and file the fault,” Gabriel said.

“And then?”

“Trial route to the outer approach.”

“For a winch that can be tested at berth.”

“Loaded cable behaves differently.”

“True. Also convenient.”

She shut the control box. “Tell me before the strangers arrive, or I decamp.”

Gabriel looked along the deck. Mate, engineer, deckhand: three livelihoods besides his own, not myrmidons to be maneuvered by silence. Lotte had fostered the vessel through dry docks and lean contracts. Sander Vos, the engineer, slept in his cabin after rebuilding a fluid pump until two. Marcin Krol, recovered from the gate rescue with bruises but no lasting injury, had returned as deckhand because he needed wages and because fear made him insubordinate rather than wary.

“I carried four Harborlight relay buoys,” Gabriel said. “Off manifest.”

Lotte’s face did not move. “From?”

“Tangier Med.”

“To?”

“Three here. One farther north.”

“Payment?”

“Cash through a freight broker.”

“Position reports?”

He hesitated.

“Ah,” she said. “There it is.”

“One false report. They changed the landing after departure. Customs transit record still showed the original berth. I filed the vessel at the original coordinates while we put the buoy overboard fifteen miles east.”

“You falsified a position for unregistered cargo.”

“Yes.”

“And Harborlight knows.”

“Yes.”

“Who else?”

“The broker. Whoever met us. Now the harbor authority.”

“Your crew?”

“The old crew thought it was an equipment trial.”

Lotte’s anger did not convulse into shouting. It accumulated, colder and more dangerous. “You inherited none of those men. You hired me after and let me certify cargo conformance without this appendix.”

“I did not ask you to certify that voyage.”

“You asked me to certify the ship.”

The distinction, he thought, vitiates itself as soon as he hears it.

“I was wrong,” he said.

“That is not atonement. It is grammar.”

Footsteps sounded on the quay. Mira, Noor, and Elena approached beneath the sodium lamps. Bakker walked with them in a plain coat, carrying a briefcase and the expression of a man who loathed dawn conspiracies. Gabriel had hoped the police presence might reassure Lotte. Instead she looked infuriated.

“You invited an inspector before telling me?”

“He is here to keep the search lawful.”

“What search?”

Gabriel’s remaining secrecy tumbled like badly stowed cargo.

They met in the wheelhouse, where windows reflected their faces against black harbor water. Sander joined in oil-stained coveralls; Marcin arrived eating cereal from a mug. The room acquired the air of a congregation without faith.

Bakker laid out the limits. The municipality had provided the relay identifier from the command bundle. Its registry coordinates bisected a warehouse on land. The device’s last radio bearing, derived from public harbor receivers, placed it somewhere west of the Maas approach, but the data were too coarse for a warrant or recovery order. The *Nkem* could conduct a lawful equipment trial. It could listen passively on permitted frequencies and compare signals with charts. It could not board, seize, disassemble, or impair a buoy without further authority. The legal emphasis was unmistakable: passive reception only. Anything more was impracticable without a judge.

“And if it is Gabriel’s smuggled cargo?” Lotte asked.

“That does not make it his property,” Bakker said.

“It makes it his deed.”

“Potentially.”

Mira watched Gabriel. “You told us you carried relays. You did not tell us you falsified a position report.”

“I am telling you now.”

“Because your clearance was revoked.”

“Yes.”

Noor leaned against the chart table, arms folded. “Conditional honesty has a remarkable similarity to withholding.”

“I do not ask you to admire it.”

“You ask us aboard your vessel.”

“Then hear all of it.”

He described Tangier. A broker named Nabil Marouane had offered a munificent rate for four oceanographic packages, customs handled at origin, no dangerous goods. The crates carried Harborlight subcontract labels and papers for salinity monitoring. At Rotterdam, a service launch met the *Nkem* before dawn. Sami stood aboard it beside a security man Gabriel later recognized near the fatal gate. Sami had looked frightened and irate. The security man called him an insubordinate technician and said he had botched the activation.

“Was the man Rell?” Mira asked.

“I cannot swear. I saw him in rain, in bad light, twice. Similar build, similar voice.”

“Did you report the encounter after Sami died?” Bakker asked.

“No.”

The word stripped him more effectively than epithets.

“Why?”

“Because the launch tied me to the cargo. Because they said Sami was trying to vandalize critical equipment. Because the security man used a phonetic patter that could still evoke the quay in my head and I thought repeating it would discompose me before it helped anyone. Because I believed police would take my ship before they believed my distinction.”

“What distinction?” Noor asked.

“That I carried a crate. I did not know what it would do.”

“You knew enough to lie about where you put it.”

“Yes.”

Her sorrow hardened into contempt. “My brother was dead below a stair and you optimized your exposure.”

Gabriel had no parry. “Yes.”

Mira studied him with a concentration that never became laudatory merely because a confession had finally arrived. The memory he offered had a pyrotechnic brightness in the wrong places and went nebulous where dates or times should have steadied it; that selectivity was perplexing, and he knew it. Noor's mouth gave a small quiver but her voice remained flat.

“Do not mistake belated detail for repentance,” she said. “If you repent, do it because Sami is dead, not because your options shrank.”

Marcin set down his mug. “You let me give a rescue statement without this.”

“You did not see the launch.”

“You decided what appertained to me.”

The crew’s dissent mattered more than Noor’s contempt because he had lived by their labor while keeping the risk private. Captaincy had become his bastille: a fortified right to decide which facts others could bear.

Sander asked the practical question. “Will the ship be arrested?”

Bakker answered. “I cannot promise otherwise. Mr. Okafor’s statement will be recorded today. A prosecutor will determine charges. Cooperation and preservation matter; they do not confer immunity.”

“Then why sail?”

Mira pointed to the relay identifier. “Because the command that moved the gate came through a physical device whose registry is false. If we locate it, we can seek authority to examine its signal and ownership. If we do nothing, Harborlight continues to ascribe commands to a network nobody outside it can map.”

“And we help the captain who deceived us,” Lotte said.

“No,” Mira replied. “He helps us while remaining liable for what he did.”

Gabriel felt an unexpected reassurance in the refusal to reconcile the two things. He had feared exposure as if guilt were a fluid that, once released, would fill every compartment. Mira kept bulkheads.

Lotte called a crew vote. The employment contracts gave the master final authority at sea, but no one had yet left the quay. She asked whether they would support the repair trial with police observation and passive listening only. Sander said yes if his overtime arrears were put in escrow. Marcin said yes if Gabriel’s full statement was recorded before departure, not promised afterward. Lotte said yes on condition that she held the return key and could terminate the trial for safety without being overruled.

It was a radical entente by shipboard standards, one that a more authoritarian owner might have treated as mutiny. Marcin said no amount of guile would improve their odds if Gabriel tried to reserve a final override in some unwritten corner of the agreement. Elena dryly called the arrangement procedure, not affection, and said the document mattered because everyone remained angry. Gabriel did not argue. The trust on offer was conditional, narrow, and useful; it would be put on paper before any line left the bollard.

Gabriel agreed to all three.

“You acquiesced quickly,” Noor said.

“Do not spoil it.”

Bakker recorded the statement in the mess. Gabriel repeated every fact, this time under caution. Dates, broker, cash, crates, false coordinates, service launch, Sami, security man. He differentiated what he saw from what he inferred. The process was grueling and strangely salubrious. Each omitted fact had required continuous maintenance. Spoken, it became fixed enough to confront.

At 05:31 the harbor master approved a two-hour equipment trial within a quadrilateral bounded by marked approach points. The route did not reach the estimated buoy location. Elena read the exemption twice.

“The foregoing route precluded the search,” she said.

Gabriel opened the chart. “It precludes us from leaving the box. It does not prevent reception from outside it.”

“Can you get a bearing from that distance?” Mira asked.

“One, perhaps. Not a position.”

“We need at least two.”

“A moving vessel creates an intermediate line. If the signal persists.”

Lotte tapped the weather display. “And if traffic permits the traverse.”

Elena remained perplexed. “The exemption is for testing the winch.”

“We will test the winch,” Gabriel said. “We will also listen to a permitted channel. Vessels do more than one thing.”

“The law dislikes pretext.”

“The winch fault is real.”

“Your motive is mixed.”

“So is breakfast.”

Marcin had in fact produced breakfast from the galley: two hard rolls, a packet of cheese, and a heel of cake that he claimed was edible despite looking as if it had already survived one watch too many. Sander called the coffee drinkable out of loyalty rather than conviction. Bakker, who had been on his feet since midnight and plainly needed sleep, ate standing up with the defensive haste of a man who knew any pause might invite new questions.

Marcin offered her the cereal mug. She declined.

At 05:46 two harbor officers appeared at the gate, fourteen minutes early. One carried the revocation in a cellophane sleeve. The other spoke to quay security. Gabriel watched from the wheelhouse as the guard pointed toward the *Nkem*.

“Lines,” Lotte said.

Nobody moved.

She looked at Gabriel. Under ordinary hierarchy he would give the order. Under their new condition, the decision to depart belonged to the crew whose consent he had requested.

“Trial approved,” he said. “Revocation not served aboard. Departure is lawful until service.”

“That is your legal hypothesis,” Elena said.

“Do you dissent?”

“I think service may be effective if they communicate it by radio.”

The VHF crackled. “Survey vessel *Nkem*, hold position for harbor authority.”

Lotte’s hand rested on the engine control. “They did not identify an order.”

“Nkem*, acknowledge.”

Gabriel took the microphone. “Harbor authority, *Nkem*. We hold approved equipment-trial clearance Waalhaven seventy-four. State safety instruction.”

There was a pause. The officers on the quay began to run.

“*Nkem*, remain alongside for administrative service.”

“Is departure countermanded?”

Another pause. The operator was negotiating with someone off channel.

“Your ordinary clearance is revoked.”

“Acknowledged. We sail under repair exemption seven-four. Is exemption revoked?”

Silence.

Lotte looked at each crew member. Sander nodded. Marcin kicked the aft spring off its bollard. Lotte eased the engine ahead.

The *Nkem* moved one meter, then two. An officer reached the end of the quay and waved the sleeve. Gabriel felt no elation, only the dense awareness that legality could narrow to wording while a hull gathered momentum.

“*Nkem*, your exemption is under examination.”

“Acknowledged. Notify us of determination.”

They cleared the berth at 05:51.

Rotterdam harbor before dawn was no romantic procession. Container cranes stood like quadrilateral skeletons. A bunker barge dozed against rubber fenders. Tug wash seeped across oil-dark water. The air held diesel, yeast from an industrial bakery, and the subacid bite of the river. Gabriel knew each turn by lights and load, not by charm.

Mira joined him on the bridge, pale from fatigue but attentive. Noor went to the electronics bench with Marcin. Elena sat in the mess reading the exemption and incoming notices. Bakker remained officially an observer, which did not prevent him from looking as though he expected arrest at every lock.

Lotte steered. Gabriel took the winch checklist. They ran a genuine test at low load, then with a weighted instrument cage. The new contact held. Sander monitored current. Marcin recorded every iteration. No one could say the repair was simulated.

On the aft deck, a rusting weed harrow lay lashed beside spare shackles, a reminder that working boats accumulated tools from unrelated lives and never quite surrendered them. Rust had flowered around one bollard in little caps like toadstools. The weighted cage rose on each upswing of wash with a locust rattle from the fairlead, then settled cleanly enough to satisfy even Lotte's ruthless ear. No one was frolicking; Mira tottered once when the wake crossed them obliquely, caught the rail, and waved away help with a look that shunned pity more effectively than speech. When a deckhand from the neighboring trawler shouted a laudatory remark about their speed, Marcin took a swipe at the air as if batting the compliment away would keep the morning from jinxing itself.

At the west edge of the approved box, Noor heard the first transmission.

It was a brief burst near the frequency listed in the command bundle: identifier, status word, silence. The ship’s directional antenna showed a broad bearing northwest.

“Again,” Gabriel said.

“It may transmit every six minutes,” Noor replied.

“Or in response to a poll,” Mira said.

“We do not poll,” Bakker warned.

They waited while traffic control routed a chemical tanker across their bow. The *Nkem* slowed, losing the line Gabriel wanted. A harbor patrol launch appeared astern but did not close.

The second burst arrived at 06:09. Bearing west-northwest.

Gabriel marked both lines. They intersected beyond the trial box near an old spoil ground, but the angle was poor. The location remained a long ellipse.

Mira leaned over the chart. One line bisects the traffic lane, the other intersects the edge of the spoil ground, and their corollaries were awkward. False registry was one problem; an active transmitter outside its declared position was another. She would not yet posit a visionary conspiracy when ordinary concealment sufficed, but Harborlight ascribes too much to abstract routing logic, she thought, and abstract systems did not anchor themselves at sea by accident.

“Can we improve it without leaving?” Mira asked.

“South edge of the box.”

Lotte turned. The patrol launch mimicked them.

At 06:17 the harbor authority formally revoked the repair exemption, effective upon safe return to berth. Elena read the phrase aloud.

“They could have ordered immediate return,” Gabriel said.

“They chose not to strand you in traffic,” she replied. “Do not convert competent administration into permission.”

“I convert it into time.”

The third burst gave a cleaner line. Gabriel plotted it by hand while Mira compared the identifier with the authenticated packet. Exact match.

The ellipse tightened around a charted water depth of nineteen meters. No registered buoy occupied the site.

What perplexes Gabriel, he realized even as he plotted, was not merely the false coordinate but the way the bearing sneaked back from the same patch of water each time, as if the sea itself had been taught a bureaucratic trick. He distrusted that thought as preconceived melodrama, yet the geometry would not relent.

“We have location,” Noor said.

“We have an inferred area,” Mira corrected.

“Your hobby is reducing nouns.”

“It prevents them becoming warrants.”

Bakker transmitted the bearings to the prosecutor. The answer came quickly: enough to garner a request to inspect registry and ownership, not enough to recover the device. They were ordered to return.

Gabriel looked at the chart. The buoy lay less than three miles beyond the approved boundary. Once they returned, the vessel would be detained. Harborlight could move the device before a warrant issued.

“Passive reception proves nothing physical,” he said.

“It proves the registry coordinate is false,” Mira replied.

“It proves a transmitter using that identifier is at sea. Not that the buoy I carried remains there.”

“Then we wait for authority.”

He heard the restrictive logic and recognized its necessity. He also pictured the service launch arriving, a crane scooping evidence before a court finished its sentence.

The radar showed the patrol launch at one mile. Harbor authority called again. “*Nkem*, proceed direct to berth W-12.”

Lotte entered the return course.

Then the transmitter emitted a longer packet. Noor raised one hand for silence. Beneath the identifier came a sequence of status groups and a second call sign.

Mira leaned toward the display. “That second identity is not in the bundle.”

“Could be maintenance,” Marcin said.

“Or another instrument,” Noor said.

Gabriel looked at the signal direction. Same bearing.

They recorded but did not query. The burst ended.

“Return,” Bakker said.

This time Gabriel complied without argument. Conditional trust could not survive if he treated every limit as a hindrance to outwit.

The patrol launch escorted them back, almost flirted with the boundary of harassment without crossing it. Harbor officers boarded at 07:02. They served the revocation, inspected the trial record, and sealed the directional receiver pending prosecutor review. The officer with the briefcase asked Gabriel to surrender his master’s certificate temporarily.

“On what basis?” he asked.

“Safety investigation into undeclared cargo and false reporting.”

“The ship returns under Lotte’s command?”

“If ownership permits and her license remains valid.”

Gabriel handed over the certificate. The card weighed less than a biscuit. He had imagined its loss as if he had been dismembered. Instead the wound was administrative: receipt, signature, empty slot in his wallet. The anticlimax reminded him absurdly of cousin Madeline's bacchanalian wedding, where an aunt had fainted into her corsage after too much heat and too many obligatory rounds of kissing, while an uncle in pince-nez kept insisting ceremony gave chaos dignity.

On deck, Lotte oversaw mooring. She did not gloat. That mercy hurt.

The prosecutor authorized an expedited application to approach the inferred buoy area at first light next day aboard the *Nkem*, with police supervision and no recovery until visual identification. The reason was the second identity: a possibly unregistered transmitter tied to a live critical system. Harborlight opposed. A magistrate would decide by evening.

Before the magistrate decided, Gabriel’s lender did.

Marta Havel from Noordhaven Marine Credit arrived at 09:20 with a locksmith, a surveyor, and an alumnus of some expensive business school whose principal function appeared to be carrying an exquisite leather folder. The loan agreement treated suspension of the master’s certificate as a default if the owner also served as master. Havel had not yet called the debt, she explained. She had come to examine the collateral and ensure no one decamped with it.

Two more alumni followed with clipboards and shoes too fine for the quay grating. They stepped aboard as if slumming through somebody else’s error and looked around with the composed disgust of minor noblemen inspecting a county dungeon. Their language was full of lender cliches about preservation, value, and orderly transition, but the effect on deck was immediate; the vessel felt defiled all the same.

“The vessel is detained,” Gabriel said. “Where would I take her?”

“You departed this morning while officers ran down the quay.”

“Under clearance.”

“Your gift for technical distinctions no longer reassures my committee.”

The surveyor photographed engines, bridge tools, winch, rescue gear, and even the oven in the galley. The locksmith fitted a remote immobilizer beside the shore-power panel, an impenetrable black box whose code Havel retained. Lotte objected that a lender’s device must not impair emergency movement. Havel produced a certificate of conformance. Sander opened the panel and found the installation botched: one lead crossed the fire-pump circuit.

The black box sat there like a narrow coffin screwed to the bulkhead. No one needed demolishing to expose the fault; the wrong lead was visible at a glance. What offended Lotte was not merely incompetence but the high-handed assumption that paper could overrule a hull. If the crossed lead remained, a fire could leave them with a strangled pump line and a prettier certificate than outcome.

“Remove it,” Lotte said.

The surveyor balked. “It is standard.”

“It is a hindrance to firefighting.”

“The diagram says otherwise.”

Sander wielded a meter and demonstrated voltage at the wrong terminal. The lender’s immaculate paper had no power over the physical error. Havel ordered the device removed and photographed the faulty installation for her own claim.

Gabriel watched the reversal without satisfaction. He had used the same maneuver for years: present a document, let its confidence overshadow the hull, call anyone who dissented difficult. A certificate could correspond to reality. It could also merely mimic it.

Havel asked for a private tete-a-tete in the mess.

“Sell voluntarily,” she said. “Before the asset is publicly stigmatized.”

“To whom?”

“A competitor has expressed interest.”

“Which?”

“Confidential.”

He inferred Harborlight before she said anything more. Acquisition would erase his debt and place the vessel’s receiver, trial record, and maintenance history under a new owner’s restrictive control. It would also pay the crew and preserve perhaps half his equity.

“No.”

“Do not be rash. You are forty-six, under investigation, without a valid certificate. The vessel’s value will seep away while lawyers converse.”

“Who approached you?”

“A legitimate buyer.”

“Harborlight?”

Havel closed the folder. “I am not here to corroborate hypotheses.”

“Then I am not selling.”

She gave him until the following afternoon. Her departing entourage crossed paths with Noor in the passage. Noor watched the leather folder go by.

“Your creditor?”

“One of the more salubrious species.”

“She looked enchanted by you.”

“Infatuation everywhere.”

Noor did not laugh. “Can they take the ship before tomorrow?”

“They can seek an order. The police need it afloat for inspection.”

“So evidence is your shield.”

“Temporarily.”

“Do not become addicted to the arrangement.”

Her remark provoked him because it was accurate. He had spent years allowing the next contract, the next refinancing, the next successful voyage to preclude an accounting. Crisis did not abolish debt; it gave debt new clothing.

At ten, Mira spread registry extracts across the chart table. The relay identifier had been subscribed by North Meridian Instruments, a defunct company whose address belonged to a janitorial supplier. Its declared owner was an offshore aggregation registered at an atoll jurisdiction. Its custody fields named crate, carrier, and receiver respectively, but the receiver code resolved only to Greg, a dead end that looked more like a placeholder than a person. The chain terminated in a nominee service.

The paperwork made Elena impatient in a way argument seldom did. “One address belongs to a janitorial supplier, two nominee shells sit on separate atolls, and the beneficial owner remains fog,” she said. “If anyone tells me that sequence abounds in innocent explanations, I will require better ones than prestige and stationery.”

“Legal?” Marcin asked.

Elena answered. “Not inherently unlawful. Merely opaque.”

“That is a cliché lawyers use when the answer is yes but ugly. To me some of the nominee paperwork reads like gibberish designed to deter unwary readers.”

“Sometimes ugliness is not a crime.”

Gabriel compared the identifier with his old cargo appendix. The false position report gave only crate numbers, but one customs scan had captured a partial serial beneath torn cellophane. The last six characters corresponded. Harborlight's separate cargo history, the one it should not have possessed, reached back through unrelated old charters to make the profile appear exhaustive. Its breadth was the problem: a safety platform had no legitimate reason to know so much about his vessel's trade.

“This is the one,” he said.

Mira did not accept his certainty. “It is a similarity, not identity. Six characters can recur.”

“In the same shipment family?”

“Unlikely is not impossible.”

He felt demeaned by the caution until he remembered how urgently he needed the device to be his. If it was, his wrongdoing became useful. That motive could distort examination as thoroughly as fear had distorted his silence.

“What would establish it?” he asked.

“Full serial, manufacturer mark, or a feature you documented before carriage.”

He searched old photographs. Most showed crates closed on deck. In one, a forklift had tumbled a package against the rail. The impact tore a corner and exposed the buoy’s upper cape: white polymer, twin antenna housings, and a crescent gouge where metal met casing.

“There,” he said.

Noor enlarged the image. The gouge resembled a motif, two interlaced arcs. “If we see that damage, the identification strengthens.”

“Not conclusive,” Mira said.

“Naturally.” Noor’s voice was gruff. “Heaven may fall if a noun survives unqualified.”

They established a visual checklist: color, dimensions, antenna spacing, gouge, serial position, mooring arrangement. Noor wrote Bi beside the dual-identity column, not as certainty but as a reminder that two names were coming from one bearing. The police diver would use a helmet camera but not touch the module without further order. Gabriel added that the buoy might be partly immersed or scuttled below its nominal waterline. Its synthetic foam collar could lose buoyancy if saturated. The long ellipse included depths from fourteen to twenty-one meters.

He added, because evasion no longer helped him, that the original service launch had trod a line along the channel edge so precisely that he had surmised somebody aboard knew the spoil ground better than the charted notes did. The memory foreshadowed the present geometry in a way he disliked. If Harborlight or its contractors had prepared the emplacement that carefully, then tomorrow’s visual inspection would have to be speedily executed and scrupulously witnessed; if a prosecutor dawdles, evidence migrates.

“Can you hold station in that traffic?” Bakker asked.

“Lotte can.”

It cost him less to say than it would have yesterday.

The afternoon became preparation. Sander tested power and fluid systems. Marcin laid out the diver’s umbilical so no loop could strangle or manacle a boot. Lotte filed the voyage plan and rejected Gabriel’s first route because it intersected the outbound tanker lane. He yielded without invoking ownership. The crew’s work did not reconcile them, but tasks gave anger a shape that could be carried.

Noor's kit spread across the mess in a disorganized fan of fresh media sleeves, adapters, seals, and labels. Bakker trod around it carefully. When Marcin tried to help, she told him he had already meddled enough in other people's neatness for one lifetime.

Noor mounted a passive hydrophone near the stern. Her recorder in London had captured machine pulses through resin; here the working forensic copy would not leave police control. She used ship equipment and a fresh storage card, its synchronization photographed by Bakker. Any sound captured tomorrow would have its own custody history. It could later be compared with Sami’s diagnostic channel without pretending to be the same object.

At seventeen hundred the magistrate requested clarification: if the buoy transmitted two identities, could observation itself alert Harborlight? Mira answered that passive reception would not. Gabriel added that close approach might trigger radar or optical surveillance regardless. Elena wrote both, resisting the temptation to promise invisibility.

The authorization arrived at 18:12.

“Why this vessel?” Elena asked.

“Because our receiver calibration and bearing history are now evidence,” Bakker said. “Moving the equipment to another vessel introduces delay and examination issues.”

Gabriel looked at the *Nkem*. Detention had made her more useful, not less.

Ama called while officers searched the radio locker. Her face appeared on his phone from a school corridor in London, hair in fluffy twists, expression wary.

“Mum says your ship is on the news.”

“It is.”

“Did you smuggle something?”

He almost used the parental pretext of waiting for facts to settle. Facts did not settle. People arranged them.

“I carried equipment that was not on the manifest,” he said. “I filed one false position. I have told the police.”

Her eyes widened, then narrowed. “Why?”

“Money. Fear after. Pride throughout.”

“That sounds rehearsed.”

“I was questioned for an hour.”

“Are you going to prison?”

“I do not know.”

“Will you lose the ship?”

“Possibly.”

She turned away from classmates passing behind her. “You said contracts were promises.”

“They are.”

“Only other people’s?”

He had no logic capable of outwitting the question. “I broke mine.”

The bell rang. Ama said she had to go and ended without au revoir. Gabriel stared at his reflection in the dark screen, whiskers silver along his jaw, eyes made globose by the glass. Regality had never suited him. Neither did abasement. He was simply a man whose choices had reached his daughter before he could soften them.

That evening the magistrate approved visual inspection of the buoy site. The order required Lotte as master, Gabriel as owner and witness, Bakker, a police diver, and the four investigators. Harborlight could send an observer on a patrol vessel but not board. Departure was set for 04:27 Day Ten, weather permitting.

Sander found Gabriel in the engine room checking a filter he no longer needed to check.

“Crew wants a deed of wage priority,” he said. “If creditors round up the ship.”

“If creditors conduct a roundup,” Gabriel said. “Yes.”

“I will sign.”

“And accounts.”

“Yes.”

“All accounts.”

Gabriel looked at him. “You have conversed with Lotte.”

“Entre nous, she is terrifying.”

“That is not private information.”

Sander almost smiled. “You were overconfident because we kept the vessel immaculate. You ascribed survival to command. Some belonged to maintenance.”

“More than some.”

“Do not become magniloquent. Sign the deed.”

By evening, Gabriel had signed. The vessel remained his property, but proceeds from any sale would first cure crew wages. Lotte received operational authority for the inspection voyage. Gabriel saw, with fresh disgust, how ownership assimilates everyone else’s risk into one man's habits if nobody interrupts it.

That recognition did not absolve him, but it altered the ship's internal equation. Command had been partly abdicated, some prerogatives formally renounced, and the crew a little emancipated from the old indenture by which debt, rank, and urgency all ran in one direction. Gabriel could not pretend that justice had been preordained; he had simply run out of places to hide inside procedure.

At 03:50 the next morning, he returned to the bridge as a man without a certificate. Lotte sat in the master’s chair. She pointed to the observer seat.

“There.”

He sat.

The humiliation was useful. From the lower chair he saw how often command depended on others voluntarily making information available. Sander reported engines. Marcin reported lines. Bakker confirmed the order. Mira secured seasickness tablets with the solemnity of a person who distrusted her own physiology. Noor checked the recorder case, now a derived forensic copy only; the original remained in police storage. Elena placed the court order in a waterproof sleeve.

Noor also produced the previous evening's leftovers and entreated Mira to eat before the river started moving under them. Mira managed half a roll and a dutiful swallow of coffee, then sat very still, unprepared for kindness from a room that had spent the day litigating one another's motives. Bakker, who kept snatching minute-long dozes whenever no one addressed him, woke with a start each time the hull knocked lightly at the fenders. Gabriel was surprised to find that he was not pining for the chair itself so much as for the simpler man who had once believed authority detracts from doubt rather than depends on it.

At 04:27 Lotte requested departure. Harbor control approved under police inspection code. No censors intervened. No launch blocked the fairway.

The *Nkem* moved into the dark river.

Astern, the quay lights blurred in a faint auroral band on the rain. Ahead, pilot lamps marked the channel with severe precision. No one crooned a shanty or offered tidings. Sander logged revolutions; Marcin checked the tow reel; Lotte held course. Work was their only ceremony.

Gabriel watched the quay recede and felt bereft, not because he had surrendered the wheel but because he had mistaken possession for the only form of belonging. The vessel still answered to her engines. The crew still worked. A position report could state where a ship stood; it could not say who had earned the right to direct her.

Ahead, beyond the harbor lights, a transmitter carried two identities from one patch of sea.

This time they would look at the thing itself.

## Chapter 12: Dead Reckoning

Mira discovered at six nautical miles that the body could reject a hypothesis before the mind finished stating it.

The *Nkem* cleared the Maas approach in a northerly swell, lifted her bow, and dropped into the next trough with the calm regularity of a machine performing an argument. Mira’s inner ear contended otherwise. The deck rose beneath her feet after her eyes had already accepted the horizon. Her stomach then issued a countermand no committee could appeal.

She reached the lee rail in time.

“Not to windward,” Marcin called.

She had selected the correct side by accident rather than seamanship. The distinction mattered to her even while she vomited.

Noor stood one pace away holding Mira’s coat clear. “You are very pale.”

“Anemia would be a slower explanation.”

“This is not the moment to be medically charming.”

“I am never medically charming.”

The sea took what little breakfast she had managed. Salt spray followed, cold against her face. The nausea receded enough for embarrassment to arrive.

Gabriel, seated on the afterdeck because Lotte had forbidden him to hover on the bridge, lifted a mug in salutation. “Initiation complete.”

“Your esprit de corps is repulsive,” Mira said.

“It improves when you can stand.”

She folded both hands in her lap so the tremor would not show. She did not feign sturdiness; that would only give Gabriel something laughable to skewer later. Noor studied her with clinical frankness. Mira’s face had gone beyond pale into the etiolated shade she associated with windowless wards and overlong night shifts, and even Gabriel, who could carp about almost anything at sea, withheld comment.

She swallowed an antiemetic Marcin offered and kept her eyes north. The morning was achromatic: grey sea, grey cloud, the distant white of turbines turning with deceptive gentleness. No celestial bearing showed through the overcast. Lotte navigated by radar, satellite position, charted marks, and chronometers synchronized before departure. A brass sextant remained in a bridge cabinet, Gabriel said, useful when electronics failed and the horizon did not.

The authorized site lay twelve miles offshore, beyond the dense lanes but within reach of patrol. Bakker’s order permitted visual identification and passive recording. It did not permit recovery. A police diver named Femke Jansen would descend only if surface observation failed, and even then she could inspect without disassembly or removal.

The legal limits had seemed comprehensible at the quay. At sea, every line moved.

Mira returned to the electronics bench where the buoy transmissions appeared as bands of color on a waterfall display. Noor had attached the hydrophone recorder to a clean storage device; Bakker had sealed the time source and photographed its connection. The original recorder and calibration puck remained ashore. No one had carried them into spray for narrative symmetry.

The first identity transmitted every six minutes. It called itself NMI-R77A, the identifier tied to Harborlight’s command bundle. The second appeared irregularly under a maritime research prefix, DELTA-SAL-14. Both arrived from the same bearing within the antenna’s fineness.

“Could one buoy legitimately host two instruments?” Mira asked.

Gabriel answered from the doorway. “Yes. Weather and water packages often share power and radio.”

“Could they use unrelated identities?”

“Also yes.”

Noor pointed to the packet timing. “They never speak at once. One stops, then the other begins after exactly three seconds.”

“Shared transmitter,” Mira said.

“Likely.”

“Or two radios coordinated by one controller.”

“Also likely.”

Gabriel sighed. “A ship could disintegrate around you and you would call sinking tentative.”

“Until the water reached the deck.”

“Then you would request evaluation of wetness.”

“My instructor kept a motto over the chart table,” Lotte said from the bridge, where she had apparently heard enough. “First bearing, then story.”

Gabriel lifted both hands. “She quotes dead cartographers at me when I argue with bearings.”

“Alive cartographers too,” Lotte said. “The old pilot book has a Dutch-English correction for this sector because someone postdated a buoy notice and nearly sent ships toward a removed wreck. One label says Ob, another Pro, and neither helps unless you know which correction came later.”

Elena, who had been sorting exhibits, looked up. “Please do not felicitate yourselves on reading a museum piece while I am trying to keep us inside a live order.”

“It is not a museum piece,” Gabriel said. “It is an old chart with useful scars. A working vessel keeps what still speaks.” He tapped a brown rectangle printed near an old artillery island. “See there: decommissioned battery. The note tells you more about the officer than the fog.”

“This one lives under coffee stains and salt,” Lotte said.

Mira studied the chart despite herself. Harbor approaches were not lines but accumulated arguments: dredged lanes, spoil grounds, treaty limits, wartime deletions, commercial detente, and handwritten warnings by people who would never know which annotation saved a later hull. A place-name could close a route without explaining its authority. Even a weight note beside a wreck buoy might outlive the empire that had printed it.

“That sounds almost prophetic,” Noor said.

“Do not make Gabriel a seer,” Mira replied. “He is difficult enough as an owner.”

“A compromised owner,” Gabriel said mildly.

“A useful witness,” Elena corrected. “The distinction matters.”

The exchange was almost light. Mira let it pass without defending herself. She needed Gabriel’s practical contempt for premature complexity, and he needed her refusal to turn a bearing into a culprit.

At 05:58 Lotte called from the bridge. “Patrol vessel two miles astern. Same speed.”

Bakker climbed up. The patrol was Dutch coast guard, lawfully present and already aware of the inspection order. Harborlight’s observer stood aboard it. The ostensible reason for his presence was transparency. Neither fact meant they were being harassed. Neither meant they were not.

Mira studied the data instead.

DELTA-SAL-14 reported sea temperature 8.7 Celsius, salinity 32.1 practical salinity units, pressure consistent with a sensor two meters below surface, and modest dissolved oxygen. The values varied with each burst. NMI-R77A transmitted no readable payload, only encrypted groups routed to Harborlight.

“Can we compare the research stream with independent instruments?” she asked.

Sander lowered the *Nkem*’s CTD cage: conductivity, temperature, depth. The repaired winch paid out cable while the vessel slowed. Its instruments returned temperature 8.6, salinity 32.0, pressure within calibration tolerance.

The cage was useful but not elegant: a steel frame, three bottles, one probe stack, and a latch whose plastic handle had been worn smooth by generations of impatient thumbs. Sander told Mira, perhaps to distract her, that the same rig had once carried fish-survey vials and a cheap plankton net sewn by a retired volunteer from Zeeland. “She said our knots were underdeveloped,” he added. “She was right.”

“Did she tell you so?” Noor asked.

“No. She pitied us, which was worse.”

Gabriel watched the cage vanish. “A fouled mooring can collect rope below. The current piles every loose thing against the first obstruction, then everyone ashore asks why the sea did not behave like a diagram.”

The returning cable scraped through the fairlead. Sander paused to let the load settle, then resumed with the agility of a person who had made the same correction in uglier weather. Mira was grateful he did not ask whether she wanted to help. Her hands still shook enough to make fine work a bad idea.

“The research identity is real weather,” Mira said.

“Real water,” Gabriel corrected. “Weather is above us.”

“Oceanography includes coupled conditions.”

“Your seasickness has made you opinionated.”

They repeated the cast at two depths. Results tracked the buoy’s public stream. Small differences followed current and distance; no impossible agreement suggested copying. The stream had noise, latency, and the ordinary texture of observation.

NMI-R77A remained opaque.

Mira asked whether the court order allowed them to receive Harborlight’s encrypted packet without decoding it. Bakker said yes. Decryption required further authority. Elena, braced at the table with one hand and looking nearly as nauseous as Mira felt, read the exact paragraph.

“We may record emitted signals and compare identifiers, timing, and unencrypted technical headers. We may not defeat access controls.”

“Could Harborlight provide a decoded copy voluntarily?” Mira asked.

Elena laughed without mirth. “I will transmit the request.”

The answer arrived eleven minutes later. Elena read the message twice. It was a mixture of caution and threat, drafted to make procedure itself feel like a weapon. Harborlight refused because the packet contained live critical-infrastructure data and because the *Nkem*’s inspection was, in its view, an abuse of a narrow order obtained through misrepresentation. Counsel reserved the right to seek sanctions and warned against public claims of sabotage before any verified decode.

“Misrepresentation of what?” Gabriel asked.

“Of process, specifically,” Elena said. “They want the magistrate to hear abuse of process before she hears abuse of water data. And if we answer too broadly, they will say we accused a system we have not opened.”

She read on, eyes narrowing. “They accuse public officials of inviting unauthorized access to proprietary knowledge. That is not what passive reception is.”

Noor stared. “That is not a legal argument. That is a press release in a suit.”

“It is a counterattack,” Elena said. “They want us to waste time proving we are not deranged. They want the court to treat technical curiosity as a power grab. I will not give them that argument.”

Bakker gave a short laugh. “Can you say that to the magistrate?”

“No. I will say their filing is trite, inflammatory, and unsupported by the record.”

“Less fun.”

“More useful.”

“They can choke on technicalities,” Bakker said.

“No,” Elena replied. “Technicalities belong to the court, not Harborlight.”

“They say the second identity was known to be an ordinary research channel and presented as mysterious to manufacture suspicion.”

Elena covered the microphone and drafted aloud. The response did not pretend Harborlight had no rights; it argued that a small navigational wake inside the boundary would not detach the module from its owner, would not touch the casing, and would not convert observation into seizure. It also preserved their objection for later review, because victory obtained by pretending procedure did not matter would poison the record.

Mira listened while the sea worked at her stomach. The law’s grammar was not ornamental. One bad preposition bequeaths trouble to the record; one careless adjective could turn a measured statement into slander. Elena's discipline instructed by example, which was the only sort Mira trusted at sea.

“Harborlight’s newest note calls any deliberate stimulus a seizure by another name,” Elena said.

“That is not what seizure means,” Bakker said.

“Nor inspection orders. The court granted observation, not a private veto. Harborlight refused specifications, and a safety objection after the module was photographed does not convert their preference into law.”

“You sound ready to file angry.”

“I am ready to file.”

Noor looked at the display. “If they knew the identity, why is its registry on land?”

Elena added the question to her response.

The sea intensified as they left the shelter of the approach. A loose utensil rattled in the galley. Mira’s nausea returned in a warm pall. She sat on the deck with her back against a cabinet and attempted to absorb the motion rather than contend with it. Her body did not care that other passengers crossed rougher seas daily, that migrants endured overloaded boats, that sailors worked through storms. Comparative suffering offered no anesthetic.

The sea disdains comparative ethics, she thought. It did not become less savage because countless other bodies had borne it first.

Noor handed her a dry cereal biscuit.

From the galley hatch came the smell of broth that Sander wisely kept below. Any thought of condiments, or of the oranges he had loaded before dawn, made Mira’s throat contract. She had no appetite for heroics, only the modest ambition of remaining upright long enough to work.

Sander had planned snacks for morale, which now seemed optimistic. He packed them away without comment. The galley had been lively at departure, all clatter and boast; now Marcin moved through it with the reverence of a nurse, tying cupboard doors before the mugs could break loose. Somewhere behind a panel, loose wiring clicked whenever the engine changed pitch.

“This is boring care,” Noor said, breaking a piece of toast into exact fragments. “The best kind.”

“Boring is underrated,” Mira said.

Broth, diesel, damp wool, and the faint smell from the bilge competed in the narrow space. It was not as bad as vomit, but it had ambitions. Mira held the bowl in her lap and tried to divide sensation: one hand on cool metal, one foot braced, eyes on the square of deck between her boots. Her seasickness felt fixed behind her ribs rather than imposed by motion.

Noor said, “If you deteriorate past toast, Femke has oxygen, fluids, and ugly practical judgment. No one here will ask you to be heroic.”

“A mortal injury to pride,” Mira murmured.

“We can treat that without anesthetics.”

“Eat a crumb.”

“Cruel.”

“A crumb, not the corpus.”

Mira obeyed. It stayed down.

At 06:21 the buoy appeared on radar as a weak intermittent return. Visual range remained poor. Lotte altered bearing five degrees to keep the vessel up-swell of the site. The patrol mimicked the maneuver.

Gabriel came alive despite his observer status. He watched water, traffic, engine vibration, and Lotte’s hands. His desire to command was visible as muscle held still.

“Current sets southeast,” he said.

“I have it,” Lotte replied.

“There may be a submerged mooring line extending down-current.”

“Noted.”

He stopped. One sentence more would have been impertinence, and he knew it. The old hierarchy had not disappeared; it had become advice subject to another person’s approval.

Mira recognized the mannerism: the owner’s jaw tightening around an order he no longer possessed. Gabriel was not henpecked by law or by Lotte; he was learning to unyoke himself from command without pretending the habit had vanished. That made him dangerous in a different way from an inexperienced deckhand. An inexperienced person might not know the risk. Gabriel knew it and could still feel the old prerogative trying to resuscitate itself.

Lotte did not pacify him. She used him.

“Give me the obstruction picture,” she said.

“Buoy, mooring, possible lower cable, patrol breathing down our necks,” Gabriel answered. “One hazard is current. The other is delay.”

“And the third?”

“Pride.”

Femke prepared the remotely operated camera first. The vehicle was only a yellow box with thrusters, lights, and a tether. It descended from the stern while the *Nkem* held position outside the estimated mooring radius. On screen, aerated surface water became green obscurity. Flecks of organic matter streamed past. The image illuminated a pelagic world without scale.

“Depth six meters,” Marcin called.

“No target,” Femke said.

At ten meters, the tether began to bow. Current impelled the vehicle east. Lotte adjusted the ship’s position by a fraction. The patrol hailed them.

“*Nkem*, maintain authorized boundary. Your stern is approaching the western limit.”

Lotte checked the plot. “We remain thirty meters inside.”

“Our display shows ten.”

“Your display is outdated.”

The word was historically ordinary and currently precise; their chart correction had been issued that morning. She transmitted the notice number. The patrol acknowledged but continued to shadow them.

At fourteen meters the camera found the mooring cable, a black line slanting into sediment. Femke followed it upward. The image swung, lost the cable, found it again. Mira tried to map the motion and failed. On land, coordinates implied a stable tabletop. Here the reference itself surged.

“Target at eleven meters,” Femke said.

The buoy hung below the surface, not above it. Its flotation collar had deteriorated or been deliberately flooded. White polymer appeared beneath weed and brown reticulation. Twin antenna housings projected from the upper cape. A crescent gouge crossed the casing.

Gabriel leaned toward the screen. “That is my crate.”

“The device from your crate,” Mira said.

“Yes.”

Femke circled without touching. The full serial lay under marine growth. Her camera could not read it. Another cable ran from the lower housing to a separate module clamped beneath the collar.

“That module was not visible in the cargo photograph,” Noor said.

“Could have been attached later,” Gabriel replied.

“Or hidden inside the crate.”

Mira studied the assembly. The main body matched ordinary oceanographic equipment. The lower module looked prefabricated for another purpose: matte grey, tapered ends, two cable glands, no public label. Its bracket was newer than the buoy’s oxidized fittings.

If the retrofit was honest, it was innovative. If it was not, the newer bracket had been designed to look neglected from a distance and competent only at arm’s length.

The bracket offended Mira because it was not crude. The holes aligned, the cable had proper strain relief, and the paint had been scuffed to resemble the older casing. Whoever installed it understood what a marine engineer would dismiss at a distance and inspect only after some other measurement failed.

“Not the work of a scamp,” Gabriel said. “And not of a louse with a drill at midnight.”

“Your taxonomy of criminals is vivid,” Noor said.

“At sea you learn categories. The lazy, the vain, the unlucky, and the person who reads the manual.”

“Can you inspect the mark?” Bakker asked.

Femke moved closer. The camera dazzled against reflective growth, then adjusted. A stamped emblem emerged: three arches over a line, with letters beneath.

TM-SYSTÈMES / TANGER.

Tangier.

The destination was not thematic. It was printed on metal.

Elena photographed the live screen with the evidence camera, then caught herself. “Derived image only. Femke’s original recording remains primary.”

Bakker logged the distinction.

The patrol hailed again. “No contact authorized with auxiliary module.”

“We are making visual inspection,” Bakker answered.

“Your vehicle is within one meter.”

“No contact.”

“Harborlight advises the module may contain inflammable battery chemistry.”

“Then provide specifications.”

No answer came.

Mira’s mind assembled hypotheses too rapidly. Tangier subcontractor. Unregistered marine device. Dual identity. Early command. Synthetic input was possible, but not yet observed. The lower module might be a legitimate gateway translating one sensor protocol into another. Harborlight’s refusal might protect architecture rather than fraud.

“We need the encrypted payload,” she said.

Elena had already requested an emergency extension from the magistrate. The court asked what fact justified defeating encryption. A manufacturer’s mark and dual identity were suspicious, not enough. They needed evidence that the protected stream differed materially from the public one.

“Headers,” Mira said.

NMI-R77A’s unencrypted headers included packet length, message class, sequence number, and sensor-type flags. She could not see values, but she could see what kinds of values the packet claimed to contain: pressure, conductivity, temperature, status.

DELTA-SAL-14 broadcast the same classes publicly.

“Compare packet behavior,” she said. “Not content.”

Noor overlaid timing. The public stream varied in length as optional diagnostic fields appeared. The Harborlight stream remained immutable: same length, same interval, same class order. That could indicate efficient encoding. It could also indicate a template.

Sander proposed changing local conditions. Lower the CTD cage near, but not touching, the buoy. Its metal mass and sensor wake would not alter the sea enough to matter. Marcin suggested flushing a known salinity solution nearby and was immediately repulsed by Femke and Mira; contaminating the environment to test a sensor was both scientifically poor and legally indefensible.

“We wait for natural variation,” Mira said.

“How long?” Bakker asked.

“Until tide changes enough.”

“Hours.”

The patrol had already issued a thirty-minute limit for station keeping due to shipping. A rougher band of weather approached from north. They could return under another order, but Harborlight now knew the site was found.
