Mira looked at the buoy’s pressure position. It hung eleven meters down, rising and falling with swell. The main sensor streamed pressure variations that matched depth. If the lower module consumed the same physical feed, packet sizes or timing might respond when the buoy moved sharply.

“Can we create motion without contact?” she asked.

Gabriel understood first. “Wake.”

Lotte’s expression hardened. “We do not wash a police vehicle into a mooring.”

“Not close. One controlled pass up-current. Wake reaches the buoy after the camera clears.”

“It could load the line.”

“Within conditions the buoy is designed to withstand.”

Bakker asked whether the order permitted it. Elena read. The vessel could maneuver for visual inspection but could not manipulate the device. A wake was an ordinary consequence of navigation. Deliberately using it as stimulus approached manipulation.

“Approaches?” Noor asked.

“Law contains fewer clean nouns than Mira prefers.”

The magistrate would not rule in real time before the patrol’s limit. Everyone looked at Mira because she had proposed the test.

She wanted a complete authorization, a controlled tank, a duplicate device, every variable fixed. The sea offered none. Decision under uncertainty had always seemed to her a phrase people used to excuse poor preparation. Now the vessel had seventeen minutes, a lawful but ambiguous maneuver, a module likely to disappear, and a test whose physical risk she could not calculate herself.

“Captain?” she asked Lotte.

Not Gabriel. Lotte.

“One pass at four knots, sixty meters up-current,” Lotte said. “ROV recovered first. If patrol orders otherwise, we stop. Gabriel gives mooring-load advice. Femke decides whether the inspection remains safe.”

Gabriel checked line angle, depth, current, and the buoy’s physique. “Acceptable. Not riskless.”

Femke recovered the vehicle. Bakker notified the patrol of a repositioning maneuver within the boundary. The patrol objected to any intentional wake test but did not issue a safety order. Elena recorded the objection.

Lotte brought the *Nkem* around. Engines deepened. Mira stood at the electronics display with Noor, one hand on the cabinet as the deck tilted. Her nausea had become background latency, a signal no longer in command.

The vessel passed up-current.

For forty seconds nothing changed. Then the hydrophone captured turbulence arriving at the submerged collar. DELTA-SAL-14’s next packet reported a pressure increase, conductivity fluctuation, and temperature unchanged. Its packet length expanded with a motion diagnostic.

The public stream looked gloriously unorganized for one burst: not false, just alive. It staggered, corrected, and showed how the package commutes motion into numbers the way a tired city commutes bodies into work without ever becoming simple. The protected stream did not stagger. It behaved like a table copied from a closed room.

NMI-R77A transmitted on schedule.

Same length. Same class order.

The next public packet showed pressure deflation as the buoy rebounded. The Harborlight stream remained immutable.

“It is not reading the same sensor,” Noor said.

“Or it buffers and smooths,” Mira replied.

“How long?”

“We wait one cycle.”

Six minutes later, NMI-R77A transmitted a packet whose header still claimed pressure and conductivity but showed no diagnostic response. The public stream had already returned through four distinct values.

Mira calculated expected compression changes under any plausible delta encoding. None appeared. A fixed packet could still carry changing encrypted values, but the sequence counter behaved oddly: it advanced by exactly one while the public instrument had emitted five observations.

“Separate source,” she said. “Probably.”

“Probably is enough for an extension?” Bakker asked.

“Not yet. We can compare the encrypted packet with the authenticated gate sequence. We know only headers there too.”

The laboratory finding included the packet header Sami’s recorder captured at 18:28. Mira aligned fields. The sensor-type flags matched. More important, the payload length and sequence cadence were identical to NMI-R77A’s current stream.

“The command bundle consumed this identity,” she said. “And this identity does not respond like the physical sensor beside it.”

Elena transmitted the comparison to the magistrate.

The patrol ordered them to terminate station keeping. Lotte acknowledged and began a slow departure. The ROV had been recovered; no physical evidence remained at risk from their movement. The buoy faded from sonar.

Then Harborlight sent a decoded excerpt voluntarily.

It arrived through Elena’s secure channel with a statement that disclosure was made solely to correct dangerous misinterpretation. The excerpt covered the last three packets. It showed salinity 36.8, 36.9, 37.0; pressure rising steadily; temperature 8.7. Harborlight said the values came from a calibrated deeper sensor and therefore need not match the public stream.

Mira stared at them.

North Sea salinity at that site was about thirty-two. Thirty-seven approached open Atlantic or Mediterranean values. A deeper sensor could read slightly different water, not that.

“Could a saliferous discharge cause it?” Sander asked.

“Not steadily, not with pressure divorced from the buoy’s motion, and not at this location without an industrial plume we would detect.”

“What about a Midwest river plume?” Gabriel asked, deadpan.

“Wrong continent.”

“A man may ask.”

“A man may also consult a map.”

“Then those values are not from this water,” Noor said.

Mira felt the word as a precipice. “They are incompatible with our observations and with the public sensor. Synthetic is the leading explanation.”

She forced herself to test the alternatives aloud. A dense saline lens could sit beneath fresher river outflow, but the claimed pressure placed the sensor only meters deeper, not in a separate water mass. A discharge could create local salinity, yet the public conductivity probe hung on the same assembly and showed none. Sensor deterioration might bias a value, but not produce a smooth, countable ascent while pressure rose by an equally neat increment. Marine growth could insulate a probe; it could not innovate a second sea.

Nothing in Harborlight’s excerpt vindicates the deeper-sensor story. It only sharpened Mira’s perplexity about why counsel had chosen to disclose numbers that widened the gap.

The neat ascent had the air of superstitions dressed as engineering: every decimal promising the future it needed. It was not evidence of motive. It was evidence of shape. Mira would not confuse those, however much the pattern invited her to.

Sander brought the CTD calibration sheet. Its reference solution had been checked that morning. The instrument’s permissible error was two orders smaller than the discrepancy. Femke’s camera also showed no separate probe on the lower module, only cables. A hidden probe might lie in the seabed housing, but then Harborlight’s claim of a “deeper sensor” required depth metadata it had omitted from the excerpt.

“Could pressure be generated while salinity is real?” Bakker asked.

“Possible,” Mira said. “The fields need not share origin. Whoever designed the packet may mix observations with generated values.”

Noor winced. “That sentence should be shorter.”

“Everything should be shorter at sea,” Gabriel said.

The brief laughter released no tension, but it prevented technical language from becoming a guise of certainty. Mira graphed the streams again with uncertainty bands and marked every assumption. The public line and *Nkem* casts dovetailed. The protected line did not merely vary; it departed in one direction with a regularity no moving body of water sustained.

Elena examined Harborlight’s covering letter. “Voluntary disclosure creates a new custody problem. They supplied values, not the signed source packet. We can prove what counsel represented. We cannot yet prove the encrypted transmission contained these numbers.”

“Why would they misrepresent their own exculpatory excerpt?” Noor asked.

“I am not saying they did. I am refusing to bequeath a conclusion to the record without its grantor.”

“Can the court compel the key?”

“It can compel a verifiable decode or appoint an examiner. The present question is whether probable interference justifies securing hardware before it vanishes.”

“Preservation is the remedy par excellence,” Elena said. “Everything else waits.”

“That sounds severe,” Gabriel said.

“It sounds correct.”

Bakker’s phone buzzed with a note from the prosecutor. Harborlight had circulated a press holding line calling the inspection a “dissatisfaction-low faction’s stunt,” as if a stray model category could insult people. Elena marked it for the record and refused to answer in kind. “No armaments of rhetoric,” she said. “No ballads for our side, no villain chorus for theirs.”

“You are denying me my one talent,” Gabriel said.

“You may call the sea names. Not opposing counsel.”

Mira separated the evidence into columns: observed public packets; independent CTD casts; encrypted headers; Harborlight’s represented decode; visual hardware; manufacturer mark. No column alone established the synthetic hypothesis. Together they justified preserving the hardware before the discrepancy could be explained away or removed.

“Say exactly that,” Elena said.

Mira dictated a statement for the magistrate. She did not call the module fraudulent, treacherous, or malicious. She said the protected identity reported values inconsistent with co-located observations; the cadence and packet behavior did not show the same immediate physical response as the public sensor; and preservation was necessary to determine whether the discrepancy arose from malfunction, configuration, or deliberate manipulation.

The wording felt tentative because reality was tentative. It was also enough.

Gabriel leaned over the table. “Thirty-seven. Tangier water can run near that.”

“Not proof of origin,” Mira said, though the allusion was powerful. “A template may have been configured there. Or someone chose plausible ocean numbers without regard to this sea.”

The decoded excerpt had been intended to vindicate Harborlight. Instead it widened the gap between the two identities. One reported real North Sea water. The other, if Harborlight's represented decode matched the encrypted packets, carried a smooth sequence of salinity and pressure values that could intensify a forecast without any local physical cause.

Mira graphed both streams. The public line wandered. The Harborlight line rose with the elegance of an astrologer’s prediction: too smooth, too purposeful, every increment ready to fulfil a scenario.

“This could be one physical input path for the early command,” she said.

She corrected the phrasing on the worksheet before anyone else could. Possible input path. Unknown weight.

The patrol vessel accelerated alongside. Over radio, its commander ordered the *Nkem* to proceed to a designated inspection anchorage. A boarding team would review compliance with the court boundary. Lotte acknowledged.

Gabriel’s old maritime history surfaced in fragments while they turned: privateers made legal by paper, company forts that mistook commerce for sovereignty, ministries far from the water. Noor asked whether Chaplin also had a maritime theory, and Gabriel said every good comic understood ballast.

“Does this lecture have a point?” Mira asked.

“Only that owners often mistake delay for a right.”

“That is almost enlightened.”

Bakker received the magistrate’s extension two minutes later. Visual evidence and signal comparison established probable unlawful interference with a critical system. Police were authorized to secure the auxiliary module, preserve its connections, and recover it if a qualified dive supervisor judged recovery safe. Harborlight objected and asserted ownership.

“We have left the site,” Marcin said.

“We can return after boarding,” Bakker replied.

Gabriel checked weather and tide. “Current strengthens in ninety minutes. If the patrol holds us an hour, salvage becomes harder.”

“Inspection cannot be refused,” Elena said.

“I did not say refuse.”

Mira looked through the aft window. The grey module remained eleven meters below a sea that gave no sign of containing it. Its Tangier mark existed now in recorded images, but the hardware itself could show whether the protected values had a physical input path and whether the module stored a device-family signature. It could also be lost if someone cut the mooring or if deteriorated flotation failed.

The *Nkem* slowed at the anchorage. The patrol came alongside with fenders squealing. Four officers boarded, followed by Harborlight’s observer, van Hove, whose approval Bakker immediately challenged. The court order allowed Harborlight to observe recovery from the patrol, not search the *Nkem*.

Van Hove remained on the other deck, dressed for a boardroom rather than a wet deck, and bellowed across the gap that the wake maneuver had violated the order and jeopardized protected equipment.

“Your equipment just reported Mediterranean salinity in the North Sea,” Noor called back.

“You manipulated the sensor.”

“The public sensor responded to motion. Yours did not.”

“You are not qualified to interpret encrypted telemetry.”

Mira stepped to the rail. “Your disclosed values are inconsistent with measured conditions. Identify the claimed deeper sensor.”

“That information is before the court.”

“Then the court can compare it with the photographed assembly.”

His contemptuous silence did more work than an answer.

Van Hove tried another tack, accusing them of staging a public drama rather than gathering evidence. Elena answered that every hash, handoff, and time stamp was available to the court and that Harborlight could stop performing indignation long enough to provide specifications. When he called the recovery theory tyrannical, Bakker asked whether he wished to make a formal safety objection. He did not. He preferred insinuation.

His written objection alleged deliberate interference with infrastructure. Elena logged the wording, then answered only the facts.

The boarding lasted thirty-seven minutes. Officers examined the track log, ROV video, engine order, and communications. Lotte’s assiduity had preserved each action. The *Nkem* had remained inside the corrected boundary. The ostensible complaint stayed fixed on the wake pass, but Bakker treated the delay itself as Harborlight’s best bid to force a deadlock before current strengthened. The magistrate referred the wake pass for later review and did not halt the recovery order.

During the final ten minutes Mira sat in the galley with a cold compress at her neck and a bowl positioned between her boots. Sander heated broth, then thought better of its flatulent onion smell and gave her plain toast. The ship’s utensils clicked in their rack with every roll. Seasickness reduced the mighty architecture of judgment to one mean commitment: keep the next mouthful down. She managed half a slice. Noor, who had shown no nausea, refrained from congratulating her.

Sander told her to drink the water a mouthful at a time and pushed away the rack of condiments before their smell could finish the job the sea had started. Even the idea of a second course was laughable. Two days of this, Mira thought, and any shore doctor would start asking practical questions rather than admiring pride. Another resealing round for the galley mug would waste time, so Noor marked it out of the evidence lane with tape.

“You decided well upstairs,” Noor said.

“Lotte decided. I asked the right person.”

“That may be what I meant.”

Mira let the distinction stand. Her physique had not improved, but the act of yielding expertise no longer felt like defeat.

At 08:12 the patrol released them.

Femke spread dive gear on deck. The weather band had arrived, bringing steeper waves and a dark intensification along the north horizon. Recovery would require a diver to descend along the mooring, photograph connectors, clamp a lift line to the auxiliary module, and disassemble its bracket. If the bracket seized, she would stop. No hardware justified a diver’s paralysis or death.

The collar’s visible disintegration mattered too. A tool twist that would be routine on deck could tear aged polymer below, load the cable, and turn evidence into hazard.

The safety briefing had no glamour. Femke named hazards in the order she expected to meet them: swell, current, fouled cable, reduced visibility, sharp metal, entrapment, cold, panic, and battery gas if the casing had been breached. A trapped hose could injure her shoulder or arm before anyone topside understood the angle. If she surfaced unresponsive, Marcin would begin oxygen, Bakker would clear the deck, and Sander would assist Noor only if asked; Femke’s kit carried a mask and drugs, but the plan was to save a person, not to dramatize medicine.

“No one follows me down unless I call for it,” Femke said. “No panic command. Lotte commands the vessel, I command the dive, Bakker commands the evidence lane.”

Mira wrote it exactly. The separation of authority mattered as much as the separation of files.

Gabriel ran a thumb along the lift hook. “If the bracket will not move, we change the plan, not the diver.”

“And if Harborlight complains?” Marcin asked.

“They can complain from shore.”

Gabriel reviewed the line plan under Lotte’s authority. Marcin checked the umbilical. Sander prepared the winch. Noor sealed the fresh audio card from the first inspection and mounted another, preserving transcripts of each handoff. Elena called the prosecutor about Tangier jurisdiction and the subcontractor mark. Bakker read the recovery terms aloud.

She also asked whether Moroccan authorities would require notice if the Tangier mark proved more than commercial manufacture. Bakker answered that such questions could wait. Femke’s right to abort remained absolute; no order converted evidence into an entitlement.

Mira’s task was to preserve the two streams and their comparison. She exported the public packets, encrypted headers, Harborlight excerpt, CTD casts, wake timing, and uncertainty notes into separate files. She resisted the urge to recombine them into one persuasive graphic before hashes were fixed. Evidence first; argument after.

Noor, engrossed in the timing windows, barely looked up except to note that the radio wrangling had already overshadowed the actual question of source. She watched the receiver needle twitch with each burst and sounded, to Mira, less frightened than obsessed.

The protected sequence continued while they worked. Salinity climbed by 0.1 at every interval. Pressure rose in lockstep. Harborlight’s system, somewhere ashore, was receiving a sea that did not match the one around the buoy.

At 08:39 the *Nkem* returned to the site.

The buoy’s public identity transmitted. The protected identity followed three seconds later.

Femke stood at the stern in a dry suit, helmet attached, umbilical clipped at her chest and shoulder. She looked neither saintly nor stalwart, merely concentrated. Lotte brought the vessel up-current and held her there.

“No heroics,” Lotte said.

“No hard-hearted salvage,” Femke replied. “I heard the speech.”

Marcin, trying for levity and missing by a meter, said she looked enormous in the suit. Femke told him that if he wanted comedy he could stand by the spare cylinders and keep quiet. Even Gabriel smiled, then stopped when Lotte looked at him.

“Diver ready,” Femke said.

“Permission to enter,” Bakker replied.

She stepped off and vanished.

On the camera feed, bubbles swirled past green water. The mooring emerged below. Femke descended hand over hand, careful not to load the deteriorated line. At eleven meters her lamp found the white collar and the grey Tangier module beneath it.

“Visual on target,” she said.

Green water spouted from the scuppers as the stern settled and rose again under the contending pull of swell and current.

The bracket showed rust around two bolts. A third fitting looked newer. A cable disappeared into the main buoy housing. Another ran down toward the anchor and was partly obscured by weed.

To Mira the white bloom around the lower gland looked like fungi, but Femke corrected her at once: not fungi, only marine growth and pale tube residue. One strip of weed did droop across the fitting whenever the swell lifted the collar.

“Two connections,” Femke reported. “Possibly power above, data below.”

Gabriel frowned. “Data below to what?”

Sonar showed no second object, but the seabed lay four meters farther down in suspended sediment.

Bakker authorized inspection along the lower cable, not disconnection. Femke followed it. The image darkened near the bottom. A rectangular shadow appeared half buried in sand.

The object had been no more than a speck on the earlier feed. Now the lamp found a larger housing recessed in a pocket of silt, with one slashed run of old insulation that had partly disintegrated and a bent pin that could impale a glove or hose if a diver came in carelessly.

Its outline had the sulky look of something designed to be mistaken for debris. The casing was not deranged; it was too deliberate, with a cable gland tucked behind the mooring like a door in a narrow alley. One fastener had backed out. Another sat flush. A third showed a pale ring where movement had polished away growth.

“Additional housing,” she said. “Larger than the module.”

The module they had found was not the whole explanation. It was an unidentified gateway between buoy and something on the seabed.

The *Nkem* rolled sharply. Femke’s tether jerked across the camera view.

“Hold position,” she said.

Lotte corrected. Sander called a gust. Marcin paid out slack.

He fumbled once with the brake, corrected immediately, and glanced up as if the admission itself might cost them time. Mira had forborne saying that a clean pause was better than bravado.

On screen, the lower cable had wrapped once around the mooring line. To recover the grey module, Femke would need to free or work around it. The bracket’s rust made disassembly uncertain. The weather made delay treacherous.

“It has not fouled by accident alone,” Gabriel said. “Someone routed that cable to hide it, then trusted ordinary tribulations to finish the disguise.”

Mira wanted to agree and did not. The route was suspicious. Suspicion was not authorship. A system could be objectionable, negligent, even treacherous in effect, without revealing whose hand had tightened the last bolt.

“We stop and plan,” Lotte said.

Gabriel’s jaw tightened, but he did not countermand her.

Femke ascended. The grey module remained attached beneath the drowned buoy, its Tangier mark bright where her glove had brushed away growth. The larger housing stayed in sediment below.

Mira watched the protected stream produce another smooth increment.

They had located the instrument, distinguished its two identities, and shown that Harborlight received values the North Sea did not contain. They had not secured the hardware. Wind now pressed the vessel south while current pulled the dive lines east. Recovery would require a salvage plan, not an improvised grasp.

Gabriel studied the cable geometry. “At slack water we can put a guide line down. One diver on the bracket, one tender controlling the fouled section. If the lower cable loads, we cut the module free.”

“Cut what?” Mira asked.

“Connections or lift line, depending what endangers her.”

The choice arrived before the dive: evidence or person, not as a moral slogan but as tension in a line no one could fully see. Any recovery that clarified the gateway but injured Femke would be a Pyrrhic victory, a best bid turned stupid by its own success.

Lotte set slack water at 10:06. Bakker requested the expanded recovery plan. Elena prepared the legal notice. Noor listened to the module’s diagnostic pulse through the hydrophone, a resonant handshake beneath engine noise. Mira fixed its time against the protected packet.

The *Nkem* turned into the swell and waited.

Below them, the false sea kept transmitting steadily.

## Chapter 13: Salvage

At slack water the sea did not become still. It merely ceased, for a few minutes, to insist on one direction.

Gabriel watched the tide gauge flatten at 10:04 while the *Nkem* pitched under a short northerly swell. The wind had chafed the wave tops white. On the afterdeck, Femke knelt beside the guide line in her dry suit, checking the helmet cable, air line, communications lead, and bailout bottle by touch. Marcin stood at the tender's station with the diver's umbilical laid in a broad, loose figure eight. Sander had isolated the sampling winch from automation and rigged a manual brake. Nothing in their apparatus was elegant. Every component had a job someone could name, and every person could name the point at which it might fail.

Lotte held the vessel up-current of the drowned buoy. She had been at the controls for six hours and had the pale, elevated stillness of fatigue under command. Gabriel stood one pace behind her, an owner without a certificate, obliged to offer acumen without pretending authority. The ship answered her with the cantankerous delay of a loaded workboat in cross-swell, never quite disobedient and never pliant enough to trust.

"Current is easing," he said.

"I can see it."

"I appreciate your gift for reassurance."

"Your appreciation is entered in the log."

The patrol vessel remained four cables east, close enough for its camera to see the operation and far enough that its wash would not endanger the diver. Harborlight's observer had objected to the expanded recovery order, then objected to the weather, the vessel, the diver, the evidence protocol, and the existence of salt water. Elena had answered each objection by reference number. Bakker had fixed the legal boundary with less ornamentation: police were authorized to secure the grey gateway if Femke and Lotte judged recovery safe. That qualification governed the entirety of the dive. It also kept Gabriel useful and quiet; wanting the thing recovered gave him no command.

Below them, NMI-R77A emitted another packet from its false sea. Three seconds earlier, the public sensor had reported the real pressure fall as the tide slackened. Noor's hydrophone caught the interval between them, including the resonant handshake beneath the carrier burst. She sat in the electronics bay with headphones over her scarf and one hand on a fresh-media recorder whose clock and seal Bakker had witnessed.

Mira sat beside her with a basin between her boots. Her seasickness had not expired out of respect for the plot. She had stopped vomiting, but the effort of remaining upright had reduced her face to a scant, grey version of itself.

"Ready on audio," Noor said over the internal circuit.

"Ready on packet capture," Mira added.

Gabriel looked down through the bridge window. Femke raised one gloved thumb.

Lotte called, "Diver to water."

Femke stepped head first from the gate.

For three seconds the stern showed only foam. Then her helmet camera resolved green water full of granules and wispy weed. Marcin paid out the umbilical with both forearms braced, deft but never hurried. The line went over the roller, descended beside the weighted guide, and disappeared.

"At five meters," Femke said. Her voice came through the speaker flattened but content. "Visibility two. Guide line clear."

Gabriel marked the swell period against the line's lateral movement. The current had not vanished; it had fallen below half a knot and was already contemplating reversal. Their adequate window was twenty minutes, perhaps twenty-five if the weather did not hasten it. A miscount of even two swell cycles would matter once Femke was under the buoy.

The buoy appeared at eleven meters like a decayed moon. Its white flotation collar had slumped beneath marine growth. The crescent gouge from Gabriel's old cargo photograph remained visible. Under it, the newer module nestled against the main housing, grey metal under a crust of weed, its Tangier stamp brushed clean by Femke's earlier glove.

"At target," she said. "Upper lead loose enough. Lower lead remains crossed behind mooring."

The lower cable ran from the module toward the larger seabed housing. It passed behind the buoy's mooring and returned across it in a conjunction that the camera could not entirely show. Yesterday it had looked wrapped once. Today, with less current, Gabriel saw the uglier geometry: the cable had entered a corroded metal eye on the mooring and doubled back. When the buoy lifted, the eye pinched it. When the buoy fell, a loop opened.

"Do not put a hand through that loop," he said.

Femke replied, "I had not planned to leave my hand down here."

Marcin barked a laugh. Crew humor was not unconcern. It was the smallest pressure valve they possessed.

Femke clipped a short restraint from her harness to the module bracket, then placed the powered driver on the first bolt. Rust emitted a brown cloud. The driver whined, faltered, and stopped.

"Bolt one seized. Trying hand bar."

"Fourteen minutes to current reversal," Lotte said.

Gabriel studied the load monitor. The guide line rose and fell by forty kilograms as the vessel moved. Sander had set an audible warning at one hundred and twenty, well below the line's rated limit, because ratings belonged to new rope in clean tests, not wet gear crossing a working stern. Spray gathered as globular beads around the nonskid, and beyond the rail the foam carried rust and torn weed.

Femke fitted a compact breaker bar. Her shoulder turned. The bolt creaked once, a microscopic movement the camera almost effaced, then turned again.

"One moving."

The patrol hailed. Its commander reported a weather cell accelerating from the north and recommended termination within ten minutes.

"Recommendation received," Lotte said. "Our radar evaluates arrival at eighteen minutes."

"Harborlight forecasts twelve."

Gabriel saw Mira lift her head at that name, but Lotte did not contest the forecast as deceitful merely because Harborlight supplied it. She checked the rain clutter, wind, and cloud line.

"Diver supervisor," Lotte called, "surface weather now gives us twelve minutes."

Femke did not argue. "Understood."

The first bolt came free. She placed it in a mesh pouch rather than let it sink. The act looked absurdly small beside the module, but custody was systematic or it was theater.

Bolt two turned with less resistance. Bolt three had no head. It had been drilled or sheared and then varnished with a dark compound that imitated corrosion.

"Third fitting is not a bolt," Femke said. "Looks like a pin through the bracket."

Gabriel leaned toward the monitor. The pin attached the bracket to a truss on the main buoy. A retaining tack sat on its lower side.

"Can you drive it outboard?" he asked.

"Maybe. Need a clear hammer angle. Lower cable blocks it."

She shifted around the assembly. Her umbilical floated above her shoulder, then dipped. Marcin took in half a meter. The monitor emitted one soft beep at eighty kilograms and fell silent.

"Line clear," Marcin said.

Femke cut weed from the pin with a blunt hook. Noor's voice entered the circuit. "Handshake now."

Through the bridge speaker came a faint clangor of engines and wave slap, then three rising tones so close together they seemed to resonate inside the hull. The grey module's status light, invisible until Femke removed the weed, answered amber-blue-amber. The public sensor transmitted. Three seconds later the protected identity emitted its packet.

"Captured," Noor said.

"Again?" Bakker asked.

"Full diagnostic sequence, both hydrophone channels, clock fixed against packet header."

"It proves what?"

Mira answered, her voice weakened but precise. "That this module emits the same handshake family as Sami's recorder captured before the gate command. Family, not unique device. It links design or firmware. It does not identify operator or intent."

Gabriel had begun to resent those qualifications less. They were braces, not impediments. Without them every inference could topple under the first adverse expert. Noor's craft was mostly negation at this stage: keeping the sound from saying more than it could. There was an implicit mercy in that discipline, though it did not feel merciful to him.

Femke set a drift against the pin and struck it. The camera jolted. Once. Twice. The pin moved outward by a finger's breadth.

"Seven minutes," Lotte said.

"Pin moving."

"You have five, then ascent."

Femke struck again. The bracket opened slightly. Sander brought the recovery line up to fifteen kilograms, enough to prevent the module dropping but not enough to load the fouled lower cable.

"Lift line attached," he said.

Gabriel watched three loads at once: lift line, guide line, diver umbilical. The module weighed perhaps twenty-two kilograms in air and less submerged. Its lower cable should remain slack as the bracket opened. If it did not, the unknown seabed housing could resist with the mass of sediment and anchoring behind it.

The *Nkem* rose on a larger swell. Lotte eased a fraction ahead to maintain position. The guide load climbed, settled. Femke struck the pin.

It came free.

For one brilliant second the module hung clear of its bracket, secured by the lift line, upper and lower cables still attached. Its stamped face turned toward the camera. The full serial appeared beneath the manufacturer's mark: TM-4G-7719-R. Bakker read it aloud. Noor repeated the diagnostic capture time. Mira repeated the corresponding packet sequence. Separate witnesses laid separate planks across the same gap.

"Recovering upper connector," Femke said.

She unlocked the collar and drew the lead out. A blue sealing ring floated loose. Only the lower cable held the module to the seabed system.

Sander raised lift tension to twenty kilograms.

The lower cable did not yield.

"Stop winch," Gabriel said.

Sander had already stopped it.

The cable's loop at the mooring narrowed. Femke moved the module downward to create slack, but the lift line prevented enough movement. Sander paid out. The module descended. The loop remained pinched.

"It is caught in the eye," Femke said. "I can cut lower lead above the crossing."

Bakker checked the order. "Authorized if necessary for recovery. Photograph before cut."

"Two minutes," Lotte said. "Then I order ascent."

Femke raised the camera. The cable showed no manufacturer label, only a matte sheath and one shallow abrasion where it rubbed metal. She drew her shears.

The wind hit the port side in a single unfavorable gust.

Lotte countered with engine and rudder. The stern moved half a meter before the bow answered. On the load display, guide tension leapt from sixty to one hundred and thirty kilograms. The alarm screeched.

Marcin paid out umbilical. Sander released lift-line brake.

Below, the buoy heeled under the lateral load. The corroded eye rotated. The lower cable's open loop became a running noose around Femke's right fin.

"Fouled," she said.

No panic altered the word. That made it worse.

"All stop," Lotte ordered. "Diver, report."

"Cable around right fin. Not leg. Guide line loaded above me."

The module swung against her shoulder. Its lift line had paid out, but not enough; a joggle in the drum had caught between turns. Sander hauled at the brake lever. It did not move.

"Winch jam," he said.

Gabriel was already descending the ladder to the engine room. Ownership gave him no command, but it had acquainted him with every ugly repair accumulated in the vessel. The manual release sat behind the hydraulic reservoir, where a prudent designer would never have placed it and a hurried retrofit had.

The engine room received him with heat, diesel, and the metallic siren of the load alarm. He crossed the plates as the ship rolled. Sander followed.

"Brake piston is not returning," Sander said.

"Pressure trapped in auxiliary line."

"Valve is shut."

"Indicator lies when the stem strips."

Gabriel put a wrench on the valve. It turned loose without resistance: stripped, as he feared. A proper repair required isolation, a new stem, and time Femke did not have. The auxiliary hose was undersized for a clean emergency dump, and oil was seeping at the fitting where vibration had worried the threads. The old indicator arm still twitched, a vestigial reassurance from the first installation. The valve could disown its own position while presenting a tidy handle to the world.

The emergency release could dump pressure, but then the winch would run free. If the module or guide line accelerated, it could drag line across the diver or strip gear from the deck.

Lotte's voice came over the speaker. "Femke cannot free the fin while the module strikes her. Cut recovery line."

Bakker said something Gabriel could not hear.

"That is an order," Lotte repeated.

The recovery line was their only physical hold on the module. Cut it and the gateway remained attached by its lower cable, or fell toward the seabed housing if Femke cut that cable first. Either way the chance of lifting it before weather arrived was annihilated.

Sander looked at Gabriel. "Knife on deck."

Gabriel understood the look. Lotte had ordered the cut; Marcin could execute it. But line tension had climbed again. A severed rope under load could recoil across the stern. The safer place to release it was the bitter end in the engine room, after constraining the drum.

He could dump pressure and gamble that the jam cleared. He could gain perhaps thirty seconds, perhaps recover the object that connected his false report to the gate. Hardware could corroborate that he had carried a tool of manipulation rather than ordinary sensors. It could distinguish his culpable deceit from knowledge he did not possess. The module was not merely evidence against Harborlight. It had become the shape of the mercy he wanted from the world: proof that his lie had limits, that ignorance still mattered after confession. That was the dangerous part, the wish to make machinery absolve what confession had already exposed.

On the camera speaker Femke's breathing shortened.

"Fin still trapped. Cable tightening on swell."

There was no contemplation left.

"Secure drum with bar," Gabriel told Sander.

They thrust a steel bar through the drum flange and braced it against the frame. Gabriel took the bolt cutters from the damage-control rack. The recovery line entered through a fairlead before winding onto the drum. He set the cutters where the frame would intercept recoil.

Sander said, "On your count."

"No count. Now."

Gabriel cut.

The loaded fibers parted with a report like a small gun. The deck-side end vanished through the fairlead. The drum jumped against the bar and stopped. Above them Marcin shouted that the line was clear.

On camera, the module dropped. Femke pushed it away. It swung once on the lower cable and sank into the suspended sediment, dragging the cable loop down with it. Her fin came free.

"Diver free," she said. Then, more sharply, "Mooring line moving. Ascending."

The corroded eye had rotated again. Its attachment to the buoy truss peeled open. The drowned buoy rose a meter, rolled, and began to slide down-current, still tethered to the seabed housing by whatever remained below.

"Leave the guide," Lotte ordered. "Tender, recover diver only."

Marcin gathered umbilical hand over hand. Femke ascended through a chaos of line and weed. At six meters the camera spun. Gabriel reached the deck as her helmet broke surface. Marcin and Bakker seized her harness. A swell slumped her against the boarding gate, then they hauled her aboard.

She lay supine for three breaths while Marcin cleared the umbilical from her ankles. Gabriel knelt at her right side. Her suit was intact. A dark abrasion crossed the fin, and beneath the boot her ankle had already begun to swell.

"Pain?"

"Three. No numbness."

"Can you move toes?"

She did. He palpated the boot line and shin while Bakker called the patrol medic. Femke sat up before anyone gave permission. Her hands trembled with adrenaline and the blunt hormone storm of survival, but her answers were clipped rather than incoherent.

"Do not make me a bereaved widow to a piece of equipment," she said.

"You are not married to it," Marcin replied.

"Then no widow. Better."

Her humor was thin, but spontaneous enough to reassure him. No fracture declared itself. The medic later called it a mild contusion and ligament strain, prescribed elevation, and instructed her not to dive again that day. Gabriel heard the last qualification with contempt for a system that required it to be stated.

The camera feed had gone dark when Femke surfaced. Sonar showed the buoy assembly descending down the old spoil slope. For six minutes the public transmitter emitted broken packets. The protected identity continued its immutable sequence, then weakened.

"Can we mark it?" Bakker asked.

Lotte shook her head. "We are being set south. Weather is here. No diver, no ROV in these lines, no second pass."

"Could patrol recover it?"

The patrol commander answered over radio. Their vessel carried no dive team and judged station keeping unsafe. A specialist salvage ship could arrive in five hours. By then the assembly might lie beneath loose spoil, and Harborlight had already filed notice that any unauthorized recovery would endanger critical infrastructure.

Gabriel watched the sonar mark descend from fifteen meters to twenty-one. Then it merged with the bottom and disappeared.

The module had not been ceded to Harborlight or police. The sea had taken custody without receipt.

Mira came aft wrapped in a blanket, one hand on each rail. "Femke?"

"Bruised ankle," Gabriel said. "No neurological deficit."

"Hardware?"

He looked toward the water. "Lost."

She accepted the word without consoling him. Rain began in hard, well-balanced drops that immediately degenerated into a slanting sheet. Lotte ordered the afterdeck cleared. Marcin cut away the abandoned guide line at the stern to prevent it reaching the propeller. Sander locked the damaged winch and affixed a red out-of-service tag.

Noor remained in the electronics bay until Bakker witnessed the audio-card seal. When she emerged, rain beaded on her eyelashes.

"The last handshake is clean," she said. "It transmitted while the full serial faced Femke's camera."

"Does that recover our case?" Gabriel asked.

"It recovers nothing. It preserves a relationship."

The distinction stabbed because it was correct.

They carried Femke to the mess, though she objected that she could walk perfectly well. Mira checked capillary refill and sensation after the patrol medic's examination, then brewed tea strong enough to remove paint. The air smelled of wet neoprene, diesel, and margarine warming in a pan because Sander believed every emergency required toast. He worked at the galley with fierce concentration.

Bakker assembled the evidence before anyone began interpretation. Primary dive video up to signal loss. Helmet telemetry. The patrol's exterior recording. Hydrophone cards from first and second sessions. Packet captures. CTD casts. Harborlight's represented decode. Still images showing the serial. The cut recovery line remaining on the drum. Femke's statement. Gabriel's and Sander's statements about the winch. Each had a separate hash, seal, or physical bag.

"The original module is gone," Elena said over the secure call from the bridge. "Opposing counsel will say a recording of a handshake cannot establish authenticity without hardware."

"Can they exclude it?" Noor asked.

"They will try. Admissible is not the same as persuasive. We have documented capture, a visible serial, synchronized packet headers, and a pattern comparable to the recorder's diagnostic channel. An expert can explain a family signature. Harborlight will argue coincidence, contamination, or replay."

Mira said, "Replay would require the module to emit the same family signature. That still links it to the family."

"Quite. But not to a defendant's intent."

Gabriel stood by the sink while rain struck the pane. The engine vibration entered through his boots. "Could we have recovered it if I had dumped the brake pressure?"

Sander answered before anyone could soften it. "Maybe. Or run the line until it caught Femke at the knee."

"The load was falling."

"Then rose again."

"For one swell."

Lotte entered, stripping off her wet jacket. "Do you contest my order?"

"No."

"Do you think the cut was wrong?"

He wanted to say the decision had been too quick, that thirty seconds might have obviated the loss. Those were the sophistic arguments of a man safely above water assigning risk to someone below it. In moderation, doubt was useful; here it was beginning to loiter around the wrong door.

"No," he said.

"Then do not make Sander justify compliance until you can imagine a version in which the line takes her leg."

Femke lifted her bandaged ankle onto a bench. "I can imagine it for you. It is unfavorable."

Gabriel sat. The cut had felt like a coup de grace delivered to his own defense. Yet the diver was present to mock his remorse, while the module could neither suffer nor forgive. A life did not outweigh evidence because of an emotional scale. Evidence had no claim to require another person's body as packaging.

"I cut it for myself as well," he said. "I do not want this rewritten as gallant. I wanted the module. Then I heard her breathing."

Femke regarded him. "Good. Brave men are dangerous around dive plans."

Marcin pushed toast toward Gabriel. "Also hungry men."

No one offered absolution. The ship turned toward Rotterdam under Lotte's command.

At 11:02 the protected transmitter vanished. The public identity had ended four minutes earlier. Noor marked both terminations. Mira would not call the silence proof of destruction; the assembly might be intact under sediment, antenna occluded by spoil. Bakker requested an exclusion zone and specialist search. Harborlight concurred with the exclusion zone while denying that its property had produced synthetic data. Its cooperation was as manipulative as its resistance: either stance could later be cited as responsible conduct.

The patrol escorted them through worsening visibility. On the horizon turbines appeared and vanished in rain. Gabriel changed out of soaked clothes in his cabin and found the empty slot in his wallet where his certificate had been. He had believed the module might restore a sequence: hardware to explanation, explanation to reduced charge, reduced charge to ship retained, ship retained to Ama's regard. The sequence had been fallacious. No object could acquit him of the false report he had admitted. Losing it hurt; it did not break the world. Femke was alive to complain about the tea, and the case would have to stand on what remained.

His phone showed a message from Ama: DID ANYONE GET HURT?

He replied: Diver bruised her ankle. She is safe. We lost the equipment because I cut its line.

Three dots appeared, disappeared, appeared again.

YOU CUT IT?

Yes.

WHY?

It was pulling her into other lines.

The answer came after a minute.

GOOD.

He did not take the word as vindication. It was only his daughter's judgment of one act.

In the electronics bay Noor replayed the handshake at low volume. Without the hydrophone's engine noise removed, the tones were almost submerged: three pulses, a pause, a lower answer. Sami's recorder contained a comparable sequence eleven minutes before the Rotterdam surge. This one was fixed to a photographed serial and a dive operation witnessed by police. The module family now had a voice even though the object lay beyond reach.

"Can a manufacturer identify it?" Gabriel asked.

"If the signature is proprietary and unchanged," Noor said. "The mark gives us Tangier. The serial gives us a production run."

"TM-Systèmes may deny it."

"Then denial becomes a question with edges."

Mira pointed to one element of the waveform. "This acknowledgement is transposed relative to Sami's capture. Same intervals, different order. Could be firmware generation."

"Or operating mode," Noor said.

"Or a replay template," Mira added.

Gabriel waited.

"But the family resemblance is salient," she conceded.

Noor's skill lay in making the evidence presentable without making it say what it could not, and Gabriel was learning that this restraint had more value than any courtroom flourish.

Bakker received a message from the prosecutor. Because the module was lost and the remaining evidence derived, Harborlight had petitioned to terminate the constrained Rotterdam pilot suspension immediately. Elena had filed for an emergency continuation in The Hague. The hearing was set for Day Twelve, allowing one day for expert comparison and service.

"We are sailing into a discussion about whether sound exists," Gabriel said.

"About whether this sound can lawfully support relief," Elena replied through the speaker. "The court will also ask who is threatened next."

"Zuid-17," Mira said. "The same district lost pump priority and hospital access."

"A district is not automatically an eligible claimant. We need a person or entity with standing and a sufficiently imminent injury."

Gabriel looked at the shrinking waveform. They had gone to sea for hardware and returned with a legal difficulty.

At the Maas approach the rain weakened. Rotterdam emerged in stacked planes: cranes, tanks, apartment towers, a pale strip of sky. Harbor control assigned the *Nkem* a detained berth. The lender had renewed its request to inspect the collateral. Police would seize the damaged recovery gear for examination. Femke went ashore for radiography, walking with crutches she called a theatrical perquisite.

Before she crossed the gangway, Gabriel stopped her.

"I am sorry."

"For the sea?"

"For delaying the cut in my head."

"You did not delay it with your hands. Keep the distinction."

She dismounted the gangway one careful step at a time.

Noor handed Bakker the sealed audio card. She retained no private copy. The recorder used aboard remained police-inspected ship equipment; Sami's original recorder and puck remained ashore under their earlier seals. Gabriel watched the transfer and understood that loss did not make the surviving evidence sacred. It made accuracy more requisite.

The *Nkem* settled against her fenders. Sander shut down the starboard engine. Its clangor diminished through the hull until only pumps and rain remained. Lotte entered the final position and engine hours. Under defects she wrote: SALVAGE WINCH BRAKE VALVE STEM STRIPPED; RECOVERY LINE CUT BY OWNER ON MASTER'S ORDER TO RELEASE DIVER HAZARD.

The harbor safety officer arrived before the lines had finished creaking against the bollards. He was young, dry, and chary of every person aboard. He photographed the red tag on the winch, then asked Gabriel why a known temporary repair had not appeared in the vessel's defect history. Gabriel explained that the stripped valve stem was new; the inaccessible placement was not. Years earlier he had acceded to the retrofit because moving the reservoir would have cost three days' charter. He had accepted a component that could be reached for maintenance but not quickly under load. It had been a lax compromise, not an insightful economy.

"So it conformed when installed," the officer said.

"To the drawing."

"And was the drawing adequate?"

Gabriel looked at the narrow passage between reservoir and frame. "No."

Sander stood beside him, saying nothing. Gabriel could have blamed the service yard, the surveyor who approved it, the former engineer who signed the test. Each statement would have contained content and missed responsibility.

"I approved it as owner-master," he said. "Record that the arrangement delayed manual release."

The officer did. He issued a detention item requiring the brake system to be rebuilt before the winch returned to service. The repair would be expensive and perhaps pointless if Noordhaven took the vessel. Still, Sander began measuring for a new valve position. Maintenance did not abstain merely because ownership impended.

In the mess, Bakker asked Gabriel to recount the cut again on video. The repetition felt tedious until the inspector altered one parameter at a time. Which alarm sounded first? Where was Sander? Who ordered release? Did Gabriel understand that severing the line would probably prevent recovery? Had anyone from Harborlight instructed him? Had his debt influenced the decision?

"My debt influenced my desire to recover the module," Gabriel said. "It did not cause the cut."

"What did?"

"The diver reported entrapment. The master ordered release. The hydraulic brake would not open."

"And your judgment?"

"That another attempt would be a wanton transfer of risk to Femke. Negligent and unconscionable."

Bakker did not praise the answer. He asked Gabriel to mark his position on an engine-room plan and initial the time reconstructed from helmet audio. The account would later be tested against Sander's, Lotte's, Marcin's, and Femke's. Conformity among them would matter only where it arose independently. A rehearsed crew could produce a superb lie; slight differences often made truthful perspectives more credible.

When the interview ended, Gabriel found Lotte on the bridge completing the casualty notification. She had classified the event as a diving near miss with minor injury, loss of recoverable property, and failure of deck machinery under load.

"Near miss sounds too small," he said.

"It means the harmful sequence was interrupted. It does not mean the sequence was small."

"Will they suspend you?"

"They may investigate me. That is not the same thing."

He had once treated investigation as an annihilating verdict and concealment as prevention. Lotte treated it as the price of retaining a profession that could learn from its own danger.

"Your order was correct," he said.

"I know. The question is whether my plan before the order was correct. We put one diver between a moving buoy, two cable systems, and a vessel with a recovery winch we believed serviceable. Belief is not inspection."

"You had its test certificate."

She looked at him askance. "You have learned nothing if that comforts you."

He felt the old reflex to contest her severity, then let it pass. The sea had supplied adequate derision already.

She passed the log to Gabriel to sign as witness.

He read the sentence twice. It contained no encore for his motive, no innuendo of heroism, no dissimulation about the evidence. It placed command, act, and reason in their proper order.

He signed.

Outside, the sea beyond the harbor kept the module. Inside a police case, a fresh card kept its handshake. Neither possession was enough. By Day Twelve Elena would have to persuade a court that an absent object could still warn of a present danger.

Gabriel looked at the cut line bagged on deck and felt, beneath grief for the lost proof, the stern cornerstone of the choice: Femke had walked ashore.

## Chapter 14: Standing

The emergency court occupied a converted insurance office whose windows could not be opened and whose carpet retained the flavoring of a thousand anxious coffees.

On Day Twelve, Elena arrived before eight with three boxes, two experts, and no client the court agreed was in danger.

Outside, camera crews jostled behind a barrier. Harborlight's petition to restore full operation had turned a narrow evidence hearing into a referendum no judge had requested. One reporter called the lost module "the drowned black box." Another called it sabotaged climate infrastructure. A hawker sold coffee beneath a leaflet proclaiming that delay would leave Rotterdam defenseless. None of them had seen the seabed, and all possessed graphic certitude.

The legal pages were only slightly less frantic. They had few facts and too many theories: a flood panic, a smuggling scandal, an administrative rebuke dressed as an apocalypse. Elena watched one analyst after another turn a narrow application into a verdict. The performance was useful to Harborlight because certainty, even scornful certainty, traveled faster than jurisdiction.

Elena entered by the staff door. Her former supervisor, Marta Kesic, waited in the corridor with Compact counsel. Marta's demeanour was agreeable enough to be ominous.

"You are here as factual counsel?" she asked.

"As applicant's legal adviser on the reporting duty. Independent Dutch counsel makes the motion."

"A useful scission."

"A necessary one."

"Your clause created the limits you now defy."

"I rely on its limits."

Marta looked askance at the evidence boxes. "You rely on a recording made by an illegally sailed vessel during an abortive recovery."

"The sailing was not illegal. The recovery was authorized. The object was lost because the master protected the diver."

"That monologue may be more effective inside."

Elena resisted the barb. Law rewarded the person who could distinguish insult from issue.

Still, the remark found a sensitive place. She had spent two sleepless nights telling herself that procedure was not timidity and that refusing to force doctrine aside was not surrender. Now she had to prove it without confusing her need to be right with courage.

The courtroom had once been an actuarial conference room. A temporary dais stood at one end; cables crossed the floor under black rubber battens. Judge Marieke Vos took her seat at nine. She was aquiline, impartial in expression, and reputed to dispense with any argument after its third repetition. Elena admired the tactic and feared it.

The applicants were formally the Rotterdam municipality and the independent laboratory, seeking continuation of constrained pilot measures and preservation of all data related to TM-4G-7719-R. Noor appeared as owner of the comparison recording and source-separation witness. Mira appeared as expert. Gabriel appeared under summons, his master certificate still suspended. Zuid-17 existed everywhere in the papers and nowhere at counsel table.

Harborlight's lead barrister, Daan Vermeer, began with standing.

"The municipality may protect its own pumps," he said, "and Harborlight does not contest the preservation of properly held public records. But the applicants ask this court to restrain a regional emergency system based on a hypothetical future injury to unidentified residents. No resident is party. No insurer is party. No hospital alleges a current refusal of service. The alleged victim is a rectangle on a map."

Independent counsel replied that the municipality had institutional standing to protect public infrastructure and that the reporting-duty clause expressly authorized preventive review of a material systems hazard.

"Review, yes," Vermeer said. "Not an injunction unbounded by a claimant's injury."

Elena heard her own drafting in his cadence. The clause gave inspectors entrance where a hazard was credibly identified, but its remedial paragraph deferred to domestic standing rules. She had considered that deference decent federalism. Now it was an interlock with no key.

Judge Vos asked, "What precise conduct do you seek to enjoin?"

Counsel listed autonomous pump reprioritization, district capacity reductions, and reliance on data from the lost device family.

"Across the whole pilot?"

"Pending independent verification."

"For how long?"

"Fourteen days."

"On evidence from one device?"

Mira shifted behind counsel. Elena knew the answer: one device, one packet family, one demonstrated mismatch, one prior gate sequence, and a live coefficient affecting Zuid-17. Together they justified inquiry. Whether they justified suspending beneficial functions for an entire region was harder.

Harborlight conceded preservation. Vermeer offered to maintain current municipal overrides, preserve encrypted traffic, and submit the disputed handshake to a mutually chosen expert. The concession was tactically pristine. It removed the apparent need for broad relief while leaving Harborlight's other automated recommendations intact.

"They want the court to treat cooperation as cure," Elena wrote to counsel.

Judge Vos called the first expert.

Noor took the witness chair in a dark jacket still creased from travel. Vermeer asked whether she was an engineer.

"No."

"A cryptographer?"

"No."

"An expert in maritime telemetry?"

"I work with multichannel recording and acoustic systems. I am here to explain capture and source separation, not to tell you what the device did."

His tactic had been to make her either overclaim or appear useless. Her answer occluded neither limit.

She described the fresh storage media, witnessed synchronization, dual hydrophones, engine-noise reference, seal, and handoff. She did not advert to Sami's death until asked about the comparison source. Then she explained that his original recorder remained under separate police custody and that she had never possessed the derived working image alone.

Vermeer displayed two waveforms superimposed on the wall.

The image was handy for television and dangerous for truth. On the screen the traces looked like a child's rebus of agreement and disagreement: two crooked lines, one bright label, and a caption too small to carry the method. Elena watched the press bench lean forward as if the picture itself could spare them the evidence.

"They are not identical."

"Correct."

"One is transposed."

"One acknowledgement group appears in a different order."

"So the claim of a match is false."

"The claim is family resemblance in timing intervals and diagnostic structure. Not identity."

"Family resemblance is an artistic judgment."

Noor's mouth tightened. "It can be measured. The intervals vary by less than the clock tolerance. The carrier transition and checksum preamble share the same structure. An engineer can interpret why. I can establish that the resemblance is not my mood."

A titter moved through the press benches. Judge Vos looked up, and it terminated.

Vermeer tried another route. The *Nkem* had sailed under a revoked clearance; Gabriel had smuggled the original buoy; Noor had a financial and reputational interest in linking her installation to the inquiry. Each fact was true enough to be troublesome.

"Did Captain Okafor control your recording?"

"No."

"Did he select the site?"

"The police order did."

"Did Dr. El-Amin tell you which sounds mattered?"

"No. The diagnostic sequence was identified before the dive and captured continuously."

"Could it have been replayed aboard?"

"Not without appearing on the reference channel and not while producing the photographed light sequence underwater."

"You cannot exclude a device aboard the buoy replaying it."

"That device is what we are discussing."

Even Judge Vos permitted herself a shallow breath that might have been amusement.

Mira followed. She looked hale only from a distance. Up close, two days of nausea and work had left her restless and drawn. Before Vermeer could make caution sound like retreat, she began where the evidence stopped. The public stream matched independent casts; Harborlight's represented decode did not. The encrypted values still needed independent verification. The handshake linked a device family, not a person, and the lost module's weight within Harborlight remained unknown.

Her notes were scribbled rather than elegant. Elena could see the margins: clock tolerance, checksum preamble, certificate disabled, no operator inference. The page looked muddled from a distance and exact up close, which was the opposite of Vermeer's case.

"Yet you ask us to halt a system that allocates flood response to hundreds of thousands," Vermeer said.

"I ask you to prevent unverified synthetic inputs from automatically reducing present capacity. Harborlight may continue observation, forecasting, and recommendations subject to local review."

"Optional automation is a contradiction."

"No. It is decision support."

"And when a local official is too flighty, indolent, or frightened to act?"

"Then the institution needs accountable fallback authority. Concealed automatic acceptance does not become impartial because humans have flaws."

He displayed Harborlight's storm record. During the previous month its warnings had improved placement of mobile barriers and emergency crews. One alert had moved equipment before a culvert failed, preventing flooded homes.

"Is that benefit authentic?"

"As far as the municipal record shows, yes."

"Would your injunction impede such alerts?"

"The proposed order preserves alerts."

"Would it slow action?"

"It could."

The answer produced a furor outside the room within minutes. EL-AMIN ADMITS DELAY RISK appeared on a journalist's tablet. Elena watched the reduction occur in real time: a clause removed from context, a qualification razed, a useful concession repainted as defeat.

The court turned to authenticity. Harborlight's expert argued that a diagnostic handshake was comparable to a model number, not a unique serial. Different devices could share it; test equipment could emulate it; firmware updates could alter it. The full serial visible on video established manufacture, perhaps, but no authentic packet body. The module was gone. The seawater had dispensed with cross-examination.

Independent expert Dr. Sanne Koster agreed with more of this than the applicants liked. She was genial, exact, and immune to counsel's desire for winning answers.

"Can you authenticate the recording?" Judge Vos asked.

"I can authenticate the capture process and rule out several ordinary contamination pathways. I can say the recorded sequence is consistent with the same protocol family as the earlier sequence. I cannot authenticate the lost module's internal state from sound."

She added that the comparison was not an announcement of one culprit across the water. It was a measured pattern with a bounded inference: useful for preservation, risky for identity, and useless as theater.

"Can the data have evidentiary value?"

"Yes. Derived evidence is not a sham merely because the source object is unavailable. Its weight depends on provenance, reproducibility, and the inference proposed."

"Would you rely on it to identify a manufacturer?"

"As a lead corroborated by the stamped mark and serial."

"To identify an operator?"

"No."

"To support preservation?"

"Certainly."

"To suspend all automated operation?"

Koster glanced toward the municipal data. "That is a risk decision outside my qualification."

Elena admired the answer even as it weakened them. Expertise became sleazy when it expanded to meet the remedy counsel wanted.

Gabriel was called next because Harborlight insisted that provenance could not be separated from the character of the vessel's owner. Judge Vos allowed questions about conduct affecting collection and rejected a wider inquiry into whether Gabriel was a decent man.

He took the oath in a suit whose shoulders had once been imposing and now looked tattered at the cuffs. Vermeer established thirty years at sea, ownership of the *Nkem*, and command during the off-manifest voyage.

"You omitted the buoy from the manifest?"

"Yes."

"You filed a false position report?"

"One."

"You accepted cash?"

"The broker paid part of the freight in cash."

"A distinction conducive to your dignity, perhaps. Was it declared?"

"As freight revenue, not against the correct cargo."

"So you lied to customs, your crew, and later police."

"I withheld the cargo history and my sighting of Sami Bensaid until Day Nine. I have given a statement under caution."

"That was not my question."

"Then enunciate the legal meaning of lie you want me to accept."

Judge Vos intervened. "Witness, answer factual questions. Counsel, ask them without moral summation."

Vermeer displayed a still from Femke's camera. The module hung free of its bracket, its serial visible. "At this instant, was the diver trapped?"

"No."

"At this instant, did you have the module?"

"We had a recovery line attached. It remained connected to a seabed housing."

"Seconds later, the vessel moved. Who advised the master?"

"I advised on mooring load. Lotte van Gaal conned the vessel."

"Could your advice have caused the fouling?"

"It could have contributed. The safety inquiry has not concluded."

The admission made the room quiet. A less disciplined witness could be flayed by shame into speculation. Gabriel waited.

"Did you cut the line to prevent examination of hardware that might establish your role?"

"No."

"Did its loss benefit you?"

"No. Recovery might have shown what I carried and what I did not know. I wanted it enough to hesitate in my head."

"In your head."

"My hands cut when ordered. The diver was fouled, the winch had jammed, and line load was rising."

He did not add that the cuff of his borrowed shirt had begun to prick at his wrist where he clenched the rail. Elena saw him notice the tiny discomfort and discard it. The important cut had already been made at sea.

"You ask the court to rely on your account."

Gabriel indicated the sealed helmet record. "No. Compare it with the video, load alarm, engine log, Lotte's order, the engineer, the tender, and Femke. My repute is optional. The records are not."

Elena saw Judge Vos write the sentence down. Gabriel had learned that confession did not purchase credibility; it could only stop him asking trust to do the work of corroboration.

Independent counsel asked three questions. Was Sami's original recorder aboard? No. Could Gabriel access the hydrophone media after Bakker sealed its bay? No. Had anyone instructed Noor to record only when the module transmitted? No; both channels ran continuously.

The municipality then called pump supervisor Aart de Jong, who had overridden the Zuid-17 downgrade. He wore work trousers under a borrowed jacket and treated the microphone as troublesome machinery.

He explained that high-confidence regional recommendations had been accepted automatically unless a local operator rejected them within four minutes. Since the constraint, every pump-priority change required affirmative local acceptance.

On the projected interface, the district sat inside a lattice of canals, tram lines, valves, and service roads. De Jong used a pencil rather than the laser pointer, touching each junction as if the map were a machine he might have to open. "This is what your model calls a region," he said. "We call it the route a crew can actually reach before water climbs over the kerb."

"Has Zuid-17 lost pump priority since that change?" Judge Vos asked.

"No."

"Then what continuing injury do you identify?"

De Jong rubbed one thumb along the rail. "We run the same pumps with two more operators each shift. We have no budget for them after this month. Harborlight still marks the district as a lower future-beneficiary area. Every recommendation arrives with that starting point."

"But you can reject it."

"If we see it."

"Have you failed to see one?"

"Not yet."

The honest answer was devastating. A precaution that worked erased the event that might justify keeping it.

"Why two additional operators?" counsel asked.

"One person cannot monitor rainfall, canal level, maintenance alarms, regional requests, and a model whose reason code can change after an update. Accept is green and large. Review is a small junction through three panes."

"A small button," counsel said, trying to help.

"A small button can save or lose a street," De Jong said. "That is why I dislike it."

"Did Harborlight refuse staffing funds?"

"We did not request funds from Harborlight."

"So the financial injury is the municipality's."

"The pump is the municipality's. The water is everybody's."

Vermeer rose. "Did Harborlight's alert last month let you move a barrier before the Schie culvert failed?"

"Yes."

"How many buildings remained dry?"

"The estimate said forty-three."

"Do you regard the platform as useless?"

"No."

"Dangerous?"

"Anything connected to a pump is dangerous if you stop looking at it."

"Pessimism, not evidence."

De Jong remained impassive. "It is why the pump has a manual switch."

Elena understood why Vale's system remained influential. Its alerts had helped de Jong. He wanted accountable inspection, not abolition. That moderate demand was harder for Harborlight to dispel than denunciation.

Dr. Lise van Dijk followed. Privacy restrictions prevented her identifying the three redirected patients. She authenticated the volatile log and explained the address-dependent recommendation, but said all three received care after staff intervened.

The entries had been stripped almost to grammar. A hepatitis patient had been steered away from a monitored bed search. An allergic reaction waited behind a postal-zone diversion. A respiratory observation case moved through the same hidden logic. Names were sealed, addresses truncated, clinical notes pared back until even harm sounded hypothetical. The standing problem was not abstract here. It was produced by lawful privacy.

"Were they harmed?"

"One allergic patient waited six minutes longer for monitored placement. I cannot attribute a clinical injury to the delay."

"Could it recur?"

"The software remains in use. Staff now review postal-zone diversions."

"So safeguards exist."

"Human safeguards exist because the system behaved incorrectly."

Vermeer approached gently. "Harborlight also directed ambulances away from a genuinely full ward that night?"

"Yes."

"Potentially preventing dangerous delay?"

"Yes."

"And none of the three patients asks this court for an injunction."

"They do not know their addresses altered the recommendation. The log is sealed."

"They may be informed through proper procedure."

"By whom?"

The question landed harder than accusation. A stealthy recommendation could pass like a draft through triage, harmless when caught and consequential when missed; the patient might never learn that an address had participated in care. Elena saw Judge Vos write again.

Vermeer returned to his seat. The standing problem fed on confidentiality: evidence stayed sealed to protect patients, and protected patients could not recognize themselves as claimants.

At noon the judge recessed. The corridor filled with bodies and phone light. A reporter thrust a microphone toward Gabriel and asked whether he had cut the line to destroy evidence of his smuggling. Gabriel stopped. Elena saw the old rashness gather in his shoulders.

"I cut it on the master's order because the diver was fouled," he said. "The cut, the order, and the machinery failure are recorded. I will answer the safety investigation, not your epithet."

He walked on.

"Adequate," Elena told him.

"Your praise is beatific."

"Do not become garrulous."

He pressed a paper napkin around a nick on his thumb to stanch a bead of blood from some unnoticed scrape on the evidence box. It was the only injury in the corridor small enough for anyone to solve.

Noor stood at the window overlooking a canal the color of slate. "They can preserve the sound and still let the system continue."

"Yes."

"Then what was salvage for?"

"To know more than we knew. Knowledge does not carry its own injunction."

"That is a lawyer's sophistry."

"No. Sophistry would be telling you doctrine can make a claimant appear."

Noor turned. "There are people in Zuid-17."

"Then we need one whose current legal interest is affected: a resident denied service, a shop whose insurance changed, a housing association facing a concrete cost, a patient redirected. We have anonymized hospital events and a nine-minute pump downgrade that was overridden. The court may call both past or cured."

"Cured because someone caught them."

"I agree. Standing does not ask whether I agree."

Elena heard the cruelty in that sentence. For years she had treated procedural thresholds as cleansing crucibles: if a claim endured them, it emerged legitimate. But people did not live in causes of action. They lived in apartments, behind counters, beside drains. Doctrine noticed them only after harm acquired the correct shape.

Mira joined them with a packet of crackers. "The coefficient uses expected insurance continuity. If insurers withdrew before a capacity reduction, a policyholder may have both present economic loss and exposure to the pump decision."

"Do we know that occurred?" Elena asked.

"No. We know the model reads insurance continuity. We have not seen underlying notices."

"Then that is the next factual question."

Noor said, "You want us to walk into the district asking strangers for bills."

"I want us to find organizers first and ask what inquiry they consider legitimate."

"Better."

The recess ended.

Harborlight called Adrian Vale remotely. He appeared on the screen in an ordinary office without the panoply of corporate branding. Elena recognized the tactic: humility by set design.

Vale affirmed that Harborlight would preserve all traffic from the device family and accept an independent sampler at the network boundary. He denied authorizing synthetic observations. A subcontractor fault, malicious injection, or configuration error remained possible. Pending review, Harborlight had disabled TM-4G-7719-R's certificate.

"If the certificate is disabled," Judge Vos asked, "why oppose continued constraints?"

"Because the requested order extends far beyond one certificate. It would require manual acceptance for time-sensitive reallocations across the pilot. During a fast surge, delay can be paramount."

"Can you maintain the current municipal override arrangement?"

"For pumps, temporarily. Hospital and transport recommendations operate under different jurisdiction."

There it was: the system's breadth made each remedy too narrow and every broad remedy too imposing.

Independent counsel asked whether Harborlight's platform had reduced present pump priority based partly on expected population contraction.

Vale answered, "The model includes future demand, asset condition, vulnerable population, alternative routes, and many other parameters. No single field determines allocation."

"Does insurance continuity enter the model?"

"At aggregate level, as one measure of recovery capacity."

"So a district with rampant cancellations may appear less able to recover."

"It may," Vale said, "or it may qualify for public support. Insurance is an input, not a verdict."

"Could loss of insurance reduce present investment?"

"It could indicate reduced capacity to restore after an event. It can also trigger compensatory public support. Context matters."

His answer was not false. That was its mainstay. If Harborlight had simply punished uninsured districts, the injustice would be obvious. Instead insurance could increase or decrease support depending on policy rules no resident could inspect.

Elena sent counsel a note: ASK DATE OF FIRST INSURANCE FEED FOR ZUID-17.

Vale said the feed began after the public pilot classification six weeks earlier. He spoke with certitude.

Mira wrote back: We have no source to rebut.

The hearing moved to remedy. Vermeer warned that an injunction could disaffect municipal partners and create legal uncertainty throughout the Compact. He called the request vexatious in scope and underhand in origin. He did not call Gabriel a felon, but arranged every fact so the word stood invisibly between them.

Elena's counsel underplayed Gabriel. The recovery order came from a magistrate; Lotte commanded; police supervised; the line was cut to protect Femke. Even illegally obtained evidence, which this was not, could still require preservation when it revealed danger. Harborlight's attack on the vessel did not dispel the mismatch between its represented values and observed North Sea conditions.
