Noor's father did not embrace her until she had finished telling him why Gabriel waited outside.

The courtyard held the last blue of Day Sixteen above its square of white walls. A lemon tree rose from a tiled basin in the center, its leaves dusty, its fruit still green. On three sides, doors stood open to rooms made dim by the heat. The fourth wall carried an antique clock beneath a shallow cedar awning. Its minute hand had stopped at twelve past six.

Noor spoke beside the basin while the calls to prayer crossed the roofs in imperfect succession. Her mother, Amina, sat on a low chair with both hands flat on her knees. Her father, Driss, remained standing. Mira waited near the blue door, neither guest nor witness yet, and looked where Noor had told her to look: nowhere that could be mistaken for judgment.

Noor gave the account without an eloquent beginning. Gabriel had carried unregistered equipment. He had seen Sami on a Harborlight launch months later. He had feared for his ship and license and had not told police on the evening Sami died. He had now corrected the carriage record under caution, surrendered his originals to customs, and probably lost his vessel.

"Probably?" Driss asked.

"The lender has possession. A judicial sale is pending."

"And this purchases his entrance?"

"No. Nothing purchases it. I thought you should decide whether he enters."

Driss's face was equable in the way of a clock case after its spring had broken: the stillness concealed force rather than its absence. He had taught mathematics at a technical lycée before retirement. Noor remembered his patience with error and his absolute intolerance of concealed work.

"Did he touch Sami?"

"No. He saw him with a security man. He cannot truthfully affirm the man's identity."

"Did he know our son was in danger?"

"He knew Sami was frightened and involved with the buoys. He did not know what would happen in Rotterdam."

Driss looked toward the door. "Let him enter the courtyard. Not the house tonight."

Noor opened the door. Gabriel stood where she had left him, his bag at his feet, his shirt dark along the spine. The street behind him was emptying toward supper. Press vans had not yet found the lane, though messages on Noor's phone showed they were searching the district.

"My father will hear you," she said. "Brevity will be a charity."

Gabriel picked up his bag, then left it outside when he crossed the threshold.

He did not offer his hand. He stood before Driss and repeated what Noor had said, but with the dates, bearings, and omissions that belonged to him. He did not call himself a pawn or claim Rell had victimized him. He described accepting cash, falsifying position, seeing Sami beside the black service launch, and choosing silence. His voice was low. At the end he said, "I cannot requite what that silence cost. I can give every truthful account when asked and accept what follows."

Driss asked, "Why now?"

"Because each concealment made the next one easier. Because your son died while I was still husbanding my ship as if steel were sacred. Because my daughter told me she did not want an inheritance bought with evidence."

"Your daughter was required to be your conscience?"

"No. She was required to bear the consequence before I allowed her the facts. That was another wrong."

Amina rose. She was shorter than Noor remembered, or grief had altered the comparison. She went to Gabriel and studied his face with neither adoration nor hate.

"You will eat after sunset," she said. "Then you will leave. Tomorrow, if my husband asks you back, you return."

Gabriel bowed his head. "Thank you."

"Do not thank me for food. It confounds the matter."

The family broke the fast with the ritual's domestic plainness, no public piety attached to it. Amina passed dates and milk first. Driss drank water in sparing swallows. Noor had imagined homecoming as accusation, then as absolution, then had recognized both as wishful. The mundane work of plates counteracted every grand design. Her aunt Khadija carried in harira fragrant with celery and ginger; a cousin brought bread; a neighbor sent chebakia under a cloth and did not enter. Steam rose in a vaporous sheet when Amina lifted the lid, and the meal looked bounteous only because grief had made every ordinary quantity seem miscounted. Amina corrected the seasoning while insisting it required none.

Mira took one date and waited until Amina nodded before eating. Gabriel remained near the courtyard wall, ravenous but deliberate. Amina told him to sit before the soup cooled; no one would leave him to languish there as a spectacle. No one made him perform shame between mouthfuls. Noor heard spoons, distant traffic, a radio recitation in the next house, and the soft recurrent click of the stopped courtyard clock attempting to advance.

Sami's chair had not been marked as a shrine. It was the same ladder-backed chair with one loose rung, pushed under the table because space was needed. His absence did not require an oddment or bauble to consecrate it. It existed in the quantity of soup Amina had made and in the extra glass she removed before anyone sat down.

After the meal, Driss led Gabriel to the door.

"Tomorrow at nine," he said. "Bring no press, counsel, or entourage."

"I have no passport and very little entourage."

The slight humor did not assuage anything, but Driss allowed it to pass. Gabriel collected his bag and left for the small hotel customs had approved. Mira remained because Amina had prepared the upstairs room Noor once shared with visiting cousins. Noor understood the hospitality as practical, not beneficent theater.

The first press intrusion came at 21:07. A reporter rang the bell, then pressed an intercom button meant for the adjoining house. His producer called Noor while he waited outside and asked whether the Bensaid family would authorize publication of Sami's childhood photographs. Within minutes another message offered an honorarium for an exclusive interview. A third cited an unnamed forensic source and said the family opposed an independent autopsy on religious grounds.

"We have opposed nothing," Driss said.

"We have not consented in Morocco," Amina replied.

"The Rotterdam authorization stands," Noor said. "I gave it as next of kin. The post-mortem began under Dutch authority. What they need now is permission for an independent pathologist to review retained samples and, if necessary, examine him again before burial. They cannot file him away as a mishap because that is easier to administer."

The phrase examine him again struck the courtyard like a dropped utensil.

Driss turned on her. "You authorized this without us."

"Police asked me before I could reach you. There were bruises on both arms and a discrepancy in the time of death. Waiting could have destroyed evidence."

"You decided haste was sovereign."

"I decided his body should not be disposed of as an accident before we knew."

Amina said, "Do not speak of disposal in this house."

Noor stopped. She had brought forensic language across the threshold as though precision made it harmless. "I'm sorry."

Mira sat beside the stopped clock, hands visible. Driss looked at her for the first time since supper.

"Doctor, tell us what has been done. Not what should be done."

Mira gave a lucid account. Dutch authorities had performed external examination and imaging, then a conventional autopsy authorized by Noor. Tissue and fluid samples were retained according to law. An independent observer had not been present at the first procedure because one could not be arranged in time. The family could now authorize a Moroccan forensic pathologist to inspect the record, images, retained samples, and body before release. A second full dissection was not automatically required and might add little. The bilateral bruises and time interval remained questions, not proof of restraint or homicide.

"Will it avert another cutting?" Amina asked.

"A competent reviewer may decide the existing record is sufficient. I cannot promise."

"And burial?"

"The Dutch prosecutor says release could occur within three days if the independent review begins tomorrow. Without it, perhaps sooner. With disputed findings, later."

Driss said, "Religion is now blamed for delay by people who delayed telling us our son was dead."

"The reporter's claim is false," Mira said. "There is no simple theological prohibition that answers every forensic circumstance. Toxicology has not supplied an alcohol or depressant explanation that makes the bruises irrelevant. Your imam, your family, and the reviewing physician should speak about the specific acts."

"You are Muslim?"

"Yes. That does not make me your theologian. It also does not make me evenhanded by default."

The answer pleased him only because it restricted her authority.

They walked after the meal to the neighborhood mosque, leaving by a rear lane to shun the cameras at the blue door. Ramadan made the streets wake after dark. Children chased a ball beneath strings of lights. Cafes filled. A man hawked fruit from a cart with a stentorian call that rose above scooters. The city was joyous without being free of mourning; Noor resented that for half a block, then resented herself for expecting the district to dim in sympathy.

The mosque adjoined a small school and an older charitable kitchen whose ledgers recorded flour, gas cylinders, and funeral meals with the same staid care. Its square minaret had been rebuilt after a storm in the nineteen-eighties, but the lower masonry was medieval, patched by generations whose repairs did not tally in color or method. Charity here was ordinary bookkeeping, not public beneficence. At the entrance, Driss and Mira performed ablution. Noor washed because the water on her face helped, though she did not pretend devotion had returned on command.

Imam Younes met them in a plain office behind the prayer hall. He was a former engineer with a trim grey beard and an old hearing aid. Shelves held scripture, municipal notices, a gazetteer of the strait, and maintenance binders more frequently consulted than the learned works above them. He listened to the proposed review and asked exact questions about incisions, retained tissue, transport, and timing.

"The sanctity of the body does not require us to sanctify ignorance," he said. "Nor does inquiry permit every intrusion merely because police desire it. The rite of burial matters. So does establishing whether harm was inflicted. Religion is not a form one stamps after fear has already decided. Ask for the least additional examination capable of answering the question. If your family wishes, request a Muslim pathologist who is competent and independent, but do not confuse identity with competence or evenhandedness, or kinship with nepotism."

Driss asked, "You would consent?"

"I would convoke the family and let the closest kin decide. I officiate prayer. I do not inherit your grief. Theology has limits; it cannot sign away your son."

Noor had expected something oracular and felt ashamed of the expectation. Younes's answer was administrative, spiritual, and bounded. The theology was casework as much as doctrine. Religious authority here was neither absolute nor decorative, and the body's sacrosanct claim did not make every requested cut divine.

He produced a pamphlet from the national forensic council on post-mortem practice and burial. A paragraph described review after suspicious death. Someone had underlined least invasive means in blue cursive.

"Sami," Driss said.

Younes nodded. "He asked me about this last year after a dockworker died. He said the wording was slapdash. Then he rewrote it, though nobody requested his editorial service."

Amina touched the ink without smiling. "Always improving other people's papers."

At Driss's request, the imam let the family use the office telephone to call Dr. Salma Chafai, a forensic physician in Rabat. She answered at 22:14 and agreed to review the digital file overnight if Dutch authorities released it through the established channel. She would travel the next afternoon if the imaging left material doubt. She refused the press description of an "Islamic autopsy dispute" as an invented schism.

"This is a question of proportional examination, not Christendom versus Islam, not secular science versus sacred body," she said. "Those categories are useful to television because conflict is inexpensive. The law should inquire after necessity, not theatre."

Driss authorized access to the existing record. Amina authorized examination only if Dr. Chafai first stated in writing why the existing material was inadequate. Noor signed as the original consenting relative. The imam witnessed the boundaries. Mira transmitted no medical file herself; Elena arranged prosecutor-to-physician access from Marseille.

When the call ended, Younes asked Driss whether he had shown Noor the clock.

"Which clock?" Noor said.

Her father looked toward the ceiling as if patience were an inheritance he had depleted. "The tide clock. Your brother repaired it in this tower."

"There is no tide clock in a mosque."

"There is one in this mosque," Younes said. "A conventional clock tells prayer times badly when its owner neglects it. Ours also recorded harbor tide for the kitchen cistern and old quay workers. Its purpose has changed more than once."

He led them up a narrow stair inside the minaret. The ascent spiraled through stone cool enough to retain winter. A meandering conduit had been clipped along the inner wall after the last storm, inelegant but dry. Noor heard Driss's breath behind her and slowed without acknowledging it. At the first landing stood a mechanical regulator in a glass-fronted case. Brass wheels turned beneath a cable descending toward a float chamber now disconnected from the municipal drain. Beside it, an electronic display showed tide height and corrected time.

"The mechanism is older than the French protectorate," Younes said. "The electronic appendage is younger than Sami. Harbor pilots used to leave comparison slips. Children now use the tide display to predict whether the lower football court floods. It is an offbeat use of practical horology, perhaps, but it is not a curiosity cabinet."

Driss opened the maintenance binder. The annals of the machine were mundane: oil, corrosion, torque, battery, cable stretch, leakage. A 1931 French municipal note called the float chamber "antiquated but serviceable"; Sami had penciled beneath it, dated can be true, and then written in English: Do not let a modern purchase antiquate a good baseline. His handwriting appeared again three months earlier. He had replaced a resistive sensor, aligned the minute shaft, and fitted a calibration puck to compare oscillator drift. He had signed the work with his full autograph and the serial number `TM-PK-1184`.

Noor read the entry twice. "He was here in March?"

"For two nights," Amina said. She had followed them up and now stood on the stair. "He asked us not to tell you."

The revelation produced no crescendo, only a small internal cessation. Noor had been sending Sami messages in March about the London sculpture. He had replied from what she assumed was Rotterdam. He had been sleeping in the room below hers, perhaps touching the same stopped courtyard clock.

"Why?"

Driss said, "He believed his employer watched his travel. He said he needed an independent clock with a long local history. He would not explain more. I resented the secrecy. I permitted it anyway."

"Where is the puck?"

"In the clock case," Younes said. "Still sealed where he installed it."

Mira moved closer, then stopped before touching the glass. "Do not open it tonight."

Driss's petulance returned. "Must every object become foreign evidence?"

"No. That is why it should stay here until customs, the mosque trustees, and an independent metrologist agree on a protocol. The installation date can be corroborated by the maintenance entry, the clock's public display logs, and witness statements. If its diagnostic family matches the Rotterdam puck and North Sea handshake, it could authenticate that family independently. It cannot tell us who altered a buoy. Opening the case with a chisel and good intentions would be tantamount to spoiling the question we need it to answer."

Younes studied her. "You restrict your claims before anyone has made them."

"Experience."

"Or religion," he said. "A discipline of limits."

"Sometimes."

Noor looked through the narrow window. The old harbor lay below, an expanse of black water interrupted by lamps. Farther west, Tangier Med's cranes made a separate constellation. Sami had returned not to a numinous relic but to a clock with a documented baseline, maintained by a community that required tides for ordinary work. He had chosen the mosque because its timekeeping joined observance to water without allowing either to become metaphor alone. It was patrimony, not a private bequest; no scion of one family could carry it away for proof.

"Did he leave notebooks?" she asked.

Driss said, "At home. Two. One is school mathematics and complaints about his employer. One contains clock readings. Neither is a dossier."

"May I see them?"

"Tomorrow."

"Why tomorrow?"

"Because tonight you are my daughter and he is dead. Investigation does not wipe out the course of mourning."

They descended. At the base of the stair, Noor's phone caught the network and displayed nineteen new messages. One was from a broadcaster asking whether she would condemn Harborlight's sacrilegious seizure of Sami's body. Another asked whether the family wished to denigrate Dutch medicine. The better story had already begun assembling itself from words nobody in the family had used.

Outside the mosque, two cameras waited behind the paling. A reporter tried to waylay Driss and asked whether he believed European authorities had victimized his son because he was Moroccan. Driss did not answer. Noor placed herself between lens and parents, then understood that turning the confrontation into her own image would serve the same appetite.

"The family will issue a statement tomorrow," she said. "There is no religious dispute. Please leave the entrance clear."

"Did Harborlight murder Sami?"

"We do not know who caused his death."

"Do you deny he was restrained?"

"The bruises require forensic review. That is all."

The reporter tried to foment anger by repeating that Harborlight had called Sami unstable. Noor resisted. A crowd leaving prayer asked the crew to move. No one booed or threatened them. The cameras withdrew a few meters and remained.

Back in the courtyard, Amina put the notebooks on the table despite Driss's instruction to wait. "Tomorrow has arrived somewhere," she said.

The first was an old exercise book reused from Noor's lycée years, the kind Driss had kept after proctor duty because blank pages offended him. Her name remained on the cover beneath a peeling label. Sami had filled it with diagrams of clock escapements, oscillator comparisons, and complaints in a fluent mixture of French, Arabic, Dutch, and engineering shorthand. His humor survived in the margins. A drawing of the courtyard clock called it PREHISTORIC BUT TRUTHFUL. Beneath a sketch of the mosque mechanism he had written: OLD DOES NOT MEAN IMPRECISE. NEW DOES NOT MEAN INDEPENDENT. Another note marked a sensor tweak after cleaning and warned that comparison required parsimony: subtract dust, battery sag, and temperature before blaming fraud.

The second notebook collated dates. Sami had compared three pucks: the London unit later sealed in Noor's sculpture; the mosque unit; and a factory reference identified only as `GOLD BENCH`. Entries showed similar drift until a firmware revision numbered `4G-R17`. After that, field devices reported offsets not present in the physical pucks. He had underlined: comparison is against signal treatment, not quartz. Do not impute packet to instrument. The interplay was narrow and incredible enough: honest oscillators agreed while transmitted values began to lie.

Mira photographed nothing. She asked Driss to place each notebook in a separate clean envelope and sign across the flap. The family would retain them. Customs could make witnessed images tomorrow. The mosque puck would remain installed until a court-approved examination. Evidence custody began by saying where objects would not go.

"He knew the firmware was false," Noor said.

"He knew a discrepancy recurred after a revision," Mira replied. "He may have suspected manipulation. This does not establish where the update occurred or who ordered it."

"You make him sound timid."

"No. I make his evidence truthful."

The words might once have provoked an altercation. Instead Noor heard the care inside them. Treating Sami as an idol would make him omniscient, then make every imperfect inference a weapon against his credibility. His legacy was narrower and stronger: he had noticed that honest clocks and transmitted values diverged after service.

Amina turned pages until she found a list of calls. Rotterdam police. A metrology laboratory. Noor. Beside Noor's name Sami had written three attempts and a time.

The call Noor had ignored.

Her body knew before speech. A velvety darkness appeared at the edges of her sight. She sat, cheek cold against one hand. For days she had treated confession as an object she could keep in custody until a useful moment. Here was its autograph in Sami's hand.

"Mama," she said. "Baba. There is something I did not tell you."

Driss closed the notebook.

Noor told them Sami had asked her months earlier to safeguard the recorder and puck. She had put both inside her installation and used the recorder's audible tracks in the work without examining its diagnostic channel. On the final day, he had called three times. She was meeting a curator after weeks of his alarms and messages. She silenced the phone. Later she saw his message asking her to listen beneath the chorus. She had thought he was being dramatic, brash with danger because he was wounded by work, and she had been prodigal with explanations for not listening. She had not called back before he died.

She did not say her answer would have saved him. That conjecture was an arrogant form of self-importance. She said only what she had done.

Amina's face became wan. "You had his machine?"

"Yes."

"You knew he was afraid?"

"I knew he said he was afraid. I believed he was magnifying another workplace fight."

"And after Rotterdam?"

"I did not tell police immediately. I was afraid Harborlight would take the sculpture and make his voice theirs."

Driss asked, "How long?"

"Hours. Then I told Mira and police. Police sealed the installation and made a forensic copy under witnessed custody. The original recorder remained sealed, and the copy helped prove the early gate packet."

"That is not requital," he said.

"No."

"It does not counteract the unanswered call."

"No."

His anger did not become monstrous because it was quiet. "You speak of custody as if love were a museum. You kept your brother where nobody could contradict your picture of him."

The charge was exact. Noor had no defense except the chronology she had already given. She did not plead artistic ownership or sibling intimacy. She did not convert guilt into accusation against Vale, Rell, Gabriel, police, or herself.

Amina wept without a wail. She pressed both palms to her eyes, then upturned them as though grief had weight. Mira rose to leave, but Amina said, "Stay. You already know."

Driss walked once around the basin. The whispering leaves above him made each turn audible. "Did Sami blame you in the message?"

"No."

"Play it."

Noor used the copy police had authorized her to retain. Sami's voice entered the courtyard through the small phone speaker, tired and hasty: Nouri, I know you are angry. Keep the piece where it is. Listen beneath the chorus when you can. The pulse is not music. I need the puck untouched. Call me before you let anyone move it. I may be wrong about the route. I am not wrong about the clocks.

The message ended. A scooter passed outside. The stopped courtyard clock clicked and failed again.

Amina said, "He thought he might be wrong."

"Yes."

"And you thought that made his fear less dire."

"Yes."

"I cannot assuage you."

"I am not asking you to. I do not want undeserved mercy to masquerade as truth."

That was the first truthful sentence Noor had found that did not also seek control. She sat while her mother mourned and her father resented her. The pain did not become ineffable or sacred. It was specific: three unanswered calls; a diagnostic channel unheard; a son dead abroad; a daughter home with evidence and no power to alter time.

Near two in the morning, Dr. Chafai sent her preliminary review. The existing imaging and tissue record were adequate to confirm the skull injury and likely time interval. The arm bruises remained discrepant with an unrestrained fall, but she could assess them from calibrated photographs and histology. She requested no second dissection. She would issue an independent report after direct consultation with the Dutch pathologist and asked that Sami's body be released for burial when the prosecutor completed formalities.

Driss read the message. "We consent to the review as restricted."

Amina nodded. Noor signed beneath them. The decision did not make the autopsy beneficent; it made further intrusion unnecessary while preserving inquiry.

At dawn on Day Seventeen, after a short sleep, Driss took Noor to Sami's room. It was not untouched. Amina had washed the bedding and opened the shutters. School prizes, obsolete circuit boards, and a model steamboat remained on the shelf. One wall carried photographs of the old harbor, including the mosque tide display at different water levels. On the desk stood a cardboard archive box labeled CLOCK, not HARBORLIGHT. The label was not iconoclastic or clever; it was Sami refusing the lazy disavowal that everything began with the company.

Inside were copies, not originals: public tide tables, calibration certificates, mosque maintenance receipts, and an email from Hamid Belkacem at TM-Systèmes. The email said the gold bench had passed tolerance before the `R17` recall and asked Sami why Harborlight wanted all field gateways returned through the bonded warehouse instead of the cooperative's service room.

Noor read the date. Two weeks before the unregistered buoys shipped.

"Hamid," she said. "He is the plant engineer customs said was on leave."

Mira, called upstairs, examined the printed header. "This supports a service route. It still does not prove the field units went through it. We need the factory build records and recall manifests."

Driss said, "And the second puck?"

"It can authenticate the family signature against a unit Sami installed before the Rotterdam dispute," Mira said. "If the factory records show the shipped devices passed tolerance, and warehouse service occurred later, the combination could distinguish manufacture from alteration. That is an orthodox proof path, not a plunge toward accusation."

The causal route settled without fanfare. The family decision had preserved a body review within limits. The confession had removed Noor's last private authority over Sami's final call. The notebook and clock had produced no miraculous dossier, only an independently time-anchored instrument and the name of a living technician.

At nine, Gabriel returned. Driss admitted him to the house this time. Customs Inspector El Idrissi arrived with a metrology officer and two mosque trustees. They surveyed the clock case without opening it, photographed the seal and serial, copied the maintenance page under witness, and recorded that the puck remained in mosque custody. Noor's notebooks stayed with Driss after customs made read-only images and issued hashes.

The metrologist explained gravely that removal might disturb the long comparison series. They agreed to test it in situ first. A cable could read the public diagnostic port without changing memory. Harborlight counsel would receive notice but no authority to seize the device. The trustees restricted publication of prayer schedules and donor records captured incidentally. The mosque's philanthropy was evidence only by accident and would not be made public for a lawsuit.

"A mosque is not an evidence warehouse," Younes said.

"Nor will it become one," El Idrissi replied.

At 10:26 the test returned the same protocol-family preamble as Sami's London puck and the North Sea handshake, with an oscillator history dating continuously from the March installation. The match did not identify `TM-4G-7719-R`; it established that the diagnostic family existed in an independently maintained device before Harborlight's recent acquisition of the plant. The clock's physical tide trace also diverged from the synthetic values sent in the North Sea.

Mira wrote the conclusion herself, then gave it to each witness to amend: FAMILY PROTOCOL CONSISTENT. INDEPENDENT INSTALLATION DATE CORROBORATED. NO CONCLUSION AS TO OPERATOR, INTENT, OR FIELD-FIRMWARE CHANGE.

Noor would once have resented the final sentence as timidity. Now she saw it as the boundary that allowed the first two to stand.

At noon, Dr. Chafai formally accepted appointment. Dutch authorities scheduled Sami's release after her review. The family issued a statement of six lines: they had authorized independent forensic review; no second autopsy was presently sought; burial timing depended on lawful release; they would not discuss private mourning; evidence questions remained open; reporters were asked to keep the mosque and home entrances clear.

The statement did not denigrate Harborlight or sanctify Sami. It gave the press less than they wanted and the family more than silence.

Before leaving for the industrial zone, Noor repaired the courtyard clock with Driss. Its failure was trivial: dust on a contact and a weak battery, not a portent. Driss held the case while she cleaned the terminal. When the minute hand advanced, neither called it healing.

"You will report what happens at the factory," he said.

"Yes."

"Not what you need us to believe."

"What happens, what it supports, and what it does not."

He looked at her, still aggrieved, still her father. "That will do for today."

Mira waited at the blue door with El Idrissi. A customs van idled in the lane. Across the street, cameras rose, but Noor did not avert her face or offer it. The mosque puck remained where Sami had installed it, under trustees' custody and a new witnessed seal. His notebooks remained with his parents. His body remained in Rotterdam pending bounded review. Nothing had been wrested from the family to make the investigation proceed.

The factory had built the device family correctly or it had not. The recall had passed through cooperative hands or bypassed them. Hamid Belkacem knew enough to have questioned the route, and the bonded warehouse stood between manufacture and the false sea.

Noor closed the blue door behind her. In the courtyard, two clocks now moved: the repaired domestic clock and, above the roofs, the old tide regulator whose patient comparison had outlasted secrecy. Neither forgave anyone. Both kept time.

## Chapter 18: Tolerance

The factory manager wanted Mira to choose between sabotage and defect before she had entered the building.

On Day Eighteen, Meridian Adaptive's new fascia covered the old cooperative name but not its screw holes. The white sign reflected the industrial-zone sun with ostentatious force. Below it, workers queued at a temporary security desk while a contractor compared their badges against a list revised overnight. Those admitted wore blue coats. Those refused stood in a narrow strip of shade beside the steel palings of the perimeter fence, disgruntled and wary.

Inspector El Idrissi presented the preservation order at 07:56. The manager, Nabil Amrani, read its first page and said, "If this is about Rotterdam, the unit was defective or someone tampered with it. Those are the choices."

"They are conclusions," Mira said. "We are here for records and measurements."

"You are the analyst from television."

"Today I am an observer designated by customs. Dr. Leila Hmoud performs the quality review."

Leila, a materials engineer from the national metrology institute, lifted one eyebrow. She had brought two sealed instrument cases and the unpretentious impatience of someone accustomed to executives introducing her own expertise. Hamid Belkacem had not answered calls. His personnel status showed medical leave, yet his address on file was an old harbor workshop that no longer housed residents.

El Idrissi required Nabil to preserve production, test, recall, payroll, chemical-safety, and access records. Meridian's counsel attended by video and objected to the breadth. El Idrissi narrowed one clause, refused three others, and sealed the server room before anyone could withdraw a drive. The order did not grant carte blanche: employee medical records would remain with occupational health; unrelated client designs would be segregated; customs could inspect lot `TM-4G` and the `R17` service campaign.

At the gate, a woman named Zohra Mansouri demanded entry. She had assembled gateway boards for twelve years and served on the former cooperative council. Meridian had demoted her to temporary line inspector after acquisition. Security said her badge status was confused.

"Confused is a machine word for a human decision," she said.

Nabil muttered that Zohra's outspokenness had become disciplinary misbehavior. El Idrissi asked whether she was named in the preserved production records. When he assented, customs admitted her as a material witness and required security to restore access for the inspection. It was a small decision, but it differentiated present management control from the workers who had built the devices.

The plant's interior was spartan and clean. Air moved through overhead flues. Worktables stood in islands beneath omnidirectional lamps. Brass jigs, solder extractors, microscopes, and collapsible test racks occupied marked places. Nothing resembled the clandestine workshop imagined by commentators already calling the factory a cause celebre. It was an economical facility designed to make robust instruments in modest runs, with a red fire hydrant boxed into the wall beside the coating room and a floor drain kept clear by habit rather than inspection theater.

Mira's attention went first to omission. The line displayed current safety cards, but adhesive shadows showed that older cards had been removed; one laminated evacuation sheet gave a faint flutter whenever the extraction fan cycled. A reagent cabinet had new labels. The clean-room pressure monitor showed a recurrent alarm between 14:00 and 16:00 over the preceding week. Near the conformal-coating booth, a young worker rubbed his wrist and blinked too often.

Leila opened the first test archive. Every finished gateway had undergone dimensional inspection, thermal cycling, salt-fog exposure, radio verification, and oscillator comparison. Tolerance was not a synonym for permission. It described the acceptable variance around a specified value. A housing could differ by fractions of a millimeter and remain functional; a pressure reading could wander within a stated band and remain truthful. The question was whether the North Sea device had left this line inside those bands.

"Lot records," Leila said.

Nabil produced an abstract generated by Meridian counsel. It summarized ninety-six units as conforming.

"Not the abstract. Raw bench results."

"The old database is archived."

"Then mount the archive."

He disliked the verb because it denied him discretion over what counted. A technician mounted a read-only image under customs supervision. Zohra supplied the obsolete field names when the new interface bowdlerized them into generic status labels. `GOLD BENCH` was not a metaphor: it was the nickname for a traceable reference station with gold-plated contacts resistant to corrosion. Beside it, an old maintenance chart still used the period shop word `scrap` for rejected housings and clipped wire, keeping waste out of the witness-board bins.

The `TM-4G` records appeared one unit at a time. Mira and Leila sifted without extrapolating. Serial `7719-R`, photographed before the North Sea module was lost, had passed final test eight months earlier. Housing seal compression sat near the center of tolerance. Oscillator slippage measured less than one part per million. Salinity input returned the test solutions accurately. Pressure response was linear. Firmware signature at dispatch was `4G-16.8`, signed by the cooperative's release key.

"A passing factory test does not prove later performance," Nabil said.

"Correct," Mira replied.

The quick agreement wrong-footed him. He had prepared to defend manufacture against accusation; she was not making the accusation.

Zohra showed them retained witness boards, one from every production batch. The `7719` board remained sealed in a nitrogen pouch. Customs photographed the pouch, signatures, and environmental indicator before Leila opened it. The board's chip contained the dispatch firmware. Its protocol-family preamble matched the mosque puck and recorded handshake, but its protected channel did not generate synthetic values under the same simulated inputs. The result prodded Leila away from suspicion of workmanship and toward the narrower question of what the service route had later allowed.

"So the sea unit was altered," Zohra said.

"The recorded behavior differs from this retained board," Mira said. "We still need to exclude component aging, field repair, corruption, and configuration."

"You avoid every straightforward sentence."

"I am trying to earn one."

They moved to environmental testing. A saline chamber stood beside a thermal cabinet, both scarred by years of use. The process was not glamorous: heat, cool, spray, dry, repeat. Desiccation mattered because trapped moisture could change electrical resistance; residue mattered because an inadequately washed board could become conductive in salt air. Shrinkage in a polymer gasket could admit water. None of those defects would selectively create two identities from one assembly, but each had to be examined before sabotage became the only congenial story.

Leila inspected the retained gasket under magnification. Its imperfections were ordinary mold marks. Chemical analysis found no unusual plasticizer loss. The board carried no stain, crack, or lifted pad. A pale macula of flux residue sat where the work instruction allowed it, and an infinitesimal solder void beneath one chip remained inside criterion. The solvent check used a control reactant from the cabinet; Leila would distill the rinse before spectroscopy, and the preliminary runs did not suggest a manufacturing contaminant that would explain the false stream. The instrument had not been built as an impostor.

At 10:20 the young worker near the coating booth sat abruptly on the floor.

His name was Rachid El Fassi. He was twenty-six, gregarious according to Zohra, and now pallid enough that Mira crossed the room before anyone asked. He complained of headache, nausea, chest tightness, and a metallic taste. His pulse was rapid. Sweat stood along his hairline although the production floor was cool, a sebaceous shine that had nothing to do with the torrid yard outside.

"Fresh air," Mira said. "Do not make him walk. Shut the booth process."

Nabil interposed. "The occupational nurse is coming. We cannot halt a validated line on a cursory impression."

"His symptoms began beside a solvent process and two alarms show ventilation depression. The expedient action is to stop exposure."

El Idrissi ordered the booth isolated. Zohra hit the emergency cutoff. Fans wound down. Workers moved to the assembly hall, not pell-mell but with practiced vigilance. Rachid received oxygen from the wall station while the nurse connected a portable electrocardiograph. The electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia without ischemic change. Mira checked pupils, lungs, skin, and mental status, careful not to transform epidemiology into an authority she did not possess.

The nurse, Samia Qadiri, said three workers had reported similar symptoms during the week. Meridian management attributed them to fasting, heat, and anxiety. No one had been referred because the episodes resolved after shifts. She lifted Rachid's sleeve with his consent and checked the epidermis at his wrist; there was irritation but no chemical ulcer.

"Fasting does not explain why symptoms peak by this booth," Mira said.

"I know," Samia replied. "My referral requests were withdrawn from the system."

Nabil said the word withdrawn had a defamatory connotation. Samia retrieved paper copies. Each request bore her signature and a later digital cancellation under an administrative account created after acquisition.

An ambulance arrived from the industrial clinic. Rachid's oxygen saturation remained acceptable, but wheeze developed. The physician gave a bronchodilator and transferred him for observation and toxicology. Two coworkers with headache and eye irritation went too. Their illness was not a narrative contribution to the evidence hunt. Work had made them ill, and the inquiry had happened to be present. The odorous booth air would have to be measured, not converted into rumor.

Leila sampled the booth air after donning protection. The coating process used an acrylic resin thinned with solvent. The safety sheet required local extraction and a charcoal stage. Inspection found the charcoal cassette installed backward after a contractor's service, while the pressure alarm had been made suppressible for two-hour intervals. The solvent concentration would not be known until laboratory testing. Neither Mira nor Samia called it poisoning yet. The pitfall was obvious in another way: a suppressible alarm could metamorphose a safety device into a calendar nuisance.

"Was the contractor Meridian?" Zohra asked.

"A local ventilation firm," Nabil said too quickly.

"Then this is not Harborlight's fault," one line supervisor said.

"It is not an argument about symbolic fault," Mira replied. "Someone authorized continued production through recurrent alarms. Occupational health records who."

The distinction mattered. Institutional coercion did not turn every manager into a fiend or every worker into an innocent automaton. Nabil had accepted counsel's stipulation that output continue during acquisition. He had also ignored Samia's referrals. Zohra had known the alarms were being suppressed but believed maintenance would arrive. Workers had remained because wages were in arrear. Responsibility was multiform and unequal; penny-pinching explained part of the heedlessness, but not all of it.

At the clinic, Rachid improved in clean air. Initial blood work excluded several acute hazards but did not identify the solvent. Samia arranged follow-up rather than declaring him cured. The plant remained closed pending ventilation review. El Idrissi amended the preservation order to include alarm changes and contractor instructions. Meridian counsel called the closure disproportionate. Rachid, listening from a treatment chair, said, "They acquired our patents, debts, and apparently our lungs."

Mira did not use the line publicly. His anger belonged first to him, and clinic privacy was not alienable because counsel wanted a cleaner press note.

The shutdown gave workers an unexpected forum in the canteen. Former cooperative members demanded a vote on whether to assist customs. Meridian said employment agreements forbade disclosure. Elena joined by secure call and explained that the preservation order compelled records but did not compel workers to waive personal rights. They could enlist counsel or union representation before giving factual statements, and any consent they gave that afternoon was not an irrevocable surrender of clinic privacy, immigration worries, or wage claims. No one had to become a testimonial for either side.

Zohra convened the old council anyway. Twelve workers attended; five abstained because they feared retaliation; nine nonmembers asked to observe. The factory's egalitarian origin had never erased hierarchy. Engineers had been paid more. Temporary cleaners lacked voting rights. A cooperative could reproduce exclusion while calling itself commonwealth. Its bylaws had required a provident reserve for safety shutdowns, but loan covenants and payroll had eaten through it.

"Do not make us saints because Meridian is worse," Zohra told Mira. "We economized on filters two years ago. We delayed Samia's request for a second nurse. We were beholden to one large customer and pretended that was providence."

"Who was the customer?"

"Harborlight. Nearly sixty percent at peak. Then they canceled an order and our loan failed."

"Did the cancellation require a recall?"

"Different contract. The `R17` campaign came first."

The workers voted to authorize inspection of cooperative records for the specified lot and recall. They appointed Zohra and an assembler named Karim as custodians. Meridian retained ownership of the servers; customs retained the legal image; workers retained their statements. The arrangement accommodated overlapping claims without pretending they were congruent. Elena called the delineation plain enough for a judge and narrow enough for frightened employees to understand.

Raw recall records showed that forty-eight gateways, including `7719-R`, had been called back for "regional compatibility and security hardening." The service instruction did not return them to TM-Systèmes. It directed sealed crates to Bonded Warehouse C at Tangier Med under a Harborlight logistics account. Cooperative engineers were told the update used proprietary signing infrastructure and would be performed by an approved mobile brigade. The depositor named on the bonded forms was Harborlight Maritime Services, not the cooperative that had built the instruments.

"We objected," Zohra said. "Firmware affects calibration. If you change signal treatment, we repeat tolerance testing."

"Response?" El Idrissi asked.

Karim found the email. Harborlight's service coordinator said the update was configuration-only and could not affect metrological performance. Reopening crates at the cooperative would void the cybersecurity chain. The paradox was stark: the company demanded worker confidence in a change it also forbade workers to test.

"Did units return here afterward?" Mira asked.

"Some," Zohra said. "Not these four. They went from the warehouse to Gabriel's ship."

The dispatch database corroborated her. Factory-to-warehouse transport had legitimate customs seals. Warehouse-to-vessel records used the inactive exporter code and false cargo description already preserved in Gabriel's correction. Manufacture and illicit carriage did not collide at the factory gate. A bonded interval joined them, an entanglement of lawful custody and false description.

Leila compared firmware packages. The cooperative retained only the hash Harborlight supplied after service. It did not match `4G-16.8`. The signed replacement was `4G-R17.3`. Its package was absent from the factory server. A service receipt listed successful installation, but no individual technician signed it. The performer field contained a code: `HB-04`.

"Hamid Belkacem," Nabil said.

Zohra scoffed. "Or someone using his initials. Hamid would not service blind."

Karim said `HB-04` was Hamid's authorized test account. The room shifted toward a culprit with indecent speed.

Mira asked when the account had authenticated. The log showed Hamid signing the pre-service manifest at 08:12 from the factory. Firmware completion appeared at 10:46 from the warehouse. At 10:41 Hamid's badge entered the factory clean room, where camera stills showed him working beside Zohra. He could not have been in both places.

"Credential misuse," Zohra said.

"Or remote approval, shared token, cloned badge, altered log," Mira said. "The overlap makes his physical performance unlikely. It does not establish which explanation."

Nabil wanted to call the log inadmissible because its time server had since been replaced. Leila found daily synchronization against the gold bench and a municipal timestamp. Drift was less than two seconds. Authentication might be corruptible; time was not murky enough to erase the overlap.

Hamid's personnel file contained a disciplinary notice issued after he challenged the recall. He wrote that the warehouse package exceeded configuration scope and required bench retest. Management called the claim insubordinate and suspended his signing authority. Yet `HB-04` continued to appear on twenty-one later updates. The continuity of that account did not astound Leila; it offended her because authentication systems were supposed to fail closed when authority was revoked.

"Why did the cooperative accept those receipts?" Mira asked.

Zohra answered before Nabil. "Because rejecting them meant rejecting the Harborlight contract. We had payroll in four days."

"Did you believe the units unsafe?"

"We believed the signature process was opaque. We had no evidence of fictitious measurements. Hamid was more suspicious."

"Did he report externally?"

"To the port standards office. They referred him back to the customer."

Connivance was too strong for workers forced by insolvency, and innocence too generous. They had accepted an opaque service route under economic pressure. Mira recognized the temptation to rationalize every compromise as coercion. Pressure constrained choice; it did not annihilate it. Treating payroll as an irresistible tempter would be another naivety.

The old council's minutes contained the argument. Hamid moved to suspend shipment. Zohra supported retesting but opposed a total stop. Seven members voted to release units on Harborlight's warranty; four opposed; three abstained. The vote was no hidden assassination plot. It was ordinary institutional weakness preserved in copious detail.

"You may publish my vote," Zohra said. "Do not publish the temporary workers' names."

"The report will distinguish both," El Idrissi said.

At 15:30 occupational inspectors arrived. They photographed the reversed filter, sampled residue, and interviewed Samia. Meridian tried to separate the safety closure from the customs inquiry. The inspectors agreed on legal jurisdiction but not factual isolation: acquisition instructions, production pressure, and alarm suppression had temporal overlap. One event did not prove the other, yet the same management change affected both access and working conditions. A relentless search for a single cause would obscure that conglomeration rather than clarify it.

Mira called Rachid at the clinic with his permission. His wheeze had eased. Toxicology suggested solvent exposure but remained preliminary. He was not to return until cleared. He asked whether the devices were defective.

"The retained factory board passed tolerance and behaves correctly," she said. "The North Sea recording differs after a warehouse update."

"So we did not poison the sea."

"The evidence does not support defective manufacture as the cause of the false stream."

He exhaled. Relief was followed by anger. "Management will reopen tomorrow and call today a gaffe."

"The safety inspector controls reopening, not Meridian alone."

"You believe procedure is automatic?"

"No. I believe named authority is preferable to a promise."

Before leaving, Leila ran the dispatch firmware through a controlled simulator. Honest temperature, pressure, and salinity inputs produced variable outputs consistent with the bench. Then she applied the documented `R17` configuration flags reconstructed from receipt metadata. The retained firmware rejected them as unsupported. Whatever the bonded warehouse installed had expanded the command surface. An undirected identity flag in the receipt metadata had no signification in dispatch firmware; in `R17.3` it appeared to govern how a device answered more than one profile. El Idrissi had a technician dedicate one read-only terminal to exporting that narrow log set, because a broad server pull would invite objections the evidence did not need.

The technical point changed the next action. They did not need to prove every instruction inside the missing package at the factory. They needed the service ledger, signing station, and access records at Bonded Warehouse C. Those records could show who performed or authorized updates and whether devices were selected by engineering criteria. It would be a herculean application for an evening judge because bonded goods, client secrets, and worker custody all had to be separated without losing the trail.

El Idrissi requested an immediate warrant. The port prosecutor declined emergency entry without a living witness who could identify the service process; Meridian argued the warehouse held many clients' bonded goods and that the receipts were sufficient. The prosecutor authorized preservation but scheduled inspection for Day Twenty-One after notice.

Three days was enough time for lawful obstruction to become effective.

"Hamid is the witness," Zohra said. "Find him before Meridian does."

His leave certificate had been issued by the old-harbor clinic for anxiety and insomnia. The clinic would not disclose an address. Samia, respecting confidentiality, said only that Hamid had asked about treatment for solvent headaches months earlier and had stopped attending after someone followed him from an appointment.

"Did he say who?" Mira asked.

"No. He was peery. He believed his telephone had been copied."

Nabil called that paranoia. Samia's expression became tart. "A medical impression is not yours to manufacture."

Customs found a different route. Hamid still held a port electrician's permit for maintaining the old harbor tide gauge. Permit scans showed weekly entry, most recently the previous night. He had listed an emergency contact: Captain Youssef Tazi at the pilot office. The permit was an outlying record, but it had the practical virtue of being current.

Mira wrote the name beside the warehouse code. She did not feel triumph. A living technician had been driven from the plant while colleagues became ill under its new owner. The investigation had cleared their workmanship but exposed the cost of assuming coercion left no residue on people.

At sunset the workers broke their fast in the closed canteen. Management had ordered everyone off site, but the safety inspector permitted a meal before dispersal. Families sent bread, eggs, olives, and lentil soup through the gate. No one produced a bountiful feast for cameras. Rachid's empty chair remained empty, not adorned. Zohra paused to lave her hands at the utility sink, then began afresh with the workers who had refused to vote in front of management.

Zohra gave Mira a bowl and sat across from her. "You came expecting sabotage."

"I came asking whether output differed before or after manufacture."

"That is what an analyst says when she wants to seem without inclination."

Mira considered the charge. "I expected alteration after we saw dual identities. I did not know whether factory staff performed it."

"Better."

"I also underestimated how acquisition pressure affected safety."

"Better again. Do not become addicted to self-abasement. It is another way to occupy the center."

Mira almost laughed. Zohra did not.

Karim brought the factory's original `R17` objection in a sealed folder. It bore four signatures, including Hamid's. The document stated that any update changing calibration lookup, packet routing, or identity handling required full environmental retest. Harborlight's reply asserted that no such functions changed. The juxtaposition was useful because it created a falsifiable claim. North Sea behavior showed identity handling had changed somewhere after dispatch. Warehouse records could establish whether `R17` was that change. The objection was not lapidary prose; its power lay in practical orthography, dates, signatures, and the exact spelling of account codes.

"Take a copy," Karim said.

El Idrissi made a witnessed image. The original stayed with the worker custodians under the preservation order. Meridian counsel received notice and a hash, not unilateral possession.

Nabil approached after the meal. His earlier imperious manner had collapsed into fatigue. "If you say the factory built correctly, will customs let us reopen?"

"Metrological findings do not supersede occupational safety," Leila said.

"Three hundred households depend on wages."

Zohra replied, "Then you should not have suppressed alarms."

"I did not reverse the filter."

"You kept the line running."

He looked at Mira as though she might mediate morality into a manageable defect code.

"The plant can reopen when ventilation is safe," she said. "The evidence supports correct original manufacture. It also supports a post-production update outside worker-controlled service. Both findings belong in the report."

"And me?"

"The safety inspector records what you authorized."

Institutional coercion and individual complicity could occupy the same person. Mira did not need to choose a stereotype.

After dark they drove from the industrial zone toward Tangier. Heat radiated from warehouse walls. At the port perimeter, Bonded Warehouse C loomed behind floodlights, a leviathan of corrugated steel divided into customs cages. Trucks entered through a gate controlled by biometric readers. El Idrissi's preservation notice had been served, but a Meridian legal team was already inside inventorying its own goods under supervision.

"They can inspect but not move," she said. "They can also learn exactly what we seek."

Mira watched a forklift lug sealed crates past an open bay. The selected gateways had gone into that building correctly built and emerged with a different firmware signature, a false description, and two data identities. The alteration was not proved, but the interval was now bounded. The distinction felt profound only because it was so limited.

Noor called from the family home. Dr. Chafai had completed her independent review. The bruises were consistent with forceful bilateral gripping before death; she could not identify the gripper. The head injury remained the immediate cause. Dutch authorities would release Sami after final police documentation. The family planned burial in Tangier when transport permitted, and Noor said the obsequies would remain a family decision, not an evidentiary deadline.

Mira closed her eyes. Technical causation and bodily causation advanced on different tracks, neither complete.

"There is more," Noor said. "A message came to my father's landline. A man said Hamid should stop hiding behind dead engineers."

"Recorded?"

"No. My mother answered. The caller knew Hamid had repaired a tide reader at the old harbor."

El Idrissi heard through the car speaker. "We go to the pilot office now."

Gabriel was waiting there under his customs reporting condition. Captain Tazi had known Hamid since apprenticeship. He said the technician slept intermittently in an unused chandlery above the old harbor, moving when strangers appeared. Tazi had promised not to disclose the place except to someone who could protect him.

"Can you protect him?" Tazi asked.

El Idrissi said, "I can record a witness statement, request protective measures, and prosecute obstruction. I cannot promise no one will follow him."

The honesty persuaded Tazi more than bravado would have. He drew a route through lanes inaccessible to vehicles. Gabriel would go first because Hamid knew him from the carriage investigation; El Idrissi would remain within call. Mira objected that Gabriel's presence might intimidate a man whose credentials had been misused.

"Then you come with me," Gabriel said. "He has seen you on television."

"That may be worse."

"We offer him the choice."

At 22:40 they found the chandlery door open. The room above it held a camp bed, a kettle, antibiotic tablets prescribed months earlier, a tide almanac, and a portable radio tuned to harbor traffic. A soldering iron was warm. Hamid was absent.

On the table lay a tide-gauge service manual and a slip of paper: SOUNDINGS DO NOT LIE, BUT DREDGERS MOVE THE QUESTION. ASK TAZI FOR THE LEDGER.

Gabriel read it and looked toward the black harbor. "He wants us to test his claim against physical depth."

A radio transmission crackled from the pilot channel. A man reported that the digital tide board had frozen. Another voice, quieter, said the manual clock remained sound. Gabriel recognized Hamid.

"Old breakwater," Tazi said through the phone. "He services the gauge from the tower access."

They reached the quay as Hamid descended a ladder carrying a tool case. He saw uniforms at the lane mouth and turned toward the water, not to jump but to take the narrow path along the wall. He was flustered rather than theatrical, one hand held out to keep balance on the algae-dark stone.

Gabriel called, "Hamid. The factory records show your account signed updates while you were in the clean room. We know that is not proof you performed them."

Hamid stopped.

Mira added, "The retained board passed tolerance. The workers built it correctly. We need your account of the bonded service. You may refuse and speak to counsel."

He faced them. He was thin, scraggly-bearded, and exhausted rather than furtive. "They will say I turned against the cooperative."

"The cooperative minutes already record your objection," Mira said.

"They will say I invented the sea data."

"The mosque puck and factory bench are independent."

"And the warehouse?"

"Preserved, not yet inspected."

Hamid laughed once without mirth. "Then you have the shell and not the creature."

He opened his tool case slowly. Inside were calibration leads, a handheld meter, and copies of service notices. No hidden package, no miraculous chip. He said he had been ordered to attend Bonded Warehouse C as the cooperative witness. Security took his signing token at entry, installed the updates behind an opaque partition, and returned the token after receipts had been generated. He protested. A Harborlight contractor told him the token authenticated attendance, not performance. When he later discovered his account on other jobs, he filed the standards complaint. The double-dealing lay there, in a credential used as presence for one purpose and performance for another.

"Can you identify the contractor?" El Idrissi asked.

"A woman called Voss, perhaps Vos. She wore no company badge. Rell came once. He did not touch the devices. He told port security I was agitating workers over a harmless compatibility patch."

"Did you see synthetic values installed?"

"No. I saw district profiles on the service console. I thought they were radio plans. After Sami called, I understood he suspected more."

"What profiles?"

"Codes, colors, update priorities. Not names. The four Gabriel carried were marked `RET-4`."

The code resembled Cadran Re's `CR-MED/RET-4`, but resemblance was not identity. Mira felt the pattern pull toward coordination and resisted declaring it.

"Will you give a formal statement?" El Idrissi asked.

Hamid looked at the harbor. "After we verify the water. Digital records were overwritten after the dredging. They will say my calibration was wrong because seabed depth changed. Tazi's pilots kept manual soundings. The mosque clock kept tide. Put them together. Then my statement has an observable base."

Gabriel understood first. A pressure baseline could be challenged by changed depth, dredging, and instrument relocation. Handwritten sounding routines corrected to an independent tide clock could separate seabed change from shifted datum. Hamid was not asking anyone to foretell the software path; he was asking them to measure water and bottom before argument hardened.

"Day Nineteen," he said. "First light."

Hamid agreed to sleep under customs protection at the pilot office rather than disappear again. He retained his copies after El Idrissi imaged them and issued a receipt. His testimony would be recorded with counsel in the morning. He was a living technician, not a key inserted into their theory.

Mira stood on the quay while the old harbor lifted and settled against stone. The factory had not yielded a villain. It had yielded correct workmanship, coerced compromise, a preventable illness, a stolen credential, and a bounded place where software changed. Each fact narrowed responsibility without simplifying the people inside it. The account was still incomplete, but its incompleteness was disciplined now, not hazy.

Behind them, the pilot office kept every light burning.

The sea beyond the breakwater was murky under city light. Its surface could not testify to its own baseline. For that, they would need the pilots' ledger, the repaired mosque clock, and Gabriel's willingness to place his false log beside both.

## Chapter 19: Sounding Line

At first light on Day Nineteen, Gabriel lowered a lead weight into water whose depth everybody disputed.

The old harbor was nearly absent from Harborlight's current chart. Its northern mole remained, as did the pilot office, fishing quay, and stone chamber where a tide float had once risen through a vertical well. Everything else appeared as simplified polygons labeled heritage use, intermittent navigation, or redevelopment margin. The chart was clean because it had discarded what no longer fit commercial traffic.

Captain Youssef Tazi stood at the bow of a nine-meter pilot launch and watched the line run through Gabriel's hand. Tazi was sixty-two, narrow-shouldered, and observant enough to make speech seem an optional supplement. Hamid sat aft under customs protection with Inspector El Idrissi. Noor had joined them carrying a clean recorder authorized only for the day's field work. Mira remained ashore with the metrologist at the mosque clock, where she would call corrected time and tide. The boatswain who had lent Tazi the launch stood on the quay long enough to check the painter and warn Gabriel about the undertow curling off the mole after each ferry wake.

Gabriel felt the lead strike silt. He lifted, let it settle again, then pinched the wet line at the gunwale.

"Four point seven meters," he said.

Tazi checked the launch's position against two masonry marks and a protruding warehouse corner. "At this tide, old ledger predicts four point eight."

Hamid looked toward the digital gauge, frozen since the previous evening. "Harborlight archive says six point one."

The variance was too large for abrasion on a lead line or a mariner's tired eye. It was also not yet proof of a shifted baseline. Dredging could deepen a channel. Silt could fill it. The launch could be aslant in current. Tide, atmospheric pressure, density, squat, and measurement technique all altered apparent depth. Tazi reproved Gabriel once after the line had twined around his wrist; a sounding line was evidence only if the hand holding it did not add drama of its own.

"Again," Gabriel said.

He had learned sounding before electronic charts became sovereign. A traditional line carried marks at known intervals; tallow in the hollow base brought up a sample of seabed. This one used modern braided cord and a machined alloy weight, augmented by a stamped serial tag and calibration certificate, but the manual principle was ancient. It did not worship the past. It offered an independent method whose imperfections were visible.

The second cast returned four point seven. The base held black mud and shell grit. Tazi entered time, position, depth, tide correction pending, and bottom type in a ledger ruled by hand.

"Pilots still keep this?" Noor asked.

"Harbor regulations prescribe a weekly comparison," Tazi said. "The digital system did not supersede it. Management stopped collecting the sheets. We did not stop making them."

"Why?"

"Because electronics fail. Because dredgers exaggerate. Because sailors prefer two ways home."

The harbor's historical sounding routine had survived as upkeep rather than nostalgia. Each Monday, pilots measured twelve stations along the approach. After storms or dredging, they added casts. The sheets antedated Harborlight's contract by decades. Some records had been digitized; others remained in cabinets above the pilot office, their pages rumpled by damp and use. Station Two adjoins redevelopment parcels, which made the routine useful to realty lawyers as well as pilots, but the pilots had never treated sale value as a depth correction.

Mira called from the mosque. "Clock correction plus zero point three seconds. Tide height one point twelve above local datum, rising gradually."

Tazi applied the correction. The reduced depth corresponded to four years of manual records within eight centimeters. Harborlight's six point one required a different zero.

They moved to Station Two, where a cul-de-sac of water adjoined the former customs quay. Gulls flitted above fishing boats. A dairy truck honked while reversing near the market. The city's daytime traffic began as a brewing discontent of engines.

Gabriel sounded again. Five casts at three stations agreed with the pilots' predicted depths. At Station Four, they did not. The lead struck hard at three point nine meters, nearly half a meter shallower than the ledger.

Hamid clenched the rail. "They will use that to impugn everything."

"Or it means the bottom changed," Gabriel said.

Tazi maneuvered twenty meters east. The next cast found four point four. Another found four point five. They circled back. The shallow patch remained pinpointed beside a drainage outlet.

"New deposit," Tazi said. "Probably rubble from the quay works."

Noor recorded position and the scrape of lead against stone. The anomalous cast did not undermine the routine. It exemplified why one did not force measurements to coalesce. The seabed genuinely changed in places. A truthful baseline had to accommodate change without transposing it into every station. Gabriel's fingers tingled from the wet cord and repeated casts, but the ache steadied him; fatigue was a poorer enemy than convenience.

At Station Five, a port-security launch intercepted them. Its officer said Harborlight's maintenance contractor had reported unauthorized hydrographic work in a controlled approach. Tazi produced his pilot authority. El Idrissi produced the customs order. The officer read both and asked whether Gabriel, whose certificate was surrendered, was navigating.

"I am handling a sounding line under Captain Tazi's command," Gabriel said.

"You are under investigation for false carriage."

"Yes."

"Then your evidence is impaired."

"My credibility is impaired. The line's length is available for inspection."

The officer seemed aggrieved by the distinction. He boarded, checked the calibrated meter marks, photographed the lead, and witnessed three casts. His presence strengthened rather than obstructed the record. Rell's methods depended on authority feeling like intimidation; sometimes authority, properly bounded, merely added a skeptical observer. El Idrissi made the officer sign as witness beneath the undersigned pilots rather than as commander of the work.

At 08:10 Mira reported a ten-minute plateau in the mosque float trace. The harbor water still appeared to rise. Hamid said the old float well could stick after algae accumulated. The group paused rather than smoothing the anomaly away. A mosque caretaker inspected the well under video and found a reed wedged against the guide, with a little trash and salt scale nibbling at the clearance. He removed it with a soft puff of compressed air, documented the intervention, and the float resumed. The manual tide series retained a marked gap.

"Harborlight will call the clock unreliable," Hamid said.

"It was unreliable for ten minutes and tells us so," Noor replied. "That is different from being made smooth afterward."

The sentence held the day's whole exegesis. An honest instrument could fail observably. A corrupted record concealed the failure or reassigned its meaning.

They completed the twelve stations before noon. Nine agreed with historical depths after tide correction. Two reflected recent authorized dredging and were deeper by expected amounts. One contained the new rubble shoal. None matched Harborlight's universal shift. The pattern distinguished local seabed change from a common datum change.

Back at the pilot office, Tazi unlocked the archive room. It was not commodious. Cabinets crowded a chamber once used for signal flags. Brass barometers hung above a desk, working but no longer official. Shelves held twentieth-century charts, harbor chronicles, dredging notices, tide tables, accident reports, and a gazetteer whose archaic place names corresponded to marks pilots still used on radio; Fatima later explained that the labels were period usage, kept because older pilots could still locate a quay by them.

Noor ran a finger near, not on, a row of ledgers. "How far back?"

"Continuous weekly sheets from 1987. Selected books from before independence. Older surveys at the municipal archive."

"And Harborlight overwrote the digital records?"

Tazi corrected her. "Its contractor migrated the port database. The old digital series became inaccessible after migration. We do not know whether overwritten means erased, transformed, or merely hidden."

Gabriel appreciated the nicety. A sailor could distrust a system without inventing its crime.

The ledgers for the relevant months were seated in a locked cabinet. Each weekly sheet carried two pilot signatures. Corrections were crossed through, not deleted. Tide references cited the mosque clock, municipal gauge, or both. Dredging notices were stapled to affected weeks. The documents formed a historical record with antecedents independent of Harborlight and Hamid.

El Idrissi called a registrar and two retired pilots to witness retrieval. One, Captain Fatima Berrada, arrived wearing a straw hat and carrying a demitasse of coffee despite the heat. She had supervised the sounding routine for fifteen years and was skeptical of everyone in the room. The other retired pilot, Daoud El Mansouri, said little, but his surname appeared on ledgers from the first year of the weekly routine.

"Gabriel Okafor," she said. "The sailor who moved four buoys and forgot where."

"I lied about where. I did not forget."

"A distinction that redounds magnificently to your reputation."

"It does not."

She appraised him for irony and found none. Then she scrutinized the day's sheet. At Station Four she asked why they had not averaged the rubble shoal with adjacent casts.

"Because it is a hazard, not noise," Gabriel said.

"Good. Some analysts would polish it away."

Mira entered from the stair, having completed the mosque inspection. "Some captains would call a universal shift from one shallow patch."

Fatima looked pleased to have found a remonstrant. "Then perhaps the room can function."

They placed the day's sheet beside manual records from the month when the four gateways passed through the bonded warehouse. Tide-corrected depths fluctuated locally by centimeters. Harborlight's migrated archive showed all stations deeper by 1.38 meters beginning at 00:00 on the date of the `R17` update. No dredging notice corresponded to the change. The shift was instantaneous and congruent across stations whose bottoms differed in mud, rock, rubble, and maintained channel.

"A dredger cannot deepen twelve places at the same second," Tazi said.

"Nor can erosion," Mira added. "But a datum change can."

Hamid opened his service copies. The warehouse console had displayed `BASELINE +1.380`. He had assumed it represented antenna altitude or pressure compensation. The field lacked units. His objection noted that changing a base value required calibration review; the contractor replied that it was a regional normalization.

"Can the plus sign explain Harborlight reporting deeper water?" Noor asked.

"Depending on convention," Mira said. "A positive offset could be added to pressure-derived depth or subtracted from zero. We need the implementation, not the label."

Fatima said, "You have twelve stations and a jump. How much more implementation does a body need?"

"Enough to tie the jump to the transmitted values rather than merely the display archive. Otherwise we are impugning a chart without proving the live feed moved."

Gabriel laid his private engine-room notebook on the table.

The room quieted. This was not one of the originals now in customs custody; it was the vessel log police had sealed in Rotterdam and released as a certified image for the inquiry. His handwritten page recorded the false position he later transmitted, the actual deployment coordinates, and the pressure checks performed during carriage. He had not previously offered its full technical appendix because it also showed two unregistered fuel transfers and a watch-hours violation.

"I request that the complete image enter this file," he said. "No redaction beyond crew medical privacy."

El Idrissi looked at him. "It will be referred to Dutch maritime authorities."

"I know."

"Your crew may be implicated."

"The watch violation was mine. The fuel entries name suppliers. Crew statements already distinguish orders."

"Why was this not in your corrected customs packet?"

"Customs received the relevant carriage originals. Police held the vessel log under a separate seal. I did not ask to expand production until today."

Fatima said, "Convenient conscience."

"Late conscience. Not convenient."

The log showed that before loading, each buoy's pressure transducer had been checked against dock water and shipboard barometer as part of cargo safety. The values corresponded to Tangier's physical tide within manufacturer tolerance. After the warehouse update, the shipping diagnostic displayed a baseline 1.38 meters different. Gabriel had queried the broker. The broker told him to treat it as destination calibration and forbade connecting the units again. His misgivings had been moral, not sensory: he saw the discrepancy, chose the answer that let cargo move, and wrote the safer lie.

"You saw the shift before sailing," Mira said.

"I saw a number without context. I asked once, accepted an answer that suited me, and carried them."

"Did you record the broker's response?"

"Here."

The notation included time, initials, and the phrase NORMALIZED FOR NORTHERN BASIN. No audio survived. The broker could deny the wording. Yet the date and value corresponded to Hamid's warehouse screen and the universal shift in the migrated harbor archive.

Gabriel's false log became corroboration by confessing its own falsity. The reported position was wrong; the contemporaneous instrument values and actual coordinates were preserved beside the lie. It did not vindicate him. It showed that he had noticed the altered baseline and failed to pursue it because cargo discretion and debt mattered more.

"Will you state this on television?" Noor asked.

"If required. Before immunity, before license outcome."

"They will say you manufactured the log after the voyage."

"Police imaging antedates our discovery. Paper and ink can be appraised from the original in Rotterdam. The lie is already in official records."

El Idrissi requested transfer of the full certified image and notified Dutch authorities of the additional offenses. Gabriel signed the request. The cost was no theatrical martyrdom. It was another probable charge, a harder license hearing, and damage to crew trust.
