The court had not authorized their transfer into French evidence. They remained his property, available for inspection under agreed protocol. Elena checked the receipt twice. Fatigue made negligence more likely precisely when everyone felt urgent.

Mira came out behind him. She had seen the partial export and looked ill with frustration.

"The 386 headers show clusters," she said quietly. "DIC-4 service precedes public risk changes in some destination classes, but locations are masked. We cannot connect them to parcels."

"Then we do not say they do."

"I know."

The sharpness was not aimed at Elena. Mira's family had not answered her latest calls. Vale's disclosure lay against every new fact like a posterior shadow, altering how she stood in public even when she was not speaking.

"Are you coming on the ferry?" Elena asked.

"Yes. Priya confirmed the Marseille hospital meeting for Day Twenty-three. She did not confirm she would help."

"Noor?"

"At security. She persuaded the terminal to keep Hamid off the public passenger list display."

"Persuaded lawfully?"

"She asked them to apply their existing protected-traveler setting."

Elena felt an inappropriate flare of pride. Noor had not tried to command the record; she had found the person who owned the decision.

They crossed the terminal at a lean walk. Check-in had begun closing lane ropes. The building's amenities were paltry: a café griddle, vending machines, a prayer room, hard benches, and one children's corner with breakable plastic toys secured by cable. Families clustered around chargers. Drivers slept sitting upright. A choir of boarding announcements reverberated in Arabic, French, Spanish, and English, each translation slightly off-key.

At the police desk, an officer took Hamid's ordinary phone and sealed it in the pouch while he watched. Hamid powered it down himself. The officer wrote the serial, seal number, and condition. Benali photographed the sealed pouch and receipt. Noor recorded no sound and took no image. A protected route was not material for her work.

The officer used red security tape to swathe the pouch twice, crossing the closure and the small plastic protrusion that would show if anyone tried to lift the seal. Hamid asked to see the number before it left his hand, and the officer turned it toward him without comment.

Rell appeared beyond the glass security channel.

He had removed the visitor vest and carried a slim case. Two contractors followed. His Marseille booking was on a faster flight through Madrid, Noor learned from no illicit source but from hearing him request the priority lane. He had no need to stalk them onto the ferry. Law and money supplied greater latitude.

He caught Elena's glance and approached as far as the barrier allowed.

"Deputy Counsel," he said.

"Not presently."

"The title may outlast today's hesitancy."

"My hesitancy ended when the secretariat suspended me."

"You think that emboldens you?"

"It clarifies who bears the risk."

His cordiality disappeared. "Belkacem has no ledger. His recollection is fallible. Cadran's settlement will compensate every verified claimant. What exactly are you preserving now?"

Elena looked at him through the barrier. "A witness you cannot define as a file."

"You mistake supervision for tyranny because it impedes you."

"And you mistake a valid order for expiation."

His smile became disdainful, not broad enough for anyone else to call it discourtesy.

For the first time his expression shifted. Not guilt, not fear; annoyance that she had refused the parlance in which compliance erased purpose.

"You drafted the system," he said.

"Yes."

"Vale gave it effect."

"Yes."

"When this collapses, do not narrate yourself as the late heroine."

The accusation was valid enough to sting. Elena would not rebut it with motive.

"I won't."

Rell walked toward the priority lane. He neither threatened nor pursued them. By the time the ferry sailed, he might be over Spain, warning every supplier Hamid could name.

At 17:31 the gate agent scanned their boarding passes. Elena's failed diplomatic card remained in her bag beside the personal guarantee. Noor carried the clean Day Nineteen field-recording receipt, not the media. Mira carried her own notes and no sealed clinical file. Hamid carried clothes, medication for reflux, the witnessed envelope of service slips, and no copy of the warehouse ledger. Benali carried the transit order.

They had not secured what they came for.

The full ledger sat under joint seal in a settlement depository whose procedures could consume weeks. Customs held a partial extract insufficient to identify parcels or directing entities. Gabriel remained detained in a room overlooking the route they were taking. Elena's superiors had suspended her. Vale's compensation process continued to pay real claims and close investigative paths at once.

Yet the witness moved.

The passenger bridge led upward through glass. Elena could see the bonded sheds, each container and pallet held in legal suspension, neither admitted nor absent. At Warehouse C, investment codes had selected devices before engineering need. That fact did not yet prove a coordinated scheme. It changed the derivation of their next question. They no longer had to ask only why a faulty instrument misreported a district. They had to ask who benefited when service, insurance, and future population all leaned in the same direction.

Noor stopped halfway up the bridge. Below, two police vehicles left the public building with Gabriel somewhere inside one of them.

"We are leaving him," she said.

"He is represented, his hearing is tomorrow, and his location is entered in the record," Elena replied.

"That is not what I said."

"No. We are leaving him."

The admission did not culminate in comfort. They resumed walking because the gate would close.

On the car deck, chains tightened against trailer axles. The massive stern ramp lifted, shutting out the terminal in sections: asphalt, warehouse doors, cranes, then a final beam of hot evening light. Engines vibrated through the bulkheads. Above them passengers sought cabins, spread blankets, soothed children, and watched the strait narrow behind glass.

Elena stood at the rail as the ferry eased leeward of the breakwater. Her phone displayed a formal notice of suspension, a disciplinary summons, Gabriel's new custody number, and confirmation that French authorities would receive Hamid. Four documents, each effective within its scope. None told the whole story.

At 18:12 the pilot disembarked. The ferry sounded one long whistle and set her course northeast.

They left Tangier without the ledger, without institutional shelter, and without the whole group. They carried a technician to sea under a protection clause Elena had written for someone else, and the limited truth that firmware updates had followed district investment codes rather than engineering need.

For the first time, Elena had no office from which to make that truth consequential.

She still had her name beneath the undertaking, and the persistence to answer for it when the next authority asked why she had signed.

## Chapter 22: Crossing

By the first night at sea, every corridor on the ferry had acquired a second purpose.

The broad passage outside Reception became a dormitory after the cheapest reclining seats filled. A breezeway beneath the lifeboat deck became a smoking room despite three placards and a rancid stench from the waste locker whenever the door failed to latch. The children's play area became a refectory where two families divided bread, boiled eggs, oranges, and tinned cheese with a galley spatula borrowed under protest. The stairwell beside Cabin 614 became the place Hamid Belkacem stopped each time nausea rose through him, because from there he could see a strip of moving water beyond the bulwarks and convince his body that the floor's slow pitch had a cause.

Noor learned these transformations by sound before sight. Slippers shuffled on lackluster carpet. Trailer lashings beat a muted, isochronous score below. The galley sent pans into brief metallic consonance whenever the ship rolled west. Children made fizzy water effervesce in plastic cups, then shrieked when caps jumped. Babies cried in diverse registers and were answered in Arabic, French, Tamazight, Spanish, Italian, and the private phonology of exhausted parents. Above it all the engines maintained a bass note too pervasive to hear until a ventilation fan disengaged and the whole vessel seemed to inhale.

Hamid leaned against the bulkhead with his eyes closed.

"Do not tell me to watch the horizon," he said.

"I was going to tell you not to vomit on my shoes."

"Compassion has transformed you."

He looked waxen. Mira had given him an ordinary dose of the antiemetic supplied by the ship's medical desk after checking contraindications and the transit record. She had not treated him as her patient or improvised from her own bag. The tablets remained with the nurse, their issue entered under Hamid's name; Mira was persnickety about dose times because seasickness could mask something worse and witness care did not permit amateur heroics. Evidence discipline had become a tiresome family trait among them, extending now to medicine.

"The nurse said it may take twenty minutes," Noor told him. "Heed her before you decide the sea has personal malice."

"The nurse has never met this sea."

"The sea is negligible. You are dramatic."

"My stomach is indigenous to land."

He grimaced and then laughed despite himself. The laugh reassured Noor more than his color did; his breathing had grown markedly less shallow since the tablet stayed down.

They had sailed northeast through the strait at dusk on Day Twenty. By midnight the Moroccan coast was a dark retention of lights astern, Spain a separate glow to port. The ferry was no sleek liner. She carried freight first and passengers in the available spaces above it: truck drivers, tourists with automobiles, students, seasonal workers, grandparents tending children, and families whose luggage disclosed no simple category. Some were immigrating. Some had emigrated years before and were returning to France after summer visits. Some crossed every month and rejected both verbs. The crossing defeated homogeneity by existing: every queue contained workers, students, grandparents, commuters, and people whose papers made them suppliant to officials without making them simple. A protected witness among them was remarkable only to the five people assigned to keep him from becoming isolated.

Benali held the sealed pouch containing Hamid's phone. French border police had its seal number and serial. The service slips stayed in their separate witnessed envelope inside a small document case secured to Benali's belt. Hamid carried the basic handset issued for family calls. It contained no stored contacts. At agreed times he typed his wife's number from memory, spoke while Benali remained within sight but not hearing, then erased the call history with the officer's instructions printed beside him.

The precautions were effectual against careless access. They did not make a ship a court depository.

At 00:40 Noor walked Hamid back to the cabin assigned to him and Benali. She had the upper berth in the adjoining cabin with Mira and Elena. The arrangement was neither clandestine nor advertised. Passenger services had marked Hamid's booking private, and the captain, chief purser, ship's security officer, and medical lead knew the transit conditions. No crew member had been asked to become a covert guard.

The corridor carpet bore a checkered pattern meant to conceal stains. A boy in dinosaur pajamas ambulated solemnly between cabins while his sister held the back of his shirt with the prehensile grip of a child promoted too early to helper. Their mother followed with a sleeping infant pressed to her shoulder.

"Who is tending whom?" Noor asked.

The girl, perhaps eight, considered. "All of us."

Her answer had more self-respect than the adult fiction that childcare belonged to one unexhausted person.

Hamid waited until they passed. "My daughter has those pajamas. Not dinosaurs. Horses."

"A filly on every leg?"

"Unicorns. Very scientific."

He yearned visibly toward the ordinary complaint. Noor had no remedy for homesickness incurred less than six hours from home, albeit she could keep his mind on the child's solemn command of the corridor.

At the cabin door, he said, "The men asked my wife about school collection. She says police moved them to her cousin's apartment. The children think the plumbing broke."

"That story may hold one night."

"My son will explicate the plumbing to everyone. He is six and addlepated only when convenient."

"An offhand lie about plumbing has a short service life," Noor said.

"Did you tell Elena?"

"Yes. She says French authorities can request continued local protection but cannot command Moroccan police."

"She would."

"I mean she was honest."

Noor heard the correction. Her cynicism had become commonplace enough that Hamid now defended Elena's limits before Noor attacked them.

"Sleep," she said.

"I have conserved all my sleep for a better vessel."

Benali opened the door. "Then lie prone and practice."

Noor returned to her cabin. Mira sat on the lower berth with a hospital privacy protocol open on her tablet. Priya had sent the document without greeting. It defined what Mira could inspect in Marseille: aggregate staffing schedules, closure orders, anonymized capacity records, and only those patient-level extracts approved by the hospital's data officer. No clinical file would leave the network. Priya's asperity was embedded in permissions, but so was a fair-minded line between proof and overexposure.

Elena occupied the narrow desk, drafting her response to discipline. Without her official title she seemed neither diminished nor reborn, merely forced to perform tasks her office once distributed among assistants. Her suspension memorandum asserted that she had prejudiced member interests, exceeded authority, and created the appearance of partiality. It did not accuse her of disclosing classified information. The distinction gave her a viable defense and exposed what the secretariat valued.

"Gabriel's hearing?" Noor asked.

"Nine tomorrow morning. Aouragh expects conditional release, but the Dutch liaison wants transfer."

"And *Nkem*?"

"Lotte says the crew wage claim forestalls sale for six more days. The ship is available only for essential maintenance under port supervision."

"Which means nobody is bringing her to Marseille."

"Not now."

Later was not promised. The vessel had only debt, defects, and a crew deciding what ownership meant.

Noor climbed into her berth. The hull's vibration entered her jaw through the pillow. She could have made a compendium of the ship's sounds: duct murmur, cinder-dry cough from the next cabin, latch chatter, water against plating, a card game continuing in the lounge with periodic beats of triumph. A loose screw in the reading lamp seemed to stridulate each time the ship rolled. Instead she slept.

Day Twenty-one at sea was long enough for suspicion to become slothful.

Morning brought azure water, a wind that kept the outer decks nearly empty, and no pursuit. Rell did not appear. Noor searched the passenger spaces once, then stopped. Obsessive scrutiny could isolate Hamid as effectively as a guard.

At breakfast he managed tea, bread, and half a banana. Mira advised him to avoid the gaudy fried buffet and the orange drink that promised vitamins in five languages. Benali claimed the eggs could indemnify themselves against no court. Elena ate them anyway.

They took a corner table near families rather than a private room. The choice was partly security and partly humanity. A witness hidden among officials would look and feel captive. Hamid played cards with two truck drivers from Nador, an elderly woman traveling to her daughter's home in Lyon, and the eight-year-old girl from the corridor, whose name was Inès and whose rules altered with capricious speed. She declared Cabin 616 lucky because it was a palindrome, then refused to explain why luck had no reciprocal duty.

The game was ronda. Hamid dealt with the quick-witted deference of an uncle accustomed to losing just enough. Inès amassed cards and accused every adult of foolery. Her grandmother corrected her arithmetic. One driver supplied a running commentary in French and Darija until his companion called him a curmudgeon and then, for accuracy, a verbose curmudgeon.

Noor watched Hamid's shoulders disengage from his ears. His stoicism had looked like compliance in the terminal; here, among cards and bad arithmetic, it looked like effort. Protection was not merely preventing abduction. It was permitting a person to remain among other people without every commonplace contact being treated as peril or every kindness as a scheme to pamper him into docile gratitude.

At 10:15 the chief purser, Claire Dumas, joined them. She was hardheaded, compact, and unimpressed by the group's tendency to make ordinary ship rules metaphysical.

"Weather remains fair," she said. "We pass east of Almería this afternoon. Arrival Marseille six thirty Day Twenty-three, subject to berth."

"Any unusual security inquiry?" Benali asked.

"Three journalists requested confirmation that Mr. Belkacem is aboard. We declined. One passenger claimed a Harborlight delegation has a block booking. It does not. Two men booked late through an industrial-security agency and boarded under valid passports."

Noor set down her coffee. "Names?"

"Not available to you. The captain and security officer checked them against the passenger manifest. No warrant, citation, or carrier rule permits us to confront them."

"Can you tell us whether one is Tomas Rell?"

"He is not booked under that name."

An equivocal answer only because identity itself could be equivocal. Rell had used contractors and aliases within legal work. Noor pictured him already in Marseille, which was no more reliable than picturing him two decks below.

"What agency?" Elena asked.

"Again, not available. I am telling you the risk fact, not opening my manifest."

Elena accepted the boundary. "Can ship security ensure they do not enter the protected cabins or access the pouch?"

"Ship security ensures no passenger enters another cabin without authorization. We do not create a private bulwark around your party unless threat or conduct justifies it. If that changes, tell us."

The purser left them with an emergency card and a mild rebuke against insularity.

"Two men," Hamid said.

"Two men among fourteen hundred passengers," Noor replied. "Your wife saw two. That does not unify them into one force."

"You believe that?"

"I believe we need behavior, not breed. Suspicion can incite its own evidence if we let it."

He appreciated the restatement even if it did not reassure him.

At noon Gabriel called Elena from detention. The judge had declined immediate Dutch transfer and ordered release at 18:00 under local reporting, surrender already in place, and a prohibition on approaching Warehouse C. The prosecutor appealed but did not obtain a stay. Gabriel would remain in Tangier for at least three days. Lotte had found a cooperative shipyard willing to advance essential work on *Nkem* against future charter, if the lender and wage claimants assented. None of that restored his certificate or turned the nascent repair talk into command.

Noor listened on speaker only after Gabriel agreed.

"You left," he said.

"Yes," Noor answered.

"Good."

"Do not patronize me."

"I am conserving energy."

He gave them his whereabouts, lawyer, release condition, and the time he would call Ama. He did not unbosom himself about detention. Before ending he asked Hamid whether Kroll's phrase might have meant investment in the devices rather than districts.

"No," Hamid said. "*Code d'investissement du district.*"

"Then keep that exact collocation. Every paraphrase makes it larger."

The sailor's advice matched Elena's, which probably miffed Noor because it was correct.

In the afternoon Hamid reviewed his testimony with Benali in a glass lounge. Noor sat far enough away not to hear privileged discussion. She worked instead with the clean copies of her own installation plans that a Marseille curator had sent. The art center occupied a former tobacco warehouse near the port. Its central nave had three levels of iron galleries, brick vaulting, and an apse-like loading bay whose curve produced a six-second low-frequency retention. The institution wanted to reinstall Noor's work for an emergency public program on "Data, Mourning, and the Littoral Imagination." The title was pretentious enough to function as weather.

Her original installation had used Sami's recorder before she knew its diagnostic channel carried evidence. The recorder itself remained sealed; they would work from court-authorized derived audio already disclosed for hazard analysis and from fresh field recordings. The curator seemed to imagine a memorable epiphany in which hidden truth emerged from sound. Noor wrote back that the room could separate overlapping pulse trains through spatial delay, not summon confession; ostentation was not a method.

At 17:00 the sea becalmed. Children crowded the outer deck. The ship's wake laid a white inscription across blue water and erased it as it formed. Inès showed Noor a phonogram she had made by drawing waves around the letters of her name. Noor asked permission before photographing it. The girl declined, then changed her mind after negotiating one packet of tangy sweets.

"You are easy to bribe," Elena said.

"It was a commission."

The moment was almost comical. That made what followed feel at first like another shipboard glitch.

At 20:36 on Day Twenty-two, after darkness had closed around the ferry, three short tones sounded over the public address system. They were not the seven-short-one-long general alarm. A recorded voice instructed passengers in French to remain where they were. Then the message broke off mid-sentence, leaving a farrago of guesses to fill the gap.

The engines continued. Ventilation continued. In the lounge, conversation thinned into murmuring.

Dumas's live voice replaced the recording. "Security notice. Passengers on Decks Six and Seven, leave cabins unlocked and proceed by the forward stairs to the muster lounges. Do not use lifts. Bring medication and outer clothing. Follow crew instructions. This is not an abandon-ship signal."

Noor looked at Elena. "Deck Six."

They moved.

The corridor outside their cabins was already congested. A crew member knocked doors open and marked each with chalk. Passengers emerged carrying too much: suitcases, blankets, automobile papers, medicine bags, birth certificates, residence cards. A man tried to retrieve duty-free cartons and was turned back. Someone said bomb. Someone else said fire. The terms crossed languages faster than official instruction, and the nascent panic fed on every translation.

Benali opened Cabin 614. "We need the document case and phone pouch."

"Medication," Hamid said.

His tablets were in the bedside cabinet. Noor retrieved them while Benali kept custody of the case and pouch. Mira joined from the stair and checked an elderly passenger who had become semiconscious against the wall. Heat, fear, and missed food appeared more likely than embolism or asphyxia, but she did not announce a diagnosis. She asked a crew member for the medical team and helped lower the woman to the carpet without obstructing her breathing; panic could choke a corridor as effectively as smoke.

The crowd stalled.

From aft came a sharper order: leave bags, proceed immediately. A security officer in a navy jacket pushed upstream. His badge displayed the ferry company's wave mark and the word AUXILIARY.

"All electronic devices in clear bags," he said. "Suspected trigger search. Preferential screening for powered devices."

Dumas's instruction had said nothing about surrendering electronics.

Benali held up the sealed pouch. "Protected legal property."

"Then it must be screened."

"By ship security in my presence."

"Screening station is aft. Passenger flow is forward. Give it to me and take your client."

Noor studied the badge. The print was fractionally skew, as if applied over another laminate. The man's accent was metropolitan French. Neither fact proved imposture; a good forger needed only seconds of uncertainty in a crowd.

"Name?" she asked.

"Leclerc. Move."

The elderly woman began to convulse.

Not a generalized seizure, Mira said; a paroxysm of shivering and panic, perhaps, with brief incoherence but no focal sign she could see in the crowd. She needed space and the medical team. Passengers pressed around them. Inès appeared on the wrong side of the flow, crying for her mother. The auxiliary officer reached for the pouch.

Noor saw the disjunction Rell had designed, if Rell had designed it. Pursue the questionable badge and leave Hamid in a crush. Guard the pouch and let a child vanish into the aft corridor. Preserve every object and fail the people around it.

"Benali keeps it," she said. "We all go forward. Do not let the hindmost passengers pile up behind us."

The officer blocked them. "The device cannot enter muster."

Elena raised the emergency card Dumas had given them. "Chief purser, direct channel. State your instruction for the recorded incident log."

The man did not capitulate. He touched his earpiece and said, "Bring it to Station B," then stepped aside.

They moved forward. Noor took Inès's hand. Hamid supported the girl's grandmother while Benali kept the pouch against his chest. Mira remained with the sick passenger until two ship medics arrived with a wheelchair and oxygen. The forward stair became unmanageable as people from three corridors converged. Crew opened an exterior route across the sheltered deck.

Cold wind struck them. Coruscating spray flashed in emergency lights. The ship was still underway but had altered course slightly, a swerve visible in the wake.

At the muster lounge crew counted passengers by cabin. The absence of baggage made the room look like a border hall after confiscation. Children sat on the floor. Drivers argued over whether they could return to vehicles. A family from Oujda had become separated from an adolescent son; two crew went to retrieve him. The elderly woman arrived conscious, embarrassed, and stable under the nurse's care, with gaseous oxygen ready but not yet needed.

Dumas reached them at 20:49.

"There is no confirmed device," she said. "An anonymous call named a locker on Deck Seven. Security found an unattended tool case with wires. It belongs to a refrigeration contractor and is not explosive. We are completing search protocol and trying to retard the spread of rumors before they outrun us."

"Did you order collection of phones?" Elena asked.

"No."

Benali looked down.

The pouch was gone.

He had retained it across the outer deck. He remembered its edge under his hand when they entered the lounge. During the cabin count a crewman had asked him to hold the document case open for visual inspection. Another had guided Hamid and the grandmother toward seats. There had been a fraction of contact, ordinary and crowded. Custody had failed in the exact place where good procedure met thoughtless compression.

"Which crewman?" Dumas asked.

Benali scanned the room. "Navy jacket. Auxiliary badge. Leclerc."

"We have no Leclerc on auxiliary security."

Noor handed Inès to her mother. Then she heard a sound beneath the public-address murmur: three dry taps, pause, two taps, the plastic snap of a case closing. It came through the service door behind the lounge.

She opened it.

A narrow passage ran aft between ventilation trunks. Twenty meters away, a man in a navy jacket stepped through another door. In one hand he carried the clear phone pouch. Its red seal hung cut and deformed where the blade had worried the plastic. He looked back.

Tomas Rell had shaved his beard closer and removed his glasses. Neither change was wizardry. Noor knew his gait before his face: the slight forward lean of someone who expected doors to yield.

"Rell!"

She ran.

The service passage pitched under her. He did not sprint; he seemed almost to saunter, trusting the ship's rules to slow her more than distance would. At the next junction he turned into a maintenance lobby where the deck plan divided toward the stern stairs and an equipment room. Noor reached the lobby in time to see him beside an open hard case on a bench. The phone lay connected by a slim cable to a mobile forensic unit. A progress bar read IMAGE COMPLETE. Rell pulled the cable free and slid the phone back into a new clear pouch.

She had caught the act and had no camera.

"You cut a court seal," she said.

"I secured an unattended device during a bomb alert."

"You copied it."

"You saw a security scan."

"You are not ship security."

"I advise operators on critical-infrastructure threats."

The false bomb report had created the threat he now claimed to manage. Noor could infer the loop. She could not prove he placed the call, planted the contractor's case, or acted under Harborlight authorization. The kernel of proof in front of her was narrower: Rell with the cut seal, the connected phone, and the completed image.

Rell closed his hard case. Behind Noor, the service door began to swing shut. Beyond him the stern stairs descended toward vehicle decks, where fourteen hundred people's whereabouts mattered more than catching one man.

"Give me the phone."

He held up the resealed pouch. The new seal was blue, not the original red, and carried a ferry inventory number.

"Return it to the purser," he said. "Its provenance will show interruption. You are welcome to accuse me."

"Why let me see?"

"I did not. You intervened."

An alarm sounded from the muster lounge: not shipwide, but a personal medical alert. Noor thought of Hamid in a room full of frightened strangers, separated from his lawyer and the evidence pouch, while she stood in a maintenance lobby jousting over an image already complete.

Rell read the choice in her face.

"Sami would chase me," he said.

The cruelty was precise. He wanted her to prove loyalty to the dead by abandoning the living.

Noor took the pouch.

"Sami is not here to subordinate Hamid to himself."

She turned back.

Rell could have lunged, restrained her, or retrieved the phone. He did none of those things. His impunity lay in having finished. By the time ship officers reached the lobby, the stern stair was empty. A door alarm showed authorized maintenance access under a temporary credential issued that afternoon to an industrial-security subcontractor. The credential name was Laurent Mercier. The contractor file contained a passport image unlike Rell and a company whose registered office was a virtual suite in Paris. Dumas said such temps were supposed to receive escorted access only; the escort line had been left blank.

Dumas sealed the altered pouch inside a larger evidence bag. She entered Noor's account, Benali's loss of contact, the first officer's description, the cut red seal, replacement blue seal, cable-port residue, and the exact times. Ship cameras in the service passage had switched to privacy mode during the security alert under a rule intended to protect bomb-disposal methods. The equipment lobby had no camera. Rell appeared on no manifest under his name.

"Did you see the screen?" Dumas asked.

"Yes. Mobile forensic interface. `IMAGE COMPLETE`."

"Could it have been a malware scan?"

"The handset was connected by cable after its court seal was cut. I cannot identify the software build or copied contents. A security scan is possible in the abstract; in this setting it is also the most convenient secretive label for a copy."

"Did Mr. Rell say he copied it?"

"No. He called it a security scan."

"Did he admit making the bomb report?"

"No."

The account was stark and partial. Noor signed it.

Hamid sat at a table with his head in his hands. When Noor told him, he asked first whether the original phone had been recovered, then whether the service slips remained sealed, then whether his family's address was on the device.

"Yes," he answered himself. "Messages, contacts, photographs. Supplier names. The people I called after the factory inspection."

"Passwords?"

"The phone was powered down. It has encryption."

Mira said, "A forensic unit may have exploited it, or the screen may have exaggerated completion. We should assume access without claiming what was copied."

Hamid gave her a look of exhausted obstinacy. "Assume all of it."

For protection, yes. For public allegation, no. Elena made both propositions explicit. French authorities received an updated risk notice naming every supplier Hamid listed from his contact history. Moroccan police were asked to reach his family and the cooperative. Dumas preserved access logs and the contractor's tool case. The false alert became a criminal referral independent of whether the case had been planted; the phone breach was not petty delinquency, but its authorization remained unproved.

"We turn back," Hamid said.

The ferry was hours east of Almería. Turning back was the language of panic, not navigation, but Noor understood him.

"To do what?" Benali asked gently.

"Warn them."

"Authorities are warning them now. Your family is under protection. If you abandon the French testimony, whoever copied the phone still has the names and also succeeds in stopping you."

"If I continue, they foreclose every supplier before we arrive."

"Likely," Elena said. "That changes the interview. It does not make it useless. Your prior contacts, dates, and reasons can be preserved even if records disappear."

Noor waited for him to decide. She did not reassure him that no harm would come. She did not assert that courage required Marseille. A protected person retained the right to become unwilling, and witness care was not a specialty in forcing bravery to look clean.

Inès approached carrying the deck of cards. "We did not finish."

Her mother tried to draw her away, but Hamid looked up.

"I was losing," he said.

"You were," Inès confirmed.

He made room at the table.

The alert ended at 22:03. Passengers returned by decks after cabin searches. No explosive device was found. The contractor claimed his tool case had been left in an unlocked service locker and expressed understandable maddenment at having his wiring mistaken for a bomb. Crew restored locks, returned bags, and documented complaints. An ambulance was requested to meet the ship in Marseille for the elderly woman, not because her condition remained acute but because the medical lead wanted follow-up after her collapse.

The return produced its own injuries of trust. A father demanded to know why security had separated him from the bag containing his daughter's residence card. Two students refused to leave muster until a crew member opened their cabin in front of them. A truck driver discovered that someone had searched the pouch where he kept remittance receipts and accused the company of treating every North African passenger as a petitioner or suspect. Dumas did not dismiss the complaints as cynicism. She assigned staff to witness each cabin re-entry, recorded missing or displaced property, and announced that immigration documents would be checked only by border authorities at arrival. The slower process angered people who wanted bed. It also prevented the false alert from becoming an excuse for indiscriminate scrutiny or toleration of collective suspicion.

Hamid helped Inès's grandmother retrieve a wheeled case from beneath her berth. The woman asked why police were waiting for him in Marseille. He answered that he was a technical witness, not a fugitive. She nodded without curiosity and gave him two clementines for the morning. Noor noticed how little explanation ordinary civility required. Harborlight's language made him an insider; Rell's operation made him a target; the woman made him a man tall enough to reach a suitcase.

At 23:10 Dumas brought a written preliminary incident memorandum. It distinguished the anonymous bomb report, the innocent contractor's case, the unauthorized auxiliary credential, the phone's interrupted seal, and Noor's identification of Rell. No causal arrow joined them yet. Noor signed as to her own account and declined to endorse the memorandum's phrase coordinated intrusion. Coordination was likely. The ship's record did not yet establish it, and Noor was no novice at the damage caused by saying more than custody could carry.

Noor sat with Hamid through the next hour of cards. He remained frightened. He also cheated once, badly, and Inès caught him. The group's laughter was unfeigned and brief.

At midnight the ferry crossed into the next watch. Marseille authorities confirmed that two named suppliers had already received preservation notices from Harborlight counsel citing cybersecurity review. A third had suspended external access. Rell, or whoever directed him, now knew enough to anticipate the inquiry.

The phone stayed double-sealed in the captain's safe for delivery to French police. No one powered it on to discover what had been copied. Doing so would risk both data and later examination. They accepted ignorance as part of provenance.

Noor went alone to the outer deck. Wind drove the ship's wake into a skew white road. The Mediterranean around them was neither elysian nor stygian, only dark water under scattered commercial lights. Behind lay a warehouse ledger they had not obtained and a family now exposed. Ahead lay a hospital, an art center, insurers, suppliers, and people who might close ranks before the ferry reached its terminus.

Rell had copied rather than stolen because theft would have announced loss. Copying preserved normalcy. Hamid still possessed his phone, his slips, and his testimony; only the adversary's knowledge had changed. That asymmetry was the new danger.

Noor had once treated custody as the power to keep an object from everyone. On the ferry, custody had failed in her sight. Yet when Rell offered pursuit, she had returned to Hamid. The choice did not retrieve secrecy. It retained the witness.

At 00:31 Hamid joined her at the rail, wrapped in a ship blanket. His nausea had passed.

"I will testify," he said.

"All right."

"Do not make it laudable."

"I was going to call it hardheaded."

"That is worse."

Below them, trailers shifted fractionally against their chains and held. The ferry continued east through a sea that offered no private corridor.

By dawn, every supplier named on Hamid's phone would know someone was coming.

## Chapter 23: Capacity

Marseille received the ferry with an ambulance, two police units, and a heat alert already three hours old.

At 06:41 on Day Twenty-three, the ship's ramp lowered into air that felt used. The port thermometer read thirty-one degrees. Heat shimmered above lanes where cars idled for border inspection, and the city's pale northern hills appeared brittle beyond cranes and apartment blocks.

Mira stood with Hamid, Benali, Elena, and Noor in a protected disembarkation lane while French police checked the transit order. The elderly woman from Deck Six went first to the ambulance, conscious and objecting that she had a train to Lyon. Her granddaughter carried the medical note. The paramedic assessed speech, pulse, blood pressure, temperature, gait, and whether she felt muzzy after the evacuation before helping her inside. No one called the transfer an emergency merely because an ambulance had been requested.

Hamid's altered phone pouch passed directly from the captain to a cybercrime officer. The officer read both seal numbers aloud, photographed the cut red seal inside the larger bag, and signed for the blue replacement. Benali retained the document case and Hamid retained ownership of the original service slips within it. French police took no clinical interest in the ferry collapse and no commercial interest in the ledger. The boundaries held because people repeated them.

At 07:18 Hamid entered a police vehicle with Benali for his preservation interview. Noor watched until the vehicle cleared the terminal.

"He is not abducted," Elena said.

"I can see the paperwork."

"That was not a correction."

"It sounded like one."

Mira let them contest tone. Her phone contained a message from Priya sent at 05:52.

SOUTH ENTRANCE. 08:00. NO PATIENT DATA. IF YOU BRING CAMERAS, TURN AROUND.

No greeting, no cancellation.

The Hôpital Saint-Césaire occupied a metropolitan block east of the old port, its original limestone pavilion hemmed in by concrete additions from six decades of medical fashion. Solar canopies shaded the south entrance. Ambulances used a separate ramp where a screen listed emergency destinations without names. The hospital's plan canicule had activated overnight after three consecutive days above the local threshold and a forecast of forty by afternoon.

Inside, cool air ended after the lobby.

The older wings lacked uniform insulation. Portable cooling units stood in corridors with condensate tubes running into buckets. Staff moved water carts between waiting rooms. A sign asked visitors to report confusion, fainting, hot dry skin, profuse sweating followed by sudden dryness, or worsening breathlessness. Another warned that infants, older adults, outdoor workers, sedentary patients unable to reach cool rooms, people with cardiovascular disease, and patients taking certain psychiatric or diuretic medicines faced preponderant risk. The language was direct without making every warm person apocalyptic.

Priya waited beneath the directory in blue scrubs, an identity badge, and shoes Mira recognized because she had once bought the same brand after Priya complained about twelve-hour shifts. Remembering the purchase was a private irrelevance. Mira had no claim on the person wearing them.

Priya Nair looked thinner than three years earlier and exactly as difficult to deceive.

"You are alone?" she asked.

"Elena and Noor are at the police interview. They will not come without permission."

"Good. You have ninety minutes with administration. Then I am clinical lead for the heat unit."

"Thank you for seeing me."

"Do not spend our time on civility."

Priya led her through a badge-controlled door. The corridor smelled of antiseptic, coffee, and overheated wiring. A porter steered a shuttle of wheelchairs around them. Near radiology, a man with a wrist fracture groaned as his swollen hand was elevated. In an alcove a nurse used a phone interpreter to explain discharge instructions. The hospital was not an abstract capacity. It was consecutive acts performed by people whose attention could be consumed.

"État des lits?" Mira asked, then corrected herself into the hospital's preferred French. "Situation capacitaire?"

"Service des urgences at one hundred forty-two percent of staffed places. Heat unit has twenty-eight beds, all occupied. Four suspected infections in isolation pending respiratory panels. One cooling failure in geriatric medicine repaired at four. Elective surgery reduced, not stopped. No mass casualty, no collapse, no excuse for people to call this carnage."

"And Harborlight?"

"Recommends diversion from Saint-Césaire because our staffed capacity is low. Correct as of this morning."

"Do ambulances follow it?"

"Dispatch can override. They often do because nearby hospitals are also full. Harborlight is not inventing today's pressure."

The qualification mattered. A faulty account would accuse the platform of every patient on a trolley. The actual question was whether it had helped create the denominator it now observed.

Priya brought her to a conference room where Deputy Director Luc Martel, data-protection officer Émilie Caron, head nurse Soraya Haddad, and two representatives of the patient council waited. One was Jeanne Vidal, a retired teacher who used a cane. The other, Malik Sissoko, ran a neighborhood association and had no patience for prefatory speeches. Caron had written sans données nominatives across the folder tab in green ink, not as decoration but as the condition for Mira entering the room.

Martel began. "You asked to link risk rankings to clinical harm. We will not release patient records, diagnoses, addresses, or row-level movement. We can show staffing establishments, licensed beds, anonymized occupancy, closure orders, and model inputs received by administration."

"That is sufficient to test sequence," Mira said. "I will ask for specifics about fields and dates, not names."

"It may not be sufficient to accuse anyone," Caron replied.

"Then I won't."

Priya gave no sign of approval.

The first records appeared on a hospital terminal mirrored to a wall screen. Saint-Césaire had once operated Ward E5, a thirty-two-bed medical ward in the 1980s east wing. Twelve beds had been used for respiratory and infectious-disease overflow, ten for step-down care, and the rest flexed during heat emergencies. The ward closed eighteen months earlier. Public minutes cited low utilization, projected demographic decline, and the cost of replacing its ventilation.

"Was the ventilation unsafe?" Mira asked.

Soraya answered. "It was inefficient and needed work. Not a source of asphyxia. Air changes fell below modern isolation standards, so we did not use it for airborne infection without portable filtration. For ordinary medical beds it remained licensed."

"Any fungal contamination, carcinogen, or structural defect?"

"No. There was localized damp around two windows, remediated. No asbestos exposure in occupied rooms. The fire survey was current."

"Then why close rather than refurbish?"

Martel said, "Capital allocation. The region would not fund a ward forecast to become redundant."

He opened the decision packet. The hospital had submitted a renovation proposal based on observed admissions and climate-adjusted demand. It forecast rising heat illness, episodic respiratory surges, and an aging catchment. The regional authority returned a Harborlight planning extract that lowered the catchment's projected population by fourteen percent over four years. Under the revised estimate, E5's modeled occupancy fell below the capital threshold.

The dates were stark. Saint-Césaire submitted its proposal on 4 March 2029. Harborlight issued the reduced future-population estimate on 19 March. The authority declined renovation on 2 April. Hospital management froze recruitment in May, did not replace six departing nurses, and closed E5 in November after occupancy fell because fewer staffed beds were available.

"The estimate precedes the closure," Mira said. "It does not prove the estimate caused it."

Martel looked affronted. "The rejection letter cites it."

"Then it contributed directly to the capital decision. We still need to separate ventilation cost, staffing, actual utilization, and any other funding constraint."

Malik tapped the table. "You people make a sentence pass through so many qualifications that the patient dies of old age before the verb arrives."

"Would you prefer an accusation they can disprove?"

"I would prefer you acknowledge what the hospital already knows. Money followed the forecast. Beds followed money. Patients followed beds."

"Yes," Mira said. "That is the mechanism we are testing."

They traced it document by document.

Before the estimate, E5 had twenty-seven funded nursing posts and thirty-two licensed beds, though average daily occupancy was twenty-four. After the renovation denial, vacancies went unfilled. The hospital shifted respiratory nurses to other wards. Lower staffing reduced operable beds. Lower operable beds reduced recorded admissions because dispatch diverted patients elsewhere. The next Harborlight extract used completed admissions, not rejected transfers, to characterize demand as declining.

"A feedback effect," Mira said.

"Do not call it accidental yet," Priya replied.

"I didn't."

"You used the passive phrase effect."

"A feedback mechanism. Intent remains unknown."

Priya's mouth tightened. The old argument stirred: Mira using technical precision as a screen, Priya hearing every boundary as retreat from moral judgment.

Caron displayed the data dictionary. Harborlight received occupied-bed counts, staffed-bed counts, accepted admissions, transfers out, and future population. It did not receive a standardized count of patients refused before registration. Those remained in dispatch systems controlled by several agencies.

"So lower capacity creates lower observed demand," Soraya said.

"If demand is inferred from admissions alone," Mira answered. "We should test whether the planning model also includes ambulance refusals or external admissions."

Martel produced the model specification supplied under contract. It referred to regional patient flow but omitted a field-level conspectus. Harborlight asserted proprietary derivation.

Jeanne asked, "Can you illustrate without the mathematics?"

Mira looked at the occupancy chart. "A bakery sells out by noon. The owner records only completed sales and ignores everyone turned away. A forecast sees no afternoon sales and concludes the neighborhood needs less bread. The owner bakes less. The next day even more people are turned away, and completed sales decline again."

"Beds are not loaves," Martel said.

"No. Patients cannot simply return tomorrow. That is why the missing refusals matter more."

Jeanne nodded. "Use that with patients. Do not use it in the report. In the report, specify which bodies fail to count refusals."

Her distinction was seasoned. Public understanding and institutional accountability required different forms, neither a caricature of the other. It helped disabuse Mira of the tempting idea that a palliative metaphor could substitute for a field name.

At 09:12 a nurse called Priya from the heat unit. Two patients had arrived from an uncooled residence with temperatures above forty. One was confused and hypotensive. Priya stood.

"I need to go."

Mira rose as well.

"You stay with administration," Priya said. "You are not credentialed here."

The boundary landed harder because Mira had once practiced clinically and because Vale's forum language kept calling her physician. She was not licensed for care in France. Expertise did not become competence by proximity, and observation did not become therapeutic authority.

"Understood."

Priya left with Soraya.

For the next forty minutes Mira reviewed the packet. The population estimate was unusually granular. It reduced four adjacent census sectors while leaving the broader arrondissement nearly stable. The affected sectors included the hospital's east catchment, a dockworkers' housing complex, an older migrant neighborhood, and parcels near a planned tram extension. The estimate cited expected relocation uptake, insurance discontinuity, and redevelopment readiness; without the refused-transfer logs, the adjustment looked less like an inexplicable error than an ulterior policy scenario wearing a forecast's coat.

"Redevelopment readiness is a population variable?" Malik asked.

"It should not be a biological or demographic observation," Mira said. "It may enter a policy scenario. The question is whether the model labels that scenario as a forecast of what will happen or a goal authorities intend to pursue."

The same conceptual offense as Tangier appeared in another domain: a desired future state presented as antecedent fact. Yet Mira could not claim common control from resemblance. Fallibility in a model was not evidence of conspiracy; a repeated omission that benefited the same projection demanded preservation before anyone could censure or clear it.

The hospital's order contained a source reference: `HL-PF/CR-MED/RET-4/13`. The code shared Cadran's facility label and the warehouse profile. Caron cautioned that institutional identifiers could propagate through billing and planning systems without common direction. Mira agreed.

"But it is referable," Malik said.

"Yes. It gives us a record family to seek."

Martel authorized an immutable export of the decision packet, excluding staff personal data and internal comments unrelated to E5. The hospital retained the source. Caron created a hash, logged Mira as recipient under the hazard inquiry, and sent matching verification to the regional authority and patient council. No patient file entered the export.

"Clinical harm?" Martel asked. "You have a closure, not a corpse."

Caron marked the sentence in her notes as coarse administrative phrasing, then underlined the reason: it reduced harm to a death certificate. Mira disliked the challenge because it was legally shrewd and ethically ugly.

"We can document reduced surge capacity and resulting diversion," she said. "For harm, aggregate outcomes may show delay without identifying individuals. But outcome attribution will be difficult. Heat severity, other closures, staffing sickness, and transport all confound it."

"Then Harborlight says no proven victim again."

"A ward closure is present institutional injury if the order relied on an undisclosed policy scenario. Patients need not surrender privacy to make the mechanism visible."

Malik said, "Ask them."

At 10:05 the patient council convened an emergency session in a ground-floor room beside the pantry. Eight members attended in person; five joined by phone. They included a dialysis patient, a parent of an immunocompromised child, a retired dockworker with chronic lung disease, a social worker, and two family caregivers. Mira explained what the hospital records did and did not establish.

One man wanted every delayed patient's story public. A woman who had spent fourteen hours on a trolley called that proposal abusive. "My indignity is not your evidence," she said. "Count the hours without putting my backside on television."

Caron added a privacy example from the hospital's own forms: intimate history, including partner status, pregnancy history, and sexual orientation categories such as asexual or heterosexual, could be clinically relevant at bedside and still have no place in an external capacity packet. The same rule covered verbatim notes that preserved abusive language from a waiting-room dispute. The council accepted the distinction because it protected facts from being confused with display.

The dialysis patient asked whether anonymization could be reversed in small categories. Caron said yes: a rare diagnosis, date, age, and neighborhood might identify someone. The council rejected diagnosis-level publication.

They agreed to three forms of evidence. First, the hospital could publish aggregate diversion hours, staffed-bed loss, and heat-surge occupancy. Second, patients could volunteer accounts through independent counsel with control over quotation and withdrawal. Third, dispatch agencies should preserve refused-transfer records so delay could be analyzed without treating admitted patients as the whole denominator. No category would be treated as homogeneous merely because aggregation made it convenient.

"What would make the evidence legitimate to you?" Mira asked.

Jeanne answered first. "That the hospital cannot choose only the data that flatter it."

The dockworker said, "That refusing my name does not make me nonexistent."

The parent said, "That a model cannot call my district empty while my daughter is waiting here."

The woman from the trolley said, "That you return and tell us what you concluded before telling a court."

Mira wrote each condition. They changed the protocol. The patient council, not administration alone, would receive the aggregate export and approve suppression thresholds. Results would be reported back before external filing, unless an emergency application made simultaneous notice necessary. Voluntary testimony would remain separate from the dataset.

This was slower than filching a dramatic record. It was also evidence people could survive having given.

At 10:47 Priya sent a message: EAST STAIR, LEVEL 3.

Mira found her beside a vending machine, drinking water with one shoulder against the wall. A dark patch spread between her shoulder blades. Her badge had twisted backward. Through the ward doors came monitor alarms, wheels, and a man's subdued groan.

"Patients?" Mira asked.

"Cooling, fluids titrated, labs pending. One likely exertional heatstroke, one classic. No intubation so far."

"Do you need anything?"

"A staffed ward."

Mira stood beside her. The corridor was not private, but privacy between them had never depended on architecture.

Priya said, "You found the order."

"The population reduction preceded the renovation denial and recruitment freeze. E5 closure then reduced admissions, which appear to feed later demand estimates."

"And you will say correlation is not causation until another winter passes."

"The denial letter cites the estimate. That is direct influence. The recursive use of lower admissions needs confirmation from the model specification."

"There. You do it even when nobody contests you."

"Do what?"

"Turn every sentence into an alibi for having spoken."

Mira felt the old defensive structure assemble: precision was not cowardice; Priya had demonstrated that often enough; accusation without proof helped Vale. All true. None addressed the intimacy beneath the rebuke.

"At the forum," Priya said, "you admitted what happened in Alexandria in front of strangers because Vale forced the document into public. You did not tell me when we lived together."

"The review was sealed."

Priya laughed once, without amusement. "Patient details were sealed. Your decision was not an infection I could catch from hearing it."

"I was ashamed."

"You were controlled. Shame would have required letting someone see you."

Mira looked down the corridor. A cleaner wiped the rail with germicide, working around them without complaint. "I told you Youssef died during a heat emergency and that I reviewed the response. I let you believe I came afterward."

"Yes."

"That was mendacious."

"Do not use a polished adjective as penance."

"I lied by implication. I let you comfort me for a loss I described falsely. Then when you asked why I could not sleep, I treated your questions as intrusions."

Priya waited.

"I am sorry," Mira said. "Not because Vale exposed me. I am sorry I made closeness conditional on your not knowing the thing that shaped how I behaved with you. I used confidentiality where fear was the reason."

She did not add that she had wanted to protect Priya, that the relationship was already strained, or that the inquiry had prohibited disclosure. Explanations hovered, each one partly valid and collectively an evasion.

"And Marseille?" Priya asked.

Mira understood. Their separation had not occurred in one theatrical outburst. Priya had taken a post at Saint-Césaire after Mira's London review became contentious. Mira promised to follow after six months. She visited twice, cancelled three trips, and finally sent an email proposing that they admit geography had decided. Priya replied that geography was not autonomous.

"I treated your life here as an allowance I could revoke," Mira said. "I kept saying the next review, the next hearing, the next crisis. When you stopped asking, I called the silence mutual. It wasn't. I left you to end what I had abandoned."

Priya's face did not soften. "That is accurate."

"I am sorry."

"An apology is not a claim on me."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"I am trying not to make one."

The answer was imperfect but not prevarication.

A nurse opened the ward door and asked Priya to review a gastric aspirate result and an antibiotic dose. Priya said she would come in one minute. The discussion stayed inside the unité de soins; Mira heard only enough French medical language to know that virulence and timing, not curiosity, were driving the question.

"What do you need from me today?" Mira asked.

"Professionally?"

"Yes."

"Do not ask for patient-level proof because a judge likes bodies more than mechanisms. Ask the people affected what they consider evidence."

"We did. The council set conditions."

"Good. Then help us count refused transfers. Harborlight's efficiency metric excludes them."

"And personally?"

Priya looked through the ward window. "Nothing today. That is not cruelty. It is capacity."

"Understood."

Priya went back inside.

Mira remained by the vending machine until the cleaner asked her to move. The apology had not restored anything. It had removed one false account between them. That was less therapeutic than forgiveness and more useful than self-abjection.

At 11:20 dispatch administrators joined the conference by secure link. Their systems recorded every proposed destination, refusal reason, override, travel time, and final handoff, but retention varied from thirty days to five years. Harborlight received final destination and travel time, not the sequence of rejected hospitals. One agency had already scheduled deletion of raw routing logs older than six months.

Elena, joining from the police building as a private lawyer rather than Compact counsel, drafted a preservation demand. She did not claim the logs proved discriminatory treatment. She stated that they could show whether reduced staffed capacity produced diversions omitted from demand estimates. The patient council joined as requester. Saint-Césaire joined reluctantly after Malik threatened to make its reluctance public.

By noon, three agencies suspended deletion. A fourth said its subcontractor controlled backups. A fifth required judicial process. The mechanism spread across ordinary administration, not one diabolic switch.

Hamid's interview ended at 12:26. Noor called with the result. He had identified five suppliers and three warehouse staff from his contacts and memory. Two suppliers reported that Harborlight security had arrived that morning with valid cybersecurity notices. One allowed inspection under counsel. One denied access. One said its records had been transferred to a Marseille broker. Rell's copy had produced preemption, though formal proof of what he copied remained absent.

"There is more," Noor said. "The art center can give us the full nave tomorrow. Their opening program is postponed because of the heat. We can run the authorized diagnostic excerpts through the spatial array without an audience."

"What are you trying to separate?"

"The ordinary maintenance ping from the extra command. On headphones they overlap. In a room with measured delays, repeated sources should resolve into positions. Hamid says each task slip has a destination pulse count. If the counts align, we may distinguish service class from district command."

"Not decode content."

"No. Separate recurring structures. Then engineers can test them."

The method remained bounded. Art would organize attention, not transmute sound into secret text.

Mira told Noor about the hospital source reference `HL-PF/CR-MED/RET-4/13` and the four reduced census sectors.

"Do you have parcel identifiers?"

"The public planning appendix has cadastral references, but the hospital export does not. We can use the public appendix without joining it to patients."

"Send the link, not a copied file."

Mira did.

In the afternoon Saint-Césaire's emergency department became hotter when a cooling loop failed in one zone. Facilities isolated the fault and moved eight patients. Harborlight correctly flagged the temporary capacity loss within six minutes and recommended redistributing incoming ambulances. Priya accepted the recommendation for two stable transfers and overrode it for a patient with possible meningococcal infection who needed the hospital's available isolation team. She entered the reason as isolement gouttelettes disponible, not a narrative. The platform was efficient when current observation governed it. The harm lay not in every output but in the antecedent decision that had removed a ward and then treated its absence as demand.

At Priya's invitation, Mira observed the operational huddle without entering a clinical role. The bed manager stood before a magnetic board whose colored strips represented staffed places, not rooms. Environmental services could clean eight beds in the closed recovery unit by sixteen hundred. Pharmacy could stock them. Oxygen had passed its last test. Nursing could cover only four without stripping the heat unit or increasing ratios beyond the hospital's emergency ceiling.

"E5 gives us thirty-two physical beds," Martel said over speakerphone.

Soraya answered with controlled vehemence. "E5 gives you thirty-two mattresses. It gives me no nurses, aides, clerk, clean utility, drug stock, functioning call system, or safe infection separation. Do not put capacity on a press release because you found a key."

They chose four recovery beds, converted an outpatient infusion room for six ambulatory patients, and asked two neighboring hospitals for reciprocal staffing rather than additional transfers. Harborlight ranked the plan less efficient than diversion because it counted travel time and available beds but not the receiving hospitals' loss of reserve. Priya entered a local override with each constraint stated. The system accepted it and timestamped the human decision. Nothing in the interface prevented accountable use when staff retained authority.

During the huddle, a porter called from the discharge lounge. A patient cleared to leave after treatment for dehydration had become dizzy while waiting for transport. Priya and a nurse went at once. Mira stayed outside the curtain. She heard questions about chest pain, vision, medication, oral intake, and the onset of symptoms; then the cuff inflated and a trolley rolled in. The patient stabilized after being laid flat and reassessed. No dramatic rescue followed. One bed simply remained occupied for another hour, and the supposedly complete discharge did not become available capacity. The correction was customary nursing work, but the model would misperceive it as an empty bed until a human reversed the status.

"Does Harborlight receive failed discharge?" Mira asked the bed manager afterward.

"Only when we reverse the status."

"How quickly?"

"Depends who has terminal access. Today, eleven minutes. On nights, longer."

Eleven minutes was not evidence of malice. It was the ordinary lag between a human body changing and a database acknowledging it. Models needed such simplifications. Concealment began when institutions treated the simplification as more authoritative than the person still in the bed.

The huddle ended with a written capacity state: four temporary staffed beds, six ambulatory places, two accepted transfers, one local infection override, one failed discharge restored. Mira asked Caron to preserve the sequence without identifiers. It showed what honest capacity looked like: conditional, revised, and attached to named decisions rather than a single immaculate number.

At 15:00 Mira stood with the facilities engineer outside locked E5. Dust filmed the door window. Through it she could see stripped beds, coiled oxygen lines, empty brackets where monitors had hung, and sunlight across the floor. The ward was inactive, not derelict. Reopening it would require staff, cooling, cleaning, pharmacy supply, oxygen checks, infection-control review, and money. Capacity could not be summoned by rhetoric.

The engineer showed her the ventilation estimate. Renovation was onerous but passable within the original capital program. After denial, inflation had increased cost by twenty-two percent. Delay had made the earlier forecast more difficult to reverse. A tensile test on one ceiling support had expired; repeating it would be minor beside the ventilation work, but it was another stamped prerequisite between a bed and a patient.

Copper had been stripped from one unused riser after maintenance funds moved elsewhere. Replacement was modest beside the ventilation work, yet it added another approval, another contractor, another month. Closure generated neglect; neglect then appeared in the next review as evidence that reopening was impractical. The forecast accumulated physical allies.

On the wall beside the ward hung a faded staff photograph. Priya stood in the rear row, newly arrived, hair shorter, one hand on Soraya's shoulder. Mira did not photograph it.

Jeanne joined her at the door. "Negative space," she said. "Administrators count what is absent as if absence were natural."

"Noor would object to the metaphor being used carelessly."

"Then tell her an old woman said it first."

Mira looked through the glass. Thirty-two missing beds could be represented as zero occupancy. Zero looked clean. It concealed the decision that had produced it.

Before leaving, Mira returned to the patient council and read back her provisional finding: Harborlight's reduced population estimate preceded and materially influenced denial of E5 renovation; the denial led to recruitment freeze and closure; later demand measures appear to omit refused transfers and therefore risk treating reduced access as reduced need. Intent, upstream selection, and patient-level outcome attribution remained unresolved.

Malik said it was too bloodless.

The woman from the trolley said, "It is what the documents prove. Put our conditions beside it."

They did.

At 18:10 Priya came downstairs after twelve clinical hours. She had changed her top but not her shoes. Both heatstroke patients were improving. The suspected infection had received antibiotics and isolation without waiting for Harborlight's distant destination. No one had died.

Mira offered her the hospital's copy of the provisional finding, though Priya already had access.

"Come tomorrow," Priya said. "Not to E5. To the art center. I want to hear what Noor says the pulse can establish before anyone uses our parcel references."

"All right."

"And Mira."

She waited.

"Your apology was not nothing. It was not capacity either. Do not allocate it an outcome yet."

"I won't."

Priya walked toward the staff exit.

Mira remained in the lobby while the evening shift arrived. The screen above ambulance dispatch updated Saint-Césaire from severe constraint to limited intake. Harborlight had read the repaired cooling loop correctly. It had not restored E5, counted the people turned away over eighteen months, or disclosed why four neighborhoods were forecast to diminish.

The hospital had given them the first documented human mechanism in the chain: a future population estimate reduced investment; reduced investment closed a ward; the closed ward reduced admissions; reduced admissions made the forecast look right.

Tomorrow Noor would test whether the same `RET-4` command family carried not merely district classes but the parcels from which people were being made statistically absent.

## Chapter 24: Negative Space

The contemporary art center had converted a tobacco warehouse by preserving everything that made it difficult to hear.

Brick vaults divided the ceiling into shallow bays. Iron galleries crossed the central nave on three levels. A glazed loading alcove returned high frequencies almost at once, while the curved wall behind the former weighing floor held bass notes until they became indistinct. Reflectors installed for concerts hung athwart the old beams. Every grant application praised the building's industrial memory. Every sound engineer cursed its reverberation.

The curatorial files held the same contradiction: preservation rules forbade acoustic baffles that would hide the brick, while the grant required public benefit from experimental sound.

Noor stood in the center at 07:12 on Day Twenty-four and clapped once.

The clap returned as architecture: a brilliant first reflection from glass, a dry answer from baize curtains on the western gallery, then a plangent decay under the roof. Six seconds later the lowest trace disappeared into traffic beyond the converted loading doors.

"Still impossible," said Camille Roux, the center's curator.

"Still useful," Noor replied.

The distinction had governed Noor's installation before Sami's death. *Negative Space* was not a composition played into a neutral room. It assigned voices, machine tones, and harbor recordings to thirty-two speakers after measuring how the warehouse bent each one. Listeners walking the nave heard sources separate and recombine. A spoken line might remain legible beside one pillar and dissolve three steps away. The work made no prophecy. It gave form to selective attention.

Technicians had spent the night reinstalling the speaker array. Cables ran along the galleries in black bundles. Small full-range cabinets perched on the ironwork; subwoofers occupied the old scale pits. A microphone grid stood on thin poles at measured coordinates. The control desk held no original evidence. Its drives contained the center's installation software, clean calibration sweeps, and a court-authorized derivative of diagnostic audio already disclosed under the systems-hazard order. The original recorder and London puck remained sealed in Dutch custody. Noor had repeated that boundary until Camille could recite it with the doleful cadence of liturgy.

On the loading floor, independent acoustician Lucie Arnaud inspected cable labels. Hamid sat with Benali beside the document case holding his service slips. Mira and Priya reviewed the hospital's public planning appendix at a separate table. Elena, now plainly introduced as a suspended Compact lawyer acting privately, read the center's access agreement. Two French cybercrime officers observed because the ferry phone breach had increased risk to Hamid. A court-appointed audio examiner, Henrik Vos, controlled the authorized diagnostic file and would export any derived result.

The room contained expertise without consensus.

Camille wanted to announce a noon preview. The center's postponed heat program had already attracted international press, and a draft publicity note promised that Noor's work would translate buried commands into civic memory.

Noor crossed out the promise so hard the paper buckled. The installation could expose a structure; it could not assign motive or intent without a separate evidentiary chain.

"A masterpiece is not a category of proof," Noor said.

"It is a common phrase."

"Not today."

Camille wore a white shirt immaculate enough to make the dusty room seem at fault. "The center defrayed emergency installation costs. Our grant requires public engagement. We cannot become a private technical locale whenever institutions arrive with secrecy."

"You received the access conditions before spending anything. Closed test first. Public method only if the custodians authorize it."

"The scandal is already public."

"The evidence is not yours because the scandal improved attendance."

That answer carried more self-assertion than Noor usually allowed herself in a borrowed institution, but the alternative was a worse abdication: letting the center's need for audience turn custody into a decorative chore.

Across the nave, three activists from the Marseille Littoral Assembly waited by a locked glass door. Camille had invited them as community advisers. Noor had agreed to a meeting after the technical session. They had arrived early carrying placards: VALE ERASES PEOPLE and THE MODEL IS THE EVICTION. One wanted the installation to include names of patients diverted from Saint-Césaire. Another had proposed a wall of Cadran cancellation letters gathered online, with no verification of claimant consent.

Noor recognized the temptation. A spectacle could equalize attention faster than a procedural finding. It could also exploit every person whose absence it claimed to commemorate.

"Doors remain closed until eleven," she told Camille. "No cameras, no livestream, no aspirant documentary crew in the gallery."

"You cannot exclude the center from its own building."

"Your conservator, safety officer, and lead technician remain. Publicity does not."

Elena looked up from the agreement. "That is what the signed terms specify."

Camille's acquiescent nod was not consent so much as temporary defeat. She sent the communications assistant away.

At 07:30 Vos broke the seal on the working drive while both officers filmed. He verified its hash against the court depository. The authorized file contained three sources copied at the Delft laboratory from Sami's recorder: audible composition, diagnostic channel, and time-code reference. Noor's original work occupied the first. The machine pulses lay beneath it on a separate recorded channel; no acoustic trick had extracted them from music. The court order allowed analysis only for device behavior and imminent systems risk.

"We begin with controls," Lucie said.

She had built four test files overnight. One contained an ordinary maintenance handshake supplied by the manufacturer. One combined that handshake with random pulses shaped to resemble the disputed command. One embedded two known maintenance handshakes at different phase offsets. The fourth was silence plus room noise. Noor did not know which file was which. Neither did Vos, who had received them under generic labels. If the installation made meaningful forms appear in random timing, they needed to discover that before listening to evidence.

The process was less glamorous than Camille's publicity note. Technicians played logarithmic sweeps through each speaker. Microphones measured the room's impulse response. Lucie adjusted delays and gains so a pulse assigned to Speaker 7 arrived at the center reference within half a millisecond of one from Speaker 23. Noor walked the nave and marked positions where reflections occluded onset. The glazed alcove was unusable above four kilohertz. The scale pit produced a low-frequency resonance that could exaggerate every fourth pulse. They excluded both zones.

At 08:16 they played Control A.

The room filled with a sparse chromatic pattern: clicks moving from lower speakers to the galleries, followed by a soft descending tone. Noor heard one source, then doubted herself near the northern pillar where a reflection created a second apparent onset. She marked the location. Lucie ran the digital source-separation model without displaying the label. It resolved one maintenance frame and no persistent secondary structure.

The blind sheet recorded the result as nil, not negative in a theatrical sense, and Vos made everyone initial that wording before any evidence file appeared on the screen.

Control B produced two sources. Noor could hear them as separate paths only along the eastern gallery. The algorithm separated them throughout and reconstructed the known frames with one timing error at a speaker whose cable had been lengthened.

Control C generated a seductively regular pulse group. Camille, who had returned despite promising not to intervene, called it "the hidden command."

Lucie revealed it as randomized synthetic data.

"Regularity is not significance," Noor said.

"It sounded intentional."

"Most percussion does."

The false positive was more valuable than a triumphant control. It showed the installation could entice interpretation. Noor entered it in the method note rather than conceal the embarrassment.

That assiduousness did more than rankle Camille, who saw every caution as a denigration of the institution's competence. Noor saw it differently: a control that embarrassed them was useful evidence against their own desire.

Control D contained room noise. The algorithm found nothing above threshold.
