At 09:02 Vos loaded the diagnostic derivative. He did not send it first into thirty-two speakers. He ran an ordinary waveform and spectral analysis on the control computer. The channel contained the known maintenance preamble, device-family signature, status pings, and a recurring burst offset by 184 milliseconds. On headphones the burst was almost wholly occluded by the louder maintenance frame. Digital subtraction using the manufacturer sample exposed parts of it, but minor clock drift left residue that could be mistaken for content.

Noor's installation offered multiple rendered positions for the overlapping structures. It did not alter the source file. Lucie's software assigned estimated components to separate speakers based on phase and timing, then tested whether the separation remained stable as listeners moved and as the room-response correction changed.

Noor insisted the patch remain inextensible during the blind run: no discretionary filters, no hand-tuned thresholds, no new speaker assignments after the labels were opened.

"If the extra burst disappears when we perturb the model," Lucie said, "it is an artifact. If it persists across reasonable parameters and independent microphones capture the same reconstructed timing, we have a reproducible component."

Hamid asked, "Can it tell you what the component means?"

"No. It can tell us what pulse intervals are present with stated uncertainty. Meaning requires a protocol or an external correspondence."

"My slips have destination counts."

"You do not show them until we freeze the pulse result."

This prevented them from tuning separation until it matched the desired numbers.

It also spared Hamid a later recrimination. If the groups matched after he opened the slips, no one could say he had led the room toward them.

The first playback made the warehouse seem to breathe in two tempos. Maintenance pings traveled at floor level, steady and familiar. The extra burst rose through the gallery speakers in a clipped arabesque of groups: preamble, pause, five pulses, pause, two, pause, a longer run. Reflections gave the sequence luxuriance it did not possess in the file. Noor ignored the room's rhapsody and counted on the screen.

Lucie changed the correction by ten percent. The room sounded rougher. The secondary onset remained.

She removed four speakers. It remained.

Vos inverted channel assignment, introduced measured clock error, and used a different source-separation routine. The exact amplitude varied. The interval groups persisted within 0.7 milliseconds.

They repeated the test at six microphone positions. The glazed alcove failed, as predicted. Five valid positions reconstructed the same burst. Lucie froze the result at 09:47, hashed the timing table, and only then asked Hamid to open the service slips.

Benali unlocked the document case. Hamid broke no seal; the envelope had remained witnessed rather than judicially sealed, and each inspection was entered under the agreed protocol. He laid out six originals on a graphite-colored mat. The papers showed device serial, firmware package, `DIC`, destination class, and a field labeled `DEST PULSE` followed by grouped digits.

"I thought it was a transmission check," Hamid said. "The operator tapped the groups into a test pad after service. If the return pattern matched, the slip printed PASS."

Four `RET-4` slips showed different grouped values. The timing table from Sami's recorder matched one exactly: 5-2-13-4-117.

"What does it identify?" Mira asked.

Hamid shook his head. "Not device serial. Not customer account. Those are elsewhere."

Vos searched the manufacturer protocol manual. The field did not appear. The maintenance preamble and status pings did; the extra burst was undocumented in the disclosed specification.

He then began to scour the annexes for alternate usage notes and found only service vocabulary already accounted for by the maintenance frame.

"Could it be a private destination code unrelated to geography?" Elena asked.

"Yes," Lucie said. "We have correspondence with one slip, not semantics."

Priya opened the public planning appendix for Saint-Césaire. French cadastral parcels used section letters and numbers, not five numeric groups. The match seemed to fail.

Mira said, "The first groups may identify country, municipality, section, parcel, and subparcel."

"Or anything else," Noor replied.

They needed an independent mapping.

The partial Warehouse C export contained destination classes but masked locations. Gabriel's carriage record had serials but no French parcels. The Charlois Cadran schedule held parcel groups under clinic control; it could not be casually imported. The hospital's public appendix named planning sectors and linked to an open cadastral map. Noor asked Vos to document an external search before anyone entered the pulse groups.

On the French land registry's public interface, Marseille municipality code 13204 corresponded to one arrondissement but not the hospital's. Rearranged as 13-204, part of the pulse appeared plausible and wrong. They rejected it. Lucie warned against procrustean parsing: a code could be made to fit almost any registry if one lengthened or shortened groups after seeing the target.

Hamid produced a fifth slip from a unit destined for Tangier. Its `DEST PULSE` read 5-2-09-7-42. Morocco's cadastral system differed, and no obvious match emerged.

Noor returned to the sound. The preamble contained two pulses they had counted as data. Manufacturer notation treated those as field separators. Removing separators yielded 52134117, not five groups. The value was too long for a single parcel in most municipal systems.

"Coordinates?" Camille offered.

"No decimal marker, no sign, no hemisphere," Lucie said.

"An appellation can conceal anything if you refuse imagination."

"Imagination is not in short supply. Constraint is."

At 10:20 the activists knocked on the glass door. Their scheduled meeting approached. One raised a placard toward the nave. Noor felt time pressing toward spectacle.

Priya said, "What if it is not a public parcel number? Cadran might have its own property key."

Mira opened the hospital decision packet. The source reference `HL-PF/CR-MED/RET-4/13` linked to a public planning appendix because the hospital had included it, not because Harborlight exposed its internal identifiers. At the appendix margin, each affected sector carried a Cadran risk-map tile code: `CR5.2 / 13 / 4 / 117`.

The room went quiet.

Noor looked at the frozen pulse groups: 5-2-13-4-117.

"Do not celebrate," she said.

They checked provenance. The appendix had been published ten months earlier and archived by the regional authority before the current investigation. Its tile code corresponded to a cluster of cadastral parcels adjoining Saint-Césaire's east catchment. The code was not itself a legal parcel number; it was Cadran Re's grouping key for parcels within an insurance and planning tile.

The correction mattered because a tile could gather many owners and uses; calling it one parcel would invent a precision the command did not possess.

"The exhibition proposal calls them cadastral parcel numbers," Camille said. "Your studio used the phrase cadastral absences in May."

The phrase had nearly created an intolerable confusion. Noor made Vos enter the exchange in the session notes. They would not call the pulse a cadastral parcel number until the underlying mapping reached actual parcels.

The public Cadran tile expanded to seventeen cadastral references. The recurring command was keyed to the tile, which in turn enumerated parcels. That was a defensible chain: pulse groups to Hamid's destination field; destination field to a preexisting Cadran tile code; tile code to a published parcel set.

Elena called the chain lawful but narrow. A court could admit the correspondence as evidence of structure; it would not admit the same table as proof of authorship, intent, or command function.

They tested the Tangier slip. An archived Cadran Mediterranean planning map used `CR5.2 / 09 / 7 / 42` for a port redevelopment tile encompassing Bonded Warehouse C's surrounding investment district. The match was exact. A third slip matched a Rotterdam tile covering part of Charlois. Benali contacted the community clinic before opening any restricted schedule. The clinic's lawyer confirmed that the public-facing cancellation notices used the same tile family but declined to disclose claimant-level annexes. No disclosure was needed to establish the code system.

Three independent destinations matched. A fourth slip did not. Its code returned no public Cadran tile.

"Do not discard it," Mira said. "It may be obsolete, private, or evidence our interpretation fails outside selected examples."

They labeled it unresolved.

At 10:52 Lucie wrote the method in terms another laboratory could reproduce without the warehouse. Verify the authorized source hash. Measure and subtract the documented maintenance frame across a bounded clock-drift range. Recover the stable secondary pulse sequence using two independent algorithms. Freeze grouped intervals before consulting service slips. Match the groups against destination fields on original slips under witnessed inspection. Test those fields against Cadran tile codes archived before the investigation. Record matches, failures, and uncertainty.

Vos then required a deliberately impoverished replication. They moved to a concrete office behind the loading bay where the only equipment was his evidence laptop, two small active monitors, and one calibrated microphone. Noor stayed outside. Lucie received the frozen parameters but not the matched tile values. Vos supplied one evidence excerpt, the randomized control that had fooled Camille, and the unmatched fourth slip under new labels.

The office made the nave's technography look almost theatrical by comparison: no galleries, no spatial walk, no retentive bass under the roof, only a desk, two monitors, and the question of whether the timing survived without beauty.

Through the office window Noor saw Lucie work without the nave's pictorial drama. No pulses climbed galleries. No listener wandered among sources. The software produced timing tables on a grey screen. Lucie marked one stable secondary frame in the evidence excerpt, rejected the randomized control because its groups changed under clock perturbation, and recovered the unmatched frame without assigning meaning. Her evidence timing differed from the nave result by four-tenths of a millisecond, inside the declared tolerance.

Vos repeated the test using a basic open-source separation package none of Noor's studio code had touched. Resolution worsened. One pulse merged with the maintenance tail, but the grouped destination value remained recoverable after the ambiguity was entered as a range. He exported both the success and the limitation.

"The warehouse is demonstrative, not necessary," he said when they returned. "It helped a trained listener perceive the overlap and helped us design the test. The finding survives in an ordinary room."

Noor felt relief accompanied by a small, shameful loss. An artist wanted the work to be integral. A custodian should want the result to survive her. She added Vos's sentence to the method note.

The art center contributed the array, room measurement, source-separation practice, and Noor's recognition that spatial assignment could prevent one strong signal from overshadowing another. The result did not depend on believing her hearing. A lab with ordinary speakers and microphones could repeat it. Even software alone could recover the timing, though less intuitively.

Art had yielded a forensic method by refusing the demand that art become proof through charisma.

Camille read the draft result. "It needs significance."

"It has significance," Noor said. "It does not need inflation."

"The public will hear that pulses match insurance map tiles. They will conclude conspiracy."

"Then we state what remains unfounded. We do not know who generated the destination field, who chose each tile, what command the firmware executed after receiving it, or whether every tile marks withdrawal. We know an undocumented recurring frame is keyed to Cadran's parcel groupings rather than engineering need."

"That is an unorthodox wall text."

"It is a justifiable one."

"That sentence will not move anyone."

"It moves us to Cadran Re."

The causal consequence was enough.

At eleven they admitted the activists, patient council representatives, center staff, and a lawyer for the dockworkers' clinic. No press entered. Noor began by stating custody. The original recorder was not present. Hamid's slips remained his. Hospital patient data had not been used. Public archived maps supplied tile codes. The session had produced a method and a bounded finding, not a public accusation.

Every admitted observer received the same boundary: no clinical or claimant records, no image of Hamid's originals, and no inference beyond the frozen method.

Salima Benchekroun of the Littoral Assembly objected. "People are being displaced while you refine wording. The model is the eviction."

"The hospital closure was material harm," Malik said. "But patients rejected using their stories without control."

Another activist pointed toward the installation. "Play the names of the districts. Let people hear what has been erased."

Noor felt the old possessive instinct rise in altered form. Once she had wanted to keep Sami's sound from institutions. Now she wanted to keep institutions and movements from making his sound represent everyone.

"No," she said. "Not today."

"Because of legal stringency?"

"Because district names are not raw material. Because the pulse does not contain voices. Because making an elegy before asking people would turn their lives into my authorship."

Salima called that aloofness dressed as ethics.

"Perhaps," Noor said. "But you do not cure extraction by changing the claimant."

Priya explained the patient council's conditions. Malik stated them again in his own words. The dockworkers' clinic lawyer asked whether the method could test Cadran cancellation tiles without exposing policyholders. Lucie said yes: the clinic could retain its schedule, provide only tile codes under a witnessed comparison, and publish aggregate matches if claimants authorized them.

They tested the proposed display language against those limits. Camille wanted a synoptic wall map with affected tiles glowing red. Malik objected that a red map would reproduce Harborlight's visual judgment and make every resident appear doomed or displaced. Salima proposed photographs of vacant storefronts. The clinic lawyer asked who had established that each vacancy followed insurance withdrawal rather than rent, retirement, or ordinary failure. No one had.

Noor replaced the map with a table of method states: source verified, secondary frame stable, service-slip match, archived tile match, unmatched case, interpretation pending. It was modest to the point of severity. Visitors would have to move from the installation's sensuous space into a study area where uncertainty remained visible. Camille worried they would skim it. Noor said the center could provide trained facilitators, translations, and audio description, but not manufacture emotional certainty.

The table encapsulated less than the room wanted and more than a press release could safely hold.

The activists won one change. Beside every tile result, the display would state who retained the underlying record and how affected residents could contest inclusion. Custody would not be relegated to fine print. Noor had been defending authorship as if only the artist could exploit people; a correct method could also become obtrusive if the institution treated affected communities as passive subject matter.

The room's conflict did not dissolve into consensus. Two activists left in anger. One stayed and asked to join the protocol-design meeting. Camille withdrew the noon preview but insisted the center publish its grant expenditure and access terms to avoid the appearance of exclusive patronage. Noor agreed. Transparency about the room did not publicize the evidence.

At 12:30 Vos exported the timing table, parameter ranges, control results, code, microphone captures, and method note. He included the randomized control that had fooled Camille and the unresolved fourth slip. French police received one sealed copy. The court depository received another by encrypted transfer with hash confirmation. Hamid and the art center received receipts, not unrestricted evidence files. Lucie signed as analyst. Noor signed as method contributor and source-separation witness, not owner of the finding.

Vos called unrestricted copying impermissible twice, once for the officers and once for Camille, because a beautiful display could still vitiate evidence if it blurred custody.

Sami's composition had not played during the session. Only the diagnostic derivative had. When the technical work ended, Noor asked Vos to unload the drive before she tested the public installation. He sealed it. The machine evidence left the control desk.

Then she loaded the art.

Voices entered the nave from years before: dockworkers describing fog, a child counting cranes, Noor's mother naming winds in French and Arabic, Sami complaining that one speaker had a rattle. His voice came from the western gallery and crossed toward the scale pit. He sounded alive because recordings always committed that small imposture.

Noor stopped playback.

Camille waited. "You have not shown the piece since he died."

"I know."

"The reopening could commemorate him."

"It could exploit him."

"Those are not mutually exclusive."

For once the curator's answer was not avaricious. Museums converted loss into program because institutions required dates, rooms, budgets, and public language. Refusing every form would leave only private bereavement, which had its own supremacy.

Noor walked to the western speaker and touched its casing. She had used Sami's recorder in the work without inspecting the diagnostic channel because she wanted his technical help without his alarm. After his death she had feared that every public playback would make her disobedience maudlin or sacrificial.

"The piece can reopen after Tangier families and the patient council review the context," she said. "Sami's voice stays where it was. No narration makes him a prophet. The forensic method appears separately, with controls and failures."

"Two rooms?"

"No nested spectacle. The installation here. The method in the study gallery, plain tables, headphones, code, custody statement."

"That is visually gloomy."

"Use legible typography."

Camille grumbled but took notes.

In the afternoon the group followed the new lead. Elena called Cadran Re's Marseille compliance office and requested the tile dictionary, service agreements, and guarantee schedules associated with `RET-4`. She stated that the pulse method linked an undocumented firmware destination field to Cadran's archived parcel groups. She did not allege that Cadran wrote firmware or ordered ward closure.

She also refused Camille's proposed summary, which would have called the tile frame a command authored by Cadran. That phrasing was inapplicable to what they had proved and untrustworthy as a handoff to the next interview.

Cadran's counsel responded within nineteen minutes. The tile codes were ordinary catastrophe-model groupings, widely licensed and incapable of proving direction. Any guarantees were commercially confidential. The firm would receive them at 09:00 the next day for a voluntary compliance interview but would not permit devices or publication.

"They did not deny guarantees," Elena said.

"They did not admit them," Mira replied.

Priya had returned to Saint-Césaire. Before leaving, she gave Noor the patient council's formal restriction: the hospital tile could be named because it was public, but no patient story or clinical category could be incorporated into the installation without separate consent. Noor attached the condition to the center's file.

Hamid examined the unresolved fourth slip one more time. "This destination was serviced last," he said. "Kroll took it off the ordinary trolley and carried it himself."

"Where was it going?" Noor asked.

"The slip says Malta relay support. No public Cadran tile."

That lead remained inchoate. They logged it for later rather than forcing it into Marseille.

Its failure was not insignificance. It was the one result in the day's three matched pulse groups that refused their pattern, and for that reason it stayed visible in the record.

At 17:00 the art center reopened its ground-floor café and courtyard because the heat had eased. Word of the closed session had leaked despite the embargo. Journalists waited on the foreshore side. Camille issued a statement saying only that independent experts had tested an acoustic separation method and that custodians were reviewing results. She did not call it phenomenal, revolutionary, or a chef d'oeuvre.

Noor left by the service door with no evidence in her bag. On the pavement, Salima waited alone.

"You undersell what you found," the activist said.

"Perhaps."

"Cadran parcel maps are inside machine commands. What more do you need?"

"To know what the command does, who selected the parcel group, and what Cadran promised when insurers withdrew."

"People already know the consequence."

"Some do. Some received compensation. Some relocation housing saved them. Some lost coverage before anyone told them why. If we make one generic victim, Vale will rebut it with one beneficiary and call the question settled."

Salima considered that without becoming peaceable. "Then do not dally at Cadran."

"We have a meeting tomorrow."

"They will hoodwink you."

"Probably not with flair."

The wry answer earned no smile, but the belligerence eased.

At dusk Noor returned to the nave. The technicians had left calibration marks on the floor: coordinates, excluded reflection zones, microphone positions, and a straight line showing the reference axis. Against the warehouse's antiquity, the marks looked temporary and modest. They did not reveal a hidden language. They showed where listeners and instruments had stood when one signal was separated from another.

She played the disputed derivative once more from the method copy only after Vos authorized a non-exporting session. Maintenance pings moved along the floor. The parcel-keyed frame climbed the galleries. Now that Noor knew the Cadran tile, the groups seemed to announce it. That familiarity was dangerous. Knowledge changed hearing after the fact.

Noor pondered that danger longer than she liked. Evidence could become a trance after discovery, each repetition making the known answer feel inevitable.

She switched to the unmatched fourth slip. Its pulses rose and yielded no map. The unresolved sequence kept the method honest.

Negative space was not emptiness. It was the shape left by prior choices: a closed ward recorded as no demand, a cancelled policy recorded as lower resilience, a district forecast to shrink, an artwork expected to speak for people absent from the room. Today the installation had made one such choice audible and reproducible. It had not supplied motive.

At 19:14 Elena forwarded Cadran's visitor terms for the morning. Compliance would permit discussion of tile licensing and catastrophe models. Executives would claim ordinary market response. Guarantee schedules remained outside scope unless a compliance officer chose otherwise or a court compelled them.

Noor looked up at the galleries where the two pulse trains had diverged.

Traffic murmured beyond the loading doors, indifferent to their discovery.

The next question no longer belonged to acoustics. It belonged to money: whether Cadran had merely mapped parcels after risk changed, or had been paid to withdraw before the public classification that made withdrawal appear prudent.

At 09:00 they would ask the insurer.

## Chapter 25: Actuarial Life

At 08:43 on Day Twenty-five, Elena stood beneath the caduceus outside the dockworkers' clinic and watched Cadran Re's windows turn white with sun.

The insurer occupied six floors of a limestone building above the Joliette tram line. Its name appeared once, in discreet brass. The clinic across the road announced itself with peeling blue paint, a pharmacy cross, and three men altercating over whose turn it was to move a balky examination couch. Between them ran four lanes of traffic and the financial distance between an injury and its price.

Elena had slept for two hours in a chair at the police building. Fatigue made the pavement seem porous. She had changed her shirt in a lavatory and tied back her hair without a mirror. Her temporary authority consisted of a private-law mandate from Hamid, a letter from the Charlois clinic, the Saint-Césaire patient council's restricted query, and Cadran's voluntary invitation. None compelled an answer.

Benali arrived with Hamid and the document case. Henrik Vos brought no evidence drive, only the sealed method receipt from the previous day. Lucie Arnaud remained at the art center. Mira had gone ahead to the dockworkers' clinic, where a physician would explain why insurance continuity had entered Harborlight's health-capacity model. Noor stayed with the installation and would join only if Cadran disputed the acoustic method.

"They said no devices," Hamid said.

"They said no recording devices in the interview," Elena replied. "Their own access system will record our arrival. We take handwritten notes, exchange copies before leaving, and particularize every refusal."

"That sounds almost amicable."

"It is an interview with an entity that may sue us before lunch. Amicability is a seating arrangement."

Across the road, a clinic foreman lifted one end of the couch while the two disputants discovered unison. The object passed through the doorway with a scrape.

At 08:58 Cadran security admitted Elena's party. They surrendered phones into numbered lockers but retained the document case. A compliance assistant inspected the exterior seal numbers without opening it. Hamid did not transfer ownership. Vos signed only for the method receipt he carried.

The interview room was cool enough to raise gooseflesh. It held an oblong table, a carafe, six glasses, and a framed photograph of wind turbines against an effulgent sea. Three Cadran representatives entered: general counsel Alain Mercier, catastrophe-model director Dr. Sabine Lenoir, and compliance officer Marianne Aveline. Mercier was outgoing in the manner of a man who expected warmth to be construed as candor. Lenoir carried a technical bibliography thick with adhesive flags. Aveline carried nothing.

Mercier began by certifying identities and scope. Tile licensing was in scope. Catastrophe methodology was in scope. Client-specific guarantee schedules, reserves, claim files, and commercially sensitive pricing were not. Cadran's voluntary attendance constituted no waiver. The firm rejected any implication that its ordinary prudential activity had caused a hospital closure or machine command.

"We have not made that implication," Elena said.

"Your associates have made comparable statements in public."

"Name the statement and speaker."

Mercier offered a backhanded smile. "We need not start with a fracas."

"Then do not attribute an unspecified accusation to the people in this room."

Aveline looked from one lawyer to the other. "Let the record show that Cadran withdraws the characterization."

There was no official record yet, only four sets of handwritten notes. Still, the phrase changed the room. A compliance officer's first instinct was not necessarily loyalty to counsel's narration.

Lenoir explained the tiles. Cadran grouped properties to model correlated loss: flood depth, construction, access, utilities, business interruption, and recovery capacity. A tile was not a cadastral title, moral verdict, or instruction to withdraw. The `CR5.2` family covered several Mediterranean portfolios. `RET-4` signified a risk-transfer treaty class, not a firmware package.

"Does `RET-4` signify the same thing in `CR-MED/RET-4`?" Elena asked.

"It signifies a treaty layer for managed-retreat exposure."

"Define managed-retreat exposure."

Mercier intervened. "Properties subject to public policy affecting future occupation."

"Public policy already adopted?"

"Adopted, proposed, or actuarially foreseeable."

"Foreseeable by whom?"

"That is not a useful formulation."

"It is the useful formulation. A public reclassification occurs on one date. Six Charlois policies are cancelled six weeks earlier. The cancellation cites your facility. Harborlight later uses reduced insurance continuity to lower recovery capacity. Yesterday an undocumented device frame matched your tile codes. I am asking what information allowed withdrawal before the public event."

Lenoir aligned her flags with the table edge. "Primary insurers make underwriting decisions. Cadran assumes part of their aggregate risk. We do not cancel individual policies."

"Did Cadran compensate primary insurers for policies withdrawn from selected tiles before public reclassification?"

Mercier said, "Guarantee schedules are outside scope."

"Did Harborlight or an affiliate compensate Cadran for those payments?"

"Outside scope."

"Did a Cadran vehicle fund relocation housing associated with those tiles?"

For the first time Mercier's reticence looked less like discipline than calculation.

Aveline said, "Our social-resilience investments are publicly reported."

"At entity level," Elena said. "Not by tile or withdrawal window."

"That may be true."

Mercier turned to her. "Marianne."

The admonition was quiet. Aveline countenanced it without apology.

Elena asked Lenoir to describe chronology without client names. Lenoir said catastrophe models normally modified expected loss after observed hazards, building changes, or policy changes. Scenario models could also estimate future relocation. Their outputs were assumptions, not prophecy.

"Can an expected relocation rate reduce present insurance availability?"

"If cedants believe occupancy, maintenance, emergency access, or public subsidy will change, yes."

"Can reduced insurance availability then lower Harborlight's recovery-capacity score?"

"Cadran does not control Harborlight's model."

"You license the tile feed."

"A limited feed."

"Containing insurance continuity?"

"An aggregate indicator."

"Generated after withdrawals?"

"Ordinarily."

"And before public reclassification?"

Lenoir glanced at Mercier. "A scenario indicator may precede public action."

The equivocation had an actuarial elegance. A scenario went into the model as a possible future. If an insurer acted on it, the action changed present conditions. Harborlight then received those conditions as observed reality. What began as a conditional assumption returned with the authority of fact.

Elena drew a diagonal across her page. On the upper side she wrote scenario. On the lower, observed withdrawal. An arrow crossed the line.

"What prevents a scenario from creating the condition used to certify itself?"

Lenoir said, "Governance. Independent validation. Consistency tests."

"Were those controls applied to `RET-4`?"

"Guarantee schedules are outside scope," Mercier said again.

At 09:46 the interview paused. Hamid went with Benali to the corridor. Vos compared the group's notes for divergence. Cadran's assistant provided coffee in paper cups and beet-colored fruit juice no one touched.

Aveline remained seated.

"Ms. Varga," she said, "your authority under the Compact is suspended?"

"Yes."

"You drafted its emergency immunity?"

Mercier, standing at the door, looked back.

"I participated in the drafting," Elena said. "My authorship and conflict were disclosed to the Hague chambers group on Day Six. They are not yet public."

"Then you understand why firms require protection to act before loss."

"I understand the argument."

"It is more than an argument. A flood does not wait for administrative perspicuity. Capital can move first or arrive as an encomiastic speech after burial."

"And if capital pays institutions to produce the evidence that justifies its movement?"

"That would be a substantive compliance question."

Mercier said, "The break is over."

When Hamid returned, Elena asked permission to show one original service slip. Mercier objected that the acoustic interpretation was unverified. Vos supplied the court examiner's method receipt and summarized the blind controls, the frozen pulse groups, three archived tile matches, and one unresolved Malta-support frame. He did not display the derivative.

Hamid opened the witnessed envelope. He selected the Marseille `RET-4` slip while Benali entered the inspection. The paper never left the graphite mat. Lenoir leaned close enough to read `DEST PULSE 5-2-13-4-117`.

"Is that a Cadran tile?" Elena asked.

"The groups correspond to one."

"Would an engineering service worker have reason to enter it?"

"Not for catastrophe modeling."

"Would a Harborlight device need it to report engineering condition?"

"I cannot speak to the device."

"Did Cadran transmit tile dictionaries to Harborlight?"

"We license dictionaries to approved users."

"Did your license permit encoding tile keys into field-device commands?"

Mercier said, "Assumes facts not established."

"Did it permit operational use outside catastrophe modeling?"

Lenoir closed the bibliography. "The standard license permits risk aggregation, portfolio reporting, and agreed resilience applications. It does not permit hidden use."

"Hidden from whom?"

"Policyholders, if their rights are affected. Regulators. Cadran, if the use exceeds the declared purpose."

"Did Cadran audit Harborlight's use?"

"Yes."

"When?"

Mercier spoke before she could. "Audit history is outside scope."

Elena let the refusal sit. Repetition had become probative in a modest way: Cadran would explain models until an answer touched `RET-4` governance, guarantees, or audit.

She moved to the Charlois sequence. The clinic retained policy originals, so she used certified dates and facility references from the public filing. Lenoir acknowledged that the relevant tile entered a relocation scenario before cancellation. She denied knowing any individual underwriting decision. Mercier said market response to flood risk was neither arbitrary nor dishonorable.

"No one says all repricing is unjustified," Elena replied. "The narrow counter-claim is that an undisclosed guarantee removed ordinary loss from early withdrawal. If true, what appeared to be independent market judgment was selective performance underwritten by the same policy system that later treated withdrawal as evidence."

"A counterclaim to what?" Mercier asked.

"To Cadran's assertion that it merely observed ordinary market response."

Aveline wrote the sentence down.

At 10:38 an alarm sounded across the road. Through the window Elena saw workers leave the clinic and gather beneath the awning. A minute later the alarm stopped. A man in green work clothes opened a side door and waved them back.

Mira called Cadran reception from the clinic. The interruption was not theatrical. Renovation dust had clogged a smoke detector near physiotherapy. No fire, no injury. The clinic asked whether Elena's party could cross for the scheduled occupational-health session.

Mercier attempted to end the interview. Aveline asked for a recess instead. She wanted to attend the clinic because the `RET-4` treaty's public report cited dockworker health and pension resilience as compensatory benefits.

"That visit was not agreed," Mercier said.

"The report is within my compliance domain."

"Not with adverse counsel."

Elena said, "I am not counsel in any filed action against Cadran. The clinic invited all participants. You may attend."

They crossed at 11:02. Heat struck the group as the glass doors opened. The clinic's waiting room had ten molded chairs, a water dispenser, and framed photographs of retired crane operators. A child's crayon drawing of a ship hung beside notices about hernia screening, solvent exposure, hearing loss, and pension advice.

Dr. Céleste Armand met them in a room where the displaced examination couch now stood. She had treated dock labor for twenty-three years and despised the phrase resilience metric.

"A metric never lifted a mattress," she said. "People do."

The clinic served active workers, casual laborers, retired port staff, and families. Its funding mixed union dues, municipal support, employer levies, and a grant from Phare Habitat, a relocation-housing entity capitalized partly by Cadran. That grant paid for a respiratory nurse, heat screening, and transport to specialists. It was appreciable and useful.

It also depended on projected relocation numbers.

Armand showed aggregate records only. The clinic's catchment had lost two hundred twelve registered households to a new estate beyond the northern freight belt. Some moved after floods; others after insurance withdrawal or landlord sale. Phare funded transport vouchers for eighteen months, then reduced them when its model assumed residents would transfer to suburban providers. Many did not. Port shifts began before the first bus. Older patients missed appointments. Workers with chronic pulmonary disease rationed visits.

"The grant increased some services and helped atrophied others disappear," Armand said. "Both are true."

"Can you attribute missed care to relocation?" Mira asked.

"Not every case. We can show travel time, appointment nonattendance, and work schedules. We cannot assume motive for every absence."

That restraint impressed Aveline more than accusation might have.

The clinic accountant, Joël Fabre, placed audited statements on the table. He had the workmanlike patience of someone accustomed to explaining restricted funds to committees. Phare's grant appeared as program income. A separate line, `RET-4 continuity supplement`, reimbursed the clinic when registered households left selected tiles. The supplement prevented abrupt revenue loss. It was commendable in immediate effect.

"Who funded the supplement?" Elena asked.

"Phare Habitat."

"Who calculated it?"

"Cadran supplied household counts. Harborlight supplied projected departure."

"Before departures?"

"Quarterly in advance."

Fabre opened a schedule. It contained no patient names, only tile, expected departures, actual registrations, and adjustment. For the Marseille tile from Hamid's slip, the first projected departure preceded public reclassification by three months.

Mercier said, "A social program planning for likely movement is not evidence of policy withdrawal."

"No," Elena agreed. "It is evidence that Cadran and Harborlight expected movement early enough to fund its consequences."

"Climate foresight is not venality."

"No one said it was."

Aveline asked Fabre whether he had ever seen the underlying guarantee. He had not. His grant schedule referenced a master facility number: `ALP-CAD/HLG/04`.

The letters altered Aveline's countenance. Elena noticed because legal work often turned on the smallest involuntary amendment to a face.

"You know that facility," Elena said.

Mercier stood. "We are leaving."

Aveline remained seated. "It is a loss guarantee."

Silence entered the little room. Outside, someone wheeled an oxygen cylinder over an interstice in the floor, producing a treble knock.

Mercier told Aveline she was not authorized to disclose client material. She answered that the firm's regulated duty to report possible misuse was not subject to his preference. Their disagreement stayed formal, which made it more severe.

"What does the guarantee cover?" Elena asked.

"I will not answer from memory," Aveline said. "I need the instrument and schedules."

"Those are outside the voluntary interview," Mercier said.

"Then this is no longer the voluntary interview."

Aveline explained the next steps with careful desistance from accusation. As compliance officer she could place a preservation hold, inspect segregated records, and report a suspected breach to the French prudential supervisor. She could not hand Elena unrestricted client files. If the documents established imminent systems hazard or false regulatory reporting, she could make a protected disclosure to the authority and seek a judicial protocol.

"Will you?" Hamid asked.

"I will inspect."

"That is what people say when they intend to tarry."

Benali touched his sleeve, but Aveline did not glower.

"Monsieur Belkacem, I understand why the response sounds feeble. If I disclose the wrong schedule without protection, Cadran will suppress it, challenge custody, and indict my motive before anyone reads the substance. Give me until fourteen hundred."

Hamid looked at Elena.

"It is a defined act and time," Elena said. "Not trust."

At 12:07 Aveline returned to Cadran with Mercier and Lenoir. Before leaving, she signed the group's reconciled notes for the morning and added three statements in her own hand: Cadran tile codes corresponded to the demonstrated destination groups; standard licensing did not authorize undisclosed rights-affecting use; `ALP-CAD/HLG/04` was a loss-guarantee facility subject to compliance inspection. Mercier signed only to acknowledge receipt and wrote that he disputed implication and scope.

The team remained at the clinic. Heat accumulated against the shutters. Armand saw patients in the adjoining rooms while Mira and Fabre tested the grant chronology. Elena called the Charlois clinic and Saint-Césaire patient council. Neither authorized joining claimant records to Cadran schedules. Both agreed to preserve facility references and receive notice of any court application.

At 12:41 Noor arrived with bread, olives, and a paper sack fragrant with thyme. She had heard Aveline's disclosure from Mira but asked first whether the original slip had returned to Hamid's envelope. It had. Vos had left the method receipt with Benali and returned to the depository. No evidence object remained at Cadran.

"What did the money do?" Noor asked.

Elena described the clinic grant.

"So the same movement that makes people travel farther paid for a nurse here."

"Possibly the same facility family. Not yet the same account."

"You can amend my sentence after we eat."

They ate in the staff room. The air conditioner had failed, and a fan stirred paper napkins without cooling anyone. Hamid reclined on a vinyl bench and slept for twenty minutes under Benali's observation. His body had ceased treating protection as rest.

At 13:56 Aveline called Elena from a supervised line at the prudential authority. She had inspected the master instrument and five schedules. The authority had accepted an initial protected report and imposed a preservation hold. A duty judge would hear a narrow production request at 16:00.

"What can you state now?" Elena asked.

"The facility was funded by Harborlight Resilience Holdings and administered by Cadran. It reimbursed cedants for specified losses if they reduced exposure in selected `RET-4` tiles before a trigger date. Trigger dates preceded public reclassification. Reimbursement included unearned premium, transition expense, and a buffer for legal challenge."

"Who selected the tiles?"

"The schedules identify Harborlight scenario bundles and a joint selection committee. I have not established individual votes."

"Did the facility require withdrawal?"

"It did not compel any insurer. It made early withdrawal nearly lossless within the selected portfolio."

"And Phare Habitat?"

"A related but legally distinct vehicle. It received a portion of the same capital commitment for acquisition and relocation housing. There is an accounting separation. I cannot yet certify substantive independence."

"Does the instrument disclose the arrangement to policyholders or public authorities receiving the later continuity score?"

"Not in the copies I reviewed."

Elena felt the brink beneath the answer. They had the financial loop in outline, but not motive, command function, full membership, or Vale's authorization. The guarantee did not order cancellation. It changed the actuarial life of cancellation by removing its loss.

Aveline continued. "There is an internal consistency memorandum warning that withdrawal could reduce the Harborlight recovery score and thereby validate the initiating scenario. The memorandum recommends a firewall and delayed model feedback. The response marks the risk compensatory and acceptable because housing capacity would be created."

"By whom?"

"Signed committee response. Names remain under the judicial request."

"Preserve the metadata."

"Already done."

At 16:00 the hearing occurred by secure video from the clinic's meeting room. Elena appeared for Hamid only on evidence provenance, not for the Charlois claimants or Saint-Césaire patients. The prudential authority sought the master instrument, five schedules, consistency memorandum, committee response, audit history, and tile dictionary. Cadran opposed broad production but did not contest preservation.

Mercier argued that reimbursement was ordinary reinsurance, designed to forestall insolvency during climate transition. Primary insurers retained independent judgment. Phare's housing investments were the antithesis of predatory abandonment: they moved families from danger and created safer homes. Disclosure could precipitate a market slump and strand policyholders.

The authority answered that ordinary reinsurance priced loss after underwriting. This facility made payment conditional on reducing exposure before public triggers while Harborlight later treated that reduction as independent evidence. The issue was not whether relocation housing existed or helped people. It was whether concealed coordination corrupted public classifications.

Elena said little. She authenticated Hamid's slip inspection, Vos's method receipt, and the archived tile match. She refused the judge's invitation to infer what the undocumented device command did.

"You have a machine pulse and an insurance tile," the judge said. "Why should I connect them to a guarantee?"

"You should not yet connect command function," Elena replied. "The tile correspondence supplies a reason to preserve and compare schedules. The protected compliance report independently supplies the guarantee's terms. Production can test overlap without assuming coordination."

The judge granted a bounded order. Cadran would produce the master instrument, schedules for the three matched tiles and unresolved Malta-support reference if present, the consistency memorandum, response, and audit entries. The prudential authority would hold originals. Elena, Hamid, and claimant counsel would receive redacted inspection copies under undertaking. No policyholder identities or pricing beyond the selected mechanism would be disclosed. Phare housing records remained outside scope except for capital transfers and governance overlap.

It was not the sweeping seizure Mercier had warned against or the public release activists wanted. It was enough to make the loop traceable.

At 17:28 Aveline delivered the first certified extract to the authority. The Marseille schedule identified the same `CR5.2 / 13 / 4 / 117` tile recovered from the pulse. The guarantee attached ninety-one days before public reclassification. Two primary insurers withdrew within the covered window. Cadran paid their documented transition costs from Harborlight's segregated account. Thirty days later the reduced continuity indicator entered Harborlight's district model. The next quarter's report cited lower recovery capacity and increased expected relocation.

The audit entry was less tidy. Cadran's internal reviewer had sampled twelve tiles and found that four moved from scenario to withdrawal faster than the catastrophe model's confidence interval allowed. She had asked whether the guarantee itself constituted an intervention requiring disclosure. The joint committee response modified the audit label from causal risk to transition alignment and closed the item after Harborlight promised a prospective firewall.

"Was the firewall built?" Mira asked.

Aveline checked the certified index. "The implementation field says deferred pending platform consolidation."

"So no."

"Not by the date of this extract."

Mercier's written response arrived while they read. He cautioned that the phrase firewall described an enhancement, not admission of a defective control. He also asserted that public authorities had long known private capital would support retreat.

Elena wrote back through the authority, not to him directly. General awareness that capital supported relocation was not equivalent to disclosure that a loss guarantee rewarded selected withdrawal before a public model measured that withdrawal as declining resilience. She requested the committee charter, attendance records, and version history of the altered audit label.

The judge reserved those items for the next morning. She would not permit the narrow order to become a farraginous corporate inquest. Elena accepted the limit. The three documents already produced established mechanism and chronology. Governance could wait for a properly supported application.

At 18:02 the Compact disciplinary officer called. Elena took the call in Armand's empty consultation room. An anatomical chart of the shoulder hung behind the desk; a jar of wooden tongue depressors stood beside a model knee.

The officer, Marta Ivanković, had once supervised Elena's first treaty posting. She sounded neither overbearing nor sympathetic.

"Did you appear adverse to a Compact contractor after suspension?"

"I appeared for Hamid Belkacem on provenance in a French regulatory proceeding. I did not invoke Compact office or credentials."

"Did you disclose protected drafting information?"

"No. Cadran's compliance officer asked whether I drafted the immunity clause. I answered that I participated and had disclosed the conflict in private chambers on Day Six."

"The secretariat says your conduct is recriminative."

"That is not a disciplinary category."

"It is their word, not mine. They also say you are using access acquired in office to damage the project."

"Every record obtained today came from a French authority, Hamid's supervised original, public archives, or Cadran's voluntary statements."

"Will you certify that in writing?"

"Yes."

Ivanković warned that Elena could be ordered to desist from representing witnesses whose interests conflicted with the Compact. Elena replied that an order required a stated rule and competent authority, not an obscure admonition delivered by telephone.

"You have become difficult," Ivanković said.

"I was difficult when you hired me."

"You were precise. There is an appreciable difference."

Elena looked through the frosted glass at the clinic corridor. "Perhaps precision without consequence was more convenient."

"Do not orate at me. Submit your record by twenty-two hundred. Preserve everything. Speak to no press."

"Those instructions are lawful and proportionate. I will comply."

"Your complacent tone is infelicitous."

"I am not complacent."

"Good. You should not be."

The call ended without leniency or threat beyond what the process already contained. Elena drafted the certification at Armand's desk. She listed every mandate, room, participant, document, refusal, handoff, and seal. She stated that she had no original evidence and no unrestricted Cadran file. The exercise was not self-defense alone. If she became disqualified, another lawyer needed a traceable account that did not depend on her narration.

When she returned to the meeting room, Hamid was studying the grant schedule. "They knew how many would leave."

"They projected how many," Elena said. "The guarantee may have helped make the projection true. That is what we can prove so far."

"You always put a buffer around the sentence."

"Today the buffer is the difference between a sophisticated mechanism and a preposterous claim that every departure was ordered."

Hamid folded the copy on its existing crease. "I despise that you are right."

"A common but unproductive response."

For the first time that day, he laughed.

The sequence was distinct and appalling without becoming simple. Insurers had genuine climate exposure. Some properties had flooded. Withdrawal might have occurred eventually. The guarantee accelerated it selectively and concealed the subsidy. The housing vehicle had built apartments, funded clinic work, and moved families out of dangerous ground. It had also acquired distressed parcels through an affiliate after coverage disappeared.

No document yet said: make this district fail. No document said: close Ward E5. No document identified Vale's vote. The system instead contained lawful acts whose interaction had been anticipated and accepted.

Mira read the extract twice. "We need to see the housing."

"Because Vale will show it," Elena said.

"Because people live there. If we call every benefit a ransom, we repeat his error in reverse."

Noor leaned against the shutter. "And if they like their homes?"

"Then they like their homes."

"If they hate them?"

"That is also theirs."

Armand supplied the name of a residents' association at Les Amandiers, the largest Phare estate outside Marseille. Its chair had already refused two journalists and one campaign that wanted residents to denounce relocation as a monstrosity. The social worker agreed to ask, not summon.

Before dusk, Elena completed the evidence notes. Hamid's slip returned to the witnessed envelope. Cadran's originals remained with the prudential authority. Aveline retained whistleblower protection and had not joined the investigators. The clinic kept its own accounts. Each boundary preserved the fact that discovery did not constitute ownership.

Elena stepped outside at 19:03. The brass name across the road had gone dark. Clinic windows remained lit. A port worker emerged with a bandage over a small incision and a pension leaflet folded in his pocket. The city beyond him was neither saved nor condemned by the schedule she had read.

Her phone showed three messages. One notified her that the Compact disciplinary office had opened a formal inquiry into unauthorized adverse action. One came from Mercier reserving claims. The third, from the Les Amandiers association, granted Mira a visit at ten the next morning under conditions: no cameras, no unannounced activists, no patient histories, no assumption that residents were grateful or deceived.

Elena sent the conditions to Mira.

The guarantee had proved the financial loop: concealed capital made selective withdrawal prudent, withdrawal diminished measured resilience, and the diminished score supported the scenario that had selected the district. Yet the same capital had bought roofs, lifts, clinic hours, and distance from floodwater.

An actuarial life could be prolonged, priced, transferred, or averaged. Tomorrow Mira would meet the beneficiaries who refused to remain an average.

## Chapter 26: Beneficiaries

Les Amandiers began where the tram stopped.

At 09:51 on Day Twenty-six, Mira left the last carriage with Noor and found a six-lane road, a petrol station, and twelve apartment blocks standing among young trees. The estate lay outside Marseille's dense northern neighborhoods, beyond a freight viaduct and a retail park whose signs were visible from homes no footpath reached directly. Its name promised almond trees. The landscaping offered maple saplings, three cypress rows, a willow beside a dry retention basin, and one old oak preserved from the field that had preceded construction.

The air was already balmy. Irrigation hoses darkened circles in the pale soil. Under a canopy between Blocks C and D, children bent over a plastic tub containing aquatic plants and two minnows. A social worker in a yellow helmet showed them how sediment settled after water stopped moving. The exercise belonged to an estival school program about flood ecology, not a campaign display arranged for visitors.

Mira had expected cameras at the gate. There were none. The residents' association had prohibited them.

Nadia Cherif met them beside the kiosk. She was forty-eight, brisk, and unimpressed by credentials. A mobility impairment made her gait uneven; she used a folding cane and rejected Noor's offer to carry her document wallet.

"You are here because journalists have discovered beneficiaries," she said. "Last month we were victims. Before that, success stories. We reside in both categories without moving."

"We are here to test what the Cadran arrangement did," Mira replied. "Not to classify residents."

"Everyone says that before they compile."

Nadia gave them the conditions again. No apartment without invitation. No child's medical history unless a parent raised it. No linking names to insurance tiles in public. No activists appearing at lunch. Residents could withdraw a statement until the association reviewed Mira's summary that evening. They could criticize Phare Habitat and still keep services funded by it. They could praise the estate without becoming proxies for Harborlight.

"Agreed," Mira said.

"You agree too quickly."

"Would you prefer altercation?"

"I prefer evidence that you heard me."

Mira repeated each condition in her own words. Nadia corrected "withdraw" to "withdraw without penalty" and added that translations must return to speakers before quotation. Only then did she lead them inside.

The estate contained four hundred eighty apartments. Blocks A through F had lifts, shaded balconies, cross-ventilation, and rooftop solar. The later blocks had smaller windows and cheaper finishes after construction costs rose. Ground floors sat above modeled flood level. Ramps met current access standards. A bus loop existed on the plan but received only a sparse private service. The public tram extension had been promised, delayed, and promised again.

"Ambient safety improved," Nadia said. "Ambient life did not automatically follow."

In the association office, a wall map showed where residents had come from. Colored pins clustered along the old port, Saint-Césaire's east catchment, and two low streets near the Huveaune. The pins did not denote legal title or medical status. Residents placed them voluntarily to arrange carpools and neighborhood meals.

Mira noticed the map's opacity. It showed origin but not cause. A flood survivor and a tenant displaced by sale could share one pin.

"Do not infer route from color," Nadia said.

"I wasn't."

"Your face was."

Noor smiled. "She has a very legible face when a variable is missing."

The morning assembly filled a multipurpose room overlooking the retention basin. Twenty-three residents attended. Others had declined because of work, fatigue, mistrust, childcare, or simple unbelief that another inquiry would change the bus timetable. Nadia stated those absences before introductions.

Mira explained the narrow finding from Cadran: a Harborlight-funded guarantee had reimbursed insurers for selected early withdrawals; later measures treated reduced insurance continuity as declining resilience; a related vehicle funded Les Amandiers. She did not call every resident coerced. She did not claim the guarantee had selected each household.

An elderly man named Farid Boulahrouz raised his hand. "You say related. Same money?"

"The capital commitment has the same source. The accounts are legally separate. We do not yet know how decisions interacted."

"Same people?"

"Some governance overlap is under review."

"Then speak like a human."

Nadia intervened. "She is speaking like a witness who does not want a lawyer to slay the sentence later. Let her finish."

Mira described what they hoped to learn: timing of offers, alternatives presented, repair and transport conditions, and benefits residents valued. Personal accounts would not be evidence of every household. Association records could establish patterns if residents controlled their use.

"And if the pattern is that we are happier?" asked Léa Morel, a young mother with a sleeping infant against her chest.

"Then that is the pattern we report."

"You look dejected by the possibility."

"I am trying not to look pleased or dejected by an answer before hearing it."

"That must be tiring."

It was.

They began with the buildings. Residents listed what worked. Lifts accommodated wheelchairs and pushchairs. Bathrooms had level showers. Summer cooling was better than in their former flats. Mold and recurrent ground-floor damp had subsided. Children could play away from traffic. The primary school had a disability resource unit and an excellent speech therapist. A community nurse visited twice weekly. The retention basin had held during a violent downpour in spring.

The failures were equally concrete. Block H's lift broke frequently and spare parts took weeks. Balcony drains clogged with construction grit. Cheap window seals admitted mistral dust. A row of ground-floor storage rooms smelled of damp despite the elevated apartments. The nearest secondary school required two buses. Port workers on early shifts paid for informal rides. A grocery kiosk sold basics at a hefty markup because the promised market hall remained vacant.

Noor asked whether residents had modified the estate. The room became livelier.

They had built shade frames from salvaged timber, planted mint and perennials, converted a sterile lawn into vegetable plots, and persuaded the school to establish an arboretum strip. A retired arboriculture worker had taught children to prune without damaging a young tree's bole. Teenagers painted a rhythmic band of fish and reeds along the basin wall, retouching the original developer's blue waves until the mural belonged to them.

"Phare's brochure calls that co-designed ambience," Nadia said.

"We stole their paint after they refused permission," a teenager called Samiha said.

"Borrowed," her father corrected.

"The tins were dormant in a locked shed. We promoted them."

Laughter did not erase the dispute. It made the estate inhabited rather than emblematic.

At eleven the group divided. Mira went with Nadia and social worker Élodie Martin to inspect accessibility and transport records. Noor joined residents documenting repairs. The association retained every original work order. Mira received only aggregate dates and categories.

Block H's lift stood open while a technician adjusted its door sensor. A wheelchair user waited in the lobby, unable to reach his fourth-floor apartment. He had been there forty minutes. The housing manager offered a vacant guest room on the ground floor, but his medication and equipment remained upstairs.

"How often?" Mira asked.

Nadia showed the association count: fourteen outages in six months, nine longer than two hours. The official service portal counted five because repeated reports during one outage were merged and outages reset after a brief operation.

The familiar mechanism appeared in miniature. A system's definition made recurring deprivation look like one event.

"Does Harborlight receive lift reliability?"

Élodie did not know. Phare reported accessible units delivered, not hours of actual access. Mira wrote a question rather than an inference.

They climbed the stairs. On the second landing, Mira's phone showed a message from Priya: both Saint-Césaire heatstroke patients discharged; no romantic addendum. Mira put the phone away.

Nadia's apartment occupied the third floor of Block D. She invited them in after checking that her adult daughter had left for work. The rooms were bright, tidy, and modest. A fern stood beside the balcony door. Family photographs covered one wall. On the kitchen sill, an old ceramic gourd held wooden spoons.

"My former building had four steps before the lift," Nadia said. "Four steps may as well be a cliff on a bad day. Here I can leave alone. That is not propaganda."

Her previous landlord had planned to refurbish after repeated flood damage. Then the building's insurer withdrew, the bank refused new credit, and the landlord accepted a Phare affiliate's offer. Tenants received relocation options: Les Amandiers, a smaller estate farther inland, or a cash payment insufficient for a comparable accessible apartment in Marseille.

"Did anyone say you had to move?" Mira asked.

"The notice said the lease would end after sale. That is a form of grammar, not free choice."

"Were you offered legal recourse?"

"A hotline funded by the buyer. Very lenient about explaining why resistance was naive."

Nadia had chosen Les Amandiers because the apartment suited her body. She did not regret the choice. She regretted that the market had been altered before the choice arrived.

"Do not condemn my home to prove the road here was crooked," she said.

Mira repeated the sentence and asked permission to include it. Nadia said she would decide after reading the full context.

At noon they met the Rahmani family in Block B. Karim repaired refrigeration systems. His wife, Inès, worked part-time at a school cafeteria and cared for their nine-year-old son Adam, who used a power wheelchair and noninvasive ventilation at night because of a congenital neuromuscular condition. Their former ground-floor flat had flooded twice. During the second flood, water rose through the courtyard faster than municipal warnings predicted.

Inès served lentil soup and filets of grilled fish. She had invited them to lunch because interviews conducted in association rooms made people sound like delegates.

"Harborlight saved Adam," Karim said before anyone asked.

Mira set down her spoon.

During the flood, a Harborlight alert had reached Inès's phone twenty-three minutes before the municipal siren. The platform knew Adam's household required accessible transport because the family had consented to a disability-response registry. It dispatched a vehicle with a ramp while ordinary emergency lines were overwhelmed. The driver arrived as water entered the flat. Adam's ventilator battery, helmet, medicines, and chair traveled with him. The family spent two nights in a school gym, then three weeks in temporary housing.

"Without that van?" Mira asked.

"Karim could carry Adam," Inès said, "but not chair and machine. Water was at his thigh. Maybe neighbors help. Maybe battery gets wet. Maybe he lives. I do not need the counterfactual to be perfect. The warning gave us time."

They later accepted a buyout and moved to Les Amandiers. Their old street had flooded again. Adam's new school was accessible and his respiratory admissions had declined after they left the damp flat. These outcomes were not mawkish decorations on Vale's argument. They were a child's life.

"Was the buyout voluntary?" Mira asked.

Karim looked at Inès.

"We wanted to move after the flood," he said. "The offer was good enough to clear our debt. Better than auction."

"Did insurance withdrawal affect the price?"

"Our policy renewed with a surcharge, not cancellation. The bank said another flood would make the flat unsellable. Phare offered before that."

Their tile matched the same Marseille group, but their policy history differed. Selective withdrawal had not touched every property. Flood danger was real and uneven. The estate was not only a receptacle for financial coercion.

Adam entered from his bedroom, steering with practiced briskness. He had been playing an online game and regarded visitors as an interruption. A sticker of an ichthyosaur decorated his chair.

"Maman says you study floods," he said to Mira.

"I study health systems. Today I am asking about moving house."

"The old house had silverfish. Those are not fish."

"Correct."

"And there was a spider in my mask bag."

Inès said, "One arachnid becomes family history."

Adam showed Noor the adapted desk Karim had built. A hinged arm held a tablet at eye level. The commercial mount had been too weak, so Karim used a refrigeration bracket and a bicycle clamp. The result lacked modish flair and worked.

Mira asked Adam what he disliked about the estate.

"The bus. The lift. Adults saying the trees are a forest. They are sticks."

"What do you like?"

"School. My room. When the basin has frogs."

"Any frog in particular?"

"They are amphibians, not beneficiaries."

Karim looked embarrassed. Mira did not laugh until Adam did.

After lunch Inès produced the evacuation message and consent form from her own files. Mira did not copy the health registry entry. With permission, she recorded only alert time, vehicle dispatch, arrival, flood depth from municipal gauges, and shelter handoff. Harborlight's useful action was independently traceable without publishing Adam's diagnosis.

At 14:00 the association convened a transport walk. The estate's private bus ran every forty minutes in daytime and stopped at twenty-one hundred. A public route passed the retail park but required crossing the six-lane road at an underpass whose lift was out of service. The alternative was a steep, dappled path beside the viaduct.

Residents took Mira through it. Heat accumulated in the concrete trench. Gum and street-cleaning residue streaked the floor. One light flickered. The broken lift bore a municipal repair notice six weeks old.

An older resident, Solange Picard, had missed two cardiology appointments because she could not climb the ramp on breathless days. A migrant care worker named Blessing paid twenty euros a week for rides after late shifts. Teenagers crossed the road at surface level despite the traffic. The estate had forestalled flood exposure and created transport exposure.

"Do not equate them," Élodie said. "One can kill in an hour. The other wears people down."

Mira agreed. Contradictory harms did not require parity to coexist.

At the retail park, a fishmonger recognized Karim and complained that Les Amandiers residents arrived only on Saturdays. He wanted a market at the estate but said Phare's commercial rents were preposterous. The vacant market hall had been designed for six vendors; no small trader could bear the deposit and fit-out.

Noor asked whether a cooperative could take it. The fishmonger shrugged. "With subsidy. Or with usury. Those are the entrees."

The association had proposed a cooperative. Phare offered a two-year rent reduction but required a corporate guarantee. Residents lacked one. Cadran's social-resilience report nevertheless counted the hall as local food access because construction was complete.

Mira photographed the exterior only after Nadia approved. The glass doors reflected a pharmacy sign across the road and displayed nothing behind them but dust.

Back at the estate, children had released the minnows into a school pond. A teacher corrected one boy who wanted to put them in the retention basin, explaining that stocked fish could befoul a temporary aquatic habitat and consume amphibian eggs. The explanation changed an action; it was not ornament.

Noor sat with the repair group beneath the canopy. They had classified 318 work orders by building, date, urgency, recurrence, and closure reason. She had not brought the acoustic evidence. Her skill here was attention to repeated wording. Requests closed as resident unavailable often followed appointments offered during residents' work shifts. Requests labeled cosmetic included window leaks and mold retouching.

"The portal makes us look pesky," said Hakima Ouali, who coordinated Block F. "One woman sends six requests for one leak, and they call frenzy. The water does not become one because their computer is tired."

Mira asked whether the association would authorize a comparison between actual recurrence and portal closure. Nadia said yes if apartment identifiers were replaced locally and residents reviewed categories.

"This is not your main case," Nadia warned.

"No. It tests whether delivered housing remains adequate."

"And if it is mostly adequate?"

"Then repairs improve it."

Nadia's expression softened by an insignificant amount.

The school principal arrived with enrollment figures at 15:12. Madame Vaillant had resisted the estate's request because educational records were not housing evidence by default. She came only after parents specified the questions: travel, transfers, disability support, language services, and midyear departures. No marks, diagnoses, disciplinary files, or citizenship data entered the review.

The primary school had opened with two hundred pupils and now enrolled three hundred eleven. Its resource unit served children who previously traveled across Marseille for therapy. Teachers reported improved attendance among those children. The cafeteria offered breakfast after parents explained that early private buses made some pupils leave home before appetite or shops were awake.

The benefits sat beside a different curve. Fifty-eight secondary pupils commuted out of the estate. Their average journey was sixty-seven minutes each way. After-school participation fell sharply because the final connecting bus left before most activities ended. Nine pupils had transferred to nearer schools that lacked programs or friendships they valued. Three later returned despite the commute.

"Cultural isolation is too grand a phrase for a missed cornet lesson," Vaillant said. "But when the lesson, football practice, grandmother, mosque, church, and old friends all become separate expeditions, the aggregate is not trivial."

Mira asked whether the school could distinguish relocation effects from adolescence, family income, and ordinary school preference.

"Not cleanly. We can compare travel before and after for pupils whose families consent. We can count withdrawal from activities. We cannot theorize their souls."

Samiha, the teenager who had painted the basin, joined them with two friends. All three attended schools in Marseille. One was studying botany and kept an herbarium for class; another wanted an apprenticeship at the port; Samiha played bass in a youth ensemble.

"The estate brochure photographed us planting a seedling," Samiha said. "It called us the fledgling generation of climate adaptation."

"Did you consent?" Noor asked.

"My mother signed something for the school garden. Not for a billboard. They took it down after Nadia made bedlam."

Nadia said, "I made a complaint."

"With bedlam in its heart."

Samiha did not hate Les Amandiers. She liked the apartment, mural, and safety of the courtyard. She hated being described as if her family's life had begun at relocation. Their old neighborhood's bakery, cousins, music teacher, and Friday dinners had not been unhealthy vestiges to outgrow.

"They transplant a tree and discuss root shock," she said. "They transplant people and count keys."

The metaphor risked deifying botany, but its source had earned it. Mira asked what would reduce the shock.

"A real tram. Cheap rooms in the market hall. Let clubs use the school after hours. Stop closing the underpass lift. And don't call every thing we make community activation. Sometimes we revel because it is Friday."

Her friend Yacine wanted the vacant hall divided into workshops. Phare had rejected the proposal because welding and wood dust were incompatible with its retail designation. Yet young residents traveled to industrial training through the same underpass. A flexible zoning cession could keep work local without creating pollution beside homes. Nadia had submitted one and received no response.

Élodie then showed the association its social-service register. It held no case narratives. Residents themselves had selected categories and counted contacts: benefits advice, school transfer, transport, repair advocacy, employment, disability access, and crisis support. Demand peaked during the first three months after each incoming cohort, then subsided except for transport and repair, which remained unabated.

Phare's funding formula assumed social-work need would diminish by half after twelve months. It did for move-in administration. It did not for the problems produced by distance. Élodie covered the gap through a municipal grant and unpaid overtime.

"The model treats relocation as an entree," she said. "You pass through the door and the service is complete."

"What would a better measure use?" Mira asked.

"Resident-defined stability. Can you reach work, school, care, family? Can you repair the home? Can you refuse a service without risking the tenancy? Do not ask whether we have allayed complaints. Ask whether people can act."

Mira wrote the questions. They were less sophisticated than Harborlight's composite score and more difficult to manipulate without someone noticing.

The association lawyer called during the review. Cadran had requested that residents authorize use of Les Amandiers as evidence of compensatory benefit in the next day's proceeding. The proposed declaration praised accessible housing, flood safety, and social support. It omitted transport, constrained offers, and insurance timing.

Nadia read the request aloud. "They want our approbation wholesale."

"We can draft our own declaration," said Farid.

"Or no declaration," Blessing said. "We do not owe the court a performance because Cadran discovered us."

Mira stayed silent until Nadia asked whether refusing would weaken the guarantee challenge.

"It might allow Cadran to say critics ignored benefits," Mira said. "That is not a reason you must speak. If you do, the court should receive the whole resident account, not my paraphrase or Cadran's."

"Would you use it if it complicates your application?"

"Yes. The complication is the fact."

The association postponed its answer until evening review. It would not be hurried by either side's deadline.

At 16:20 a summer storm formed over the hills. Wind bent the saplings and sent a covey of pigeons from the roof. Children ran under the canopy. Rain arrived in large warm drops, then a sudden buffet. Water coursed along designed channels toward the retention basin.

Residents watched because drainage had failed in Block J during the spring storm. Today the main channels worked. One drain near the kiosk clogged with bark and litter. Karim and the housing caretaker cleared it with gloved hands before water reached the doorway. The basin filled, muddy and swift, then held.

Harborlight issued a local surface-water alert eight minutes before the heaviest rain. It recommended avoiding the underpass, correctly. The estate app displayed accessible shelter rooms in Blocks A and C. The Block C lift was operating. The advice was useful.

Nadia held up her phone. "Put that in your report too."

"I will."

"Do not hide it in a footnote after four pages of coercion."

"I won't."

The storm subsided within half an hour. Heat rose from the wet pavement. Children waded at the basin edge until the teacher called them back from the steep bank. No building flooded.

At 17:00 the association reviewed Mira's provisional account aloud. She separated five propositions.

Les Amandiers reduced flood, damp, and access risks for many residents and included services people valued. Harborlight warnings and registry-based transport had materially assisted the Rahmani evacuation. Some households chose relocation after direct experience of danger and received adequate compensation. Other households faced constrained choices after insurance withdrawal, sale, or lease termination in markets altered by the same financial structure. The estate's distance, weak transport, repair failures, and absent commerce imposed avoidable costs not captured by units-delivered metrics.
