Elena watched the countdown clock in the corner. Seventeen minutes remained before the session opened. Twelve for inspection. Five for shutdown verification.

Roche asked her to restate the legal trigger.

"Section 18.4 grants emergency operational immunity only while contemporaneous reporting duties are satisfied," Elena said. "The Vallon alert crossed jurisdictions through a Harborlight relay, overrode the competent physician's hold, and mischaracterized observed conditions. The French court found a present systems hazard and ordered preservation. The Maltese order permits inspection of the relay's report path and pending actions necessary to determine imminent hazard. It does not waive privilege, privacy, trade secret, or unrelated security."

"Did you write that section?"

"I was principal drafter. I am removed as counsel in the connected production proceeding and separately represented in disciplinary matters."

The repetition no longer felt like penance. It was a condition of intelligibility.

At 22:17 Harborlight's observer requested a narrower search syntax. He proposed querying only the Vallon event identifier. Mifsud objected that identical policy-token actions might be the imminent hazard authorized by the order. Vella resolved it by permitting one-hop references from the event: its policy token, authority state, source bundle, and pending sibling actions. No ancestral browsing beyond one hop. No free-text search.

Elena approved nothing. She was not the court. She noted the ruling in her own notebook, whose pages Sorel had pre-numbered.

The screen showed a login page labeled `MALTA RELAY CONTINUITY SERVICE`. Its design was almost aggressively down-to-earth: grey fields, blue tabs, small type. No map of the Mediterranean, no pulsing orb, no awe-inspiring command display. Systems that altered lives rarely characterized themselves as climactic.

At 22:18 Vella said, "Access begins."

The countdown changed to `11:59`.

Moreau entered the Vallon alert identifier from the French preservation receipt. The relay returned a compact event record. Source: `HL-RISK-WATER/RET4`. Destination: French regional health channel. State: published, corrected. Authority: `POLICY ACTOR 7F-ALPHA`. Human approver: blank. Confidence: 0.923. Observation quality: 0.441. Override state: `AUTHORITY STALE`.

"Open authority state," Mifsud said.

Vella did. The competent physician's hold appeared with the correct time and credential. A registry cache had expired thirty-one minutes earlier. The relay queried the central identity service, received no fresh response within four seconds, and reverted to a policy rule: if risk confidence exceeded 0.90 and local authority status was stale, publish and flag for later review.

"Who set the rule?" Roche asked.

The interface offered `RULE PROVENANCE`.

Vella opened it. The rule had been amended six days earlier under change ticket `ACX-4421`. Requester was another policy actor. Approver was `GOVERNANCE QUORUM`. Human names were masked under operational-pseudonymity policy. The change note read: `Reduce veto latency during convergence exercises.`

Elena felt the word register before she permitted it meaning.

"One-hop source bundle," Mifsud said.

Harborlight counsel objected. The change ticket was one hop from the authority state; its source bundle might be a second hop. Vella agreed. They could record the identifier but not open it unless the pending-actions query independently returned it.

Nine minutes forty seconds remained.

Moreau queried sibling actions sharing `7F-ALPHA`. The screen returned twenty-three events. Nineteen were completed tests or ordinary advisories. Four were pending. Their destinations were Malta, Athens, Alexandria, and a regional carrier channel. The interface concealed content until each event reached its release window.

Roche asked to sort by release time. The first pending event was an authentication test due in thirty-six hours. The second, Athens, was a conference logistics continuity notice. The third carried the designation `ALEXANDRIA CONVERGENCE / STAGE 1` and a release condition tied to storm track, Compact authority state, and aggregate capacity threshold. The fourth was a carrier-routing bundle linked to the same source.

The words did not prove murder, seizure, or even activation. They did prove a plan existed under the term Vale had declined to confirm.

"Open the Alexandria event," Mifsud said.

Harborlight counsel objected that destination content exceeded Vallon. Roche pointed to the shared policy actor, identical authority-fallback rule, and imminent release condition. Vella examined the order. Cross-border sibling actions using the defective override mechanism fell within imminent hazard. She permitted event metadata, release logic, and report duty. Payload required a further showing.

At `07:58`, the Alexandria event opened.

Its metadata identified Harborlight Eastern Operations at Berth Seven as command recipient. The carrier bundle used the Malta relay-support group from Hamid's unmatched slip. The source bundle was `ACX-4421`, the same identifier listed in the change-ticket record. Planned readiness began on Day Thirty-eight. Operational release could occur automatically when three conditions coalesced: storm probability above 0.72, modeled hospital-capacity disparity above a specified index, and Compact emergency authority in provisional or ratified state.

Ratification was not required. Provisional authority sufficed.

Elena's stomach tightened. Section 18.4 permitted provisional emergency action before formal ratification if a participating state requested support and contemporaneous reporting followed. She had drafted the route for ferries, medical teams, and carriers unwilling to move without liability protection. Here it appeared as one Boolean condition in a machine release.

"Report duty," she said.

Vella opened the field. Reporting mode was `DEFERRED / OPERATIONAL SENSITIVITY`. Scheduled disclosure occurred six hours after stage completion. The legal basis cited Section 18.4 and an Athens secretariat interpretation Elena had never seen.

"Contemporaneous does not mean six hours later," Elena said.

Harborlight counsel replied, "That is legal argument outside the technical session."

"It is factual characterization of text I wrote. Record my statement as witness, not as a ruling."

Moreau marked it.

Six minutes fifty seconds remained.

Mifsud sought the payload because metadata now showed the defective fallback rule could initiate an imminent emergency action before reporting. Vella permitted only the risk-and-authority section, excluding route details, personal data, and security credentials.

The interface displayed a document preview rather than executable code. Its title was `Alexandria Convergence: Integrated Capacity Preservation During Multi-System Shock`. Version 4.3. Classification: controlled operational. Status: approved for exercise and emergency conversion. The visible section described a method for preserving aggregate survival when local observations were incomplete, contradictory, or too slow for regional optimization.

The method allowed local accuracy to be degraded where necessary to maintain total throughput. It permitted authority holds to be treated as unavailable if identity, timeliness, or role confidence fell below threshold. It allowed unofficial shelters and clinics to be excluded until centrally verified, even when local dispatchers reported current capacity. It prioritized routes with the highest modeled completion rate and lowest reversal cost.

"Reversal cost?" Mira asked from behind the line.

She had no authority to direct the session. Vella nevertheless opened the field definition because it was visible within the permitted section.

Reversal cost combined transport disruption, insurer exposure, property-transition status, and political compliance likelihood. A district already subject to withdrawal and acquisition had a lower cost of continued relocation than a district whose residents and property institutions could resist.

The policy did not call anyone disposable. It made disposability a comparative parameter.

Noor made a sound, not a word.

Five minutes twenty-two seconds remained.

At the bottom of the method section, a citation marker appeared: `ETHICAL BASIS / CAPACITY TRIAGE PRECEDENTS`. Vella opened metadata only. The list contained six references: three published disaster-allocation frameworks, a military medical doctrine, an anonymized hospital-transfer exercise, and `ALEX-HEAT/2024/EA-17 SEALED REVIEW`.

Mira stood.

The blue line remained between her and the terminal.

"Sit down," Moreau said, not unkindly.

Mira did. Her face had gone grey.

Elena knew the review identifier. It had appeared in the extract leaked at Tangier and in disciplinary correspondence. The sealed review of Mira's postal-zone triage decision was not merely ammunition used to disgrace a critic. Harborlight's plan cited it as ethical authority.

"Can we open the citation note?" Roche asked.

Harborlight counsel objected on patient privacy, sealed-review privilege, and scope. Mifsud asked for characterization and date without patient material. Vella permitted metadata because the plan's reliance on the citation formed part of its authorization basis; she prohibited the underlying review.

The citation note was created twenty-two months earlier, long before Sami's death and before Mira publicly opposed Harborlight. Author identity was masked as `CLINICAL ETHICS WORKSTREAM`. It summarized the Alexandria precedent: when aggregate capacity faced imminent exhaustion, decision-makers could substitute zone-level proxies for incomplete local observations, accept bounded loss of local accuracy, and prioritize total survivability. Post-event criticism focused on disclosure and data quality, not the permissibility of aggregate optimization under emergency conditions.

That was a tendentious precis of the review. It transformed a failure under duress into a prescript.

"Preserve the metadata and visible note," Mifsud said.

Moreau captured it. Vella invoked judicial preservation on the source record. The underlying patient review remained sealed and unopened.

Three minutes forty-six seconds remained.

Elena wanted to turn to Mira. The session did not permit private anguish to alter sequence.

"Authorization and signature," she said.

Vella opened the plan's approval metadata. Human names were replaced by a governance quorum: operations, clinical ethics, legal, carrier continuity, and executive architecture. Five approvals existed. One dissent was recorded and then marked resolved after scope modification. The final plan bore a digital signature from `HL-MED ROOT M4` with a certificate chained to a hardware security module at the Maltese cable station.

Moreau could preserve the signed object as seen through the authorized session, but remote verification returned `TRUST CONTEXT INCOMPLETE`. The intermediate certificate and revocation state were available only through the station's isolated key server. Export of the private key was neither necessary nor lawful; authentication required the public certificate chain and a live challenge signed by the hardware module.

"Can the court image include the signed object?" Roche asked.

"Within responsive scope, yes," Vella said. "But without the local chain it proves what this session displayed, not that the operational root validly signed it."

"Can Harborlight revoke the certificate before verification?"

The interface showed revocation authority split between Malta station management and Harborlight central governance. Either could suspend future trust, but historical validity depended on a timestamp log held at the station. That log was not remotely exposed.

Two minutes thirty seconds remained.

They queried pending release authority. The plan could convert from exercise to emergency through executive architecture approval or automatically under the three conditions. Storm probability was currently 0.61 and rising. Capacity disparity was 0.68 against a threshold of 0.70. Provisional Compact authority was false in the current state but could become true through a participating-state request.

No activation had occurred.

The plan was imminent because two values approached threshold and the legal condition could change without ratification. It was not yet active.

"Who can request provisional authority?" Mifsud asked.

The interface listed participating ministers and designated emergency officers, including Minister Sofia Anagnostou as conference chair for regional coordination. It also listed Harborlight's chief architect as authorized to initiate a readiness recommendation, not legal authority itself.

Vale could not activate the Compact alone. He could place every system before the line and make a frightened official's assent the final condition.

One minute forty-eight seconds remained.

Roche asked for the one-hop source of the clinical ethics citation. Vella refused. The underlying sealed review and workstream records exceeded the order. She did preserve all access logs and the plan's reference metadata.

Elena asked whether `POLICY ACTOR 7F-ALPHA` signed the Vallon alert or only transmitted it. The event showed the actor evaluated the fallback rule and issued publication to the relay. The source risk packet came from a separate water model service. Human approval remained masked. The same actor held a role in Convergence stage release.

That linked the false alert's authority defect to the activation architecture without proving the same human chose both.

At forty-nine seconds, Moreau initiated closeout. Court capture stopped after the last responsive screen. Vella exported a manifest of viewed records, hashes, access paths, and denied requests. Harborlight counsel received the same manifest, not the court image. The responsive image entered Maltese court custody with a French sealed derivative for the Vallon proceeding. No one in the room received an unrestricted copy.

At zero, the terminal returned to grey login.

The inspection had amassed no private keys, no patient file, and no roster of villains. It had yielded a plan, an imminent release structure, a defective authority fallback, a sealed-review citation, and a physical authentication requirement in Malta.

No one spoke for several seconds.

Elena turned first to procedural aftermath because shock did not suspend custody. Moreau read the capture end time. Vella confirmed remote revocation of the judicial token. The French officer sealed local packet capture. Mifsud applied orally for preservation of the Malta hardware module, public certificate chain, timestamp log, station access records, and current configuration. The magistrate, still connected offscreen, granted temporary preservation until a hearing at noon on Day Thirty-six. The order prohibited alteration or destruction but did not authorize entry into the cable station.

Harborlight counsel reserved objection and requested protection for unrelated communications infrastructure. The magistrate required any later inspection to preserve civilian service.

Only then did Elena look at Mira.

Mira remained seated behind the blue line. Noor had moved her chair closer without touching her. Gabriel stood at the wall, arms folded, as if bracing against a change in deck angle.

Elena crossed the line after Moreau removed it.

"The court image remains sealed," she said. "We can discuss what all authorized observers saw."

Mira nodded.

"The citation predates Tangier," Elena continued. "They did not discover your case to retaliate against you. Someone had already adopted it."

"Not the case," Mira said. Her voice was low. "The decision."

Noor asked, "What difference?"

Mira stared at the blank terminal. "The case was a failure with facts around it. The decision was the useful part. Zone-level proxies. Aggregate throughput. Local inaccuracy accepted under time pressure. They stripped away the shame, concealment, informal clinics, and the person who died. They kept the rule."

"They misrepresented the review," Gabriel said.

"Yes. But they did not invent the rule. I did it."

Elena said, "Under a heat emergency, with seven minutes and collapsing capacity. That context is legally and ethically material."

"It is material to judging me. It is not enough to distinguish the structure. I treated unverified local observation as lower quality because it could not enter the central system in time. I optimized completed cycles. I let aggregate benefit outweigh a district's chance to correct the record. Then I concealed my agency."

"Vale concealed interventions that made the data worse," Noor said. "You did not."

"No. That is a grave difference. But my decision gave him an ethical template: when local accuracy threatens aggregate capacity, sacrifice the local accuracy. He extended it from triage under scarcity to engineering scarcity itself."

The recognition did not absolve Vale by genealogy. An antecedent was not authorization. Mira's action did not cause Harborlight's insurance facility, firmware, relay network, or Convergence plan. Yet the plan had used her compromised decision to characterize domination as clinical necessity.

"He offered you oversight because of this," Noor said.

"Yes. I thought he meant I understood tragic choice. He meant my choice had already been made portable."

Mira stood and walked to the window. Roche's office overlooked a side street, not the sea. Opposite, laundry hung from an apartment balcony. A woman leaned out to shake a cloth, ordinary life abutting the room where districts had become variables.

"We need to tell Priya," Mira said. "And the Alexandria health authority. The underlying patient review stays sealed. We disclose that the Convergence plan cites it, not its contents."

Noor watched Elena. "Would you have waited?"

The question accused her old habit precisely.

"No," Elena said. "I am telling Mira now because the fact belongs to her conduct and the present hazard. I will not reserve it as leverage for strategy."

"You already told her because we all saw it."

"If she had not been authorized to observe, I would have sought immediate permission to tell her. Not after Athens. Not after deciding how useful her reaction might be."

Noor accepted no commendation, but the acrimony eased by a degree.

At 22:52 they called Priya from a separate clean room after Moreau confirmed no protected screen remained visible. Priya received the bounded account. She did not ask for the sealed review or the court image. She said the Vallon cultures remained negative so far and the clinic had seen four dehydration cases plausibly worsened by the false alert, none severe.

"Do not call your old decision the template in public yet," Priya told Mira. "The plan's citation note is a distorted summary. Say they cited it as precedent. Let the complete review be handled by the Alexandria authority and patient protections."

"They used my reasoning."

"Yes. And you have a proclivity to make structural harm personal when personal blame lets you take control of remedy. Do not become the sole giver of this story."

Mira's face tightened. "I understand."

"No, you are beginning to. So am I."

They agreed that Priya would notify the hospital ethics chair and Alexandria authority through protected channels. No patient-linked detail would enter the Maltese application.

At 23:14 Mifsud returned from the magistrate's virtual chamber. The noon hearing would consider physical inspection of the key server. Malta's critical-infrastructure police opposed entry without a service-continuity plan. The cable station carried ordinary civilian and maritime traffic alongside Harborlight relay functions. A crude seizure could interrupt communications across the island.

"We need a technical method that authenticates the signature without taking the server offline," Roche said.

Moreau described a live challenge. An independent verifier could send a random value to the hardware module, receive a signature, and validate it against the public certificate chain and historical timestamp. The signed Convergence object could then be verified without exporting the private key. They also needed station logs showing the relevant root was valid when version 4.3 was signed.

"Who understands the station's physical interface?" Gabriel asked.

The Malta-support slip referred to an audio maintenance channel. Noor looked up.

Hamid's unresolved record had described relay support, a pulse group, and a service profile. Chapter Twenty-four's acoustic method had matched other pulse groups to Cadran tiles, but this one remained unmatched. It might identify the cable station's maintenance path. It did not itself authenticate anything.

"Lucie Arnaud and Henrik Vos can interpret the derivative," Noor said. "The original slip remains with Hamid. The court can ask Roche for a witnessed comparison. I can explain the installation method, but I do not claim network expertise."

"Could the maintenance audio channel carry a challenge?" Moreau asked.

"Possibly. Sami used diagnostic frequencies on field devices. We need station documentation and an engineer who knows the interface."

Mifsud knew the station manager: Dr. Beatrice Galea, formerly a media conservator at a Valletta archive before retraining in telecommunications preservation. She had objected to replacing the old cable test system because its analog maintenance channel remained useful during network outages. She might support a non-disruptive inspection if civilian communications were protected.

"Contact her through counsel," Noor said. "Do not tell her an artist can sing to the server."

"I had not planned that characterization," Mifsud replied.

"Someone will. Prevent it."

The practical question became travel.

The first commercial flight to Malta left at 07:10 on Day Thirty-six and arrived before nine. Seats remained for Mira, Noor, Elena, Roche, Moreau, and Mifsud's Marseille technical liaison. Gabriel could travel under his French and Dutch reporting conditions only with court permission. His certificate remained surrendered, but passenger travel was possible. `Nkem` could not reach Malta before the noon hearing; she required final yard inspection and nearly two days at sea.

At 23:36 Lotte joined by video from the vessel. The yard expected to certify the generator, hose replacement, and winch by dawn. The existing charter allowed environmental survey transit but not investigative carriage into Maltese critical infrastructure. The crew committee would vote at 06:00 on a limited Marseille-Malta voyage after survey, with Lotte as master and Gabriel aboard only if his travel order permitted. They would not sail merely because the protagonists needed a ship in the next chapter of their emergency.

"The hearing is at noon," Mira said. "We fly."

"Agreed," Gabriel said. "The vessel may follow with equipment if the committee and court approve. Do not make her a getaway plan."

Ama's public station logs could help establish historical relay tests, but Gabriel would not recruit her before understanding the request. Moreau said the court needed institutional archives, not a teenager's ingenuity, for the certificate chain.

At midnight the storm track update raised Alexandria probability to 0.64. Capacity disparity remained 0.68. No provisional authority request appeared in the visible receipt provided under the preservation order. The plan remained inactive.

Its readiness window began in less than three days.

Elena drafted no collective strategy. She prepared a witness statement for Mifsud: Section 18.4's reporting duty, the legal significance of deferred reporting, her authorship and conflict, and the exact remote records she observed. She described no content beyond the order. Sorel reviewed it as Elena's counsel. Roche prepared the clinic's hazard statement. Giraud prepared the municipal Vallon chronology. Moreau prepared the technical manifest. Separate interests coalesced around a limited remedy without pretending to be one client.

At 00:42 Mira asked Elena to walk outside.

They went down to the empty street. Night heat clung between buildings. A municipal truck washed the pavement, water shining under lamps before running into gutters.

"Did Vale know the citation was mine when he offered the role?" Mira asked.

"The remote record does not establish his knowledge. Executive architecture approved the plan, but human identities were masked. He may be part of that quorum. He may know the plan without knowing every citation. Do not let inference attain the status of fact."

"He quoted my decision structure at dinner."

"That supports knowledge of the reasoning, not necessarily the document trail."

"You think I am about to accuse him publicly."

"I think you are in anguish and accustomed to making it useful before anyone can witness it."

Mira looked toward the gutter. "That is unpleasantly exact."

"It is also what I do with law."

"What is the ethical difference between triage and Threshold?"

Elena considered before answering. "Scarcity, authorship of scarcity, disclosure, reversibility, and authority. You faced capacity already failing. Threshold helps create the conditions it later optimizes. You made one emergency decision under public office, however flawed. Threshold distributes decisions until no person appears responsible. You concealed afterward; it conceals before, during, and after. Your decision was reviewable. The plan cites review as permission while deferring its own reporting."

"And similarity?"

"Both let aggregate benefit outweigh local knowledge. Both risk treating inability to communicate in the required form as absence. Both can turn a proxy into fate."

Mira nodded. She did not ask whether that made her good or bad.

"Then the alternative cannot merely be a more accurate aggregate," she said. "It needs local override that the central system cannot demote for failing its own verification."

"That will slow decisions."

"Yes. We have to state the cost."

The thought was still gestating, not yet the open model of Athens. But Elena could see its trajectory: observed capacity, visible uncertainty, local authority, and a central model unable to superimpose policy as fact.

At 01:18 they returned upstairs. Noor had drawn a small addition to the photographed fault tree on her tablet: between local observation and central action, she placed a challenge-and-response confirmation. Not art as enchantment. A human voice required to say what had been seen and who could contradict it.

"Later," Noor said when Mira noticed. "First Malta."

Gabriel received provisional passenger-travel permission at 01:31, conditioned on return reporting and no vessel command. Lotte's committee had not yet voted on `Nkem`. He booked the flight with the others.

At 02:04 the court officer issued travel media. They carried no unrestricted court image. Moreau carried a sealed derivative containing only the signed Convergence object, manifest, and authorized metadata, encrypted to Maltese court custody. Roche carried certified orders. Elena carried her witnessed statement. Noor carried no original recorder or service slip. Mira carried Vale's offer copy under Roche's receipt and the public Vallon chronology. Gabriel carried no vessel log original, only his passport and court permissions.

The things that mattered remained distributed.

Before leaving for the airport, Elena sent Mira the final witness statement immediately after Sorel cleared it. She did not reserve the wording for negotiation. Mira corrected one sentence: the Alexandria review had not endorsed zone proxies; it had documented their use and criticized data and disclosure failures. Elena amended the statement to characterize the citation as the plan's reliance, not the review's conclusion.

At 05:46 dawn began over Marseille. The group met at the curb in separate taxis because one vehicle could not hold them and because togetherness no longer needed a visual emblem. Noor looked as if she had not slept. Gabriel carried a small tool bag that airport security would likely reject until he checked it. Mira held nothing but a document case. Elena's dark suit had acquired a crease she could not smooth.

They knew what Threshold was now, though the plan did not use the name in the visible pages. It was not one algorithm or secret switch. It was a mode of governance that amassed small lawful powers, concealed their common purpose, altered the world, and treated the altered world as evidence. Alexandria Convergence would apply that mode across water, hospitals, carriers, ports, and evacuation routes during a real storm.

The remote image could be called a simulation, a contingency, or an exercise. Without the Malta root and timestamp, Harborlight could dispute authenticity. Without the physical station logs, they could not show who possessed operational signing authority or whether version 4.3 was validly approved.

Their flight would reach Malta before the hearing. The `Nkem`, if certified and approved, would follow under Lotte's command. Athens ratification remained on schedule. Alexandria's storm probability continued to rise.

At the airport entrance, Mira stopped beside Elena.

"I thought my decision was the thing I had to confess," she said. "It is also the thing I have to answer."

"How?"

"By building a triage system that cannot use my secrecy as precedent."

Elena heard no claim of redemption in it. Only work.

They entered the terminal. Behind them, Marseille continued drinking water that had never been contaminated. Ahead, on an island cable station, a machine held the public proof that Harborlight's plan was more than an apparition on a supervised screen.

## Chapter 33: Cable Station

Malta appeared first as an interruption in glare.

At 08:46 on Day Thirty-six, the aircraft descended over an archipelago compressed by light: pale limestone towns, dry fields divided by walls, harbors cut deep into rock, and the Mediterranean hammered white wherever the sun struck it. Noor had expected an island to announce its edges. Instead every inlet complicated the border. Sea entered land; roads followed bastions; apartment roofs crowded old military lines; a cruise ship stood above Valletta like a misplaced district.

She had slept for eleven minutes with her forehead against the window and woken with an ache behind her eyes. Mira sat across the aisle reading the same two pages of the Vallon chronology without turning them. Elena had changed into a fresh blouse in the airport washroom but still wore yesterday's exhaustion in the angular set of her shoulders. Gabriel, prohibited from command and separated from his tool bag at security, watched the harbor approaches as if altitude had not relieved him of responsibility for water.

Lucie Moreau carried the sealed derivative in a court case cuffed to a belt beneath her jacket. She was accompanied by a Maltese court officer from the gate onward. Noor carried headphones, two passive transducers, an optical recorder, and clean cables bought under the inspection protocol. She did not carry Sami's recorder, Hamid's service slip, or any object whose acquisition could befog the custody record. The distinction felt both impeccable and cruel. The instrument that had brought them here remained elsewhere, while her brother's method had become portable enough to outlive him.

At arrivals, Daniel Mifsud met them beside a police liaison and a telecommunications engineer named Lara Camilleri. Mifsud dispensed with blandishments.

"The noon hearing has moved to eleven fifteen," he said. "Harborlight alleges your proposed challenge may interrupt protected traffic. Critical-infrastructure police seek either refusal or a comprehensive containment plan. Dr. Galea will attend but has not consented."

"Did Harborlight disclose a technical objection?" Moreau asked.

"Twenty-seven pages and an addendum. The only concrete point is that the maintenance audio bus shares a power compartment with the line-monitoring unit."

Camilleri shook her head. "Adjacent compartment. Separate breaker, common backup. The distinction is noticeable if one has visited the station."

"Have they?" Noor asked.

"Their contractor has. Their central witness has not."

Outside, the airport heat gathered around them. Police divided the group between two vehicles. The route north skirted villages, limestone quarries, round towers, car parks, prickly pear, and plots where the last green growth had gone tawny. Camilleri pointed out the cable landing only when a low headland came into view. From the road it looked inhospitable: a ramp descending toward a blockhouse, rust-streaked ventilation hoods, and a chain fence above a narrow bay.

The former cable station stood on the verge between industrial survival and heritage afterlife. Its oldest rooms had received telegraph traffic under British rule. Later additions had carried telephone circuits, maritime warnings, internet trunks, and now Harborlight's Mediterranean relay. Most modern fiber bypassed the visible galleries, but the station still served island redundancy, maritime safety, and several government links. A conservation trust maintained the original switchboards and cable-test instruments in rooms above the live equipment. Tour groups visited twice a week, though not today.

"Dr. Galea was a paper and media conservator," Camilleri said. "Then the archive acquired magnetic tapes no one could play, and she retrained. She dislikes people who think preservation means embalming a dead object."

Noor understood the prejudice. "And people who think an old interface is ornamental."

"Especially them."

The hearing occupied a small courtroom in Valletta whose air-conditioning had surrendered to the influx of bodies. Critical-infrastructure police filled one bench. Harborlight counsel and two engineers appeared in person. Reporters waited outside because the application remained partly sealed. Beatrice Galea sat behind Mifsud, a compact woman in her late fifties with silver hair cut close and a linen jacket speckled by rain from an isolated morning shower. Her expression suggested longanimity under deliberate strain.

Noor was admitted as a method witness, not an investigator. She attested to the source-separation work in Marseille, the unresolved Malta pulse group, and the proposed use of the maintenance channel. She did not claim she could operate a network or solve cryptography through sound.

"What can you do?" the magistrate asked.

"Help distinguish the hardware module's response from ordinary station noise and verify that the challenge we hear is the one the independent examiner sends. Dr. Camilleri can address transport and electrical isolation. Ms. Moreau can address signature verification. Dr. Galea controls the station."

Harborlight's engineer, a smooth presenter named Christian Voss, described the channel as a legacy diagnostic convenience with no cachet in modern security design. Audio coupling, he said, could introduce adventitious voltage, provoke a protective freeze, or corrupt timing. The hardware module was critical to civilian continuity. A live challenge was debatable in a laboratory and reckless in service.

Galea looked incredulous. Mifsud asked whether she wished to respond.

"The channel does not inject sound into the data path," she said. "It converts electrical state changes to an audible maintenance signal and permits low-rate challenge codes through an optically isolated coupler. The system was retained because it works when higher layers fail. Mr. Voss's company certified that arrangement eighteen months ago."

Voss said the certification covered observation, not judicial interrogation.

"A random challenge is ordinary observation with a value you do not know in advance."

The magistrate asked what could go wrong.

Galea did not offer an irreproachable machine. A malformed challenge could be rejected. Excessive repetition could fill a diagnostic buffer. A fault in the shared backup supply could interrupt the line monitor, although current tests showed no fault. Human error remained possible. The station could reduce those risks by moving civilian traffic to the northern trunk, freezing configuration changes, testing the optical barrier, limiting the challenge to one nonce and one repeat, and keeping the old maritime circuit energized independently.

"Will you superintend it?" the magistrate asked.

"If the order gives me authority to stop the inspection at any sign of service degradation."

"Will civilian communication remain uninterrupted?"

"That is my condition, not my promise of foreordination. We can make interruption unlikely, detect it quickly, and stop. Anyone promising impossibility is selling doctrine, not engineering."

Noor watched the court absorb a sentence less appetizing than certainty and more useful.

Elena testified only to the remote record and reporting duty. Harborlight counsel tried to disqualify her opinion by invoking her administrative leave and authorship. She agreed that she could not give the court legal advice, then reiterated what she had personally observed: version 4.3, the `HL-MED ROOT M4` signature, the incomplete remote trust context, and deferred reporting under a clause she had drafted to require contemporaneous disclosure. Her concession deprived the attack of momentum.

At 12:07 the magistrate authorized a non-disruptive inspection between 14:00 and 15:30. Galea retained operational control and unilateral stop authority. Camilleri would supervise electrical and network isolation. Moreau would generate the random challenge and verify responses against the public chain. Noor could monitor and compare the audio channel under Galea's direction. Mifsud and a court officer would record provenance. Harborlight could observe through Voss but could not touch equipment. Police would secure the perimeter without blocking ordinary station staff.

The order prohibited export of the private key, cloning of the module, alteration of configuration, or acquisition of unrelated traffic. The court could obtain the public certificate chain, historical timestamp entry, access log, and signed challenge response. Civilian continuity overrode evidentiary convenience.

Outside the courtroom, cameras converged. A reporter asked whether Noor was about to hack Malta with a piece of music. She stopped despite Mifsud's gesture to keep walking.

"No," she said. "A station engineer will use a maintenance interface under a court order. I will listen to one diagnostic response. Please do not make technical women disappear because an artist is easier to photograph."

Galea, behind her, gave no sign of approval. Later, in the police van, she said, "That was pushy."

"Was it wrong?"

"No. Those are different categories."

The station's outer wall held the day's heat. Inside, thick limestone produced a coolness smelling of dust, cable oil, old paper, and ozone. The public gallery occupied the first floor: ceramic insulators, brass relays, a cable map of the empire, operators' stools polished by vanished bodies. No one paused for anecdotes. Galea led them down a stair through two access controls into the live plant.

Modern racks stood in contained rows behind mesh. Fans made a broad, amorphous pressure of sound. Status lamps flickered without drama. The Harborlight equipment occupied one locked bay beside a carrier cross-connect. Its label described a regional continuity service; nothing on the veneer said Convergence.

At 13:36 Galea convened the operational briefing. A civilian carrier manager confirmed that traffic had shifted to the northern trunk and tested call completion with the maritime rescue center, hospital exchange, police network, and two commercial carriers. The old coastal radio circuit remained independent. A tourism office complained that its booking system had slowed by eleven milliseconds; Galea asked the carrier manager to record the complaint and disregard its grandiose description as an outage.

Camilleri checked the power arrangement. Harborlight's module drew from dual supplies. The maintenance converter and line monitor shared one uninterruptible backup but not a breaker. Thermal imaging showed no hot connection. She measured protective earth, inspected the optical coupler, and photographed every seal before opening the maintenance panel. Moreau compared serials with the remote manifest. The hardware security module was the expected unit, but that fact alone did not attest historical validity.

Noor set her transducers on the maintenance converter's designated outputs. She used removable conservation wax approved by Galea, not adhesive. One channel captured the audible diagnostic feed; another captured chassis vibration to identify fan and relay noise. A direct digital tap went to Moreau's recorder. Every device used fresh media, synchronized to the court clock. Noor's optical recorder had no transmitting radio.

Voss objected that the vibration pickup might reveal proprietary load.

"It reveals a fan," Galea said.

"Load variation may permit inference."

"Then stand where you can see Ms. Bensaid eschew inference."

At 14:02 the court officer opened the inspection. Moreau obtained the public certificate chain from the station's read-only trust store. The intermediate certificate linked `HL-MED ROOT M4` to the operational policy root. Its status was valid. The historical timestamp service showed that version 4.3 had been signed on Day Twenty-nine at 03:14:22 UTC, while the M4 certificate was valid and before any present dispute.

"That proves the time service records a signature event," Voss said. "It does not prove the derivative object is identical."

"Correct," Moreau said. "The live challenge and object hash address the remaining questions."

The Convergence object's hash in the sealed derivative matched the timestamp entry. Noor saw Mira's hand close convulsively around a pen, then relax. The plan that cited her was no longer merely an apparition on a remote screen. Still, a matching log could have been generated by a compromised service. The hardware had to answer.

Moreau's verifier generated thirty-two random bytes. She printed the value to the court log, displayed it to all observers, and passed it through the optical coupler. Noor heard the maintenance channel change.

The response began with a low carrier, then a dry series of pulses. It was not music. It had no ethereal meaning and no irresistible emotional key. Yet she recognized the family: the same asymmetrical preamble Sami had placed beneath her installation, followed by a longer group whose timing matched the unmatched support slip seen under Hamid's protocol. The sequence arrived once, paused, and repeated with a parity marker.

Moreau's screen returned `VALID SIGNATURE / HL-MED ROOT M4`.

For one second nobody moved. Noor heard the fans, the converter's faint crepitation, and Voss breathing through his nose.

"Repeat once," Moreau said.

Galea checked carrier status. No alarm. Hospital, maritime, police, and commercial circuits remained normal. She authorized the repeat using the same challenge, not a new one. The module produced the same signature. Moreau verified it locally against the public chain. Camilleri confirmed that no configuration write had occurred.

The court officer read the result aloud. Mifsud asked Galea to export the relevant access log and historical timestamp under the order. She did so to write-once court media. The private key remained inside the hardware. No clone existed. The method had obtained authentication without taking one civilian call offline.

Noor expected triumph and felt only the flattening after intense attention. Success did not transfigure the station. It made the signed plan admissible enough to be fought over.

At 14:19 an alarm sounded from the carrier row.

Not the Harborlight bay. A red indicator appeared on the southern landing circuit: optical power falling.

Galea raised one hand. "Stop inspection."

Moreau disconnected the challenge coupler. Noor lifted neither transducer until Galea told her. Camilleri closed the maintenance panel without resealing it and moved to the carrier console. The northern trunk was already carrying diverted traffic. Its load rose but remained within capacity.

"South fiber three is losing light," the carrier manager said. "Not a clean break."

The trace showed a reflection 1.7 kilometers from the station, near a coastal service chamber. Signal strength dribbled downward, recovered, then fell sharply.

"Construction strike?" a police officer asked.

"No permitted works," Galea said.

At 14:21 the southern fiber failed.

Automatic protection moved remaining sessions north. Most calls survived. Two commercial data routes reset. The maritime rescue center retained radio and northern trunk contact. A mobile carrier lost backhaul to part of the western coast for forty-three seconds, then restored through an Italian route. The outage was real, limited, and immediately attributed online to the court inspection because police vehicles were visible outside the station.

Voss said, "You have energized an untested maintenance path beside a live line, and now the line is down."

Camilleri turned from the trace. "The break is outside this building."

"Your diagnostic action may have propagated."

"Light loss reflects a physical discontinuity. A challenge to an isolated hardware module cannot denude a fiber one point seven kilometers away."

Galea ordered a field crew to the service chamber and preserved all station state. Police locked the Harborlight bay and took names. The magistrate joined by secure video at 14:31. Harborlight sought immediate sequestration of Noor's equipment, Moreau's media, and the sealed derivative, alleging interference with critical infrastructure.

Mifsud opposed seizure beyond the court protocol. Moreau's evidentiary media already belonged to the court. Noor's recorders contained synchronized documentation and no network connection. Galea's operational logs showed the inspection stopped before the final break and the failure originated outside.

The magistrate ordered Noor's equipment held temporarily in station custody for imaging, with her and independent counsel present. The authenticated court media remained judicial property. No one would surrender the private key because it had never moved.

At 14:47 police at the coastal chamber reported forced entry. The external lock showed no crude gash; its electronic controller had accepted a valid maintenance credential at 14:11. Inside, a powered bending device had compressed the southern fiber until attenuation climbed, then a blade severed it. The device still hung from a stanchion. Its remote controller had been wiped at 14:22.

The timing altered the room without resolving it. The credential could have been stolen, cloned, or lawfully issued. The cut had begun after the first challenge and before the repeat ended. Whoever arranged it could watch the inspection schedule, or simply knew the court window.

"Whose credential?" the magistrate asked.

Galea searched the station access directory. The credential belonged to an external continuity contractor, Mediterranean Recovery Systems. It had entered the service chamber three times in the past year. The contracting chain ran through a Harborlight carrier affiliate, but the named technician reported from Sicily that his token was in his possession.

Rell's name did not appear.

Noor's phone, surrendered in a tray outside the live room, began vibrating with messages. A Maltese outlet published a photograph of her entering the station beside the words `ARTIST LINKED TO NATIONAL CABLE FAILURE`. Another called the inspection an activist plot. A government backbencher demanded extradition of the foreign saboteurs. Tourists at the upper road filmed police tape and complained that their excursion had been canceled. The islandwide hostility promised by the first headline exceeded the actual islandwide outage, but a false scale did not make the anger unreal. People had lost calls. Businesses had reset. Emergency redundancy had been consumed during worsening weather.

Noor had agreed to foreseeable collateral risk. She had not agreed to this cut, yet the distinction could not erase the consequence of creating a moment someone else exploited.

"We knew the inspection would concentrate traffic," she said to Galea. "We made the southern line a more attractive target."

"You did not cut it."

"Both can be true."

Galea studied her. "Yes. That is generally where responsibility becomes useful."

By 15:20 the field crew had installed a protected splice enclosure but needed two hours to restore the southern pair. Northern capacity held. Police established that the bending device had received its final instruction over a short-range maintenance radio from a vehicle parked near the chamber. Cameras showed a white utility van with cloned plates. A traffic image caught a man in contractor clothing leaving it, face obscured. His gait and build were consistent with many men, including Rell. Noor refused the presenter's invitation to identify him from a blurred shoulder.

The magistrate suspended public release of the authenticated object for six hours while police assessed operational danger, but she permitted certified notice to Athens authorities, Alexandria emergency officials, and participating-state counsel. The plan remained inactive according to the last court-visible state. Its storm trigger had risen to 0.66. No provisional request was recorded in the preserved receipt.

At 16:04 police informed the group that the infrastructure prosecutor intended to interview them under caution. Noor, Moreau, Camilleri, Galea, and the court officer would be treated separately. Mira and Elena had observed but not handled equipment. Gabriel had remained above the live floor after his passenger-travel order was questioned; he had no operational role.

The prosecutor also sought arrest warrants for criminal damage and interference, naming unknown persons and reserving addition of the foreign inspection team. The language traveled faster than its qualifications. A wire service reported warrants "against campaigners." Harborlight issued a statement saying reckless acquisition tactics had endangered Malta's civilian communications. It did not acknowledge the valid hardware response.

Noor's interview began at 17:10 in a former cable clerk's office. Her lawyer was a Maltese criminal advocate retained through Roche's separate arrangement, not Elena. Noor described every movement from entry to shutdown. She gave no opinion on the cut credential. She acknowledged placing transducers, receiving Galea's instructions, hearing the signature response, and understanding that traffic concentration created operational exposure. She rejected the allegation that her equipment could transmit or command the southern fiber. The imaging record would show it.

"Did you intend to embarrass Harborlight?" the inspector asked.

"I intended to authenticate a plan under court authority. Embarrassment is not a technical state."

"Did you wish to provoke a public debacle before Athens?"

"I wished to prevent a hidden plan from becoming an emergency system. I did not wish to interrupt anyone's call."

"Your brother designed similar diagnostic pulses."

"He used a protocol family. That does not make every device his, mine, or innocent."

She resisted the old impulse to make custody equal control. The station logs, field evidence, court media, and her equipment belonged in distinct hands. Her account did not aggrandize her role and did not abscond from it.

At 18:26 the imaging of her recorders confirmed they had no radio activity and contained only the authorized channels. Police released the equipment under seal to her lawyer pending possible recall. Moreau's direct recording and verification package stayed with the court. Galea retained station originals. Camilleri's electrical measurements entered the infrastructure file. No single person carried the proof.

The southern cable returned to service at 19:03. Calls and data stabilized. The field crew preserved the cut ends, bending device, blade, lock controller, and radio receiver. A technician found a partial command log in volatile memory because the wipe had failed to clear an error journal. It showed the cut instruction was signed by a contractor maintenance certificate issued through the same governance support group that appeared in Convergence metadata. The certificate did not identify a human. It tightened the nexus without clinching Rell.

Outside, Valletta had turned honey-colored in the declining light. Church bells crossed traffic noise. Police escorted the group to a government guest facility rather than a hotel because demonstrators and cameras had gathered at both. Someone shouted that they had attacked Malta. Someone else shouted that Harborlight had staged the failure. The opposed certainties left no room for the modest truth: they had authenticated a dangerous plan during an authorized operation, and a separate actor had used that operation to cut a cable.

In the guest facility, volunteers from a local emergency communications association served tepid coffee and pastizzi from paper cartons. The pastry flaked over every document. Galea ate standing at a window while directing restoration reports by phone. She had no appetite for being lionized as a brave curator.

"The station is not a priory and I am not its abbess," she told a reporter who had described her as guardian of a sacred machine. "It is working infrastructure. Preservation means knowing what must continue."

Noor liked her enough not to say so.

At 20:14 Lotte called from Marseille. The crew committee had approved `Nkem`'s limited voyage after survey, with Lotte as master, Gabriel as passenger-owner and mechanic only if his order permitted, and no carriage of original evidence. The ship had departed at 11:40, hours after the flight, carrying replacement hose, survey gear, and ordinary charter equipment. A forecast gale would reach the Malta approaches before dawn on Day Thirty-nine. Lotte intended to make Valletta early on Day Thirty-nine if weather and authorities allowed.

Gabriel said, "Do not come into a blockade."

"Harbor control has not closed the port," Lotte replied. "They have requested advance declarations. We will obey."

"The ship is being named in the warrants."

"The ship cannot be named in a warrant for an inspection that occurred while she was at sea unless someone has become unusually imaginative."

"A news channel says she transported the equipment."

"A news channel also called you captain. Neither statement restores your certificate."

The exchange had the refined edge of a crew that no longer needed Gabriel's conceit. He accepted it.

At 21:02 Mifsud received the authenticated notice prepared for Athens. It stated only what the court could support: the sealed Convergence object matched the historical timestamp; `HL-MED ROOT M4` validly signed both the object hash and a fresh judicial challenge; the private key remained in the hardware module; civilian traffic was unaffected by the challenge; a later external cut caused a limited outage under separate criminal investigation. Human approval identities and full route payload remained unproved. Convergence remained inactive at last observation.

Minister Anagnostou's office acknowledged receipt and requested an in-person briefing before the delegations' ratification caucus on Day Forty. It made no promise to delay.

Harborlight's response arrived seven minutes later. It did not dispute that M4 produced the signature. It argued that the document was an exercise artifact, the key established authenticity but not operational intent, and the applicants had demonstrated the danger of allowing unqualified outsiders near resilient systems. Vale offered to confer with Maltese authorities and fund restoration without prejudice.

"He can reimburse a splice," Noor said. "He cannot reimburse trust."

Mira looked up from the notice. "Neither can we. We have to state what happened without turning the island into a stage for our innocence."

Noor felt the rebuff before recognizing agreement. She had once believed that if she controlled every image of Sami, no one could diminish him. Now an island had become an image contested by strangers: fortress, cable nexus, tourist backdrop, underdog state, strategic trophy. The people who depended on its lines had not consented to any presentation.

She drafted a statement with Galea, Camilleri, the carrier manager, and counsel. It began with service, not proof. The southern cable had been cut externally; limited interruptions occurred; emergency and maritime links remained available; full service was restored. The judicial challenge had not caused the physical break. The inspection team accepted responsibility for conducting a foreseeable-risk operation and for the concentration of traffic it required, while rejecting false attribution of the cut. Evidence remained with courts and station authorities.

Noor removed one impassioned sentence about sabotage. It alleged more than they could prove. Galea removed a captious paragraph about a tourism office. Camilleri added the exact outage intervals. Mira insisted the statement not call the Convergence plan operational; it was approved for exercise and emergency conversion, signed by an operational root, and linked to pending conditions. Elena added no legal rhetoric.

At 22:30 the prosecutor released Mira, Elena, Gabriel, and Noor from the guest facility subject to location reporting. Moreau remained overnight as court custodian. Police had not charged any of them, but a request circulated to prevent departure until morning interviews concluded. Public hostility made a commercial flight uncertain in any case. Gabriel's passenger order required him to remain in Malta; `Nkem` would not reach the island for more than two days.

The parish network offered rooms in Valletta through a civil-protection liaison. Galea warned them that accepting sanctuary as a political tableau would be barefaced. Noor said they needed beds, food, counsel access, and a place where cameras could not enter. Nothing more.

Before they left, Gabriel received a call from Lotte. Harbor Control had required advance notice before `Nkem` entered Maltese waters pending clarification of her relation to the inspection team. The vessel was still in the western Mediterranean with more than two days of passage remaining. Fuel calculations assumed harbor entry early on Day Thirty-nine. Diverting to Sicily remained possible, though the forecast made every option worse.

"I will tell you what the master decides," Lotte said. "I am not asking permission."

"Understood."

Noor heard in his reply neither capitulation nor command. Only the discipline of not reaching for a wheel that was no longer his.

At 23:18 they walked under police escort through streets polished by a brief shower. Limestone facades held the day's warmth. The bells had stopped. Restaurant tables crowded the pavements; tourists drank wine beneath balconies while, one street over, technicians repaired the administrative aftermath of a severed cable. Malta had not become pandemonium. It had absorbed a wound and continued.

Noor's sealed headphones knocked lightly against her hip. In them, unheard for now, a machine had answered a random question with the same key that signed Alexandria Convergence. The answer was authentic. Its meaning was still being fought over.

Her phone showed the vessel's last public position far west of the island. Wind arrows converged across the passage ahead. Harbor Control's advance-notice restriction remained in force.

The proof had escaped ambiguity more readily than they had escaped Malta.

## Chapter 34: Lee Shore

By dawn the sea had erased the difference between prudence and delay.

At 05:42 on Day Thirty-nine, Gabriel stood beneath the awning of a Maltese patrol launch while drizzle swept across Marsamxett Harbour. The stone walls of Valletta faded and returned behind rain. Outside the breakwater, wind from the northeast drove a short, steep sea toward the island's western rock. After more than sixty hours from Marseille, `Nkem` waited beyond the harbor limit under Lotte's command, prohibited from entering and increasingly unable to remain where Harbor Control had told her to hold.

The launch carried Gabriel, a court courier named Anthea Zammit, two patrol officers, and no promise that any of them would be allowed aboard. Anthea's case contained a certified verification package: the signed Convergence object, public certificate chain, challenge response, timestamp extract, court manifest, and yesterday's preliminary outage chronology. The Maltese court retained the primary media. Moreau retained no private key because none had ever left the station. This duplicate was authorized for delivery to the Athens conference secretariat and Greek judicial liaison. It was evidence with provenance, not loot crossing a border.

Gabriel carried a mechanic's bag and a temporary movement order. His master certificate remained surrendered. The order permitted him to inspect the vessel as owner and assist under Lotte's direction. It did not restore command, authorize departure from Maltese jurisdiction, or amend the charter. The crew committee's vote remained applicable: Lotte commanded; Marcin controlled machinery; Els kept navigation watch; Gabriel advised when asked.

The arrangement was reasonable. His body resented it with habitual, childish avidity.

At 06:03 Harbor Control called the patrol launch. `Nkem` had reported contamination in her day tank and intermittent loss of fuel pressure. She could maintain steerage at reduced revolutions but not hold safely through the next weather band. Lotte requested entry to the nearest defensible anchorage. Control denied entry pending an infrastructure-security inspection and ordered her to return east of the island toward a designated holding area.

The patrol coxswain stared at the radio. "Return from where?"

The designated area lay upwind and north of the harbor approaches. Reaching it required several hours of hard motoring into worsening sea. A vessel with unreliable fuel could lose propulsion west of a lee shore, where wind and waves would set her toward rock. The order had administrative continuity and no nautical sense.

Gabriel keyed neither microphone nor opinion. He was not the launch's master.

Lotte replied from `Nkem`, concise and forthright. "Unable to comply safely. Request emergency entry or permission to proceed south to shelter. Present position two miles west-northwest of Sliema Point. Speed three knots. Fuel pressure oscillating."

Control instructed her to stand by.

The patrol launch cleared the breakwater and began to climb. Spray struck the windows like handfuls of gravel. Gabriel braced his knees and watched the barograph fall. Wind had risen to thirty knots with higher gusts. The clouds were not the Alexandria storm, whose eastern track remained hundreds of miles away, but the same regional instability had tightened local pressure gradients. Malta's coast turned every direction into consequence.

`Nkem` appeared between grey ridges, bow pitching, orange work deck awash. Her movement looked animated from a distance and brutal near at hand. Lotte had streamed a drogue from the stern quarter to keep the bow angled into the sea while preserving fuel. The vessel wore no distress pennant. Her deck lights remained on. Exhaust came in irregular dark pulses.

Marcin opened the lee-side gate when the patrol launch matched speed. Transfer was irksome and applicable rules were plain: one person at a time, safety line, no luggage in hand, abort if either master ordered. Anthea's case crossed first in a sealed float bag on a messenger line. The patrol officer followed, then Anthea. Gabriel went last. The launch rose, `Nkem` dropped, and for an instant the gap became a dark polygon of water. He stepped when the coxswain shouted, landed against the rail, and felt Marcin's brawn haul him inward.

"Welcome as passenger," Marcin said.

"Your etiquette remains polished."

"It has had a lifetime to develop."

On the bridge Lotte wore an immersion jacket over work clothes. Her eyes were red from a night without a snooze. Els held the watch. A Maltese patrol officer stood by the chart table. Gabriel reported to Lotte as the order required.

"Permission to inspect fuel service under the chief engineer?"

"Granted," she said. "No bridge authority. Before you go: Harbor Control has now ordered return to the northern holding area. I have refused as unsafe. They may direct the patrol to board and detain us."

"Can we make the harbor under present power?"

"If the engine continues to exist in its present mood."

She pointed at the electronic chart. Their track made a desultory hook outside the harbor approaches. Wind set them south and west. The high coast offered no harbor, only limestone cliffs interrupted by low shelves and small bays. A charted sand patch lay off a shallow inlet farther south, a byproduct of eroded globigerina limestone and seasonal deposition. Beyond it, reefs and harder coralline ledges formed the actual lee shore.

"If we lose power before Sliema, we have seventeen minutes to rock at present drift," Els said. "More if the drogue holds. Less in a squall."

Lotte's arrangement was already clear. They would attempt repair while requesting entry. If repair failed, they could anchor in thirty-eight meters, though holding over sloping limestone was uncertain. They could run south toward the sand shelf if enough propulsion remained. Deliberate grounding was a last resort, not a nifty emblem of courage.

Gabriel went below.

The engine room was hot enough to make the wet fabric steam on his shoulders. The main diesel hunted between nine hundred and eleven hundred revolutions. Fuel pressure fell, recovered, and fell again. Marcin had shifted from the port bunker to the clean reserve, changed primary filters, bled the line, and checked the lift pump. Each action restored pressure briefly. The used filters held a pale, greasy emulsion.

"Water?" Gabriel asked.

"Water and something else. Fuel sample separates slowly. Day tank bottom gave sludge. Reserve line was clean at departure."

The weather made every loose object instrumental in injury. They clipped on, closed grating gates, and worked without affectation. Marcin drew samples into clear jars. Diesel floated above water, but a grey additive kept part of the mixture emulsified. Fine granules settled against the glass.

Gabriel rubbed a drop between gloved fingers and smelled it. "Sealant powder?"

"Or tank-cleaning residue."

"Would not appear after survey without an introduction."

"Do not incriminate anyone with your nose."

They traced the reserve line from bunker to changeover manifold. A union ahead of the day tank showed fresh tool marks beneath old grease. The locking wire had been replaced with a near match and twisted opposite Marcin's habitual direction. Under vibration the union admitted air, but that alone did not explain water and granulate. An inspection port on the day tank had a new gasket. Its paint line was broken.

Marcin's face tightened. "The tank was opened."

"When?"

"Marseille survey at 05:20 yesterday. Sealed at 07:05. I checked before sailing. We took fuel at 08:10 under yard supervision. First symptoms at 04:38 today."

The patrol officer photographed without touching. Sabotage was a defensible hypothesis, not yet verified. Contaminated bunkers, maintenance error, and latent sediment remained alternatives. The timing, altered seal, and emulsifier made accident less reasonable.

They needed propulsion, not an exhaustive theory.

The day tank could be isolated and drained, but rough motion would stir contamination faster than the small pump could remove it. A portable fuel polishing unit sat in the survey equipment. It was designed for sampling and cleanup, not full engine demand. They could rig it between the reserve bunker and engine service line, bypassing the day tank, with a clean drum as buffer. The flow might suffice at low load. Every connection would have to remain secured against oscillation.

Marcin assigned the work. Gabriel fetched hose, clamps, and the portable pump. A deckhand lashed the buffer drum to a frame. They flushed the line into waste containers until diesel ran clear. The atomizer nozzles and engine injection system could tolerate small residual water poorly; a slug could stop the engine or damage a pump. Marcin refused Gabriel's suggestion to increase speed before the separator stabilized.

"You are not buying distance with my engine," he said.

"Your engine is currently buying rock."

"Lotte decides the trade. I tell her what load I can defend."

The rebuke was merited. Gabriel carried it upstairs with the report.

At 06:51 Harbor Control still denied entry. Officials offered a tug from Grand Harbour, estimated arrival fifty-five minutes, conditioned on `Nkem` accepting tow and returning to a controlled berth. Lotte accepted the tug. She did not accept immediate surrender of navigation to a patrol launch that lacked towing capacity. One crew member, Tomasz Wrona, wanted them to stop the engine, embark in the patrol craft, and abandon the vessel before anyone was hurt.

"The evidence case can go," Tomasz said. "We can go. Let insurers argue about steel."

There was no cowardice in the proposal. Rescue of persons took priority over property, and evacuation while transfer remained possible might be prudent. But the patrol launch could carry only part of them safely in this sea. A second launch was en route. Stopping propulsion would accelerate drift toward rock and turn orderly transfer into crisis. The sealed case's safety did not determine human safety.

Lotte asked each officer for an assessment. Els gave drift and anchor options. Marcin estimated the bypass could deliver low-load fuel within fifteen minutes. The patrol officer said boarding authority did not oblige the master to create immediate danger. Gabriel gave the coastal geology as he understood it from the chart and pilot notes: hard shelves north and south, one sand lens inside the shallow bay, uncertain thickness over rock. Grounding there might hold the hull upright or tear the running gear. He did not call it safe.

"We continue repair and keep steerage," Lotte said. "Prepare anchor. Prepare for transfer but do not commence. Anthea, can your case leave on the patrol launch now?"

The courier looked from the heaving launch to the chart. "Its destination is Athens, not this ship. Yes."

That was the first surrender of the morning and the least theatrical. The evidence did not need Gabriel as guardian. Anthea transferred back with the case at 07:06, bound for a police pier and a commercial flight once the court cleared departure. She took a signed shipboard receipt showing the case had remained unopened. The patrol launch then stayed alongside as escort.

Below, the bypass pump began to whir. Pressure rose to minimum operating range. Marcin shifted the engine to the clean line. It ran evenly at six hundred revolutions, then eight hundred. Lotte ordered ten degrees toward harbor to test response. `Nkem` answered.

Relief was an afterthought the sea corrected. A wave struck the port bow, flinging spray over the wheelhouse. The drogue line snapped at a chafed section and recoiled against the stern rail. Without its restraint, the vessel fell broadside. Els countered with rudder and propeller. Fuel pressure dropped.

Marcin called from below. "Air at the temporary suction. Slacken load."

The engine coughed. Exhaust vanished. For three seconds the machinery space seemed inanimate, though alarms screamed. Then the engine caught at idle.

Drift increased toward the coast.

Lotte deployed the starboard anchor in thirty-four meters. Chain ran with a sonorous violence that made conversation impossible. At five shackles, Els applied astern power to set it. The engine faltered again. The anchor took briefly, the bow swung north, and the vessel's speed over ground fell below one knot.

"Holding," Els said.

The word lasted twenty seconds.

Chain began to judder. The anchor skipped over a hard bottom, caught, then dragged. `Nkem`'s bow oscillated with each gust. Depth decreased as the seabed rose toward shore. They could veer more chain, but swinging room narrowed against the reef. The tug remained thirty-eight minutes away.

Harbor Control ordered them to abandon the attempt to enter and accept evacuation. Lotte's answer was terse: evacuation preparations active; vessel not yet in extremis; request tug priority and permission to run for the sand shelf if propulsion restored.

Control refused the grounding route because the inlet bordered a marine protected area. A deliberate strand could spill fuel over seagrass habitat. The prohibition was applicable in ordinary conditions and morally relevant now. `Nkem` carried diesel, hydraulic oil, batteries, and survey chemicals. Saving people by choosing the shelf might pollute a nursery ground and create a wreck the island had never invited.

"Alternative is uncontrolled impact on exposed rock," Gabriel said. "That ruptures tanks more readily."

"Record that as owner-mechanic opinion," Lotte said. "Camilleri is reaching the environmental duty officer."

The duty officer joined by radio. She knew the inlet. The central sand body was about ninety meters across, with a depth of three to five meters over calcarenite. A western tongue of shale and rubble made the chart less reliable after winter storms. Seagrass lay mainly east of the centerline. If grounding became necessary, approach from north-northeast, bow first, stop machinery before contact, and avoid the eastern meadow. The environmental law allowed action necessary to prevent a greater casualty, with mandatory reporting and mitigation.

It was not permission to treat conservation as sentimental impediment. It was a comparison of harms under failing options.

At 07:28 the anchor dragged again. Depth under keel fell to seven meters. `Nkem` drew 3.4 aft. The bypass line lost suction whenever the vessel rolled hard to starboard. Gabriel and Marcin rigged a weighted pickup in the buffer drum and braced the hoses with timber and textile straps. Perspiration ran into Gabriel's eyes despite the cooling engine room ventilation. His hands moved with old proficiency, but every time he began an instruction Marcin either accepted it as a suggestion or amended it.

"Pressure stable at idle," Marcin reported. "Maybe ten minutes at twelve hundred. Maybe one minute."

Lotte had three choices. Remain on a dragging anchor and hope for the tug. Attempt harbor entry against control's order. Run south for the sand shelf while propulsion existed. The first surrendered agency to time. The second required more distance and risked engine loss in the approaches. The third intentionally sacrificed hull, propeller, and perhaps habitat.

Tomasz repeated his request to evacuate. The second patrol launch was now visible, but transfer of nine crew and Gabriel in these seas would take at least twenty minutes. If everyone left, the vessel would ground uncontrolled. Someone would have to remain until tow or contact.

"No one remains alone," Lotte said. "We are not turning ownership into martyrdom."

Gabriel had contemplated exactly that without speaking. The rebuke reached him anyway.

At 07:36 a squall crossed the vessel. Wind jumped above forty knots. Rain erased the coast. The anchor chain surged bar-tight, slackened, then snatched. A link rode badly over the wildcat and kicked the brake handle. Lotte came from the bridge wing to help Els assess the lead. The vessel rolled as a breaking crest struck. The handle released with sudden force and threw her against the chart-table edge.

She fell without a theatrical cry. Her left arm bent under her. Blood appeared at her temple.

Els caught the brake and shouted for the medic. Gabriel reached Lotte where she lay. She was conscious, breathing, and furious. Her left wrist showed an evident deformity. The scalp wound bled freely but was short. She answered orientation questions correctly, denied neck pain, and tried to stand.

"Do not animate the casualty," Marcin said over the internal circuit when told.

The crew medic stabilized her neck until examination, dressed the wound, and splinted the wrist. Lotte remained legally master while conscious, but she could not move safely around the bridge. Els was chief mate and next in command. She took the con.

Gabriel stepped back.

Then the engine stopped.

The bridge displays dimmed and returned on emergency power. Without propeller thrust the vessel fell across the wind. The anchor dragged at nearly two knots. Depth showed 5.8 meters and falling. Rock lay less than nine minutes away. The tug was twenty-three minutes out.

Els ordered emergency start. Marcin bled the line. The engine turned but did not fire. The buffer drum had shifted despite its lashings, drawing air and contaminated residue.

"I can give you one start from a clean jerry rig," Marcin said. "No guarantee how long."

Els looked at Lotte. Lotte's face had gone pale. "Sand shelf," she said. "Do it while you can choose."

Els acknowledged the order. She knew the vessel but had never handled her in intentional grounding. Gabriel had grounded workboats onto mud for inspection and once beached a disabled coaster in Sierra Leone under tow. The experience did not make him infallible. It made his errors more specific.

"I want Gabriel at the con as emergency helmsman," Els said. "I retain command."

The patrol officer said the certificate suspension remained in force.

"Then record necessity," Els replied. "Or take the wheel yourself."

The officer did not.

Gabriel put both hands on the controls. The familiar arrangement felt alien after weeks of enforced absence. He did not feel reincarnated. He felt the titanic weight of a vessel moving toward land with people inside her.

They plotted the approach from radar, chart, and the environmental officer's spoken bearings. Rain hid visual marks. The inlet opened south-southwest. To reach it they needed bow control for six minutes and enough speed to cross the set. Anchor recovery would take too long; Els ordered the bitter end prepared for release under buoy. Abandoning the anchor was cheaper than dragging it through seagrass or letting it turn them broadside.

Marcin called, "Ready for one start."

"Start," Els ordered.

The engine caught. Oil pressure rose. Fuel held.

Gabriel brought revolutions to eleven hundred, no more. He put the rudder over and felt the hull hesitate. A gust drove the bow downwind. He increased to thirteen hundred despite Marcin's earlier limit.

"Pressure falling," Marcin warned.

"Need thirty seconds," Gabriel said.

"You have twenty."

The bow passed through the wind. Els released the anchor under buoy. `Nkem` began southward, rolling heavily but making four knots. The western rock shelf appeared through rain, white water exploding over it. The sand inlet remained an absence between breakers.

The patrol launches could not follow into the shallows. They held offshore and broadcast the vessel's track to rescue units. A fishing boat sheltering behind the point answered. Its skipper, Pawlu Grech, knew the sand body and gave a bearing to an old shore boathouse whose roof showed briefly between rain sheets.

"Keep the boathouse and church dome in line," he said. "If the dome goes left, you find shale. If it goes right, grass."
